title: Trump targets Omar for deportation in escalating drive toward dictatorship
description:
The Trump administration is seeking to strip Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar of her US citizenship and deport her, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing US officials and others familiar with the investigation.
The Journal reported that HSI examined a similar tip under Biden but did not move forward because it lacked evidence of fraud.
The Washington Post reported Thursday evening that a review under Trump in 2019 also found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing by Omar.
The threatened deportation of Omar takes place amid the campaign by the Trump administration to greatly accelerate the pace of deportations, which exposes its victims to imprisonment, persecution and death.
The attack coincides with Trump administration demands to exclude the ballots of supposedly ineligible voters in California and a wider campaign against the election itself.
text:
The Trump administration is seeking to strip Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar of her US citizenship and deport her, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing US officials and others familiar with the investigation. The revelation follows Monday’s raid on her Washington D.C. home, and the issuing of more than a dozen subpoenas, including to members of her family.

The administration is using the persecution of Omar as a battering ram against citizenship itself. Its political objective is to make the right to remain in the country contingent on loyalty and submission to the president. A sitting congresswoman who arrived in the United States as a child refugee and became a citizen more than a quarter-century ago is being threatened with expulsion for opposing Trump.

According to the Journal, agents seized Omar’s cellphone, personal computers, notebooks and passport during the early-morning search on October 12. Only Omar and her husband were home. The Justice Department confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), executed a court-authorized warrant, but declined to elaborate.

CNN reported Wednesday that US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the D.C. federal district court in Washington authorized the search. Prosecutors first spent several days pressing for broad access to records in Omar’s home. Sharbaugh required a screening process to protect material concerning her legislative work under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause. Those restrictions did not prevent the raid or the seizure of her personal records and devices.

The New York Times reported that relatives of Omar have also received subpoenas, while the Journal reported that authorities had issued more than a dozen seeking testimony before a Minnesota grand jury. Investigators are examining the family’s immigration paperwork, including the actions of Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, who died in 2020.

The central allegation concerns whether Omar or her father misrepresented her age when she obtained citizenship in 2000. Investigators are seeking to establish that she was already 18, rather than 17, and therefore did not qualify to acquire citizenship through her father as a minor. Omar maintains that she was born in 1982 and has denied committing immigration fraud.

“President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this,” her office told the Journal on Wednesday.

Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, Omar fled the country with her family after civil war broke out. They spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before being admitted to the United States in 1995. In her memoir, she described the opportunity to immigrate as a “golden ticket.” The family initially settled in Arlington, Virginia, outside Washington, before moving to Minnesota. Omar has said she was 12 when she arrived and became a citizen in 2000.

The administration is revisiting allegations that officials previously declined to pursue. The Journal reported that HSI examined a similar tip under Biden but did not move forward because it lacked evidence of fraud. CNN reported that the immigration case was reopened in 2025. This is distinct from a financial investigation initiated under Biden in June 2024, which stalled for a lack of evidence.

The Washington Post reported Thursday evening that a review under Trump in 2019 also found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing by Omar.

No immigration fraud charges against Omar have been announced. The government has not publicly established that either she or her father falsified the information now under scrutiny. Yet the administration is openly discussing the punishment it wants to impose while investigators search for a basis to carry it out.

Trump has spent years directing racist and dehumanizing attacks against Omar and Somali Americans. At his Ohio rally on Monday evening, hours after the raid, the audience chanted “deport” as he attacked Omar and other Somalis. “They cheat on everything,” Trump declared. “We’re not going to stand for it.”

The same president who incessantly denounced the prosecution over his January 6 coup attempt as political persecution is deploying federal police against his opponents on the basis of unproven allegations concerning decades-old paperwork. Whether Omar was 17 or 18 when her father became a citizen cannot justify this campaign of political banishment.

Socialists defend the right of workers and their children to live and work in the country of their choice, with full democratic rights. Modern society depends on the coordinated labor of workers across the world, linked through international production and transportation networks. While capital moves across borders in pursuit of profit, workers are confined, detained and deported by the rival nation-states that defend capitalist property. The struggle for workers’ freedom of movement is inseparable from the struggle to abolish the capitalist nation-state system and establish world socialism.

The threatened deportation of Omar takes place amid the campaign by the Trump administration to greatly accelerate the pace of deportations, which exposes its victims to imprisonment, persecution and death. This summer, deportation flights to Haiti increased from monthly to weekly despite the country’s violence and humanitarian crisis. Human Rights Watch documented five consecutive weekly flights between August 20 and September 17 carrying a total of 474 people.

The administration has also expanded renditions to third countries, sending people to places where they have no ties or legal status. On September 29, the Supreme Court lifted restrictions on these removals while litigation continues. Deportees have faced arbitrary detention, beatings and disappearance.

Monday’s raid came just 22 days before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Omar is heavily favored to retain her Minneapolis-based seat. The attack coincides with Trump administration demands to exclude the ballots of supposedly ineligible voters in California and a wider campaign against the election itself. The investigation could provide a pretext for Trump and his congressional allies to challenge Omar’s legitimacy and attempt to block her taking her seat if she wins.

The pursuit of Omar is part of a sweeping expansion of the government’s campaign to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship. According to administration officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, more than 200 denaturalization lawsuits have been filed since Trump returned to office.

An August 21 report by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC) identified at least 105 denaturalization suits in the first seven months of 2026, including 50 in July alone, which it described as “an all-time high.” By comparison, it identified 125 suits during the entire period from 2008 through 2025, with no filings found in 30 states. Sixteen of those states recorded filings in 2026 through July.

TRAC warned that its figures could understate the actual scale of the campaign. The true number of suits, it explained, “may be higher since there is no reliable way to identify every court action.” It added: “While claiming that it is filing a record number of denaturalization suits, the DoJ is highly selective about which suits it publicizes and which ones it fails to make public.”

As the Trump administration moves to strip a Democratic congresswoman of her citizenship and deport her on bogus pretexts, leading figures in her own party have responded with silence or empty denunciations.

As of Thursday, no public statements could be found from Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer condemning the attack on Omar, while House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries has uttered only platitudes. This response was accompanied by other Democrats’ milquetoast denunciations unaccompanied by concrete action. Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, for example, accused Trump of “abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election,” but proposed nothing to stop him.

Walz explained the political outlook behind this inaction at Georgetown University on Thursday: “I am a product of the institutions, I defend the status quo.” He coupled this declaration with the claim that he was under no obligation to meet fascism “halfway.” Yet during Operation Metro Surge, his deployment of the National Guard and Minnesota police forces in support of the immigration Gestapo, together with the trade union bureaucracies’ containment of opposition within one-day protests, blocked the development of the mass movement building in response to the murders of Renée Good and Alex Pretti.

Such actions actively defend the institutions through which fascism develops. One-day protests and appeals to “remember in November” have brought no justice to the families of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, murdered in Minneapolis by federal agents, or the thousands of other families whose lives have been shattered by the mass deportation operation. As the attack on Ilhan Omar demonstrates, that operation is being expanded into a weapon against all political opposition.

The capitalist status quo defended by Walz and the Democrats has produced staggering concentrations of wealth and power and nurtured the fascist forces now attacking citizenship itself. text:
Three voting and privacy rights organizations asked a federal court Thursday to declare the Trump administration’s “secretive and unlawful effort” to collect millions of Americans’ voter records illegal under federal privacy laws.

In the new lawsuit, the groups also requested that the court order the federal government to delete the data it’s collected so far.

The groups — the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens — alleged that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) over the past year and a half has illegally obtained voter records from at least 47 states as part of a sweeping effort to investigate unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud.

“DHS has no authority to stockpile voter data for a nationwide election-law dragnet, and in carrying out this policy it has disregarded federal safeguards and violated the privacy rights of millions of Americans,” the organizations said.

Since last year, DHS and the Department of Justice (DOJ) have worked to obtain state voter registration records. Some states complied with the Trump administration’s demands and gave the federal government their unredacted voter rolls, which may include people’s sensitive personal information like Social Security numbers.

But the DOJ also sued 30 states and D.C. for their voter rolls, and DHS has sought to obtain records in multiple other ways.

The three civic organizations said DHS abused its legal authority throughout the voter data initiative.

“Congress created DHS to prevent terrorism, secure the border, and address other specified threats — not to conduct a voter-fraud dragnet centered on the private voting information of millions of Americans and records reflecting the exercise of constitutional rights essential to democracy,” they said.

The legal nonprofit Democracy Forward* is representing the organizations in the suit.

The new lawsuit comes just days after a federal judge in D.C. found the DOJ’s crusade for state rolls illegal. Specifically, the judge said the effort amounted to an “attempt to decide who gets to vote.”

Internal government documents released last week through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit filed by Democracy Forward revealed that DHS — specifically U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — received 50.6 million voter records from the DOJ.

ICE received another 48.4 million voter records from “independent sources of information” connected to Heather Honey, a longtime promoter of false election conspiracy theories who is now a senior DHS official.

The full scope of what DHS has done with the voter records it received from the DOJ and other sources remains unclear.

Legal proceedings in other cases have revealed that the Trump administration sent millions of records through a flawed DHS citizenship-status database as part of its hunt for noncitizens registered to vote. However, due to flaws in federal data, that database has routinely flagged eligible voters — particularly naturalized citizens — as noncitizens.

Separately, DHS has used immigration data in its possession and citizenship data from other federal agencies to conduct massive reviews of public versions of state registration lists.

This week, the DOJ used what it said were findings from DHS’s audit of California’s public voter roll to challenge around 20,000 people’s right to vote in the upcoming midterms.

In a lawsuit against the state Thursday, the DOJ claimed that DHS flagged those voters as potential noncitizens and asked a federal court to force the state and Los Angeles County to set aside those ballots until their citizenship status is confirmed.

Falsely claiming citizenship to register to vote is a federal crime. But the DOJ has not charged any of the 20,000 people it claimed were illegally registered in the state. Though the department asked a federal court to disenfranchise those 20,000 voters, it asserted it was “not practicable or feasible” to investigate all 20,000 for potentially committing a crime.

*Democracy Docket Founder Marc Elias is the chair of Democracy Forward’s board.

This is a breaking news story. Please check back for additional information.

text:

(CNN) — A political appointee with deep ties to the Trump family has been remove…



(CNN) — A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.

Under President Donald Trump, unaccompanied migrant children have been increasingly forced to navigate a complicated and accelerated immigration process with dwindling help after the administration ended a long-standing contract for legal services this summer — and as administration officials try to wrap their cases at an unprecedented pace.

“This is not the immigration process that Congress intended for unaccompanied children; it is a deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights,” the lawsuit states. Thursday’s lawsuit was filed by six legal service providers who work with unaccompanied migrant kids.

It focuses on unaccompanied migrant children who are residing with family in the US or are detained, either after recently crossing the US southern border or because their guardians were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Detained children are held in shelters operated by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is charged with their care.

CNN previously reported that children are contending with a fast-tracked immigration process, including abruptly rescheduled asylum interviews, sometimes with only a 24-hour notice — and increasingly without legal help. Migrant children as young as 2 are also showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.

Like adults, children must also go through immigration proceedings and present evidence to back up their asylum claim, and there’s no requirement for them to have legal representation throughout the process.

According to attorneys, asylum interviews have been abruptly pushed up.

“Since August 1, 2026, Plaintiffs have collectively received more than 600 notices of asylum interviews scheduled to take place in quick succession. Their attorneys are expected to represent children in multiple asylum interviews on the same day, sometimes at the same time, forcing them to forgo preparation and severely limiting their ability to effectively represent their unaccompanied child clients,” the lawsuit states.

“For these children, who risk being sent back to the countries they fled, the stakes could not be higher,” it continues.

The lawsuit calls for a return to the status quo — for example, when children were given at least 21 days notice prior to their asylum interview — and cites a federal law that’s been in place for nearly two decades, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, that’s supposed to provide protections for unaccompanied migrant children.

The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland.

The Trump administration has previously denied claims that cases are being fast-tracked, arguing that officials prioritize timely completion of cases. And in a statement to CNN last month, an HHS spokesperson said, “ORR will continue facilitating the ability of [unaccompanied alien children] in its custody to fully participate in immigration legal proceedings with representation by counsel, including hearings before EOIR immigration judges, who manage their own juvenile case dockets and schedules and make independent decisions on asylum claims under consideration.”

title: DOL Announces Enforcement Actions Against Employers in H-1B and PERM Fraud Probe
description:
H-1B workers are typically limited to up to six years of validity in the United States.
For affected H-1B workers, an employer losing access to the PERM process means losing a clear pathway to US permanent residence.
That foundation covers internal audits, sound PERM recruitment practices, wage compliance, whistleblower response, and training.
Employers must ensure that H-1B workers are paid at or above the required prevailing wage and actual wage levels.
Companies that sponsor H-1B workers or utilize the PERM process should treat immigration compliance as a core enterprise risk.
text:
Introduction: An Escalating Enforcement Environment

On October 8, 2026, Vice President J.D. Vance led a press conference announcing that the Department of Labor (“DOL”) “will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications” involving eight employers. The affected employers include well-known technology companies and global information technology (“IT”) services firms.

The announcement has practical consequences for employers whose workforce decisions and sponsorship activity could draw similar attention. Beyond its focus on prominent US employers and its White House-level involvement, three features of the action stand out:

The government is focused on major technology companies that sponsor their own long-term employees for permanent residence, not only outsourcing-model firms.

The government publicly justified the suspensions by pointing to employers’ layoff histories and recruitment practices, rather than limiting its rationale to concerns about the accuracy of specific filings.

The Vice President stated that a suspension would last “as long as it needs to” and that the Administration wants the companies to change how they hire.

The announcement did not indicate that an official finding of wrongdoing has been made against any of the affected employers, and DOL’s regulations allow it to suspend permanent labor certification (Program Electronic Review Management, “PERM”) processing while an investigation is pending, before any determination has been made. If an investigation ends without an adverse finding, DOL must resume processing the affected applications.

The government’s announcement drew attention to the relationship between two distinct programs:

The H-1B is a temporary (nonimmigrant) visa program that permits US organizations to petition for work authorization to employ foreign workers in “specialty occupations.” These are positions that require at least a bachelor’s degree, or its equivalent, in a specific specialty. H-1B workers are typically limited to up to six years of validity in the United States.

PERM labor certification is DOL’s process for an employer to conduct a mandatory recruitment process before sponsoring a foreign worker for certain types employment-based permanent residence (green cards), and is typically needed for H-1B workers to remain in the United States beyond the H-1B six-year limitation. Through this labor market test, DOL determines whether there are sufficient able, willing, qualified, and available US workers for the position. If, based on the employer’s recruitment results, there are not sufficient US workers, the employer may sponsor employees for green cards to fill the position.

While the October 8 action does not suspend any employer from the H-1B program, the two programs are inextricably linked. For instance, DOL reports that more than 50% of FY 2024 PERM applications were filed for workers in the United States in H-1B status. For affected H-1B workers, an employer losing access to the PERM process means losing a clear pathway to US permanent residence.

The Legal Framework and Its Limits

DOL’s regulations allow it to suspend processing of PERM applications involving an employer, attorney, or agent in two situations. The first is when DOL learns of possible fraud or willful misrepresentation. The second is when it learns that the party is under investigation for possible fraud or willful misrepresentation by the Department of Justice (“DOJ”), the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”), or another agency.

A suspension may initially last up to 180 days. At that point, DOL may resume processing some or all applications, or extend the suspension until the investigation or court proceedings are complete. If no fraud or willful misrepresentation is found, DOL must decide each pending application on its merits. If fraud is found, DOL must decide each pending application on its merits, but may deny applications containing fraudulent or false statements. It may also issue a written notice debarring the employer, attorney, or agent from the PERM program for up to three years.

The regulation therefore treats a suspension as a temporary hold tied to an investigation with a defined point for review. The recent announcement by the Administration suggested an open-ended suspension meant to change corporate hiring behavior. That gap is likely to shape how affected employers respond. If processing remains frozen past the 180-day mark without an indictment or a completed investigation, this could serve as an opportunity for employers to press DOL for an update on the status of the investigation. Employers should also keep in mind that a suspension is not a finding of fraud. Certifications that have already been approved by DOL would require a separate revocation or invalidation process upon a fraud finding. Nothing announced so far revokes them automatically.

The announcement builds on President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14431, signed September 18, 2026. That order directs the Departments of State, Labor, and Homeland Security to consider whether a sponsoring employer conducted layoffs in the past year, or plans layoffs, affecting similarly situated US workers. The agencies must weigh this in H-1B labor condition applications, petitions, visas, and admissions. The order also directs DOL’s Wage and Hour Division to review previously filed labor condition applications for possible enforcement action.

While the October 8 actions did not accuse the named companies of any specific violations of law, the Vice President pointed to an employer’s layoffs of American workers alongside its reliance on H-1B visas and green card sponsorship as justification for the action, making it clear that the Administration believes that an employer’s layoff history now directly affects its access to immigration benefits.

Responding to Subpoenas and Government Inquiries

During the October 8 announcement, DOL Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito confirmed that subpoenas have already been served to the relevant organizations, which shows that this enforcement effort has moved into active investigation. Employers that receive a subpoena, a request for documents, or a notice of an investigation involving H-1B or PERM filings face exposure on several fronts. This can include administrative sanctions, civil penalties, and criminal liability. The first decisions an employer makes often shape how the matter unfolds.

A federal inquiry, or subpoena, concerning an employer’s H-1B or PERM program presents two critical questions: what the government is entitled to obtain, and what the company needs to consider about its own conduct. Proactive steps taken before any inquiry, and decisions made at the outset of an investigation, can shape the company’s legal position, its interactions with investigators, and its ability to manage ongoing immigration obligations. Companies should: (i) conduct a privileged audit of H-1B and PERM practices now under scrutiny; (ii) build a rapid-response protocol before agents or subpoenas arrive; and (iii) manage any inquiry as a potential parallel civil, administrative, and criminal matter from day one.

Identify the agency and posture: First understand who is asking and why. A records request from DOL’s Wage and Hour Division typically signals a civil or administrative inquiry, while a subpoena from the DOL Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), or contact from a US Attorney’s Office, indicates that a criminal referral is a more immediate consideration. Employers should determine as early as possible whether the company is viewed as a witness, subject, or target, and whether particular employees, outside immigration counsel, or vendors are themselves a focus. That assessment drives staffing and it informs decisions, from how documents are produced to whether individual employees need separate counsel.

Immediate obligations: Some obligations apply as soon as an inquiry begins, including requirements to preserve relevant records and cooperate with investigators, while others can be negotiated and discussed. For instance, the scope of a subpoena, the custodians, and the timing of production can often be negotiated, and early, informed engagement with the investigating office can narrow the issues and avoid unnecessary escalation.

However, statements made during an inquiry also carry meaningful risk. Knowingly and willfully furnishing false information to investigators is a federal offense punishable by fine or imprisonment, and separate penalties apply to fraud or misuse of immigration documents. The law also protects from retaliation employees who disclose suspected violations or cooperate with an investigation. Employers must therefore handle internal communications and employment decisions with care.

Preservation and internal review: An effective response starts before documents are produced. Employers should promptly issue a targeted legal hold covering relevant data, documents, and communications. They should consider whether to conduct a privileged internal review, including employee interviews with appropriate guardrails, to understand the facts before engaging substantively with investigators. Investigators increasingly cross-match data, including data disclosed in government filings with employer payroll records, employee profiles, recruitment results, and hiring and layoff data. The internal review should run the same comparisons the government will run.

On-site visits: Inquiries do not always begin with paper. When agents arrive on site, frontline staff should request identification and the purpose of the visit, obtain copies of any notice, subpoena, or warrant, and contact counsel before documents are produced or interviews proceed. A judicial warrant generally must be honored, but an administrative warrant does not by itself authorize entry into non-public areas without consent. Employees may decide for themselves whether to speak with agents, and the company should neither discourage cooperation nor allow interviews of managers to proceed before counsel has considered the company’s position.

Self-disclosure: An investigation also forces a disclosure decision. Under DOJ’s Criminal Division Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (which we previously discussed in our March 2026 Legal Update), timely self-reporting, full cooperation, and remediation can support a presumption of declination, and a company may still qualify if it self-reports within 120 days after receiving an internal whistleblower report, even if the whistleblower reached DOJ first. The expanded DOJ whistleblower program now covers immigration violations, meaning employees and former employees have increased financial incentives to report suspected violations directly to the government. Any internal complaint about wages, recruitment, or filings should therefore trigger prompt triage and a documented disclosure decision, and discrepancies between wages paid and wages attested should be corrected without waiting for the government to identify them.

Coordinated defense and collateral consequences: Employers should manage the matter as a coordinated, multifront defense from the start. Cross-agency coordination now characterizes immigration-related enforcement, and a Wage and Hour inquiry can expand into scrutiny from other agencies, including US Citizenship and Immigration Services, DOJ, or Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The factual narrative presented to each agency must be consistent, because positions taken in a routine audit response may later be tested in a criminal proceeding. Employers should also plan for collateral consequences, including a PERM suspension or debarment, securities disclosure considerations for public companies, and communications with sponsored employees whose immigration status may depend on the outcome. Because DOL’s suspension authority is tied to whether an investigation is pending, how an employer conducts itself during the investigation may directly affect how long its PERM filings remain frozen.

Building on Our Earlier Recommendations

We have tracked this trend in a series of prior Legal Updates: our February 2025 Legal Update analyzed government directives making immigration enforcement a top DOJ priority and the legal ramifications for employers; our May 2025 Legal Update examined DOJ’s expanded whistleblower pilot program focused on immigration enforcement; our October 2025 Inside Track podcast examined DOL’s Project Firewall initiative and its focus on wage compliance, worksite accuracy, labor condition applications, and public access files; and our December 2025 Legal Update addressed the heightened vetting and screening environment affecting travelers, visa holders, and employers.

The compliance foundation in our September 2026 Legal Update still applies. That foundation covers internal audits, sound PERM recruitment practices, wage compliance, whistleblower response, and training. The October 8 action calls for further steps.

First, review workforce reductions and immigration sponsorship together.

The Administration has made the link between layoffs and foreign worker sponsorship explicit, both in Executive Order 14431 and in its public justification for the suspensions. Before a reduction in force, employers should identify pending and planned H-1B and PERM filings in the affected occupations and locations. They should assess how the timing and the record will be viewed by the government and, when appropriate, document the business reasons that distinguish eliminated roles from sponsored ones.

Second, evaluate PERM recruitment from the government’s perspective, not just against the regulatory checklist.

The Administration has criticized employers that run what is viewed as ineffective job advertisements and then cite the lack of applicants to justify hiring foreign workers. Recruitment that meets the technical requirements but may be unlikely to attract qualified US workers may be highly scrutinized by the government.

Third, conduct an audit of wage compliance.

Employers must ensure that H-1B workers are paid at or above the required prevailing wage and actual wage levels. The OIG has specifically highlighted “coercive wage-kickback arrangements” as a focus of its investigation. Reviews should also capture unpaid “benching” between assignments and deductions that effectively reduce pay below the attested rate. Any discrepancies between wages paid and wages reported should be identified and addressed promptly.

Fourth, examine relationships with third-party staffing firms and labor brokers.

Companies that engage staffing firms or labor brokers to place H-1B workers should review those relationships for potential issues, including irregularities in billing, wage pass-through arrangements, or recruitment practices. Vendor contracts should include audit, cooperation, and indemnification rights.

Finally, plan for a possible suspension or subpoena before either arrives.

Unless the investigating agency requests otherwise, DOL must notify the employer of a suspension in writing. Employers should decide in advance who receives government correspondence, who will lead the response, and how affected employees will be identified and told. A rapid-response plan should include written protocols and scripts for frontline staff, a call tree for immediate notice to counsel, and clear procedures for document handling, and it should be tested through mock audits. Employers should also decide how the 180-day review point will be monitored and, if appropriate, how to address next steps.

Looking Ahead

The October 8 action represents a further escalation, and the speed with which the Administration has moved from investigation to enforcement signals that additional actions are likely in the coming weeks and months. The Administration has tied employers’ access to the PERM program to their layoff histories and recruitment practices, the DOL OIG has confirmed that subpoenas are outstanding, and the regulation’s 180-day review point will test whether the suspensions remain tethered to an investigation. Companies that sponsor H-1B workers or utilize the PERM process should treat immigration compliance as a core enterprise risk. That means reviewing sponsorship and workforce decisions together, auditing wage and recruitment practices under privilege, treating internal complaints as potential disclosure triggers, and having a response plan in place before a subpoena or suspension notice arrives.

How Mayer Brown Can Help

Mayer Brown’s Global Mobility & Migration group, one of the nation’s top-ranked employment-based immigration practices, works alongside seasoned white-collar defense leaders in the firm’s Global Investigations & White Collar Defense practice, including former DOJ, DOL, and DHS officials, and experienced labor and employment practitioners.

We regularly advise employers on:

Responding to subpoenas and investigative demands;

Negotiating the scope and timing of document productions;

Conducting privileged internal investigations;

Preparing employees for interviews;

Engaging with agencies on suspension and debarment matters; and

Managing the interaction between immigration compliance and potential criminal exposure.

We also help employers proactively assess their recruitment, wage, and workforce-planning practices before they draw government attention.

For more information about the issues raised in this Legal Update, please contact the authors.

title: Trump administration sues CA to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
authors: ALANNA DURKIN RICHER and SOPHIE AUSTIN
description:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month's midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn't comply.
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare.

text:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month's midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.

The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.

The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn't comply.

PREVIOUS STORY: Justice Department threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls

The federal government didn't specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. His office said the list contained names of voters throughout California, not just Los Angeles, even though Logan is the only county election official named as a defendant in the lawsuit. He doesn't have jurisdiction over ballots outside Los Angeles County.

In a statement Thursday, Logan said his office can’t withhold ballots or refuse to count them “based solely on unverified allegations.”

Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.

Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn't provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state's voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada's voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens.

She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”

California's elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added.

David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.”

“If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.”

List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive

Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”

Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department's request as it was sent.

“Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said.

The Justice Department's lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.”

“The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined.”

Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government's outreach had not been collaborative.

She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.

In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”

Letters sent weeks before elections

The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration's alleged number of noncitizens on the state's voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department.

“What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said.

He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election.

“They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said.

The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.

Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court.

“This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.”

text:
Corporations given lucrative government contracts to carry out President Trump’s immigration agenda have contributed millions of dollars in campaign donations to Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterm election.

A Scripps News review of Federal Election Commission records shows The GEO Group, the nation’s largest owner of immigration detention centers, is also one of the biggest corporate donors supporting Republicans this midterm election.

A GEO subsidiary, GEO Reentry Services LLC, has contributed $4.4 million dollars to MAGA Inc. a super PAC supporting President Trump.

RELATED STORY | AI interest groups pour tens of millions of dollars into 2026 election

Companies will sometimes make campaign contributions through a subsidiary that is itself not a federal contractor to avoid violating an FEC rule that bars contractors from giving to candidates and political committees, said Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigations at the Campaign Legal Center.

“We think that's a really big problematic loophole in the law,” Fischer said. “The reason that federal contractors are prohibited from making political contributions is to prevent pay to play in the contracting process.”

The GEO Group donated through its subsidiary as the company reports record revenue tied to President Trump’s administration reopening profit-detention immigration centers closed during President Biden’s term.

“Last year was the most successful period for new business wins in our company’s history,” GEO Group Chairman and CEO George Zoley told investors during a public quarterly financial update in August.

The GEO subsidiary has also given $1.3 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC focused on keeping the GOP’s majority in Congress.

GEO Group did not respond to questions about its 2026 campaign spending.

FEC records show political action committees for both GEO Group and CoreCivic, the second largest operator of ICE detention centers, are also contributing directly to dozens of Republicans on the ballot.

Several recipients are incumbent lawmakers who sit on committees that set DHS spending levels or have immigration oversight power.

Both GEO Group and CoreCivic PACs have given the maximum allowed $10,000 contribution to Rep. Andrew Garbarino, R-New York, who is the chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premium

The PACs have also donated to Maine Sen. Susan Collins, the top Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Ashley Moody, a Florida Republican who sits on both the judiciary and homeland security committees.

The PACs are also giving to the Republican National committee and two main congressional committees working to elect GOP members. GEO Group's PAC has already donated three times as much money to those three committees compared to the 2024 election, the Scripps News analysis of FEC records showed.

A CoreCivic spokesperson responded to questions with a statement that said the company supports candidates and elected officials who understand the “limited but important solutions” the company can provide to address national challenges.

“Our political engagement is focused on educating policymakers about those solutions and the services we provide,” the statement said.

While major corporations often donated to both Democrats and Republicans, GEO Group and CoreCivic’s support overwhelmingly is going to Republicans.

CoreCivic’s spokesperson pointed to Democrats refusing to accept donations from certain businesses. Democrats have called for shuttering immigration detention centers.

“Political contributions from the private prison industry have become politically toxic for Democrats,” Fischer said. “I think it's very likely just a pure business decision that they see Republicans as being more beneficial to their financial interests. With many federal contractors, they don't see red and blue, they see green.”

(The Center Square) – California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the Trump administration's practice of conducting civil immigration enforcement in and around courthouses.
The legal challenge marks Bonta's 100th lawsuit against the administration since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, but the White House is pointing to court rulings up holding the administration's immigration enforcement as lawful.
According to the California Department of Justice, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have conducted disruptive and often violent civil immigration enforcement actions at courthouses across the state since the policy was initiated in May 2025. State officials report that witnesses, victims, and survivors of domestic violence increasingly fear appearing in court, creating what the state calls a profound chilling effect that undermines public safety and judicial operations.

“In California, our courthouses aren't proving grounds for unlawful immigration enforcement tactics,” said Bonta at a press conference in Sacramento. “When people come knocking at the court's door, justice should welcome them in with equal access and application regardless of their immigration status.”
Data cited in the lawsuit reveals that the average monthly number of ICE arrests in and around state courthouses spiked by more than 550% in the year following the policy change.
“Immigration arrests at courthouses have been documented in at least 22 California counties, from Los Angeles and San Diego to Shasta, Butte, and Glen, all throughout our state,” said Bonta. “That includes the five largest counties, each home to a significant percentage of non-citizen residents and families of mixed immigration status.”
The White House sharply criticized the litigation, pointing to the administration's legal track record.
"Instead of bragging about filing frivolous lawsuits against the Trump Administration, the California Attorney General should focus on addressing problems in his own state – like the countless criminal illegal aliens extreme Democrats allow to roam free and kill innocent Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told The Center Square in an email Thursday. "The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the Administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions."
Acting ICE Director David Venturella and Secretary of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named in the lawsuit. The Center Square reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, but did not hear back by publication time.
Although a federal court vacated ICE's written directive in late June 2026 in Pablo Sequen v. Albarran, Bonta said enforcement actions have persisted. State records show 34 reported incidents resulting in 30 civil arrests in June 2026, followed by 28 reported incidents and 28 arrests in July, with activity continuing through the summer and fall.
Filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE, Bonta's lawsuit outlines multiple arguments. First, the lawsuit claims the immigration enforcement directive is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because the agency failed to evaluate the directive's chilling effect on access to justice and did not provide a reasoned explanation for removing prior restrictions on courthouse enforcement. Second, Bonta argues that the agency exceeded its statutory authority under the APA, asserting that the Immigration and Nationality Act was enacted against a centuries-old common law privilege barring civil arrests at courthouses — a protection Congress is presumed to have incorporated.
Finally, the lawsuit contends that the directive is contrary to constitutional rights and violates the 10th Amendment by infringing on the state's sovereign power to maintain a judicial system, prosecute crimes and execute core police powers.
Meanwhile, legal defenders of federal policy argue that state powers cannot override federal authority.
Christopher Hajec, deputy general counsel for the Federation for American Immigration Reform, noted that the immunity doctrine protects federal officials performing their duties from state interference. For example, Hajec said that California once arrested a U.S. marshal for murder because of actions he took to protect a Supreme Court justice. The Supreme Court ruled that the prosecution had to be dismissed, because California law could not stop the marshal from doing his job. Pointing to Bonta’s lawsuit, Hajec said California cannot invoke its state powers or property rights to block ICE from doing its job.
"When the federal government comes into a situation anywhere in the United States, federal law is supreme, not that of the state where the activity takes place," Hajec told The Center Square in an email.
"There is no common-law privilege, silently incorporated into the INA against immigration arrest at courthouses," Hajec added.
The old privilege, he said, had the far different purpose of stopping litigants from arresting each other (as then could be done) when they came to a courthouse to have their differences decided.

text:
An 805 UndocuFund volunteer was detained by ICE on Thursday morning in Santa Maria.

Alexandria Quintanar, a rapid response volunteer for the organization, was followed by an ICE agent after she dropped off signs for a protest hosted by Indivisible Santa Maria on McCoy Lane and Depot Street.

The ICE agent allegedly ran through red lights and drove recklessly for half an hour as he followed Quintanar in her car before stopping her.

“What happened to me today, being chased erratically by that ICE agent, could have been anybody’s family member,” said Quintanar, who was released from custody shortly after.

The incident comes on the heels of another volunteer for 805 UndocuFund, Joseph Dobzynski, having been detained at gunpoint while observing federal immigration enforcement in Camarillo on Wednesday.

Dobzynski was released and has a scheduled court hearing in December, according to a post on Instagram.

Since Oct. 5, an estimated 84 people have been taken by ICE agents in North Santa Barbara County, according to data from 805 Undocufund.

The organization hosted a press conference outside of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office located at 740 W. Century St. in Santa Maria Thursday evening to address the recent detainments.

At the meeting, 805 UndocuFund Executive Director Primitiva Hernandez spoke alongside Quintanar and other rapid response volunteers. Santa Maria City Councilwoman Gloria Soto also shared her thoughts on Thursday’s events.

“We need more eyes on the street,” said Hernandez, who asked for more people to volunteer to document ICE activity in the community.

805 UndocuFund works with volunteers throughout San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara and Ventura counties to document the activity of federal immigration agents. The organization also provides legal and financial resources for people affected by ICE, along with fundraising events.

Over the last two weeks, volunteers have observed a surge of enforcement throughout the Central Coast. Last week, the parent of an Allan Hancock Student was detained after leaving campus, and on Monday a man was detained outside of Albertsons in Carpinteria.

But Santa Maria has been hit the hardest by immigration enforcement of any city in Santa Barbara County, Hernandez said.

On Wednesday, Joel Mendoza witnessed ICE agents detain a man outside of SM Wireless on 307 W. Main St. in Santa Maria. 805 UndocuFund later confirmed the arrest on their social media.

“I walk inside and I’m just kind of shocked how they can just pull up and take somebody like that,” said Mendoza, who is an employee at the cellphone and repair store.

He works with many immigrant families to help them navigate Facebook and Whatsapp on their phones.

Mendoza said he has noticed less foot traffic in his store and along Main Street, a normally bustling area of the city, this week.

“We need ICE out of Santa Maria,” Soto said. “We need ICE out of the 805.”

Soto urged her colleagues on the City Council to stand up for immigrant families in Santa Maria.

She said the Santa Maria Police Department also needs to affirm it will not cooperate with ICE nor infringe on the rights of rapid response volunteers as they document immigration enforcement.

“I’m calling on our police department to publicly communicate its policies, ensure every officer receives appropriate training and to reaffirm its commitment to protecting the constitutional rights of every Santa Marian.”

805 UndocuFund’s hotline number, 805-870-8855, is the primary way for people to alert the organization of potential ICE activity in their community. Families affected by federal immigration enforcement can also call the number for legal and financial support.

text:
A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.

Under President Donald Trump, unaccompanied migrant children have been increasingly forced to navigate a complicated and accelerated immigration process with dwindling help after the administration ended a long-standing contract for legal services this summer — and as administration officials try to wrap their cases at an unprecedented pace.

“This is not the immigration process that Congress intended for unaccompanied children; it is a deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights,” the lawsuit states. Thursday’s lawsuit was filed by six legal service providers who work with unaccompanied migrant kids.

It focuses on unaccompanied migrant children who are residing with family in the US or are detained, either after recently crossing the US southern border or because their guardians were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Detained children are held in shelters operated by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is charged with their care.

CNN previously reported that children are contending with a fast-tracked immigration process, including abruptly rescheduled asylum interviews, sometimes with only a 24-hour notice — and increasingly without legal help. Migrant children as young as 2 are also showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.

Like adults, children must also go through immigration proceedings and present evidence to back up their asylum claim, and there’s no requirement for them to have legal representation throughout the process.

According to attorneys, asylum interviews have been abruptly pushed up.

“Since August 1, 2026, Plaintiffs have collectively received more than 600 notices of asylum interviews scheduled to take place in quick succession. Their attorneys are expected to represent children in multiple asylum interviews on the same day, sometimes at the same time, forcing them to forgo preparation and severely limiting their ability to effectively represent their unaccompanied child clients,” the lawsuit states.

“For these children, who risk being sent back to the countries they fled, the stakes could not be higher,” it continues.

The lawsuit calls for a return to the status quo — for example, when children were given at least 21 days notice prior to their asylum interview — and cites a federal law that’s been in place for nearly two decades, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, that’s supposed to provide protections for unaccompanied migrant children.

The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland.

The Trump administration has previously denied claims that cases are being fast-tracked, arguing that officials prioritize timely completion of cases. And in a statement to CNN last month, an HHS spokesperson said, “ORR will continue facilitating the ability of [unaccompanied alien children] in its custody to fully participate in immigration legal proceedings with representation by counsel, including hearings before EOIR immigration judges, who manage their own juvenile case dockets and schedules and make independent decisions on asylum claims under consideration.”

text:
This story was first published in partnership between Injustice Watch and The Intercept, a nonprofit news organization dedicated to holding the powerful accountable through fearless, adversarial journalism. Sign up for The Intercept’s newsletter.

CHICAGO — After being detained for five days in an airport hotel, a mother filed suit against a longtime Immigration and Customs Enforcement contractor on behalf of herself and her now 23-month-old son, alleging false imprisonment among other counts.

The lawsuit was filed on September 29, more than a year after an investigation by Injustice Watch and The Intercept revealed MVM Inc. had confined Valentina Galvis, an asylum-seeker from Colombia, and her then seven-month-old infant, a U.S. citizen, in a room at the Sonesta Chicago O’Hare Airport Rosemont last summer. In that reporting, Galvis had described her captivity in stark terms, detailing how she and her son were locked in a room with no way to communicate with the outside world and no idea when, if ever, they would be set free.

Galvis is seeking monetary damages for the alleged harm and injury she and her child suffered as a result of the detention following their arrest by ICE at a Chicago immigration court in June 2025. Galvis named the Sonesta International Hotels Corporation and affiliated companies that own and operate the hotel as defendants in the complaint.

The lawsuit also named five Sonesta and two MVM executives and employees. It identifies JoAnna Granado as the MVM employee who transported Galvis and her son from the hotel to a federal office in Chicago on the day they were released, drawing on the original reporting in which Granado confirmed she was involved in the family’s detention.

Granado and other individuals named in the suit couldn’t be reached for comment. MVM didn’t respond to questions about the lawsuit. During the original investigation, Sonesta said that it “does not condone illegal behavior of any kind” at its hotels. The company declined to comment on the lawsuit.

The suit accused both the ICE contractor and the hotel of detaining Galvis and her child for profit, and alleged the companies engaged in a civil conspiracy by working together to use the hotel room as a detention cell.

“MVM, a federal contractor, physically seized, transported, and confined Ms. Galvis and her infant son,” the suit claimed. “Sonesta knowingly provided and maintained the hotel room used as a makeshift detention cell, profiting from the arrangement while a mother and her infant were locked inside.”

The suit seeks more than $50,000 in compensatory damages, plus punitive damages, and demands a jury trial.

In the complaint, Galvis alleged that her detention at MVM’s hands caused her and her baby a range of physical, emotional, and caregiving harm. Her son had just recently started transitioning to solid foods before the pair were seized by ICE; the suit alleged the infant was provided only scraps of food that were nutritionally inadequate for his age. Meanwhile, confinement-induced stress caused Galvis to decrease her breastmilk production at a time when her son needed it most.

Her baby suffered sleep disturbance and a worsening skin condition, the lawsuit claimed. While MVM had given Galvis an adequate change of clothing, the garments provided for her baby didn’t fit him. Because no laundry service was available, Galvis “washed [the infant’s] clothing in the bathroom sink multiple times,” she stated in an affidavit filed with the court, hanging “the wet clothes near the bed where the air conditioning would dry them quickly.” The infant wore only diapers while his clothes were being washed, and left the hotel on a Tuesday wearing the same outfit he’d worn since he and Galvis were detained by ICE the previous Thursday, according to the affidavit.

In court documents, Galvis alleged MVM confined her and her infant to a room near O’Hare International Airport. Galvis said she was sometimes told she would be taken to a Texas detention center and, on one occasion, that she would be deported to Colombia. She was released by MVM after a federal judge ordered that Galvis and her baby couldn’t be removed from Illinois.

The practice of using hotel rooms as makeshift detention sites has drawn little media attention; far more scrutiny has centered on conditions inside the growing network of ICE detention centers around the country. An inspector general’s report published last month found that ICE had failed to manage its detention space contracts. When asked about it at a September 30 press conference, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended facility conditions, saying detention centers meet and often exceed federal standards — and that comfort isn’t the department’s priority.

“We’re not providing Holiday Inns,” said Mullin.

While ICE agents don’t generally place people in hotels, the agency contracts with MVM to transport immigrant children and families; the contractor sometimes places them in hotel rooms across the U.S. Since fiscal year 2020, MVM has received more than $1.3 billion in ICE contracts, much of it for transporting families.

The lawsuit doesn’t name the federal government as a defendant.

William G. McLean III, who represents Galvis and her baby, underscored the companies’ role in their confinement. “The corporate defendants in this case unlawfully imprisoned and permanently traumatized my clients,” he said, “over five terrifying days after the Department of Homeland Security illegally arrested them.”

Galvis remains at risk of deportation — a final decision on her asylum claim is still pending in immigration court. She’s currently in therapy after an evaluation determined she’s experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the detention.

“I isolate myself to avoid anything that reminds me of what happened. I stay home and I do not go outside unless I really need to,” she said in an affidavit.

“Even now, when I go out, I get very nervous, and I feel terror.”

description:
The report raises new questions about the identity of the man ICE said it was pursuing during Saturday’s operation in northwest Harris County, when an agent allegedly struck 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez with an SUV as he ran away.
What ICE says happened In a statement Saturday, ICE said agents conducting surveillance had seen Mendoza-Cervantes enter a vehicle driven by Parra Hernandez.
When agents attempted to stop the vehicle, Parra Hernandez and a second man fled on foot, according to the agency.
ICE said Parra Hernandez ran in front of one of its vehicles and was struck.
Parra Hernandez’s brother and supporters also said Parra Hernandez had never crossed paths with Mendoza-Cervantes.
text:
HOUSTON – Federal immigration agents involved in an operation that left a Houston construction worker seriously injured were searching for a man whose family says died nearly nine years ago, according to a new report from The New York Times.

The Times reported Wednesday that Jamie Jimenez, of Dallas, identified the man pictured in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement wanted bulletin as her father, Jose Hector Jimenez Mendoza. She said he died in October 2017 after falling from a cliff near the southern border while fleeing immigration agents.

A Mexican death certificate provided by Jimenez to the Times states her father was 43 when he died in Laredo, Texas.

The report raises new questions about the identity of the man ICE said it was pursuing during Saturday’s operation in northwest Harris County, when an agent allegedly struck 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez with an SUV as he ran away.

ICE identified its target as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, an undocumented Mexican immigrant with a deportation order and multiple prior arrests. Jimenez told the Times her father used aliases, including the name released by ICE, and that the photograph in the agency’s bulletin appeared to show him.

The Times said it reviewed photographs provided by Jimenez that appeared to match the image in the Department of Homeland Security bulletin. The newspaper also reviewed court records showing her father faced the same types of criminal charges ICE attributed to its target.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Times’ questions about Jimenez’s father or requests for additional information about the man the agency was seeking.

What ICE says happened

In a statement Saturday, ICE said agents conducting surveillance had seen Mendoza-Cervantes enter a vehicle driven by Parra Hernandez.

When agents attempted to stop the vehicle, Parra Hernandez and a second man fled on foot, according to the agency. ICE said Parra Hernandez ran in front of one of its vehicles and was struck.

The agency described its target as a public safety threat, citing four prior arrests for driving under the influence and an arrest for unlawful possession of a firearm. ICE also said the man had been deported twice and illegally reentered the United States five times.

However, Jimenez told the Times her father died in 2017, and the newspaper reported that records showed he had faced similar charges and used aliases.

During a Wednesday news conference, Cesar Espinosa, executive director of immigrant rights organization FIEL Houston, displayed a photograph of the passenger who fled during the operation. Espinosa said the passenger did not resemble the man pictured in ICE’s wanted bulletin.

Parra Hernandez’s brother and supporters also said Parra Hernandez had never crossed paths with Mendoza-Cervantes. His family said he had lived in Houston for 34 years and had not previously been stopped by immigration authorities.

A search of court records using Parra Hernandez’s name and age found several traffic tickets but no criminal charges, according to the Times.

ICE agent placed on administrative leave

The ICE officer who allegedly struck Parra Hernandez has been placed on administrative leave while an internal investigation continues, according to a senior Department of Homeland Security official cited by NBC News.

Multiple officers at the scene were wearing body cameras, and ICE is reviewing the footage internally, NBC News reported. It remains unclear whether the footage will be released publicly or shared with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office is investigating the incident with the Harris County Sheriff’s Office and considering whether the officer could face an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon charge.

“From my perspective and from the perspective of a lot of different investigators who have looked at this, that individual was intentionally struck and run over,” Teare previously told KPRC 2.

ICE has denied allegations that its officer intentionally struck Parra Hernandez.

The investigation also includes allegations that federal agents removed critical evidence after the incident. The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has raised concerns about ICE’s handling of evidence, as detailed in KPRC 2’s previous reporting.

Parra Hernandez remains hospitalized

Surveillance footage appeared to show an ICE SUV veering toward Parra Hernandez and striking him from behind as he ran away, according to the Times.

The impact shattered his leg and injured his hip and ankle. His attorney, Kim Bruno, said Parra Hernandez underwent surgery Saturday and needs additional surgery.

He remains in ICE custody at the hospital, according to his attorney.

FIEL Houston has been assisting Parra Hernandez’s family and has raised concerns about the circumstances of the operation and the treatment of the injured man.

The second man who was in the vehicle escaped on foot and was not captured, according to the Times.

The case is unfolding amid heightened scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in the Houston area. Harris County prosecutors are also investigating the July killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, during an encounter involving federal immigration enforcement in east Houston.

Teare has previously criticized the Department of Homeland Security for not responding to his office’s requests for information in that investigation.

FIEL released the following statement after the news broke:

Brockport, N.Y. (WHAM) — Faculty, staff, and students rallied at SUNY Brockport on Thursday, calling for the immediate release of German Machado from ICE detention, a demand echoed by Gov. Kathy Hochul.

BACKGROUND: Family fears for future after ICE detains SUNY Brockport employee outside home | SUNY Brockport employee detained by ICE outside home, union says

Over a two-hour period, Machado’s fellow SUNY employees and students gathered at a visibility event held by United University Professions (UUP) to show their support, with the U.S. flag flying overhead.

“He's a valuable member of our society, of our campus community, of our union chapter," said Anne Macpherson, a SUNY Brockport history teacher. "So, the law must be respected. Due process must be respected. That's what the flag means to me."

The union said Machado, a father and husband from Batavia, was arrested by ICE outside his home Tuesday while preparing to go to his job as an IT technician at the university. According to his family, Machado has a valid federal employment authorization document and no criminal record.

At Thursday’s rally, supporters held signs reading “Bring German home,” and signed messages of support.

“It shows that there's a lot of love between the student body and the faculty at campus,” said Brockport student Shawn Victory. “Bring German home!"

“We don't like what's happening throughout the entire country, and now it's hitting home,” said Jerry Hickey of Brockport.

In a social media post Thursday, Hochul called for Machado's immediate release, saying her team had contacted the Department of Homeland Security.

"German Machado was on his way out the door for work Tuesday morning when ICE agents snatched him outside his home," Hochul wrote. "He is a law-abiding husband, father, and New York State employee with federal authorization to work through 2029. Imagine the fear and heartbreak his family is feeling."

Hochul also criticized President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, questioning the administration's immigration enforcement priorities.

"Donald Trump and Secretary Mullin said they were only going after the 'worst of the worst.' Is this who they meant? Shame on them," Hochul wrote. "My team has reached out to DHS to demand his immediate release. German belongs home with his family."

Machado's family fled Venezuela in 2016 after his wife faced threats for her work as a journalist. They sought asylum in the United States, but their application has remained pending since then. Immigration attorney Gadi Zohar said the delay could be due to a significant backlog of asylum cases.

“I think 10 years isn't really outside the realm of possibility," said Zohar, a managing partner at Zohar Law. "Usually it's less than 10 years, maybe five, six, seven-year mark. But it's been a problem for years."

The Department of Homeland Security said Machado lawfully entered the U.S. in August 2016 with permission to stay until February 2017. The federal agency said he “overstayed his welcome by almost a decade and failed to depart," emphasizing that work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status.

Zohar said ICE can arrest someone with a pending asylum case under circumstances involving criminal activity or through a process tied to a policy change implemented in July.

“Now, to try to expedite the process, the policy is that they could put you directly in front of an immigration judge even before you have an interview," Zohar explained. "So, they can waive the interview which once you're in front of an immigration judge, they have the ability to detain you and put you in a detention center awaiting a hearing."

Zohar said it can take years for a final hearing to occur.

“What we're seeing is that a lot of people either will really just stay for a long time and fight it out, but the more likely scenario is that they just give up, because they're not criminals, and they're being housed with criminals a lot of times,” Zohar said.

On the SUNY Brockport campus, union representatives said they will continue supporting Machado and monitoring his case.

"We're going to respond accordingly with the events or the outreach or the resources that are in accordance with the family's wishes and what's going to be best to bring him home," said Alissa Karl, vice president of United University Professions and a Brockport faculty member.

DHS said Machado will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. —

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced the filing of the 100th lawsuit against the Trump administration, targeting a Department of Homeland Security directive that allows Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to conduct enforcement at or near courthouses.

"We brought the lawsuit because we have data showing the impact of the immigration enforcement at courthouses and what it has on the impact that it has on the administration of justice in our court system,” Bonta said. “It has interfered with the administration of justice. It has intimidated and created fear for witnesses and victims."

Bonta explained that the enforcement actions have discouraged witnesses and victims from coming forward, forcing prosecutors to drop cases. "It is anti-public safety,” he said. “The Judicial Council has been collecting data, and that data shows a 550% increase in the number of immigration enforcement incidents at or near courthouses."

Bonta said the lawsuit seeks to vacate the Department of Homeland Security directive, effectively prohibiting ICE from conducting immigration enforcement at courthouses.

"We are looking for an order that says that directive from the Department of Homeland Security is no longer effective and ICE is no longer allowed, and they’re actually prohibited from enforcing immigration law at or near courthouses," he said.

Bonta responded to a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration against California, alleging that 20,000 non-citizens are on the state’s voter rolls. He dismissed the claim as baseless and politically motivated.

"Completely unimpressed. We think this case is completely without legal merit, without factual basis. They have provided absolutely no justification for the claim,” Bonta said. He criticized the administration for advancing debunked conspiracy theories about voter fraud and questioned the timing of the lawsuit, which coincides with an ongoing election in California.
