On a recent Zoom meeting of Habeas Flight Watch users, flight trackers from Las Vegas, San Diego, and Ann Arbor, Michigan, do a round of introductions.
These on-the-ground flight trackers have a symbiotic relationship with remote virtual trackers like JJ, Mimi, and Toby: Online trackers provide information that helps activists know what they’re looking for on the ground, and in person flight trackers are able to verify aircraft codes and arrival and departure times that confirm suspected ICE flights as they happen in real time.
As seasoned ICE flight watchers, Susan and Wayne decided to devote their retirement road trip to documenting flights at airports across the country and providing mentorship to the newer flight trackers they’ve met along the way.
ICE flight tracking is not without its personal risks, either.
text:
In May 2025, a Bedford, Massachusetts-based computer programmer and pilot named Mimi came upon an account on Bluesky that piqued her interest. Each day, the account owner—a man named JJ—posted a list of cities with outbound deportation flights by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as their final destinations, most of which were outside of the United States. JJ’s posts typically included up to ten flights per day. Mimi, who requested that her last name be withheld to protect her privacy, tells The Progressive she couldn’t comprehend how a single individual was able to glean so much detail about the flight logistics of an agency that has gone to increasing lengths to obfuscate its day-to-day operations from the general public.

Among people who track ICE flights both on the ground at airports and online using free, publicly available flight locator websites such as Flight Aware, JJ has become well-known: his Bluesky profile, almost entirely dedicated to sharing the daily, precise details of ICE deportation and detention flights, has garnered nearly 30,000 followers. Within a few weeks of monitoring JJ’s page, Mimi reached out via direct message. Through their conversation, she discovered JJ was running his extraordinarily time-intensive flight tracking operation manually and independently. So she offered to assist him—and in doing so, began a trajectory that would lead to a nationwide effort to help defend immigrant detainees and their families.

JJ, who lives in Washington, D.C., and also asked that his last name be withheld, learned how to track flights using publicly available software during his service in the U.S. military in his late twenties. After leaving the military, he continued flight tracking as a hobby and was interested in how commercial and military planes involved in conflicts moved around the globe.

In 2025, as the Trump Administration began ramping up its systemic targeting of immigrant communities across the country, JJ found himself in between jobs and figuring out what to do next. A self-described “boring liberal,” he was horrified to see the photos and videos of people being ripped from their homes, cars, and sidewalks in broad daylight. He says he found it particularly disturbing how little information was available to the general public regarding ICE’s operational logistics and where the individuals they detained were being taken.

“I figured if they’re trying to hide [the flights], then we should definitely be looking at them closer,” he tells The Progressive. “It’s not a classified military mission. You’re just doing a law enforcement function, supposedly, of taking people overseas or moving them between different detention centers in the United States.”

When he began tracking ICE flights in April 2025, JJ tells The Progressive, he used a basic flight tracking tool called Flight Radar 24. Since the federal government provides no public schedules of ICE flights, JJ relies on different sets of publicly available data, such as flight logs and air traffic control broadcasts. But ICE follows a regular schedule of facility transfer and deportation flights—so the art of ICE flight tracking lies in pattern recognition.

JJ says he began to see patterns in the numbers used for call signs reserved for government charter flights; certain numbers were exclusively reserved for ICE flights. He also has a particular eye for noticing repetition of unusual repetitive routes—governement chartered flights that were bound for countries outside of the U.S., and departed not from major cities, but airports in smaller cities that had become ICE hubs, such as Alexandria, Louisiana.

In July 2025, amid Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s wrongful deportation to El Salvador and ensuing legal battle against the Trump Administration, JJ monitored GlobalX—the airline which operated the plane on which Garcia was initially deported—in search of ICE flights into and out of El Salvador. He’d been tracking GlobalX for two weeks when the flight codes suddenly disappeared from his radar completely.

He broke out some of the techniques he’d learned in the military, and searched for planes that were following similar patterns as the El Salvador flights he’d previously been watching. But they were no longer visible on the public flight tracker. Now, they were shielded behind a privacy radar called Limiting Aircraft Data Displayed, a program that restricts aircraft flight data to paid subscribers alone, blocking the information from public flight-tracking websites—which celebrities like Elon Musk and Taylor Swift use to hide their private jets from trackers. JJ realized that GlobalX had changed the call sign of nearly every ICE flight it operated to “TYSON”—a specially designated sign that had previously only been used for President Trump’s personal aircraft.

Because JJ had already established a weekly predicted schedule of ICE flight from his weeks of studying aircraft routes, the TYSON call sign was only a momentary barrier–the name may have changed but he could see flights following the exact same patterns as the ones he had been monitoring continuing to operate. By the time Mimi made JJ’s acquaintance in September 2025, ICE flight tracking was taking up a significant amount of his time. Mimi was eager to help—but even with both of them working to update their spreadsheet of potential ICE flights, the tracking had become nearly equivalent to a full-time job. Mimi quickly realized that in order to keep up their operation, they would need to find a way to automate their work.

Around this time, Mimi’s close friend Toby—a computer programmer and flight tracker based in Bedford, Massachusetts, who also requested that his last name be withheld due to privacy concerns—had been introduced to a group of pro bono attorneys in Massachusetts. The attorneys rapid-file habeas-corpus petitions—legal proceedings that are often the last option for immigrants who have been detained by ICE illegally, or whose civil rights have been violated over the course of their detainment. The attorneys had seen local news coverage about demonstrations outside the Hanscom Air Field in Bedford, calling for a halt to all ICE deportations flights. The demonstrations were organized by a local flight watch group of which Toby is an active member. The attorneys asked Toby to create a database that could help them document and verify information about their clients’ deportation flights. When Toby called Mimi up to pick her brain, she immediately knew she had to introduce him to JJ.

Over the course of several months in late 2025, JJ, Mimi, and Toby worked together to develop a tool called Habeas Flight Watch, which automates the tracking process JJ had been performing manually by compiling the predicted ICE flights of any given day and auto-populating their call-signs, arrival and departure destinations and times. What initially struck Mimi about JJ was his incredible aptitude for identifying unusual patterns in large sets of flight data; it felt like he needed only to stare at a week's worth of flight information to be able to point to the particular planes and routes that were ICE flights. “Part of the program we wrote is called ‘JJ’s Brain,’” Mimi says. “We basically just tried to translate his mind into software.”

In May 2026, JJ, Mimi and Toby, launched Habeas Flight Watch as a first-of-its-kind, publicly available website. Its dashboard displays a map of the U.S. with color-coded boxes indicating major airports. When a user clicks on a box with an active flight, a pop-up window shows the exact flight code, how long the plane was on the ground before departing, its final destination, and its expected arrival time.

Even before its public launch, Habeas Flight Watch was used by immigration attorneys to help provide documentation for habeas-corpus petition filings. But over the course of the past year, the effort has grown larger than JJ, Mimi, or Toby could have ever imagined. In Dallas,Texas, ICE flight tracker activists regularly coordinate with the Habeas Flight Watch network as part of their work to draw attention to the increased use of the city-owned airport, Dallas Love Field, for detainee transfer and deportation flights. JJ rattles off other cities from which he has near-daily communication with local flight trackers, including Minneapolis, Minnesota; Twin Falls, Idaho; and Memphis, Tennessee. Habeas Flight Watch is now also used by family members attempting to locate their loved ones who have been detained, as well as immigrant rights non-profits, ICE watchdog groups, and investigative journalists.

On a recent Zoom meeting of Habeas Flight Watch users, flight trackers from Las Vegas, San Diego, and Ann Arbor, Michigan, do a round of introductions. While JJ, Mimi and Toby work behind the scenes in the digital realm, the participants on this Zoom call engage in the side of flight tracking that involves posting up at public parking lots or service roads near their regional airport and photographing ICE flights—and the detained immigrants aboard the flights—as they arrive or depart. These on-the-ground flight trackers have a symbiotic relationship with remote virtual trackers like JJ, Mimi, and Toby: Online trackers provide information that helps activists know what they’re looking for on the ground, and in person flight trackers are able to verify aircraft codes and arrival and departure times that confirm suspected ICE flights as they happen in real time.

One of the participants, Susan LaSante, is already well known among the group, even though this is many of the attendees’ first time meeting her. LaSante and her husband, Wayne, are based in Bedford, Massachusetts, but have spent much of the last year on the road. As seasoned ICE flight watchers, Susan and Wayne decided to devote their retirement road trip to documenting flights at airports across the country and providing mentorship to the newer flight trackers they’ve met along the way.

LaSante describes a recent encounter with a woman who had been unable to locate her detained family member after being alerted of his transfer from an ICE facility in Massachusetts. The flight tracking network was able to confirm the detained man’s flight was departing from Bedford and headed to Alexandria, Louisiana, where LaSante was already stationed at the airport with a long-range camera. “We were able to identify him by the fluorescent sweatshirt he was wearing—it was his company shirt,” LaSante says. “I didn't understand how much that would mean to them, because there wasn’t anything we did except to verify where he was. I think they just knew we cared, that there are people out there that care.”

LaSante then enthusiastically greets another meeting participant, Audrey Hines. Hines is joined by two other Las Vegas-based participants, Jill Glass and Buffy Taylor. “We met Susan and Wayne through our Democratic Socialists of America [DSA] chapter,” Hines says. “They took the time to show us the ropes of how to track the planes and document them.”

Hines, Glass, and Taylor formed a flight tracking team together after each getting the hang of staking out the planes individually. “Buffy is just like an absolute gem for this because she's an aviation enthusiast and a photographer,” Hines says. “Jill has an incredible long-range camera. We’ve got it down to a science.”

Glass, a schoolteacher who has devoted her summer break to flight tracking, says a large part of what motivated her to start this work was the fear and trauma she saw in the immigrant children that she teaches in Las Vegas. “What ICE has done to this country, it’s antithetical to everything I believe in,” she says. “It has to be fought in every possible way.”

This is a sentiment mutually acknowledged by everyone on the call. On the ground flight trackers who watch and photograph airplanes transporting ICE detainees know that the work entails seeing human beings shackled together and stripped of an identity on a daily basis. Multiple flight trackers in the meeting shared accounts of watching immigration officials casually toss pairs of shackles over their shoulders, or use them as props for jokes, while waiting to restrain the wrists and ankles of the next group of detained immigrants. Even from a distance, documenting these flights means bearing witness to acts completely devoid of humanity, the trackers on the call express. It is the shared desire to not look away from or allow that process to become normal that binds this informal group together more than anything else.

ICE flight tracking is not without its personal risks, either. Kris Olsson, a flight tracker from Ann Arbor, describes a run-in she and her husband had with immigration officials after attempting to leave the Willow Run Airport where they’d been photographing planes for the day. As they headed down the service road adjacent to the airport, they noticed four unmarked vans attempting to block their path. Through a gap in the road, the couple was able to squeeze by, but they were quickly followed by one of the vans. The van tailed them around Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor as they drove for miles aimlessly, until they finally parked at a grocery store near their house and waited for hours for the van to leave. Olsson says that although she and her husband now often feel paranoid when they leave their house, they have no plans to stop ICE flight tracking any time soon.

Before the meeting ends, Toby shares one last thought. “What I've been amazed at in this group is people's willingness and ability to take risks,” he says. “It’s a sense of ‘I'm willing to stand up and be photographed by ICE and have my name in their database. I don’t give a shit. I’m just going to do this.’ That commitment to doing something, that’s not ideological. It’s a moral sense, I believe.”

text:
The Delaware County nurse who was arrested by ICE as she took her 3-year-old son to Disneyland last month faced her first agency check-in on Thursday ― emerging free and able to go home after three hours.

Friends and family had worried ICE would rearrest Monica Ryadi, 30, when she presented herself, despite a federal magistrate judge having earlier ordered her freed from detention. She continues to have to wear an ankle monitor to track her movements.

“I’m glad it didn’t go the way I thought it was going to go,” a tired Ryadi said afterward. “I thought I was going to be redetained.”

Amid President Donald Trump’s push for mass deportations, immigrants who long thought they were safe from enforcement are suddenly at risk. ICE has increasingly taken people into custody at what were supposed to be routine check-ins, meetings that immigrants have little choice but to attend, as skipping a required appointment can itself be grounds for deportation.

Ryadi arrived at the main ICE headquarters in Center City shortly before 8 a.m., supported by about 20 friends, family members, clergy, community members, immigration activists ― and Democratic U.S. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, who called Ryadi’s arrest “absolutely unforgivable.”

A nun laid hands on Ryadi and prayed for her. Another person held a sign that said, “Stand with Monica! Our nurse and neighbor.”

Ryadi’s attorney, Eric Rosenfeld, said early Thursday morning he had received conflicting messages from the agency, one directing Ryadi to the headquarters at Eighth and Cherry Streets, and a second telling her to go to an office on Chestnut Street that handles intensive-supervision appearances.

After clarification, Ryadi went to the second office, where she was escorted inside by Rosenfeld and Scanlon, and accompanied by her husband, Steven Sary, 35, and their son, Luca.

Ryadi said afterward that she was overwhelmed and grateful for the support of so many people. Her husband said he was frustrated that his wife continues to be tracked by ICE.

“Why does she need the ankle monitor?” he said. “She’s not a criminal. Where is she going to go? We have no reason to run.”

Ryadi came lawfully to the U.S. at age 9, grew up attending Philadelphia schools, and continues to live here legally under a grant of what is called withholding of removal.

On Sept. 15, the family had barely stepped off a plane at Los Angeles International Airport when they were surrounded by four or five men in street clothes who said they were ICE agents, flashed a badge, and snapped Ryadi into handcuffs.

“It felt like I was kidnapped,” Ryadi told The Inquirer at the time. “I kept saying, ‘I’m legal, I’m a legal immigrant.’”

She and her husband were taking their son to the West Coast theme park so he could meet his favorite Cars movie characters and visit the Cars Land attraction there.

Ryadi spent 15 days in custody at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in California before being ordered released. Her husband and son flew to her immediately, and the family reunited at the Los Angeles hotel they had booked when they planned to visit Disneyland.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately reply to a request for comment on Thursday.

Homeland Security earlier said that Ryadi was “an illegal alien” who was taken into custody “during a targeted enforcement operation at Los Angeles International Airport.”

DHS said she entered the U.S. legally in 2005 but “overstayed her welcome.” An immigration judge issued a deportation order in 2010, DHS said, although the agency did not note that such an order is a standard part of receiving permission to stay, work, and live in the U.S. under a grant of withholding of removal.

Ryadi was brought to this country as a child, by parents fleeing religious persecution in Indonesia.

They entered on legal visas in 2005, and five years later were officially granted withholding. That is where an immigration court judge agrees that deporting someone to their homeland could get them hurt or killed.

It is similar to asylum, though more limited. The key difference is that under withholding, the federal government retains the right to deport someone if it can find a third country willing to take them. Withholding does not include a path to citizenship.

Traditionally, people who gained that relief were left alone.

Now that has changed, as the Trump administration takes a new, hard view ― seeing those who have withholding, even people like Ryadi who have lived here for decades, as candidates for deportation. Some immigrants are held in ICE detention for months while the administration tries to find a foreign government to accept them.

Attorney Rosenfeld has noted that Ryadi is a healthcare professional, employed at Riddle Hospital in Media, a taxpayer, the spouse of a U.S. citizen, and the mother of a citizen son. She grew up in the United States with government permission and has work authorization, a REAL ID, and a Social Security number.

The couple has arranged their lives around their son, setting schedules so one parent is always home with him. Ryadi works weekends at the hospital while her husband works Monday to Friday as a UPS truck driver.

Rosenfeld said he plans to file petitions in federal court and immigration court to try to secure Ryadi’s safety and residency. He had argued on Thursday that Ryadi should not be made to wear an ankle monitor, and hopes to have it removed or replaced with a less uncomfortable device soon.

WASHINGTON STATE — A new University of Washington Center for Human Rights report says that Washington Department of Licensing data access was tied to hundreds of immigration arrests during street and vehicle-related stops.

The report, Stopping the DMV to DHS Data Pipeline , compared Washington with Maryland, Minnesota and New York on efforts to limit federal access to DOL data. Angelina Godoy, the report’s principal author, tells Nonstop Local that they've confirmed 356 arrests as of this week where an immigration arrest on a street, parking lot or other vehicle-related stop was preceded by a query through the DOL-related data pathway.

Those four main pathways are described as the DOL database, Nlets, data brokers and local and state agencies. Godoy clarifies that the way they're being accessed is illegal.

“So just to be clear. State law doesn't prohibit Ice or CBP from gaining access to, or from seeking access, rather to the Dol database, but it prohibits the Dol from releasing that information to them in cases that are civil immigration enforcement, not in cases where there's a criminal issue,” Godoy said.

Those arrests came from a variety of counties, including some in southeastern Washington. The report also highlighted a number suggestions to help curtail access, including new strongly written laws, a private right to action, better transparency and action aimed at all four pathways.

“This is not a time for careful analysis over the course of the next five years. It's a time for action now to defend Washingtonians core civil rights. We have students afraid to go to school, families afraid to go get food, people unable to go to work. As a result of the fear that has been unleashed by these tactics being used indiscriminately,” Godoy said.

Gov. Ferguson’s office responded to a request for comment and said Washington had taken steps to protect residents’ private information in a quote:

“Washington is a national leader on protecting the private information of our residents. My administration has taken multiple actions to adapt to a Trump Administration that is intent on misusing law enforcement agencies to further the president's cruel immigration agenda,” the governor’s office said.

The governor’s office also provided these statistics saying the Washington State Patrol blocked 174,349 search attempts from federal organizations between November of 2025 and October of this year. It also said Washington state had blocked Driver and Plate Search access for ICE and HSI as well as NLETS searches of DOL data from ICE.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- Reports of increased Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity across the Central Valley in recent weeks have sparked fear and concern among many local families, according to Bishop Joseph Brennan of the Diocese of Fresno.

Brennan said he has heard stories firsthand from pastors and parishioners affected by recent immigration enforcement activity.

"Here in the city of Fresno, at least three of our parishioners have been detained. One of whom is a mom and a grandma and been here for years and we don't even know where she is," Brennan said.

He said it has been difficult to hear what families are experiencing and encouraged community members to support one another.

"They have each other and they have us," Brennan said.

In a public letter released Wednesday, Brennan addressed what he described as unrest, anxiety and fear within the community.

The letter states: "Our Church teaches that every human person possesses an inherent dignity. This dignity is not granted by governments, economic status, citizenship, or legal documentation. It is given by God."

Brennan said the Diocese of Fresno has seen ICE agents near churches but not on church grounds. According to the Department of Homeland Security, ICE agents have the authority to enter places of worship and make arrests.

He said he has encouraged pastors to make some changes, including moving religious education programs online.

"We are still going to have the mass schedule. If people do not show up because of fear, I encourage my pastors to take that with absolute pastoral care," Brennan said.

Brennan also called for immigration reform.

"There has to be some provision for people who have been here for years and who have lived a decent and good life whose only infraction was crossing the border maybe 20 years ago," he said.

Action News said it has reached out to ICE multiple times regarding recent activity across Central California. The agency said it cannot disclose or discuss its law enforcement operations and added that the Department of Homeland Security enforces the nation's laws every day.

title: The Constitution has the last word – for now | Mail & Guardian
description:
The long-awaited judgment held that asylum seekers’ claims should be assessed on their merits rather than treating irregular entry as an absolute barrier to the asylum system.
The frustrations have since entered public policy debates.
As such, the judiciary can invalidate any public policy or government action that conflicts with the principles of a constitutional democracy.
Under section 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, the Constitution is the supreme law of the country.
However, if most South Africans believe that constitutional supremacy has become too restrictive of their public demands, the Constitution allows for amendments.
text:
Amid the ongoing immigration uncertainty and instability in South Africa, the country is once again confronted with an uncomfortable question: Who gets to have the final say on immigration policy: the elected government that represents the people or the courts, which are the custodians of the Constitution? This question has become relevant, particularly after the Constitutional Court ruling in Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town versus the Minister of Home Affairs on 7 July 2026.

As the highest court in the country, the judgment declared certain provisions of the regulations governing the Refugees Act unconstitutional.

At its core, the judgment held that certain provisions could prevent foreign individuals in the country from accessing the asylum system, primarily because of procedural failures, such as entering South Africa irregularly.

The long-awaited judgment held that asylum seekers’ claims should be assessed on their merits rather than treating irregular entry as an absolute barrier to the asylum system.

From a legal perspective, the judgment is significant.

Politically, however, it exposes deeper tension in South Africa’s constitutional democracy.

In recent months, South Africans, mobilised by civil organisations and anti-immigration movements, including March and March and Operation Dudula, have expressed frustration about the influx of undocumented migration, pressure on public services, rising unemployment and competition for limited economic opportunities. The frustrations have since entered public policy debates.

However, constitutional supremacy does not operate on majority rule alone. In South Africa, the executive and parliament are compelled to respond to public demands. But public policy remains subject to constitutional review. As such, the judiciary can invalidate any public policy or government action that conflicts with the principles of a constitutional democracy.

A difficulty in a constitutional democracy is that the majority can win elections but that does not automatically mean it will prevail in every constitutional argument.

In this regard, Lekaba and Motloung (2025) offer an important perspective on this tension. They describe constitutionalism as a central feature of South Africa’s democracy. Their analysis demonstrates that the supremacy of the Constitution does not operate in a political vacuum; rather, it exists alongside growing public dissatisfaction with political institutions and therefore creates demands for fundamental changes.

The frustrations over immigration clearly highlight the conundrum. For many South Africans, the debate on immigration is not just a legal debate, especially for those who live in townships, rural areas and semi-urban areas. It is an everyday reality. It raises concerns about congested public facilities, informal businesses, housing, employment, crime and the ability of the state to control its borders.

Whether these claims are legally correct is a separate matter. What cannot be ignored is that immigration has become a powerful driver of political mobilisation and, to a larger extent, political participation.

As a result, the public frustrations have become visible on the streets and across online platforms.

From 5 to 8 October 2026, anti-immigration protests in Durban, Soweto, Pretoria West and other locations across the country erupted, with protesters blocking foreigners seeking access to refugee centres to have their asylum claims assessed.

This comes after the department of home affairs (DHA) was forced to comply with the ruling issued by the Constitutional Court allowing foreign nationals to apply for asylum.

However, the protests in Durban and Soweto escalated into violence, with multiple vehicles set alight and foreign-owned shops looted.

The protests are directly linked to the directive issued by the DHA.

Although protesters are demanding stricter action against the influx of undocumented foreign nationals, there is no excuse for violence.

The legitimate concerns behind the protests, however, should be treated as a warning that the state must not ignore.

The heightened protests bring debates on constitutional supremacy out of academic discussions and courtrooms and into communities and the streets, where immigration has become a contested socio-political issue.

For protesters who believe that the state has for years failed to control its borders, the directive from the DHA may appear to contradict public demands for tighter immigration enforcement.

From this point of view, the decision by the DHA to allow foreigners to access the asylum system can be interpreted as a sign of the government adhering to judicial requirements rather than listening to public demands.

However, the legal distinction between allowing an individual to access the asylum system and granting permission to remain legally in the country remains fundamental.

An application for asylum does not mean the automatic granting of refugee status, citizenship or permanent residence. As such, any interpretation suggesting otherwise should be treated as misinformation or disinformation.

Instead, the ruling by the Constitutional Court should be inter-preted as a requirement to protect access to the asylum system for foreign nationals.

In this regard, concerns arise when access to the asylum system is viewed as evidence of a weak immigration policy supported by constitutional requirements.

This is exactly where constitutional supremacy and public demand pro-duce democratic tension.

Under section 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, the Constitution is the supreme law of the country. Government decisions must therefore always comply with the Constitution.

Even though citizens can exercise their political power by voting for a government that advocates for their interests, that government’s policies will still be subject to constitutional review.

This creates a dilemma for a constitutional democracy.

On one hand, citizens have the right to demand tighter immigration management policies and can also hold elected representatives accountable.

On the other hand, the judiciary, led by the Constitutional Court, has the responsibility to protect constitutional rights.

These rights apply to citizens and non-citizens alike. When it comes to politically sensitive issues such as the immigration debate, the dilemma can produce conflicts, particularly when judicial decisions are perceived to run counter to public demands.

However, if most South Africans believe that constitutional supremacy has become too restrictive of their public demands, the Constitution allows for amendments. As such, an honest answer to the question posed at the beginning of this opinion piece is that the Constitution does have the final say but a Constitution that citizens believe is working against them will not remain supreme for long.

As a result, necessary changes should be made to suit lived realities. Until then, the Constitution, as it stands, remains supreme and the courts of the land have the power to agree or disagree, even if a significant majority of the public would prefer otherwise.

title: Love Field deportation, ICE 'shuffle flights' have ended - Dallas Observer
description:

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson did not say whether Fort Worth would be the new base for ICE Air in North Texas.

text:
ICE deportation and domestic “shuffle” flights have ended at Love Field, activists announced Wednesday.

For months, organizers operating under the banner of No Love For ICE Air have witnessed and documented hundreds of individuals, often shackled, being loaded onto planes at private terminals at the city-owned airport. Organizers staged multiple protests, and at the Cathedral of Hope Wednesday morning, they said their efforts paid off.

No flights have been observed since a final boarding on Sept. 29, Lanie Olmo, an organizer with No Love for ICE Air and the Democratic Socialists of America, said. Love Field spokesperson Lauren Rounds confirmed to the Observer Tuesday that Signature Aviation, the fixed-base operator (FBO) that has serviced the flights since late June, told the city that operations have ended, though she could not offer more details. Atlantic Aviation, a Plano-based FBO, previously serviced the flights.

“We believe this change is permanent, but we will remain vigilant if Signature or Atlantic Aviation decides to do a contract with Ice Air; we will be back because this fight is not over,” Olmo said. “The fight is not over; it is only moved.”

Activists say the flights have been redirected to Fort Worth’s Alliance Airport, another city-owned airfield. Jason Meyer, an airport spokesperson, said officials have no control over federal flight activity and directed the Observer to the Department of Homeland Security for more information. In a statement, a DHS spokesperson did not say whether Fort Worth would be the new base for ICE Air in North Texas.

“For operational security reasons, ICE does not discuss or confirm specific ICE Air operating locations, flight schedules, passenger totals or other operational details,” the statement reads. “ICE transportation operations are driven by operational needs, safety, security, geography and the need to move individuals in custody in a controlled and humane manner. ICE continually evaluates available ground and air transportation options to meet mission requirements efficiently, safely and responsibly.

Olmo said they have personally observed 46 domestic “shuffle flights” entering or leaving FBO terminals since May, which she estimated transported roughly 2,606 individuals. They have also observed and tracked an additional 12 flights destined for international airports, suggesting deportation operations, with an estimated 1,166 individuals boarded on the planes, Olmo said, adding that the estimates were likely undercounts. According to Human Rights First, 15 flights took place at Love Field in 2024.

“The scale of what has been normalized here in just two years is staggering,” Olmo said. “We have video and photo evidence documenting nearly 3,500 of these detained individuals, and they are not statistics to us. We looked at their faces. We watched them walk across that tarmac, and what we saw made us sick.”

Observers have frequently warned about shuffle flights specifically, which they say can be used to skirt the legal process and move detainees between holding facilities in states with especially long backlogs for immigration hearings, such as Texas.

John Putnam, another lead organizer with No Love For ICE Air and El Movimiento, said they had seen what appeared to be young adults and pregnant women being loaded onto planes.

‘We are not done’

This isn’t the first time the group has touted a victory in its pressure campaign against ICE and the FBOs that provide hangar space and refueling services for chartered flights. In July, after ICE-tied flights shifted from Atlantic Aviation to Signature’s terminal, they said their “target the money” approach had paid off.

Dallas officials have insisted the city has no authority to stop or regulate federal flight activity at the airport, a claim a local aviation attorney said was accurate in a prior interview with the Observer. Olmo said the move likely stemmed from Signature Aviation’s cancellation of a contract, which did not respond to a request for comment.

Emails obtained by The Dallas Morning News through an open records request confirmed that Love Field officials knew about the flights in July. In one email, Signature Aviation Love Field GM Brett Langsdorf requested permission to install black mesh fencing around the terminal to avoid “further media scrutiny.” The company’s request was denied, although records show high-ranking employees discussing ways to make the operation more discreet.

Even if the city didn’t decide to host operations or end the flights, Putnam said he was angry with local leaders for their silence on the issue.

“I’m not even mad at the conservative ones,” Putnam said. “I’m mad at the ones that say that they care about immigrants or that they’re progressive.”

Olmo said they are in contact with Fort Worth organizers to continue monitoring the activity in Tarrant County.

“We won something very real today,” Olmo said. “But as I said, we are not done.”

text:
Federal investigators in Minnesota abruptly stopped sharing evidence last month with state authorities investigating the fatal ICE shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

The move — which could hamper the state’s probe of the two killings by ICE agents — is the latest in a series of reversals that have frustrated Minnesota officials, with federal authorities repeatedly cooperating with state and local investigators before suddenly changing course and cutting off cooperation days, or even hours later.

Minnesota investigators said in court filings Tuesday that say the Justice Department still has not turned over key evidence to local authorities, including a statement by one of the officers who shot Pretti, a crucial piece of evidence as the Hennepin County attorney investigates the killing.

State investigators are also now blocked from accessing the cellphone of the agent who fatally shot Good, her clothing, the firearms used to shoot Pretti, the gun Pretti possessed, and other physical evidence from the scene of Pretti’s shooting, such as projectiles and shell casings, according to a sworn statement from Drew Evans, superintendent of Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA.)

The state of Minnesota investigators are also seeking evidence in the non-fatal shooting of Venezuelan immigrant Julio Sosa-Celis. The ICE officer, Christian Castro, faces state and federal charges related to the shooting and investigation.

Minnesota investigative authorities are still battling the Justice Department in federal court in Washington, DC, for access to the evidence needed to continue their investigations.

CNN has reached out to the Justice Department and the Minnesota US attorney’s office for comment.

Inconsistent sharing of evidence

The sudden change in DOJ’s posture came after a three-week period beginning in late June when the US attorney’s office for Minnesota and the BCA, the state’s lead investigative agency, negotiated an agreement to share evidence in the shootings.

According to the court records filed Tuesday, federal law enforcement provided evidence including Good’s vehicle, the gun used to shoot her, body-worn camera footage, officer statements, and other evidence. The Minnesota investigators also shared evidence its agents collected with federal agents.

The following month, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, thanked federal prosecutors at a press conference for the evidence sharing. At the time, Moriarty believed all the evidence in the cases had been shared with her office or would be soon.

Within days of the press conference, federal officials in Minnesota stopped cooperating with local authorities — and offered no explanation, the state said in their filings.

According to Tuesday’s filings, Moriarty’s team later discovered key evidence had not been shared.

Moriarty said in a sworn statement that she repeatedly reached out to Daniel Rosen, the US attorney for Minnesota, to resume evidence-sharing. Rosen told Moriarty several times his office was “pausing” cooperation but was “optimistic” that more information could be shared “soon.”

But, on September 10, Rosen informed Moriarty that his office would stop sharing evidence “indefinitely,” citing “challenges with D.C.”

Moriarty said in her statement that she “was left with the understanding” that federal authorities would not share any additional evidence with state and local investigators “unless and until there was a change in policy on that sharing coming out of Washington D.C.”

Moriarty acknowledged a notable distinction in the otherwise normal working relationship between federal and local law enforcement.

“Indeed, in all other matters including complex homicide cases, mass shootings, drug and gun cases, and many other types of cases, collaboration and information sharing with federal officials continues as normal,” Moriarty wrote. “The pause on information sharing is unique to these matters.”

text:
NEW YORK — A man who was shot by federal immigration officers in New York had his first hearing before an immigration judge Thursday, appearing remotely via video livestream from the federal jail where his lawyers say he is being held in solitary confinement.

Oscar Belgal, 28, barely spoke during the brief court session. His injury from the shooting wasn't apparent on the video feed, but his lawyers say he needs surgery to remove a bullet lodged in the back of his neck.

Belgal, a native of the Dominican Republic, tried to say something to the judge about his living conditions at the jail, but his lawyer advised him against it and cut him off.

Karene Brown, of the Legal Aid Society, said Belgal has been on 24-hour lockdown at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn with no access to a phone to speak with his family.

She told Judge Dara Reid that she has asked Immigration and Customs Enforcement to move him from solitary confinement but it has so far not honored the request. Reid said she has no say in where he's placed within the facility — the same jail holding former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

ICE officers confronted Belgal on Oct. 8 while he was trying to find a parking spot after picking his son up from school. The boy, age 5, was in the car when an ICE officer ran up and smashed one of the car windows.

In a court filing Wednesday, Belgal's lawyers said the ICE officer then fired several shots into the vehicle as Belgal attempted to drive away. The officers never identified themselves and wore masks and civilian clothes, the lawyers said.

Department of Homeland Security officials maintain the officers believed their lives were in danger and opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.

New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn't conclusively show how the shooting happened.

Belgal's next immigration court hearing is Oct. 29. His lawyers have also filed a petition in federal court seeking his release.

text:
Atlanta

‘Deepening Our Moral Witness’: A call to support immigrant families, communities

By NATALIA DURON | Published October 15, 2026 | En Español

KNOXVILLE, Tenn.—Parents are afraid to drive to work and children listen for a knock at the door. Families worry that a loved one may leave home and never return.

Those fears are reaching Catholic communities across the Southern region in the United States, said church leaders on Sept. 30 at the regional gathering, “Deepening Our Moral Witness.”

Nearly 200 people gathered in Knoxville to confront the effects of immigration enforcement and organize a plan rooted in solidarity with migrants.

The conference invited diocesan leaders and communicators, including bishops, clergy, religious sisters, Catholic ministry leaders, communication directors, journalists and community partners from across the region to discuss how the Church can better respond to the fear affecting families.

Organized by Hope Border Institute, the Diocese of Knoxville, the Diocese of Lexington and the Center for Migration Studies of New York, the day included discussions on Catholic social teaching, Hispanic ministry, communications, parish planning and Mass.

“The church stands with families who are afraid,” said Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, during a press conference at the Cathedral of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus. “The church affirms the God-given dignity of every person. And the church is calling on public leaders for meaningful immigration reforms that respond to that dignity, that respond to the contributions of migrants.”

“Parents think twice before driving to work, going to Mass, picking kids up from school, children are listening for a knock at the door,” Corbett said. “These aren’t strangers. They’re parishioners, co-workers and neighbors.”

Participating dioceses included the Archdiocese of Atlanta; Archdiocese of Louisville, Kentucky; Diocese of Charleston, South Carolina; Diocese of Memphis, Tennessee; Diocese of Nashville, Tennessee; Diocese of Owensboro, Kentucky; Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston, West Virginia; and the Episcopal Diocese of East Tennessee.

Standing with immigrant communities

The day began with a presentation on the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops’ “You Are Not Alone” campaign, which seeks to help the Church accompany immigrant communities affected by immigration enforcement.

Corbett then turned to Catholic social teaching on migration, emphasizing that migration is not separate from the Church’s identity or mission. He pointed to “Strangers No Longer: Together on the Journey of Hope,” a 2003 pastoral letter issued jointly by Catholic bishops in the U.S. and Mexico.

The letter outlines principles that include the right to remain in one’s homeland when possible, the right to migrate when basic needs cannot be met, the right of nations to regulate their borders humanely, the protection of refugees and asylum-seekers and respect for the dignity and human rights of all migrants.

“A litmus test for social justice today is the treatment of migrants,” Corbett said during his session.

The discussion emphasized that the Church could recognize a government’s responsibility to regulate its borders while also insisting that immigration policies respect human dignity. Those principles, Corbett said, cannot be separated.

That responsibility, he shared, extends beyond public statements. It requires accompanying families, protecting vulnerable people, organizing communities and advocating for policies that respect the dignity of every person.

Parishes on the front lines

A session on Hispanic ministry explored how dioceses and parishes can turn that responsibility into practical support for immigrant families.

Blanca Primm, director of Hispanic Ministry for the Diocese of Knoxville, discussed efforts to connect parish leaders with community organizations and public officials, share families’ stories and accompany people to court hearings.

Deacon Chris Gutiérrez, director of Hispanic and Latino Ministry for the Diocese of Owensboro, emphasized the importance of maintaining contact with people in detention.

Elizabeth Elfers of Christ the King Church in Nashville urged others to make connections with nonprofit organizations and educate parish communities about Catholic teaching on immigration.

These efforts reflect the role parishes can play in supporting people who may be afraid to seek help or uncertain about where to turn.

During a press conference held before the noon Mass, Bishop Mark Beckman of Knoxville called for advocacy.

“We have a responsibility to care for the dignity of each and every human person and to respect the rights and due process that are due to citizens and anyone who lives on U.S. soil,” Bishop Beckman said.

Yuri Cunza, president and CEO of the Nashville Area Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, described the impact on businesses with fewer customers, employers whose workers are afraid to leave home and the wider economic effects of immigration enforcement.

“Because behind every economic number is a person,” Cunza said. “Behind every worker is a family. And behind every immigration case is a human story.”

Bishop Brian Cole of the Episcopal Diocese of East Tennessee, who joined the Catholic leaders at the press conference, likewise emphasized that welcoming migrants is rooted in Christian faith.

“As Christians, we are called to welcome the migrant and the stranger,” he said. “We are all living in a time of fear and chaos and brutality.”

Bishop John Stowe of Lexington urged the Church to stand directly alongside immigrants rather than speak about their troubles from afar.

“Not adjacent to the suffering, not issuing statements about it from a safe distance, but right in the midst and in solidarity with immigrants and migrants,” he said.

Bishop Stowe described families who fear that a parent may not return from their job or that a child may be left waiting for someone who never comes home.

“Migrants and refugees are not an issue, are not a problem to be solved, and not a population to be managed,” he said. “They are members of the one human family.”

When asked how Catholics can help parishioners understand immigration as a pro-life issue, Bishop Stowe said the Church’s defense of life must include every person, regardless of immigration status.

“Pro-life begins with understanding that each person made in the image and likeness of God is given inalienable rights,” he said. “That doesn’t require documents. That doesn’t require papers.”

To be pro-life, Bishop Stowe said, is to affirm not only the unborn child but also life at every stage and each person’s right to live and flourish.

Communicating with shared values

Afternoon sessions focused on how dioceses and parishes can communicate about migration safely and plan an appropriate response.

Astrid Liden, communications officer for the Hope Border Institute, encouraged participants to approach conversations about immigration by starting with shared values rather than statistics alone.

The Church already has guidance from the pope, bishops and Catholic teaching, she said, including an emphasis on respecting life. The challenge is applying those principles in everyday conversations, especially when immigration has divided families and communities, she said.

Rather than beginning with numbers or descriptions of the most disturbing events, Liden encouraged Catholics to start with values people can recognize, which is the desire to keep families together and the belief that every person has dignity.

“We have to start from common ground,” she said. “And how do we start there? By using the values we share as people and the values we have as Catholics, which reflect the teachings of the Church.”

The goal is not simply to change opinions, she said, but to help people understand that immigration is not an issue affecting only immigrant communities, but also the Church and the country, she shared.

“Take a step back and realize that, maybe your parish isn’t affected, but your archdiocese is,” she said.

Parishioners can stay informed about what is happening in their communities, learn what resources their diocese already offers, and pray and discern how they can help, Liden said. Possible steps include sharing information with parishioners, speaking with a pastor, starting a parish discussion group or creating a fund to assist families in need.

“The Church can contribute a narrative of hope amid the terrible things immigrant communities are experiencing,” she said. “This cannot be done individually. It cannot be done alone.”

The wider impact

During a panel discussion, Archbishop Gregory J. Hartmayer, OFM Conv., connected the discussion to the contributions of immigrants throughout Georgia.

Archbishop Hartmayer, who previously served as bishop of Savannah, said the state’s dioceses differ in their needs and circumstances, but immigrant communities are an important part of life across Georgia.

He pointed particularly to agricultural workers in southern Georgia, where migrant labor helps sustain the production of fruits and vegetables.

“If the migrant workers weren’t there, economically, there would be a tremendous hit to the state and to the global economic area,” he said.

Archbishop Hartmayer also raised concerns about the consequences of delays in renewing work permits and visas. When people are forced to leave the country while waiting for their paperwork to be processed, families can lose their income, struggle to pay mortgages and face separation.

“It’s just making people’s lives miserable,” he said. “There’s no simple answer, but what we’re going with right now is not an answer.”

The final sessions of the gathering focused on planning next steps within dioceses and parishes. The aim was to move beyond understanding the challenges facing immigrant communities and toward discerning how the Church can respond together.

For Bishop Beckman, that work requires a sustained commitment rather than a single day of discussion.

“The work of building a civilization of love does not happen overnight,” he said during the press conference. “This is an ongoing journey.”

text:
This Friday, American Oversight and the American Historical Association (AHA) will urge the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to uphold a court order the groups secured requiring White House officials to comply with the Presidential Records Act (PRA). Ahead of oral arguments in the Trump administration’s appeal, the groups released the following statements:

Chioma Chukwu, Executive Director of American Oversight:

“Friday’s argument comes down to a simple question: Is the president above the law? For nearly 50 years, every administration of both parties has been bound by the Presidential Records Act, the law Congress passed after Watergate to make clear that presidential records belong to the American people, not to any one president. If the Trump administration can stop following the law, they can rewrite history to cover up corruption and avoid accountability.

“The Trump administration has already struck out once in court, and the Supreme Court rejected nearly identical arguments decades ago. Yet the administration keeps pressing for a power no president has ever had: the ability to defy a congressionally passed law on what will be preserved, to control what the public will know about how this president used or abused his power.

“Right now, the court’s order is all that stands in the way. If it falls, the court-ordered requirement to preserve this White House’s records ends immediately. Records that are destroyed are gone for good. We are asking the appeals court to uphold that order, because the historical record of the presidency belongs to the American people. Our democracy depends on it.”

Dr. Sarah Weicksel, Executive Director of the American Historical Association:

“Every time a record is destroyed, a piece of history is lost. We lose the ability to consult historical evidence, to fact-check, to assess one version of events over another. And that is only part of what is lost if the White House is not required to preserve records.”

“The loss of the historical record would prevent historians from understanding and contextualizing the decisions and actions of a presidential administration. What is ultimately at stake in this case is the ability of Americans to access the full documentary record of their history—something that is essential in a democracy.”

Friday’s arguments center on a May 20, 2026, order from Judge John D. Bates of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, who found the groups were likely to succeed in showing that the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) was wrong to declare the PRA unconstitutional. The injunction requires the White House Office, the National Security Council, the U.S. DOGE Service, and advisors to the president to comply in full with the PRA — including preserving all presidential and vice presidential records and refraining from using text or ephemeral messaging accounts for official business without copying an official account.

Judge Bates opened his ruling by quoting George Orwell: “Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past.”

The dispute traces back to an April 1, 2026, OLC opinion that declared the PRA unconstitutional and advised President Trump that he “need not further comply” with its requirements. The next day, the White House Counsel’s Office issued guidance directing White House staff to follow that opinion — making record preservation voluntary rather than mandatory, and specifically instructing staff not to preserve text messages except in narrow circumstances.

American Oversight and AHA filed suit days later, warning that the OLC opinion could jeopardize public access to hundreds of millions of presidential records, including from prior administrations. Legal experts and historians warned that applying the opinion could block access to more than 700 million White House emails alone. The groups sought emergency relief after the administration refused to commit to preserving records — including those created on personal devices or sent through encrypted messaging apps — while the case proceeded.

On appeal, the Trump administration’s sole argument is that the PRA is facially unconstitutional in its entirety. In their response brief, American Oversight and AHA — along with Freedom of the Press Foundation and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) — argue that the Trump administration’s appeal fails at the threshold.

They note the administration has not shown that the PRA is unconstitutional in every one of its applications, and it concedes that the law serves legitimate purposes in other contexts. On the merits, the brief argues that the Constitution’s Property Clause and Necessary and Proper Clause each independently give Congress authority to require the preservation of presidential records, and notes that the Supreme Court rejected nearly identical arguments when it upheld the PRA’s Watergate-era predecessor in Nixon v. Administrator of General Services. The brief also notes that in nearly 50 years, the administration has not identified a single instance in which the PRA actually impeded a president’s ability to do the job.

The groups’ position is backed by friend-of-the-court briefs from 106 members of Congress, 25 former senior national security officials who served under presidents of both parties, and seven former senior leaders of the National Archives and Records Administration, including former archivists of the United States. Together, the briefs argue that the PRA imposes minimal burden on the presidency, protects a sitting president’s access to a predecessor’s national security records, and reflects a deliberate balance Congress struck after Watergate.

The administration’s position also threatens access to records from Trump’s first term, which became eligible for public access under the PRA on Jan. 20, 2026, and for which American Oversight filed a sweeping set of Freedom of Information Act requests that same day.

Trump’s handling of records from that term has already drawn scrutiny: the National Archives had to recover records taken to Mar-a-Lago, and then-Special Counsel Jack Smith later brought charges against Trump for unlawfully retaining classified documents. Volume II of Smith’s report on that case remains blocked from public release under a court order that American Oversight is challenging on appeal.

Oral arguments are scheduled for 9:30 a.m. on Friday, Oct. 16, at the E. Barrett Prettyman U.S. Courthouse in Washington, D.C.

text:
A PDF version of this resource is available here.

Introduction

On October 14, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued an interim final rule reducing the time refugees have to respond when U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) initiates the termination of their refugee status. The rule, “Removing 30-Day Refugee Termination Notice,” shortens the response period from 30 days to 10 days and took effect immediately. This substantially reduces the time available to obtain legal representation, gather evidence, and contest the government’s determination before losing refugee status. The rule comes amid the administration’s broader review of refugees admitted under the Biden administration, including people whose applications for lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a “green card,” remain pending. Refugee resettlement organizations and legal advocates have raised concerns that the shorter deadline will make it difficult for affected individuals to meaningfully respond.

When Can Refugee Status Be Terminated?

Refugees generally apply for protection while outside the United States and undergo screening and processing before being admitted through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program. Their admission differs from asylum, which individuals generally seek at the U.S. border or after arriving in the country. Although both forms of protection address persecution, they are governed by distinct procedures. Under section 207(c)(4) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, refugee status may be terminated if the government determines that the individual was not a refugee within the meaning of the law at the time of admission. A subsequent change in conditions in the person’s home country is not, by itself, a basis for terminating refugee status under this provision. Historically, termination of refugee status has been “exceedingly rare.”

Before terminating status, USCIS must provide a written Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) explaining the proposed action. The individual may respond with written evidence, request an interview to present oral testimony, or both. Before the new rule, the regulation provided 30 days to respond. The NOIT is not a termination and the opportunity to respond occurs before any final termination decision by USCIS. The response is not an administrative appeal of an already completed termination of refugee status. That distinction matters because federal regulations do not provide for administrative appeals of USCIS decisions to terminate refugee status, although individuals may subsequently seek alternative protections or relief in immigration court. Recent court rulings suggest that individuals may be able to bring suit in federal court to challenge a USCIS determination that an individual did not qualify as a refugee at the time of admission.

What Does the New Rule Change?

The rule reduces the response period from 30 days to 10 days while retaining the existing grounds for termination and the opportunity to submit evidence or request an interview with USCIS to explain why their status should not be terminated. It does not change the underlying legal standard for deciding whether someone qualified as a refugee. The principal features of the revised process are:

Shorter response period. Refugees have 10 calendar days from service of the notice to submit a response, a reduction from the previous time period of 30 days.

Additional time for mailed notices. Under the applicable service rules, three days are added when the notice is served by mail, producing a 13-day response period. The period runs from the mailing date, not the date the individual receives the notice. A deadline falling on a weekend or federal holiday moves to the next business day.

Continued opportunity to request an interview. Individuals may still submit written evidence, request an interview to give oral testimony supporting their case, or both.

Consequences for failing to respond. Failure to respond within the applicable period allows USCIS to proceed with termination without a rebuttal from the individual. There remains no administrative appeal of a termination decision.

Under the new rules, individuals have an extremely limited timeframe to respond to a NOIT. The timing of service is particularly consequential. Because the deadline for mailed notices begins before delivery, individuals may have less than 10 days after receiving a NOIT to understand the allegations, contact an attorney, and prepare their response. In addition, experts caution that a refugee’s attorney may not automatically receive a copy of the notice, making prompt communication between refugees and their legal representatives especially important.

Who May Be Affected?

The rule applies to individuals who remain in refugee status and have not adjusted to lawful permanent residence, meaning they have not received a green card. It is not limited to a particular nationality or to refugees admitted during the Biden administration, even though DHS’s stated rationale emphasizes admissions during that period. Termination can also affect family members, as a spouse or child whose refugee status derives from the principal refugee may lose that status when the principal’s status is terminated. DHS identified approximately 186,000 refugees admitted during fiscal years 2015 through 2025 who had not adjusted to permanent residence as the maximum population potentially subject to the measure. It is important to note that this number is not a projection of how many people will receive termination notices, lose their status, or be removed – it is simply the larger pool of individuals who could theoretically receive a NOIT. Whether an individual receives a notice depends on USCIS’s review of the facts and circumstances of their case.

The rule does not directly change the procedures governing asylees, humanitarian parolees, Special Immigrant Visa holders, or people whose protection derives from Temporary Protected Status (TPS) rather than refugee status. These distinctions are important for Afghan arrivals, who entered the United States through several different pathways. Afghans admitted as refugees who have not adjusted to permanent residence may be affected, while those admitted through humanitarian parole or as Special Immigrant Visa holders are not covered by this refugee-termination rule solely because of those statuses.

Why Did DHS Issue the Rule?

DHS states that the shorter response period will allow it to act more quickly when it determines that a person was not eligible for refugee status at admission. The administration argues that processing changes during the Biden administration prioritized admission numbers and speed at the expense of adequate screening and eligibility review. Refugee resettlement organizations dispute that characterization, noting that refugees underwent interviews and background checks and received government approval before entering the United States.

The rule follows the administration’s November 2025 directive to review refugees admitted during the Biden administration and place affected pending green card applications on hold. The pause in green card processing in these cases is significant because affected individuals would now be subject to the rule’s shortened response period. Refugee resettlement organizations emphasize that these individuals entered through a government-approved process involving interviews and background checks. They argue that revisiting those determinations should include a realistic opportunity for refugees to obtain counsel and respond to the government’s concerns. As a result, refugees with valid grounds to contest termination stand to lose their refugee status because they cannot secure legal assistance or present supporting evidence in time.

Why Are Advocates Concerned About the Shorter Deadline?

Advocates warn that the shortened deadline could undermine refugees’ due process rights by denying them a meaningful opportunity to obtain counsel, gather evidence, and contest the proposed termination of their status. Preparing a response may require obtaining immigration records, locating documents abroad, translating evidence, and developing declarations addressing the government’s allegations. Refugees may also need to find an attorney after receiving the NOIT. Advocates and refugee resettlement organizations have criticized the rule, warning that the shortened period could undermine refugees’ ability to defend their status. The consequences extend beyond the termination decision itself. Termination of refugee status ends employment authorization associated with that status and can lead to removal proceedings, creating potential disruption for families and employers.

While termination of refugee status may lead to removal proceedings, termination itself is not itself a deportation order. Individuals placed in removal proceedings may be able to seek asylum, withholding of removal, protection under the Convention Against Torture, or other available relief before an immigration judge. Those possibilities are distinct from an administrative appeal of USCIS’s refugee termination decision and depend on the circumstances of the individual case.

What Happens Next?

DHS issued the change as an interim final rule, making it effective before completing the usual notice-and-comment rulemaking process. The Department invoked the Administrative Procedure Act’s “good cause” and foreign affairs exceptions to justify proceeding without advance public comment and without the usual delayed effective date. DHS is accepting comments through November 13, 2026, under docket USCIS-2026-0397, and may revise the policy when issuing a subsequent final rule. However, the shorter response period applies while that comment process is underway.

text:
The arrest of two immigrant advocates by Santa Ana police officers while observing ICE agents near city hall is sparking renewed scrutiny over how cooperative local law enforcement in OC’s only sanctuary city is with federal immigration agents.

It comes roughly a week after another advocate, Jackie Cordova, says she was beaten by federal agents while observing them and detained and as local immigration advocates warn of a 45-day surge in enforcement across Southern California.

According to Santa Ana police, officers arrested Santa Ana residents Madison Crabill, 25, and Adilene Tonoco, 33, on Wednesday for resisting a peace officer, stalking and criminal conspiracy after Santa Ana police received a call for help from off-duty federal agents

Immigrant advocates say the duo was observing the agents and didn’t interfere with them but were ultimately arrested by local police. Meanwhile, police officials say the activists blocked the agents’ vehicle and that the federal agents were worried for their safety.

Melissa Rios, a grassroots community organizer with LUCHA Costa Mesa, who is speaking to the press on behalf of Crabill and Tonoco, says she saw the tail end of the arrest as officers put the organizers in the squad car and towed Tonoco’s car.

“Both women were following an ICE vehicle from an appropriate distance. They remained behind the vehicle, and they weren’t blocking it, and they weren’t interfering with the car’s movement. Eventually, an ICE vehicle stopped near Santa Ana PD headquarters,” said Rios.

“And several police vehicles were already in position. One of the women pulled behind the ICE vehicle and the two Santa Ana PD vehicles pulled behind her as well.”

LUCHA Costa Mesa along with other organizations are holding a news conference in front of the Santa Ana Police Department at 3 p.m. today to demand the release of Crabill and Tonoco.

Rios and an eyewitness, who requested anonymity, are raising concerns about the interaction between Santa Ana police and the federal agents.

“What was particularly concerning, I think, is that the witness observed that the two ICE agents were communicating directly with Santa Ana PD officers, and then I believe the ICE agents received a case number from Santa Ana PD as well,” Rios said.

Rios says that another car was patrolling alongside Crabill and Tonoco, and the arrest seemed targeted towards the two women.

Santa Ana Police Spokeswoman Natalie Garcia said the pair did block the agents’ car and the agents had recognized them from previous federal operations in La Habra that same day and “expressed concerns for their safety.”

“The agents reported that the individuals began following them after they left a federal building in Santa Ana. The individuals later blocked the agents’ vehicle in an alley before continuing to follow them toward the SAPD station. While en route, they reportedly drove erratically and ran two red lights to maintain contact with the agents’ vehicle,” Garcia wrote in a Thursday email to Voice of OC.

“When the agents arrived in front of the station, the individuals parked directly behind them and used a megaphone to yell obscenities at them. SAPD officers responded and detained the two female suspects pending further investigation.”

In a statement after publication, an unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson deferred questions to the police department.

“For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE never discloses or discusses law enforcement operations,” reads the Thursday statement.

How Cooperative is Santa Ana Police With ICE?

The arrest of the two residents is raising concerns from at least two elected officials in Santa Ana on why police officers in OC’s only sanctuary city are helping ICE.

City Councilwoman Jessie Lopez, who is running for state assembly, said she demanded the city manager have the two residents released, adding she is “furious” that police helped ICE again.

“I am 100% against Santa Ana police continuing to support and help ICE in our community, and if they don’t want the public thinking that they do, then they need to stop doing what they’ve been doing,” Lopez said in a Thursday morning phone interview.

“There are other things that Santa Ana Police Department needs to be focused on in our community.”

It’s not the first time Santa Ana Police Officers have responded to a request for help from federal agents.

Earlier this year, Santa Ana police and city executives publicly said they accepted federal calls for assistance at the ICE protests in June 2025, for fear of federal officers bringing out their own reinforcements to deal with protesters.

At those protests, police officers fired hundreds of rounds of bean bags, rubber bullets and threw tear gas at ICE demonstrators over four days – costing the city nearly $400,000.

That policing response has faced ongoing criticism from some residents, a handful of council members including Lopez and one OC Supervisor – calling the officers’ actions excessive.

“I saw it with my own eyes when we were under attack by our own police department. When children in the crowd were being pepper sprayed and these chemicals were being thrown at us, I saw them form a line of defense to protect the federal agents,” Lopez said.

“So, again, why is Santa Ana police responding to calls of federal agents when they know that observing what they are doing is completely legally acceptable and it should not be criminalized?”

After publication of this article, Councilman Johnathan Hernandez said residents have a right to observe what ICE agents and police officers are doing in their community and called for the advocates to be released.

“It’s a legal right that every resident has in the city. It does worry me, and I am concerned that Santa Ana PD is pro-ICE,” Hernandez said in a phone interview.

As a sanctuary city, Hernandez said the arrest is troubling.

“When you see police officers who know we are a sanctuary city who are arresting legal observers, it sends the opposite message to our residents. It sends a message that Santa Ana PD has no regard for people’s protected constitutional rights, and it shows that Santa Ana PD has no regard for the status of a sanctuary city,” he said.

Police officials have repeatedly contended they follow the state law that bars them from assisting federal immigration enforcement and earlier this year officials banned local police officers from moonlighting for ICE and other federal immigration enforcement agencies.

A request to create a notification policy to inform residents about ICE activity in Santa Ana last year was shelved by a majority of city council members despite officials in Anaheim regularly updating residents on enforcement actions on their city website.

Officials in Santa Ana were the first to roll out a legal aid fund to help protect residents from deportation and after immigration enforcement ramped up last year launched an aid fund to help families impacted by ICE raids.

Councilman Ben Vazquez said he was upset the department arrested the women and that they have a right to observe what ICE is doing in the community. The rest of the city council did not respond to requests for comment Thursday.

“It’s just painful to see our ICE watchers going through this, putting in their own time, doing hard work, taking responsibility for their neighbors and families to do this work, and then to be harassed by our own police department-that’s part of a sanctuary city. They were just observing. There was no intent to harm the officers,” Vazquez said in a Thursday phone interview.

“Two young girls with cameras and phones were not intentionally going to harm two armed men.”
