text:
AUSTIN, TEXAS – On Thursday, October 15th, Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas), alongside Representatives Bennie G. Thompson (D-Miss.), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and five other members of Congress held a field hearing to investigate the numerous ICE shootings across Texas, including the recent shooting of Wilber Garcés-Pérez.

Representatives Greg Casar, Bennie G. Thompson, and Pramila Jayapal were joined by Representatives Troy A. Carter, Sr. (LA-02), Lou Correa (CA-46), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), and Al Green (TX-09).

The Members of Congress were joined by witnesses Ms. Rachel Reyes, mother of Ruben Ray Martinez, Kristin Etter, Director of Policy & Legal Services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, Carolina Rivera Nelson, Attorney at the ACLU of Texas, and Danny Woodward, Policy Attorney with Texas Civil Rights Project.

“Texas has become the epicenter of Trump’s deadly deportation machine, so we brought Members of Congress from across the country to Austin to see it firsthand,” said Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas). “ICE shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez, a DoorDash driver and a father, in the back then denied him medical care. They even tried to deport him so he could never speak the truth. Donald Trump's ICE isn't going after the worst of the worst — it's gone after people like Wilber, who have no criminal record. We will fight to hold the perpetrators in this administration accountable, and not provide another dime in funding to this rogue agency."

“Democrats came to Austin today to demand justice and accountability for Wilber Garcés-Pérez and the others that have been shot by immigration agents in Texas. If Republicans refuse to conduct any oversight of the Trump administration, we must do so in their place,” added Congressman Bennie G. Thompson. “What we heard today was powerful and informative. Make no mistake: we will do everything possible to hold this administration accountable for what it is doing. This violence, lawlessness, and chaos in our communities must end.”

“Twenty-five days ago, ICE agents in Austin, Texas shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez in the back. Instead of taking him to the hospital, they locked him up in a detention center and did not allow him to have surgery for 11 days. This is not the most recent shooting by ICE, and is one of nearly a dozen that we know of since Trump returned to office,” said Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal. “ICE is a lawless, rogue agency that is causing generational trauma in communities across the country. House Democrats today are doing the oversight work that Republicans refuse to do — and we will continue to do everything possible to protect our communities from Trump’s mass deportation agenda.”

"The shooting and medical neglect of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez follows the many other cases that have become synonymous with cities being swarmed with masked, armed federal agents and the nation’s dangerous descent into tyranny: Renée Nicole Good, Alex Pretti, Johan Sebastian Guerrero, and too many others. No life is meaningless, and each individual assaulted or killed by our immigration system is someone's child, someone's sibling, someone's parent, and they all still belong here with us,” said Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. “Unless you’re Native American, we all come from somewhere else. The Trump immigration system is structured and staffed as a deportation machine that violates individuals' constitutional rights. Democrats will fight for an immigration system that honors our history and sets forth a reasonable, compassionate path to citizenship."

“President Trump got elected on the promise to go after the “worst of the worst.” Instead, since January, federal immigration agents have detained over 500 U.S. citizens and killed at least three. ICE is arresting people with no criminal record to hit political quotas while cutting training and lowering hiring standards,” said Congressman Lou Correa. “There is an urgent need for major reforms to keep our communities safe from violence. DHS was created to defend Americans against foreign terrorists. Instead, we have permanent residents and American citizens being shot by ICE agents in our streets.”

"In Texas, we have witnessed at least three ICE shootings since this administration began its aggressive, unprecedented enforcement actions,” said Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher. “People across our community in Houston are still reeling from the shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Just last weekend, ICE agents ran over and gravely injured Miguel Parra Hernandez while pursuing someone else. ICE's reckless and brutal actions are not only unprecedented, they're unconstitutional. They are making us less safe, creating fear and danger for immigrants and citizens alike. This Republican-led Congress that has enabled this lawlessness has utterly failed Wilber Garcés-Pérez, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Ruben Ray Martinez, and so many others. All Americans deserve better from our government, and that is why I joined Congressman Casar, Ranking Member Thompson, Congresswoman Jayapal, and my Democratic colleagues in Austin today to hear from some of the many people impacted, learn more, and demonstrate our commitment to bringing justice, accountability, and change.”

“Trump promised to go after the worst of the worst. But judging by what we’re seeing across Texas and the country, that sounds more like ICE’s recruitment strategy. People are being shot, injured, and killed by federal agents operating without basic law enforcement standards or accountability,” said Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia. “In Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed on his way to work. One hundred days later, his family still has no answers. Instead they’ve been met with stonewalling and excuses. These families deserve the truth and justice, and we will not stop fighting until they get both.

“No President is above the law, and no federal agency should be allowed to serve as judge, jury, prosecutor, and executioner while operating with impunity,” said Congressman Al Green. “Under President Trump, ICE has been emboldened to use deadly force against people in our communities while the administration evades transparency and accountability, engaging in a cover-up. These shootings are not isolated incidents. They are part of a deeply troubling pattern of conduct that threatens the constitutional rights and lives of people in this country.”

The Members of Congress’ full remarks can be found here(link is external).

###

Congressman Greg Casar represents Texas’s 35th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives, which runs down I-35 from East Austin to Hays County to the West Side of San Antonio. A labor organizer and son of Mexican immigrants, Casar serves as the Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus for the 119th Congress. He also serves on the Committee on Education and Labor and the Committee on Oversight and Accountability.

description: (The Center Square) – California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the Trump administration's practice of conducting civil immigration enforcement in and around courthouses.
text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta speaks during a news conference, Feb. 18, 2025. Photo: State of California Department of Justice / Used with Permission.

(The Center Square) – California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the Trump administration's practice of conducting civil immigration enforcement in and around courthouses.

The legal challenge marks Bonta's 100th lawsuit against the administration since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, but the White House is pointing to court rulings up holding the administration's immigration enforcement as lawful.

According to the California Department of Justice, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have conducted disruptive and often violent civil immigration enforcement actions at courthouses across the state since the policy was initiated in May 2025. State officials report that witnesses, victims, and survivors of domestic violence increasingly fear appearing in court, creating what the state calls a profound chilling effect that undermines public safety and judicial operations.

“In California, our courthouses aren't proving grounds for unlawful immigration enforcement tactics,” said Bonta at a press conference in Sacramento. “When people come knocking at the court's door, justice should welcome them in with equal access and application regardless of their immigration status.”

Data cited in the lawsuit reveals that the average monthly number of ICE arrests in and around state courthouses spiked by more than 550% in the year following the policy change.

“Immigration arrests at courthouses have been documented in at least 22 California counties, from Los Angeles and San Diego to Shasta, Butte, and Glen, all throughout our state,” said Bonta. “That includes the five largest counties, each home to a significant percentage of non-citizen residents and families of mixed immigration status.”

The White House sharply criticized the litigation, pointing to the administration's legal track record.

"Instead of bragging about filing frivolous lawsuits against the Trump Administration, the California Attorney General should focus on addressing problems in his own state – like the countless criminal illegal aliens extreme Democrats allow to roam free and kill innocent Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told The Center Square in an email Thursday. "The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the Administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions."

Acting ICE Director David Venturella and Secretary of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named in the lawsuit. The Center Square reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, but did not hear back by publication time.

Although a federal court vacated ICE's written directive in late June 2026 in Pablo Sequen v. Albarran, Bonta said enforcement actions have persisted. State records show 34 reported incidents resulting in 30 civil arrests in June 2026, followed by 28 reported incidents and 28 arrests in July, with activity continuing through the summer and fall.

Filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE, Bonta's lawsuit outlines multiple arguments. First, the lawsuit claims the immigration enforcement directive is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because the agency failed to evaluate the directive's chilling effect on access to justice and did not provide a reasoned explanation for removing prior restrictions on courthouse enforcement. Second, Bonta argues that the agency exceeded its statutory authority under the APA, asserting that the Immigration and Nationality Act was enacted against a centuries-old common law privilege barring civil arrests at courthouses — a protection Congress is presumed to have incorporated.

Finally, the lawsuit contends that the directive is contrary to constitutional rights and violates the 10th Amendment by infringing on the state's sovereign power to maintain a judicial system, prosecute crimes and execute core police powers.

Meanwhile, legal defenders of federal policy argue that state powers cannot override federal authority.

Christopher Hajec, deputy general counsel for the Federation for American Immigration Reform, noted that the immunity doctrine protects federal officials performing their duties from state interference. For example, Hajec said that California once arrested a U.S. marshal for murder because of actions he took to protect a Supreme Court justice. The Supreme Court ruled that the prosecution had to be dismissed, because California law could not stop the marshal from doing his job. Pointing to Bonta’s lawsuit, Hajec said California cannot invoke its state powers or property rights to block ICE from doing its job.

"When the federal government comes into a situation anywhere in the United States, federal law is supreme, not that of the state where the activity takes place," Hajec told The Center Square in an email.

"There is no common-law privilege, silently incorporated into the INA against immigration arrest at courthouses," Hajec added.

The old privilege, he said, had the far different purpose of stopping litigants from arresting each other (as then could be done) when they came to a courthouse to have their differences decided.

text:
SANTA FE, N.M. —

Santa Fe County officials confirmed that ICE conducted raids at three or four construction sites in Santa Fe on Tuesday morning, leading to the arrest of at least seven workers.

Gina Auz, a member of Santa Fe Rapid Response, captured video of one raid off of Agua Fria Road in south Santa Fe. Auz said she arrived at the scene shortly after the raid began.

"When you see the families, and when you see the faces of the people over there, you feel like, 'no, it's not right,'" Auz said.

At a city council meeting Tuesday night, Santa Fe County commissioners said ICE agents likely staged at nearby Romero Park before conducting raids at construction sites. On Sep. 30, the county passed an ordinance prohibiting ICE staging on county property, alongside a similar Santa Fe city ordinance the day after. Both ordinances have 90 days to take full effect.

Miles Conway, CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, expressed concern about the emotional impacts of the raids on workers and their families.

"I think I entered that state of grieving, you know -- grieving for workers who are encountering incredibly stressful situations with their families, maybe displaced from their families," he said.

Conway noted that more than 30 percent of the state's construction workforce is foreign-born.

"They're trying to go to work," Conway said. "They're trying to earn a living, support their families and participate in our society in a very beneficial and productive way."

He also highlighted the broader economic consequences of the raids.

"People are not going to work. They're not going to supply houses. They're not going out and buying lunch," he said. "People that don't really have a reason to are laying low."

Conway said the federal government needs to provide clarity about the situation.

"My members are very eager and active and trying to find out information about what exactly is happening," he said. "Is there a targeted campaign right now, or are we just rounding up everybody that has the wrong color skin?"

Auz emphasized the need for community support for immigrant families in Santa Fe.

"Immigrant families in Santa Fe don't have help," she said.

When asked about verifying the legal statuses of construction workers, Conway said all employees are required to present employers with eligible documentation, and it is up to the employer to determine the authenticity of those documents.

KOAT has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment regarding the legal statuses and exact number of individuals arrested. A response is pending.

title: Our Lawsuit Against the Trump Administration's Social Media Surveillance Moves Forward ...
description:
That the surveillance program might affect someone’s immigration proceeding down the line doesn’t turn our lawsuit into a removal challenge.
The court held that the unions alleged concrete injuries, including a chill on members’ speech that is objectively reasonable, not just subjectively felt.
Demanding Social Media Handles Also Causes Harm Under the surveillance program, applicants for certain immigration benefits must disclose all social media handles they have used during the preceding five years and, in some instances, maintain public social media accounts.

The government must now answer our complaint and we will move forward with the discovery process, in which we anticipate getting more information from the government about its surveillance program.
text:
No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S.

Last fall, we sued on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court denied the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a big deal for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning.

Our Lawsuit

Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to broadly surveil the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. The government is targeting a broad range of views, including criticism of the Trump administration; support for Palestine or criticism of Israel; “rationalizing or making light of” Charlie Kirk’s murder; and anything nebulously “hostile” to American culture, founding principles, “traditional American views,” or “our way of life.”

It has paired that surveillance with a public intimidation campaign. High-ranking officials have explicitly threatened to punish noncitizens for their online speech, then followed through with a series of terrifying viewpoint-driven enforcement actions. This has led to a significant chilling effect on speech, not just for noncitizens, but also for their families, coworkers, and friends.

In response, three major labor unions—the United Auto Workers (UAW), the Communications Workers of America (CWA), and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT)—sued the Departments of State and Homeland Security alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The unions are represented by EFF, Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA).

The government moved to dismiss our lawsuit, arguing first that federal immigration law prevents federal district courts from hearing the case, and second, that the unions don’t have “standing” to sue. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York rejected both arguments and allowed the case to proceed. At this stage in the litigation, the court accepted all of the facts in our complaint as true and analyzed the law based on those facts. We will now prove these facts as the case proceeds.

Federal Immigration Law Doesn’t Block Our Lawsuit

The government first argued that the court had no power to hear our case at all. It pointed to three provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) that restrict when federal courts can review immigration matters. The district court disagreed and rejected each provision in turn.

The first provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9), is often called the “zipper clause.” It bars federal courts from hearing challenges that arise from efforts to deport someone, except through review of an individual’s final removal order. The government claimed the zipper clause applies here because our lawsuit is really an effort to stop it from initiating adverse immigration actions.

The district court wholly rejected this argument. Relying on the Second Circuit’s decision in Ozturk v. Hyde, it held that the zipper clause bars only challenges to a particular individual’s removal proceedings, not a lawsuit like ours that challenges the constitutionality of the surveillance program itself. That the surveillance program might affect someone’s immigration proceeding down the line doesn’t turn our lawsuit into a removal challenge.

The court similarly rejected the government’s argument that § 1252(g) and § 1252(f)(1) prevent federal courts from hearing this case. Our suit, the court explained, “challenges the constitutionality of a government policy that is collateral to any active removal proceedings,” so § 1252(g) doesn’t apply. And § 1252(f)(1) only limits what kind of relief a court can give. So while the court may not be able to stop a particular person’s removal proceedings, it can still block “an unlawful surveillance program that suppresses free speech.”

The Unions Have Standing to Sue

To sue in federal court, a plaintiff must show that it has “standing” to bring its claims. This requires a plaintiff to show an “injury in fact” that is, among other things, “concrete.” That’s often a high bar in surveillance cases, where plaintiffs can’t easily see what the government is doing behind the scenes. And the Supreme Court has held that a person’s mere subjective fear of surveillance is too speculative to confer standing.

Even so, our plaintiffs cleared the bar. The court held that the unions alleged concrete injuries, including a chill on members’ speech that is objectively reasonable, not just subjectively felt. It found that the unions had established standing in two ways: “organizational standing,” based on the unions’ own injuries, and “associational standing,” based on injuries the unions’ members have suffered.

Organizational Standing

The court first held that our plaintiffs had successfully alleged an injury to the unions themselves (injury was the only aspect of organizational standing the government disputed). The surveillance program has harmed the unions’ ability to carry out their core responsibilities, including “organizing their members and advocating for the unions’ goals.” The court made two key points:

1. Unions Are Injured When Members Go Silent

As we explained in our complaint, the surveillance program has caused members to step back from union leadership roles; stop participating in union activities online and in person; remove their names from union webpages; and avoid filling out bargaining surveys. Members who might otherwise spread the unions’ message and raise awareness of union issues are staying quiet, hampering the unions’ ability to organize. The court said this amounts to a concrete injury for purposes of standing.

2. Surveillance Doesn’t Need to Target Pro-Union Speech

The court also rejected the government’s claim that members’ retreat from union activities was “essentially an overreaction,” because the surveillance doesn't target pro-union views. The court said this misunderstands the issue: “the question is whether the Government’s conduct would deter a person of ordinary firmness from engaging in protected activity, not whether the specific expression a member forgoes is itself among the viewpoints the Government disfavors.”

Here, the surveillance program monitors noncitizens’ online activity indiscriminately, and members “cannot reliably predict which of their activities will be captured” and attributed to a disfavored viewpoint. What’s more, the court noted, the unions’ organizing often happens alongside the very advocacy the government is alleged to target, “including pro-Palestine and anti-ICE activism on college campuses.” That makes members’ retreat from union activity a foreseeable consequence of the program.

Associational Standing

The court also held that the unions established associational standing to sue on behalf of their members. Of the three requirements for associational standing, the government challenged only two. It argued that members lacked sufficiently concrete injuries to sue in their own right, and that the claims aren’t “germane” to the unions’ purpose.

The court disagreed and found associational standing for every claim but one: members’ right to receive information. That claim survives anyway, because the unions’ organizational standing covers it. Along the way, the court made several important rulings.

1. The Ongoing Surveillance Is a Present Injury

As a threshold matter, the government argued that our case is a “pre-enforcement challenge,” meaning we sued before the government actually punished anyone. That would trigger a different test, and the government argued we failed it because we hadn’t alleged a sufficiently imminent threat of prosecution.

The court disagreed, explaining that “Plaintiffs’ allegations are of an ongoing surveillance program that is actively chilling the speech of their members and otherwise causing harm.” That chilling effect is a First Amendment injury even if there isn’t a direct prohibition on speech. And when government conduct is actively chilling speech right now, a challenge to it isn’t pre-enforcement.

2. Surveillance + Public Threats Reasonably Chills Speech

The court rejected the government’s argument that we alleged only a generalized, subjective, speculative fear of surveillance, explaining that “the chilling effect” of the program can “itself be an injury when the plaintiffs are surveilled.” Here, plaintiffs have alleged that their members are under active surveillance, which has had objective chilling effects on their speech. And the government is targeting certain disfavored viewpoints, making it “viewpoint discrimination” that is “presumptively unconstitutional.”

The chill is also objectively reasonable, the court held, because the government has extensively publicized the surveillance program through public statements and social media posts, making clear that noncitizens who post disfavored views will be targeted for removal. Notably, the court agreed with us that the “threat of adverse immigration consequences, under a government whose harsh immigration crackdowns has been heavily publicized and reported on, is certainly enough to deter a person of ordinary firmness from the exercise of First Amendment rights.” This is a concrete injury sufficient for standing.

3. Demanding Social Media Handles Also Causes Harm

Under the surveillance program, applicants for certain immigration benefits must disclose all social media handles they have used during the preceding five years and, in some instances, maintain public social media accounts. The district court held that this too amounts to a First Amendment injury, undermining the rights to anonymity and freedom of association.

The judge pointed to one CWA member we identified, a lawful permanent resident with a pending naturalization application who is subject to the five-year disclosure requirement. The member has deleted one social media account, set another to private, and removed past posts expressing disfavored views. These allegations, the court said, show an actual and objectively reasonable injury due to the government’s surveillance program.

4. General, Public Threats Can Still Be Coercive

We also argued that the Trump administration is waging a campaign of coercive threats to suppress disfavored speech, which the First Amendment prohibits. The court agreed that this campaign can be an actionable injury of its own.

Notably, the court held that it didn’t matter that the government’s statements were not specifically targeted at certain individuals, and were instead made on social media or to the public. In this case, the court explained, “the number, severity, and high-profile examples of action upon those threats are such that a reasonable person would perceive the communication as coercive.”

That means it’s reasonable that the unions’ members “would, and did, limit their public speech on disfavored viewpoints” in response. That the threats were made to the general public “does not diminish this injury,” as the very purpose of the challenged surveillance program is to intimidate noncitizens into silence.

5. Free Speech is Central to Union Functioning

The court also found that the unions met the second prong of associational standing. It held that the unions’ interests in protecting their members’ rights to speak freely, organize, and advocate, are “germane” to the unions’ missions. The court put it plainly:

The freedom of Plaintiffs’ members to speak, associate, and appear publicly is not incidental to union work, but rather is the mechanism through which unions recruit, organize, communicate, and bargain. A program alleged to silence members and drive them from the unions’ rolls therefore strikes at the unions’ representational function itself.

Next Steps

When the government surveils what people post online and threatens to punish them for their viewpoints, the result is exactly what our clients have experienced. Members have deleted their accounts, scrubbed posts, and withdrawn from union activities.

The government must now answer our complaint and we will move forward with the discovery process, in which we anticipate getting more information from the government about its surveillance program. We look forward to continuing to prove our case.

text:
Weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez has made an accelerated effort to put immigration reform at the forefront of the conversation. She says the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home should worry everyone.

At 4:30 a.m. Monday, Homeland Security Investigations searched Omar's Washington home as part of what the Justice Department called a "federal criminal investigation" into decades-old paperwork. Agents took her phone, two sources told CBS News, and her relatives have been issued subpoenas.

In a statement on social media, Omar called it an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies." Her office has said she has "done nothing wrong." President Trump told reporters he "had nothing to do with" the raid.

Ramirez told CBS News Chicago that the early-morning raid pressured her to file the "Reimagining Safety Act" this week, a bill that would abolish the Department of Homeland Security and transform it into a cabinet-level Department of Community Safety. Ramirez first announced the bill at a Sept. 23 news conference in Chicago, CBS Chicago reported. According to that report, it would also abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

"What happened to my colleague and my sister, Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, is bone-chilling," she said, calling it an abuse of power against "political enemies" of the president.

Ramirez is worried about the broader implications and the precedent this sets for her constituents and everyone living in the U.S.

"It should scare everyone, because if they're willing and able to do that to Ilhan Omar, they can do it to anyone," she said.

"They're not stopping. We need to stop them," Ramirez said.

Ramirez, 43, who is the child of two Guatemalan immigrants, shared her own fears.

"I'm human, and it's actually why this work is so personal to me and why I am so persistent," she said. "But it doesn't mean I don't worry."

Ramirez has been an outspoken critic of Mr. Trump. She said she is sometimes nervous about what an administration "obsessed with targeting people with whom they disagree" could try to do to her, and that it is why she continues to raise the alarm about her colleagues.

Ramirez also stood alongside local and national immigration and civil rights groups at a press conference to introduce the "People's Vision for Immigration Reform," a platform to preserve and expand pathways to citizenship.

The resolution has 19 congressional co-sponsors and the backing of 54 civil and immigration rights organizations. The press conference, held at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights office, was packed with representatives from local and national advocacy groups.

"We've seen the consequences of the inability of Congress to prioritize legislation and the overreach of the Trump administration that has taken a sledgehammer to refugee admissions, temporary protected status, healthcare, food access, and due process," said Lawrence Benito, the coalition's executive director.

He said the coalition was formed 40 years ago, in direct response to the last time Congress, under then-President Ronald Reagan, enacted major immigration reform legislation. It has helped hundreds of thousands of people prepare applications and gain access to citizenship, and has helped pass numerous pro-immigrant state-level laws.

The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 was the last sweeping, multifaceted overhaul of U.S. immigration laws. It created a pathway to citizenship for more than 2.7 million people and strengthened border protection.

Representation was broad, from Korean to African organizations, as well as the ACLU of Illinois.

"Immigration policy can be based on a commitment to family unification, fairness, and due process, and recognize the dignity and worth of people from other countries," said Ed Yohnka, director of communications for the ACLU of Illinois.

The 71-page bill proposes how and where to redistribute DHS's funds and responsibilities across other departments, including the creation of the Department of Community Safety.

The bill would preserve FEMA and cybersecurity functions within the new Department of Community Safety, while moving immigration enforcement back to the Department of Justice, which initially oversaw it before the Sept. 11 attacks. Customs functions would move to the Department of the Treasury, and the TSA and Coast Guard to the Department of Transportation.

The bill would also redirect DHS funds into Medicare for All, housing and education. It would also limit government surveillance, rein in what Ramirez called "unlawful abuses of data," and curb militarized enforcement.

The bill has fewer than seven co-sponsors and faces long odds in a Republican-controlled Congress that is out of session until after the Nov. 3 midterms.

The National Republican Congressional Committee called the legislation "utterly insane."

"The radical socialist agenda for the Democrat Party is on full display, and it's utterly insane," committee spokesman Mike Marinella said. "Democrats are rolling out the welcome mat for criminals and cartels, and expecting Americans to go along."

Some moderate Democrats, such as Rahm Emanuel, also think abolishing ICE goes too far. Ramirez said border work would continue.

"I'm not saying that there's no work in the border," she said to CBS News Chicago. "The work of the border needs to be done by the Department of Treasury, as we know that at ports of entry, we are handling and managing imports and exports all the time," she said, referencing drugs and guns.

Abolishing ICE has become a campaign issue for many candidates, most notably Juliana Stratton, who won her primary running on it, compared to her competitor Raja Krishnamoorthi's call to "abolish Trump's ICE." A January Economist/YouGov poll found 46% of Americans support abolishing ICE, compared to 43% who oppose it.

"What is radical about calling out and dismantling an agency that is less than 23 years old? An agency that has proven to us for the last 23 years that it cannot be trusted with our tax dollars to protect people. That is now the biggest threat to the homeland," she said.

Both Ramirez and the community groups emphasized that this issue did not start or end with Mr. Trump, and called on Congress to be more courageous and reassert its power.

"The fact that Ronald Reagan, in November of 1986, passed the bill that established some form of immigration reform, and that neither Democrats nor Republicans have been able to do anything since then, tells us that the only permanent safety for people in this country is actually a roadmap," Ramirez said.

"But really it's the bills that we have to actually pass in Congress that actually get to legal pathways, so people don't have to go through a border, or experience what they've experienced," she said.

Even with that push, Ramirez said it all comes down to people's advocacy.

"The community is ready," she said. "And it's the community that's going to lead the charge — whether it's to dismantle DHS, or to actually get this Congress to give a damn and actually do something about immigration reform."

title: Dying in ICE custody: Inside one family's story of heartbreak | Donald Trump News
description:
Ismael was one of more than 50 people to die in ICE custody during the first 500 days of Trump's second term.
What it found was that 2025, the year Ismael died, was the deadliest year in history for those in ICE custody.
'Not proportional' The Trump administration has consistently denied reports that deaths in ICE custody are increasing.
In total, 33 people died in ICE custody last year, according to the agency's own statistics.
Detainee Jesus Jacobo Ortiz Ruiz estimated that, for every 320 people in ICE custody, there is only one doctor.
text:
Los Angeles, California – Saturdays marked a weekly pilgrimage for Lucia Uribe. Every weekend, she would travel to the edge of California's desert to visit her son, Ismael Ayala-Uribe, in detention.

Ismael was among the hundreds of thousands of people swept up in United States President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

Born in Mexico and brought to the US as a child, he was arrested on August 17 while working at a car wash. Ever since, he had been in the custody of immigration authorities, first at a local jail and later at a detention centre for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Adelanto, California.

But one Saturday was different. Lucia remembers that Ismael’s hands looked paler, his eyes were bloodshot, and the fever he had was rising.

“Mom, I’m not going to make it,” Lucia recalls Ismael telling her. There was little she could do but reassure him.

“I told him, ‘Oh, my son, just hang in there as long as you can,’” Lucia said. “When I said goodbye to him, I felt something in my chest, a tightness, and it made me want to cry.”

It was the last time she would see her son alive. Lucia’s fears were confirmed by a knock at her door two days later, when police told her that her son had died at 2:32am on September 22, 2025.

Ismael was one of more than 50 people to die in ICE custody during the first 500 days of Trump's second term.

A coroner's report from the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department in southern California found that his death was caused by complications from an abscess in his pelvic region.

Ismael's family, however, has argued that insufficient medical treatment in ICE facilities led a preventable infection to fester into a deadly condition.

For months, the Al Jazeera documentary series Fault Lines has spoken to people in ICE custody and the families of those who never made it out alive, to understand the conditions that could have led to deaths like Ismael's.

What it found was that 2025, the year Ismael died, was the deadliest year in history for those in ICE custody. But experts fear 2026 is on track to match or surpass that record.

'Not proportional'

The Trump administration has consistently denied reports that deaths in ICE custody are increasing.

In a social media post in June, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, claimed that the death rate has remained "consistent with data over the last decade".

"There has been NO spike in deaths," the department wrote, pointing to the percentage of deaths relative to the overall population of ICE detainees.

But experts and watchdog organisations warn that ICE's framing may be misleading.

“What has often been claimed is that the overall detained population is going up," said Nicholas Cuneo, an expert in immigrant health with Physicians for Human Rights, an advocacy organisation.

But he pointed to statistics that show the death rate has nearly tripled. “That clearly is not proportional to the detained population," Cuneo said.

In June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights published a joint report revealing that, since Trump returned to office, immigrants in ICE custody are dying at a rate roughly three times higher than under his predecessor Joe Biden.

The annualised mortality rate during Biden's four-year term was 2.24 for every 10,000 detainees. Since Trump began his second term, that proportion has risen to 6.38 deaths for every 10,000 people in custody.

In total, 33 people died in ICE custody last year, according to the agency's own statistics. So far in 2026, at least 26 people have died.

Reagan Williams, a human rights lawyer and researcher who worked on the June report, said that the increase in overall detentions does not explain the spike in deaths.

"The administration has incarcerated record numbers of immigrants," Williams said.

"And yet this rapid rise in detention does not fully account for the staggering increase in deaths. A higher percentage of detained immigrants are dying under this administration."

While overcrowding at ICE facilities is a factor, experts at Physicians for Human Rights also found a pattern of delayed emergency care, understaffing and failure to provide adequate medical treatment.

Those factors have raised concerns that many ICE deaths may have been preventable, including Ismael’s.

'A major failure'

A round-faced man with dark-rimmed glasses, a moustache and short-trimmed hair, Ismael came to the US when he was only five years old.

Southern California became his home, and as an adult, he qualified for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) programme, which offered temporary protection against deportation.

He lost his DACA status, however, in 2015 after a conviction for driving under the influence.

His family remembers him as a caring son and uncle, always willing to buy his niece and nephew new clothes or school supplies.

“Ismael was always looking after his siblings. He just had a big heart,” said his brother, Jose Miguel Ayala. “He was very protective of not just us, but my mum and dad too.”

He was 39 years old when he was brought to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.

Two weeks after his arrival, Ismael told his family that he developed a high fever and a painful sore on his backside.

On September 18, 2025, workers at Adelanto initiated a Code Blue alert for Ismael, signalling a life-threatening medical emergency. Medical staff rushed him from his dorm to the infirmary in a wheelchair.

ICE documents show that Ismael was given pain medication, an ointment and a fibre supplement.

But according to Physicians for Human Rights' Cuneo, who reviewed the case, Ismael should have received a physical examination and antibiotics.

"That is a major failure," Cuneo said.

That weekend, hours after Lucia’s visit, Ismael’s condition worsened. Just after midnight on Sunday, ICE records say he was vomiting, shaking and sweating.

According to ICE documents, he was later sent to an intensive care unit, where he went into cardiac arrest within minutes of his arrival and subsequently died.

“I believe Ismael’s death could have fully been prevented by timely care,” Cuneo said. “It was a simple abscess that was not treated in a timely manner.”

Fault Lines obtained a coroner's investigation that reveals Ismael was critically ill when he first arrived at the hospital, a fact that was left out of ICE's public report on his death.

The coroner's report also contradicts ICE's timeline for Ismael's death. It indicates Ismael went into cardiac arrest early on September 21, nearly a full day before he passed away. Medical staff, however, managed to restore his heartbeat after intubating him.

That conflicts with ICE's report, which only notes his pulse stopping once: shortly before his death was announced on the morning of September 22. ICE described his condition on September 21 as "calm and cooperative", but it signalled no heart problems.

“If they had given him the medical care and what he needed, maybe he would be here with us,” Lucia said.

In a statement about Ismael’s death, ICE said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” throughout their time in custody.

But California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta told Fault Lines that his office found “the exact opposite" during its inspections of the state's detention centres.

“We've gone to these facilities. We've gone into Adelanto. We have done our own physical inspections," Bonta explained.

“If what the ICE spokesperson said was true, Mr Ayala-Uribe would be with us today.”

An internal mortality review committee also found that the care provided to Ismael at Adelanto "deviated beyond safe limits of practice", according to a document obtained by US media earlier this year.

It also suggests that medical staff delayed responding to calls about Ismael's declining health in the days leading up to his death.

'We want to go outside alive, not dead'

Fault Lines spoke to current detainees in the Adelanto detention centre who say they, too, fear the conditions could be harmful to their health.

Many described inadequate medical care, mouldy food and retaliation for protesting against the subpar conditions.

Some are part of a class-action lawsuit, filed in January, accusing the US government of "inhumane and illegal conditions" at Adelanto.

"They don't take things seriously," one detainee, Kurt Campbell, said of the Adelanto staff.

"They think everyone's a liar. So when you're going through something and you express what you're going through, they act like you're lying. We do want to go outside, but we want to go outside alive, not dead."

Four men have died in Adelanto between September 2025 and March 2026, including Ismael. Campbell, who is originally from Jamaica, said he knew one of the detainees who passed away.

"His last days were spent in confinement and in Adelanto instead of being with his family," Campbell said. "He didn't kill anyone. He didn't hurt anyone. His crime was coming over the border."

Guadalupe Moreno Cristin, another detainee in Adelanto, recalls experiencing rectal bleeding for more than a week, in addition to heart issues.

When he was taken to the infirmary, the only treatment he said he was given was Tylenol and a serum. His health has continued to deteriorate.

"I haven't had a bath for, like, eight days now because I can't lift my hands up," Cristin said. "I can't change myself on my own. I can't stand for long, and I can't walk much."

Detainee Jesus Jacobo Ortiz Ruiz estimated that, for every 320 people in ICE custody, there is only one doctor. "You've got to be literally dying in here for you to get sent to the hospital," Ruiz added.

Fault Lines spoke to US Representative Judy Chu, who represents a congressional district near Adelanto. For the past decade, she has been conducting oversight visits at the facility.

"I've seen firsthand for over a decade how they've cut corners, how they don't want to spend money on food, and most importantly, they don't want to spend money on medical care," Chu said.

To push for change, roughly 150 detainees signed a petition and went on hunger strike earlier this year to denounce the "unbearable and inhuman" conditions at Adelanto.

Campbell said he was placed into solitary confinement for 30 days for participating in the hunger strike. Other detainees reported receiving physical retaliation, including Ashraf Abujama.

"They just enjoy using force on me," Abujama said. "They want to just use me as an example to all the detainees, that '[this is] what we can do'."

'An emptiness that wasn't there before'

In recent weeks, changes have been under way at Adelanto.

The facility, formerly owned by the private prison firm Geo Group, has been sold to the Department of Homeland Security for $950m, as the federal government seeks to acquire more detention centres.

Critics, however, warn that the switch to federal ownership could make conditions inside Adelanto more opaque, limiting the ability of state and local authorities to exercise their oversight roles.

It is a change that concerns families of detainees like Ismael. Where once his mother Lucia visited him at Adelanto, she now spends her weekends with a new ritual: visiting his grave on Sundays.

Jose, Ismael’s brother, often joins her, along with his sister and her two kids.

Their father often stays behind. "My dad still has a hard time going," Jose explained.

More than a year has passed, but the entire family is still grappling with the loss.

"There's a time where I just feel like he's just going to walk in," Jose said. "There's just an emptiness that wasn't there before."

text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed the state’s 100th lawsuit against the federal government since President Trump took office for a second time in 2025.

Bonta reached that milestone in 21 months. During the first Trump administration, California officials sued the federal government a total of 123 times in four years.

The lawsuit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California alleges that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement overstepped its Constitutional limits by taking people into custody at state courthouses, a practice forbidden by a U.S. District Court judge that the lawsuit alleges ICE nevertheless continues to employ.

For instance, the California Justice Department found that ICE detained 34 people at state courthouses in June 2026. In July 2026, the month after the judicial order to stop making arrests at courthouses, ICE detained 28 people at courthouses.

“ICE’s directive on courthouse enforcement and the resulting enforcement activities have had a profound chilling effect that has hindered California’s ability to enforce the law and protect public safety,” the state Justice Department said in a news release.

Picking people up at a courthouse can have a chilling effect on witnesses, victims and even suspects who are afraid to show up for court, California Supreme Court Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero said last year.

“Making courthouses a focus of immigration enforcement hinders, rather than helps, the administration of justice by deterring witnesses and victims from coming forward and discouraging individuals from asserting their rights,” Guerrero said.

text:
The leaders Catholics and evangelicals in the United States asked to address the immigration debate from compassion, public responsibility and Christian principles, with special attention to children and families facing uncertainty due to their immigration status.

In the statement entitledA call to Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate, the Reverend Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, andMonsignor Brendan Cahill, president of the Migration Committee of the Conference of Bishops Catholics of the United States, expressed a common position regarding the human consequences of immigration policies.

“How Catholic and evangelical Christians, we have our doctrinal differences, but we are united in our conviction that God calls us to support both our fellow Americans who face concerns economic and cultural as well as our immigrant neighbors who face existential challenges”, they expressed.

Human dignity

The signatories maintain that the dignity of each person is prior to their immigration status and does not depend on its recognition by the authorities.From this perspective, they consider that public policies They must respect human rights and prevent differences between citizens and foreigners become reasons for confrontation.“This dignity comes from God, not the government, and no earthly power can delete it”, maintains the document, which bases its position on passages biblical texts about the creation of human beings in the image of God and the commandment of love your neighbor.

The declaration also recalls the biblical tradition of welcoming the stranger and proposes recovering the figure of the good Samaritan as a reference to recognize to others beyond their origin.In that sense, Christian leaders question practices that present migrants only as a burden on society.

“The foreigner is not simply a burden to bear”, they point out, remembering that migrants can also contribute to the renewal of the communities and congregations that receive them.The text extends this concern to American citizens living situations of poverty and vulnerability.They maintain that the defense of migrant families should not be understood as an opposition to the needs of the local population, but as part of a shared responsibility towards those who are going through difficulties.

Concern about arrests and separation family

The leaders warn that detentions and deportations can cause separations that They especially affect children and those who depend on their parents or spouses.“Their fear is our fear; their tears are ours to dry”, express when referring to migrants who live with uncertainty of losing their legal status or sharing their home with someone in that situation.

The declaration recognizes the responsibility of the State to protect its citizens, maintain secure borders and establish immigration policies.Without However, it emphasizes that these obligations must be exercised proportionally, respect for human dignity and legal guarantees.

The ecclesiastical authorities express their recognition to the police forces and their service to society, but they warn that the application of the law does not is exempt from unfair consequences. In particular, they question the measures that indiscriminately affect peaceful and productive people.“Start a mother of his children or leaving a citizen spouse to raise a family alone is to create the same widowers and orphans that Scripture tells us orders to defend”, they maintain, appealing to the moral responsibility of those They design and apply public policies.

Proposals for immigration reform

Before this scenario, the Evangelical-Catholic Dialogue on Immigration considers it necessary a legislative reform that expands the possibilities of regularization for those They have been residing in the United States for years.The document indicates that the routes legal opportunities to access permanent status are limited and are inaccessible to many people.

The leaders identify three priority areas for a migration policy that combines security and respect for human rights: Secure borders and enforcement proportional of the law;limits on the detention of nonviolent people;ways accessible and effective laws.

Religious freedom also occupies a relevant place in the declaration.In The document states that this right must be protected for all people, regardless of their beliefs or immigration status, and put special attention to those who remain detained.Consequently, express their willingness to work with the authorities to ensure that people in custody can receive spiritual assistance and participate in the sacraments.

From faith

The statement places the immigration debate in the context of values foundations of the United States, as the country approaches the commemoration of the 250th anniversary of its Declaration of Independence, in 2026. Leaders evoke the principle e pluribus unum—of many, one—and the tradition of welcome represented by the Statue of Liberty.They also remember the declaration of independence on the equality of all human beings and their fundamental rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

From These principles propose generating more spaces for education and dialogue between the different Christian traditions, as well as within the congregations local, to reflect on the responses that reality requires current immigration.

The statement concludes with an invitation to pray for the authorities, the legislators, judges, law enforcement officers and all persons They work for the common good.The signatories present reconciliation as a Christian responsibility that must be expressed both in words and in actions actions: “We do not offer these words with anger or partisanship, but with hope, trusting that the God of exile and the foreigner has not abandoned to his people.”

text:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear an appeal by the federal government seeking to deny asylum to Izuchukwu Ozurumba, a Nigerian who was allegedly held against his will and forced to cook for a suspected separatist group known as Unknown Gunmen.

According to Reuters, the court agreed to review a lower court ruling that found Ozurumba’s work as a cook did not amount to providing material support for terrorism under US immigration law.

The case centres on whether preparing meals for members of a group designated as a terrorist organisation amounts to providing material support, even when the person involved claims to have been coerced.

According to court documents, Ozurumba travelled to a remote camp outside Lagos in 2022 after learning of a job opportunity. He was employed as a cook but later discovered that the camp was allegedly operated by the Unknown Gunmen, a group believed to have links to separatist activities in Nigeria.

His lawyers said he became suspicious of the group after noticing that the movements of some young men from the camp coincided with reports of killings and arson.

Ozurumba allegedly attempted to leave but was prevented from doing so and forced to continue working without pay.

After six months, he reportedly escaped during a trip to purchase supplies and returned to Lagos. His lawyers said he subsequently received death threats, prompting him to flee to Venezuela. He added that the threats continued there.

In July 2023, Ozurumba entered the US illegally through its southern border and applied for asylum and other forms of protection against deportation.

However, an immigration judge ruled that the Unknown Gunmen constituted a terrorist organisation and that Ozurumba’s work as a cook amounted to material support for terrorism.

The judge reasoned that preparing meals helped the group pursue its objectives by meeting members’ “basic human needs”.

The judge also ruled that Ozurumba’s claim that he had been forced to remain at the camp did not exempt him from the immigration restrictions. His applications for protection against deportation were consequently denied.

Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in 2025 while his appeal was pending.

In September 2025, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, based in Richmond, Virginia, overturned the immigration judge’s interpretation of Ozurumba’s activities.

In a two-to-one decision, the appellate panel ruled that Ozurumba was a captive labourer and that preparing meals for the group did not amount to material support for terrorism.

The court held that his work provided nothing that the organisation could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities.

However, the appellate court declined to order US authorities to return Ozurumba to the country while the legal proceedings continued. Instead, it ordered a fresh consideration of his asylum case.

Dissatisfied with the decision, the administration of President Donald Trump, through the US Department of Justice, appealed to the Supreme Court.

In its submission, the department argued that cooking for members of a terrorist organisation constituted material support under US immigration law.

“Providing meals to a terrorist organisation’s members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles,” the department argued.

The administration also warned that allowing the appellate court’s decision to stand would substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism.

The dispute centres on provisions of US immigration law restricting the admission of non-citizens who have engaged in terrorist activities, including providing material support to terrorist organisations.

Reacting to the Supreme Court’s decision to hear the appeal, Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which represents Ozurumba, criticised the government’s interpretation of the law.

“At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum,” Mayer-Salins said.

She maintained that the appellate court correctly recognised that asylum should not be denied to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and issue its ruling by the end of June 2027.

text:
LOS ANGELES – The Justice Department, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), today filed a complaint against the State of California over its voter list after determining that more than 20,000 people who are likely aliens are registered to vote in California. Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot. It is unlawful for aliens to vote in federal elections.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), in coordination with federal partners, analyzed publicly available voter-registration records to identify potential indicators that aliens may have registered to vote, cast ballots, or received election-related mail. The Department of Justice has filed a complaint against the State of California alleging that these individuals, who are likely noncitizens, registered to vote and/or voted in a federal election. HSI and its federal partners used multiple data-enrichment and verification methods to assess whether the individuals identified were likely aliens.

According to the lawsuit, the federal government sent relevant California officials a list of more than 20,000 names of people that it believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot from California to participate in the federal election. The federal government asked California to review the list and, in partnership with federal agencies, to determine whether citizens were listed. California failed to do so.

“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation’s representative system of government. The Department of Justice will continue working to uncover cases of voter fraud, hold fraudsters accountable, and restore trust in American elections.”

“California election officials were given an opportunity to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls and to sequester ballots returned from suspected ineligible voters. They refused,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. “We are taking California to federal court to demand that the votes of American citizens not be diluted by noncitizens.”

“It is unlawful for noncitizens to vote in federal elections,” said Secretary Markwayne Mullin of DHS. “The Department of Homeland Security and our federal partners reviewed publicly available California voter-registration files and compared relevant records with federal immigration data to identify alien registrants. This preliminary analysis has identified a significant number of individuals in California who are likely noncitizens and appear to be registered to vote; the analysis and review remain ongoing. This is completely unacceptable — as even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen and undermines our elections. DHS is committed to identifying unlawful voting, protecting the integrity of federal elections, and ensuring that only eligible American citizens elect America’s leaders.”

“The law is clear, aliens in the United States cannot vote in federal elections,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “What our complaint alleges is that California is facilitating unlawful voting by knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. This needs to stop.”

The United States is requesting the court prevent California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined. The lawsuit seeks an order that California set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the federal government likely to be noncitizens and to independently – or in collaboration with the federal government – verify their citizenship status beyond relying on unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.

The United States seeks to prevent unlawful dilution of American citizens’ votes and to protect the integrity of our nation’s elections.

text:
The Trump administration is working to build a case against Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota) with the hopes of ultimately denaturalizing and deporting the progressive Somali American lawmaker, The Wall Street Journal reports.

The alarming, unprecedented effort — denounced as outright fascism by critics — is wide-ranging, encompassing several federal agencies. U.S. officials and other sources familiar with the investigation told the Journal that the effort is focused, in part, on unearthing information about her deceased father, the circumstances surrounding her arrival in the U.S. when she was a child, and her citizenship.

The Justice Department has issued over a dozen subpoenas in relation to the investigation to Omar’s family, including to her sister and other relatives. The New York Times reported this week that federal officials are attempting to establish a case that Omar’s father lied or omitted information on his immigration forms when he came to the U.S. with Omar in 1995.

Other reports also say that the Trump administration is also looking into whether she lied on papers to obtain legal status and citizenship, and specifically on whether she or her father intentionally misstated her birthdate to obtain citizenship as a minor alongside her father when she was naturalized. The Department of Homeland Security looked into similar allegations of immigration fraud under the Biden administration, but did not move forward because of a lack of evidence, the Times reported.

In a drastic escalation on Monday, agents from Homeland Security Investigations conducted a predawn raid on Omar’s house in Washington, D.C. Officers seized her phone, notebooks, personal computers, and passport.

“President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this,” Omar told the Journal.

Omar was 12 years old when she arrived as a refugee in the U.S. Her family had fled a bloody civil war and a “human rights disaster,” as dubbed by Amnesty International, in Somalia. She became a U.S. citizen at the age of 17, in the year 2000.

Omar has weathered racist and bigoted personal attacks against her by President Donald Trump and other political figures for years. The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the Minnesota representative have been widely condemned by Democrats as a naked attempt to go after a political opponent just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is up for reelection; as well as a tyrannical, fascist act by the increasingly bold and out-of-control Trump administration.

The allegation that Omar was actually 18 when she was naturalized originally gained traction on conservative social media through a viral video posted in 2019. Her congressional office had her birth year changed on official paperwork from 1981 to 1982, which conservative conspiracy theorists framed as suspicious.

However, her office said it was already in the process of getting her biographical information changed through official channels. Further, it is common for people from war-torn and underresourced countries to put an approximate date on immigration paperwork because they have no official record of their births; a 2020 report found only 6 percent of births are registered with the government in Somalia.

After the raid on Monday, Trump once again spewed racist rhetoric against Omar and Somalis.

“She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said at a rally in Ohio. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

The crowd chanted “deport” as he incited violence against Somalis. Just last Friday, Trump openly encouraged a race war against Somalis in Minnesota in a post on Truth Social, telling followers to “fight back.”

Omar has stood up against Trump’s attacks. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” said Omar on Monday following the raid. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

The lawmaker is left-leaning and has been a consistent advocate for Palestinian rights, especially amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza. In 2025, she marked her 30th year in the U.S., and recalled the story about her family’s arrival in the U.S. She said that her grandfather was a major catalyst for their immigration.

text:
United States President Donald Trump’s mandate for aggressive immigration enforcement has fractured public support in advance of next month’s critical midterm elections.

In the lead-up to the November 3 vote, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.

That rate was even higher among demographics that may be key to the Republican Party’s prospects in November.

The poll, conducted in September, found that 60 percent of independent voters agreed with the idea that Trump’s immigration efforts have overreached. Two-thirds of Hispanic participants also agreed with the campaign having “gone too far”.

Experts say the political debate about immigration in the US has shifted since the last major election in 2024. At the time, the focus was largely on border security. But increasingly, attention has fallen on how enforcement operations are being conducted.

Cynthia Penaloza is among those questioning the Trump administration’s tactics.

In August, her sister, 23-year-old Joceline Penaloza Magana, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Houston, Texas, during a traffic stop. Joceline remains in custody to this day.

“We’re always afraid. We’re uncertain of what’s going to happen, if she’s going to be sent back to Mexico, if we’re ever going to be together again or how this is going to change our lives forever,” Cynthia told Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle.

She rejects Trump’s assertion that his administration’s immigration enforcement operations have targeted “the worst of the worst”.

Joceline, according to the Penaloza family, was an honour roll student who does not have a criminal record. She was brought to the US as a young child, about five years old.

“She’s always been a good girl,” Cynthia told Lavelle.

A focus on ‘criminals’

Still, the Trump administration has tied its campaign of mass deportation to efforts to control crime.

In a statement earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, credited Trump’s policies with having “unleashed ICE to target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens, including pedophiles, murderers, gang members, terrorists, and rapists”.

Immigration arrests have been on the rise under Trump. In September, ICE announced it had tallied two consecutive months with more than 50,000 immigration arrests, beating a record set in June, when 43,900 people were detained.

Homeland Security has argued that approximately 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in.

But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.

In other words, many of the accused could be acquitted or see their charges dropped. A large portion of those with criminal charges may also be accused of non-violent crimes.

Analysts have found that a majority of people currently in immigration custody are not considered criminals under the law. According to the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government data sets, some 70 percent of those held in ICE detention have no criminal record.

The Trump administration has nevertheless pushed to increase detentions.

“We need more. We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” Tom Homan, the White House “border czar”, said in an interview in July.

Pushback on the campaign trail

The aggressive arrest tactics may have repercussions on the Republican campaign for the midterms, though.

Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as in key state and local elections.

Trump made significant gains in the 2024 elections with Hispanic voters. During his re-election bid, he received nearly 48 percent support among Latinos, according to an exit poll from the Pew Research Center — up 12 percentage points from the 2020 election.

But Pew found that his gains may be eroding. Among the Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024, his approval rating has steadily declined, from a high of 93 percent at the start of 2025 to a low of 57 percent as of last week.

Some Republicans running in the midterm election, including Congress member Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, have even openly criticised the president’s hardline immigration policies.

“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in an advertisement campaign launched in September. She cited the large number of immigrants who were arrested without a criminal record.

Other Republicans, however, blame previous presidencies for creating the conflict over immigration enforcement.

“A mess was created, and now cleaning it up is dirty business,” Jeremy Price, a Republican in Texas, told Al Jazeera. “You’re having to find people, arrest them against their will and remove them from the country because they don’t want to leave.”

Democrats, meanwhile, hope to convert that outrage over immigration enforcement tactics into votes, come November.

“I would hope they’d abolish ICE,” Richard Gonzales, the chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party in Texas, said in an interview with Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.

“I mean, in my perspective, I think that they’ve, the agency has just lost its identity, and there’s no way to rehabilitate that.”
