When other states, like Nevada, Texas, and Missouri, have used the DHS system to vet their voter rolls for noncitizens, investigations have found that it incorrectly flagged hundreds of US citizens as ineligible to vote.

California officials have said the list of names was provided to them on a thumb drive, which came with a password written on a sticky note. They did not consider this to be a secure device and refused to open it. The letter was sent more than a week after California began sending mail ballots to 23 million registered voters.

The state refused to set the ballots aside, saying that the administration had not provided credible evidence that the voters were not citizens and that eligible voters could be disenfranchised. In its complaint Thursday, the DOJ called on the court to stop the ballots from being tallied until the citizenship status of each voter could be independently verified. It also requested that the state not send a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one.

The DOJ's batch of roughly 20,000 supposedly ineligible voters is a significant reduction from the 190,000 that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged were registered in the state back in July. When California asked for the underlying data and methodology for that figure, DHS declined to provide it.

"What happened to those 170,000?" said California Attorney General Rob Bonta at a press conference on Thursday. "They just got those wrong."

This highlights the concerns states have expressed about using the DHS system to purge their voter rolls. In refusing the DOJ's request, state officials have noted that in Nevada, the system flagged 185 voters as possible noncitizens only for state officials to determine that every single one of them was a US citizen.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber responded to the DOJ's lawsuit with a sharply worded letter, accusing it of “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians' right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”

Weber described it as an effort to block “thousands of Californians’ right to vote” weeks before an election and said, “The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law.” Federal law prohibits states from systematically purging voter rolls within 90 days of an election.

“We are not impressed with the federal government’s letter. We are not impressed with its lawsuit," Bonta said. “This is what the federal government does. They lie, they advance misinformation, disinformation, they advance conspiracy theories. They try to sow distrust with those lies."

“Their timing is rife with and smacks of and reeks of desperation and bad faith, to do this during an election,” he said.

Stephen Richer, the former Republican Maricopa County recorder in Arizona, described the government's lawsuit as "a real escalation by the federal government."

"I've mostly said 'Calm, calm. It's going to be OK' with respect to federal involvement in election administration," he wrote on social media. "This lawsuit—in October, in the middle of early voting—that asks election officials to disqualify certain voters based on suspect databases, not conclusive evidence, which definitely could have been alleged before early voting began... This does represent an escalation."

The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Voting Rights Project filed an emergency brief on Thursday seeking to stop the DOJ from using its list to withhold ballots.

"With voting already underway, eligible citizens should not have their ballots withheld based on a federal list they have never seen and have had no opportunity to challenge," said its director, Chad Dunn. "We are asking the court to intervene before voters suffer harm that cannot be corrected after Election Day."

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said in a statement that the Trump DOJ "is now actively trying to interfere in the 2026 elections and strong-arm California into purging names from our voter rolls and blocking mail ballots based purely on vague allegations less than three weeks before Election Day."

He added, "This lawsuit has no legal basis or evidence behind it and is nothing more than a blatant abuse of power designed to sow distrust in our elections and threaten Americans’ right to vote."

Trapped inside the burning apartment was Awad's daughter, Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, whose age has been reported as between 2 and 4 years old. Prominent Palestinian author Mosab Abu Toha said family friends confirmed the child was born in February 2024.

Palestinian journalist Ali al-Jaafrawi witnessed and recorded the immediate aftermath of the strike.

"There are children are screaming alive inside," al-Jaafrawi is heard saying as he approached the building.

"I went up to the apartment. There were flames everywhere," al-Jaafrawi told Al Jazeera. "I went in despite the fire and smoke and heard a little girl screaming inside. I went in, found her, and rescued her immediately. I carried her and handed her to people so they could take her to hospital."

"I went back to rescue others and to document what happened, but I suffocated and lost consciousness because of the thick smoke," he added. "I saw a woman on fire inside the apartment."

Photos and video recordings show Ghanem being treated for injuries, including burns, at al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, which is struggling to operate after much of the facility was destroyed or damaged by Israeli forces, who besieged and raided the complex multiple times since October 2023.

Abu Toha, who saw Ghanem in the hospital, said the child "kept repeating the same heartbreaking words: 'I want my mum. My body hurts. There was a lot of fire.'"

Ghanem—whose father, Ahmad Ghanem, was reportedly killed by Israeli forces early in their genocidal assault—has joined the ranks of the more than 56,000 Gaza children who have lost at least one of their parents in the war, according to the United Nations Children's Fund.

"Reem and Ahmad had waited four years to conceive Maryam," Abu Toha wrote. "Four years of waiting and hoping to bring a child into this world. Ahmad never lived to see his daughter’s face. Reem lived long enough to watch her little girl grow for two-and-a-half years before she was burned alive in front of her. Now Maryam is an orphan, fighting to survive her horrific burns."

Ghanem's grandfather told Middle East Eye that the child and her mother "did nothing wrong."

"They were sleeping quietly at night," he said. "There was no one in the apartment except the two of them."

Israel said it is investigating the strike, which it claimed—without providing evidence—targeted a member of Hamas.

Dismissing a nominal yearlong ceasefire during which at least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed and over 5,000 others wounded by Israeli attacks, the grandfather said that "honestly, there is no security."

"I fear for my family," he added. "All people are afraid, not just me. There is still assassination, war, hunger, poverty, and destruction... Nothing has changed."

The horrific footage of the strike's fiery aftermath evoked imagery from earlier in Israel's onslaught, including video of a 7-year-old girl trying to escape an inferno caused by bombing that killed dozens of Palestinians—among them her mother and siblings—and a teenager photographed burning alive after Israeli forces bombed a tent encampment.

Some observers noted the almost complete absence of US media reporting on the story, with the apparent exception of CBS News, which published video of the burning apartment in a Facebook Reel.

"This little girl watched her mother be burned alive in Gaza. If she was Israeli, this image would be front-page news. But Israel can kill Palestinians in the most horrific ways without generating any headlines," US historian, author, and political analyst Assal Rad said on social media.

"Video has been circulating all day; you can hear the little girl cry and see her engulfed in smoke," Rad said in a separate post. "I can’t find headlines in Western media *because* the story is horrific. They want you to forget."

The Washington, DC-based Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) issued a statement calling on members of Congress "to condemn Israel for burning a Palestinian mother alive while her daughter watched in Gaza."

“The horrific video of a little girl surrounded by fire as her mother burns to death in their home exemplifies the reality of Israel’s genocide in Gaza," CAIR said. "We cannot comprehend how any political leader with a conscience could continue to fund the sheer cruelty of the Israeli government and the war criminals who carry out its orders."

"Members of Congress must condemn this atrocity and demand an immediate end to all US support for Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza," the group added.

The US has provided Israel with tens of billions of dollars in armed aid, as well as diplomatic cover, including repeated vetoes of a series of United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions, throughout the three-year annihilation of Gaza, which has left more than 250,000 Palestinians dead or wounded.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, weighed in on the attack on Bluesky.

"I have reached the limits of my ability to put words to pure evil," he wrote. "Once again, Israel burned another family in Gaza alive. But the image of the... daughter in the family watching the rest of her family die in the flames will haunt me for the rest of my life."

"But," Parsi added, "will it haunt Israel?"

Omar spokesperson Jackie Rogers responded to the report by accusing President Donald Trump of engaging in "desperate attempt to justify his extraordinary abuse of power."

"This is politically motivated and an escalation of Trump’s personal vendetta against her lasting over a decade," Rogers told HuffPost. "He has lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country."

To Trump, no American value or principle is too important to be shredded for his own personal gain."

Author John Ganz on Thursday published an analysis of the reported Omar deportation plot, which he said is "undoubtedly driven by racial and religious animus" and also "a serious assault on the constitutional order being carried out through the executive branch’s legal and bureaucratic machinery."

Ganz argued that a serious attempt to strip Omar of her citizenship and remove her from the country would be a major escalation from the Trump administration toward establishing an outright totalitarian state.

"Authoritarian governments suppress political opposition and deprive their subjects of particular rights," Ganz explained. "Totalitarian movements aspire to something much more radical: the destruction of the independent political and juridical personhood. They attack not merely the liberties of particular citizens they seek to repress, but the concept of citizenship itself—and then, ultimately, the concept of shared humanity."

(Graphic by Data for Progress)

In recent years, states and municipalities have sued fossil fuel companies over their well-documented history of misleading the public about their products' role in warming the planet. These lawsuits have sought compensation for damages from worsening floods, wildfires, droughts, and other climate-related disasters.

Eleven US states—California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Vermont—as well as the District of Columbia, have active lawsuits, as do at least two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities around the country, according to a tracker by the Center for Climate Integrity.

The new poll suggests voters are even more opposed to shielding oil companies from these lawsuits than they were five months ago. Another Data for Progress poll in May showed just 65% opposed legislation to shield oil companies, compared with 75% now.

"Big Oil is desperate to secure legal immunity and escape accountability for its role in the climate crisis—and the billions of dollars of damages that have followed," said Iyla Shornstein, the political director at the Center for Climate Integrity. "These poll results show that Americans across the political spectrum are opposed to putting Big Oil above the law.”

Protesters hold a banner outside the US Supreme Court as it considers the Suncor v. Boulder case in Washington, DC, on October 5, 2026. (Photo by Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)

The oil industry's lobbying arm, the American Petroleum Institute, has described stopping state climate lawsuits as a top priority for 2026. Their Republican allies have pushed at all levels of government to advance that goal.

In April, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and several GOP cosponsors joined Rep. Harriet Hageman (R-Wyo.) to introduce legislation that would shield fossil fuel companies from any climate-related lawsuits, dismiss pending cases, and overturn state "superfund" laws requiring the industry to pay for climate damages.

That bill failed to pass out of the House Judiciary Committee last month but could be brought forth again during the "lame-duck" session after the midterm elections in November.

ProPublica has identified at least 15 bills across 11 states that have either been enacted or proposed to shield companies, either by granting them broad immunity from liability for greenhouse gas emissions or restricting the ability of communities to sue over climate-related damages. Groups linked to Leonard Leo, the co-chair of the right-wing Federalist Society, have coordinated many of these efforts.

Republican attorneys general in 16 states have proposed creating a "liability shield" for fossil fuel companies modeled on the one that protects gun manufacturers from liability for the misuse of their products. The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), a leading conservative policy shop, approved a model bill in August aiming to establish this shield in state legislatures nationwide.

The oil industry has also pushed for the right-wing Supreme Court to step in to block these lawsuits. Earlier this month, during oral arguments, oil giants ExxonMobil and Suncor urged the court to block a lawsuit brought by Boulder, Colorado, that accused oil companies of deceiving the public about climate change and sought to hold them financially responsible.

If the court blocks the Boulder suit before it gets to trial, it could set a precedent that derails dozens of similar lawsuits around the country.

Meanwhile, Trump, who pledged to help Big Oil executives in exchange for their donations to his presidential campaign, signed an executive order last year directing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to identify and challenge state lawsuits that seek to impose financial penalties on fossil fuel companies.

His DOJ has weighed in on the Suncor v. Boulder case on the side of the oil industry and has sued at least five states that have sought to hold fossil fuel companies accountable.

The question about climate lawsuits was part of a broader set of questions Data for Progress asked voters about rising insurance costs and corporate accountability in partnership with the Insurance Fairness Project. Other results showed that many Americans want legal recourse against insurers and other companies that impose costs on consumers.

"As rising home insurance costs directly threaten housing affordability for the majority of Americans, voters are tired of their prices rising while insurance companies, energy providers, and the oil and gas industry go unchecked," said Grace Adcox, senior climate strategist for the Insurance Fairness Project. "There is a strong appetite for holding corporations accountable, both for their role in driving up costs and their role in contributing to the climate crisis."

It also reveals previously undisclosed donors who have benefited from a presidential pardon as well as government contracts and at least one closed federal investigation.

The 57 donors whose names were published by the Post had committed to contributing at least $100,000 to the ballroom construction project, which is proceeding for now following a Supreme Court ruling in August.

The list shows a total of $333 million contributed from private donors, but does not include Trump's name, though the president has said the demolition of the White House's East Wing and the construction of the ballroom would be "paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine."

It also falls short of the $600 million projected price tag; according to the Post, taxpayer funds have been used to partially fund the project, along with donations from companies with business before the government.

Nvidia's $25 million donation came three months after the company reached a deal with the Trump administration to sell advanced microchips to China.

A $25 million donation from Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of the telecommunications company Dish Network, came shortly after the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) dropped an investigation into the failure of EchoStar, which owns Dish Network, to upgrade its cellphone network.

FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr had threatened last May to revoke government licenses from EchoStar, and a month later, Ergen met with Carr and Trump in a closed-door meeting where his political donations were discussed, Bloomberg reported.

Ergen then negotiated a deal to sell some of the licenses to AT&T. Carr dropped the investigation the following month, and months later, with the sale pending, the executive donated $12.5 million to Trump's ballroom construction. A second $12.5 million contribution came soon after, according to the list published by the Post.

“Big Tech giants didn’t just chip in for Trump’s ballroom," said Sacha Haworth of the Tech Oversight Project, a watchdog group. "The same companies funding Trump’s vanity project lined up for tax breaks, chip deals, federal contracts, and a blind eye to lawbreaking. Under Donald Trump, there’s a two-tiered justice system. Big Tech plays by a different set of rules because they bought their way in."

The Post also detailed a $2.5 million contribution from Isabela Herrera, the daughter of international banker Julio Herrera Velutini, whom the US Department of Justice indicted on bribery charges in 2022.

Herrera Velutini's charges were reduced to a misdemeanor months after his daughter donated millions of dollars to Trump's MAGA Inc. political action committee, and a month later, she committed to a $2.5 million donation for the ballroom. Soon after, Herrera Velutini was pardoned.

The transactions detailed by the Post amount to "blatant corruption," said progressive news outlet The Tennessee Holler.

Companies with massive stakes in decisions before President Trump and his administration gave many millions to the White House ballroom project, which the President has made clear is important to him. So are you confident he'll make those decisions based only on what's good for the American people?

[image or embed]

— Noah Bookbinder (@noahbookbinder.bsky.social) October 15, 2026 at 10:43 AM

Cryptocurrency investors Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss donated more than $5 million in bitcoin—a portion of the more than $18 million the industry contributed to the ballroom. Trump has pushed for loose regulations for the industry.

Other top donors include Google, Lockheed Martin, Amazon, and Palantir.

Government watchdog Public Citizen said a new tax filing from the Trust for the National Mall, a nonprofit charity that manages the donations for the ballroom, shows that $169.7 million came from just 10 big donors.

“One year after the people’s house was abruptly bulldozed for a gold-plated ballroom that most Americans will never be allowed inside, we are uncovering who paid the most to fund it," said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate for Public Citizen. "The question these ballroom megadonors all now need to answer is—why?”

Haworth said that "when Democrats take back gavels in January, they need to investigate Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and others for potentially breaking the law to buy get-out-of-jail-free passes and sweetheart deals in exchange for their donation."

This concern with corruption appears likely to benefit Democratic candidates, as respondents say they trust Democrats to handle corruption better than Republicans by a 10-point margin.

Overall, the poll finds Democrats hold a nine-point lead on the generic congressional ballot.

Trump's personal net worth has increased by billions of dollars since the 2024 election, driven in large part by his family's cryptcurrency venture, which is nearly half owned by a fund backed by the United Arab Emirates.

Many legal experts also believe that Trump brazenly violated the US Constitution's emoluments clause when he accepted a $400 million luxury jet as a gift from the Qatari government.

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, said that widespread concerns about corruption were not surprising given how President Donald Trump and his family have shamelessly enriched themselves since returning to power.

"The public is furious about the corruption they see from the government," said Gilbert. "Even Fox News polling says as much."

Gilbert emphasized that Democrats must hit the ground running to further uncover Trump corruption if they win the upcoming 2026 elections, as voters will be demanding accountability.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO – Anxiety has been the defining hallmark of life for Samir since he lost Temporary Protected Status (TPS) in 2025. The 32-year-old Venezuelan now finds himself adrift in a legal limbo, stripped of his livelihood and with no clear path ahead.

Adding to his fears, he says, is the explosion of surveillance cameras across San Francisco and nationwide, fueling a pervasive sense of his own vulnerability.

“From the moment I step outside the door, I look forward, I look back, I look in every direction constantly,” said Samir (who asked that we not use his real name). “Anything looks suspicious to me. It’s paranoia. You end up feeling like a criminal without having done anything wrong.”

That sentiment is part of what is behind the growing public backlash against the government’s expanding surveillance capacity, one now being deployed as part of the Trump Administration’s ongoing anti-immigrant crackdown.

‘Like Amazon, but with human beings’

There are, according to estimates, between 70 and 80 million surveillance cameras installed across the country, or roughly 1 camera for every 4 to 4.5 residents. Among these are some 120,000 Flock Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPRs) deployed across roads and highways nationwide.

The rapid spread of these “public safety” tools is raising alarm bells among privacy and civil rights advocates as well as immigrant rights defenders.

“Immigration enforcement and ‘national security’ have long served as the justification for increasingly authoritarian systems that erode civil liberties [and] weaken democratic protections,” write the authors of a recent report, The Tech Behind ICE: Oligarchs, Immigration Enforcement and the Threat to Democracy.

In turning to expanded tech-driven surveillance, the administration’s vision, the authors note, quoting former ICE Acting Dir. Todd Lyons, is to create a deportation process “like [Amazon] Prime, but with human beings.”

‘We can’t keep you’

Samir first left his native Caracas in 2017, a year marked by massive protests, a brutal crackdown by former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and the first in a series of crippling sanctions imposed on the South American nation by the US.

A musician by training, Samir initially fled to Mexico, where he would spend the next three years eking out a living as a teacher in a local music school. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and his life was once again turned upside down.

Unemployed and unsure of where to turn, Samir decided to head to the US. He secured a tourist visa, giving him entry into the country, and boarded a plane to San Francisco, where a friend lived, in December of 2020. In March of the following year, he applied for and was eventually granted TPS, reserved for individuals fleeing countries shaken by violence, political persecution or natural disasters.

Now able to work legally, Samir returned to music, landing gigs teaching guitar, piano, music theory, and improvisation at Bay Area music schools. He also found a position with the stagehands union, Local 16, working shows around San Francisco.

But events would once again upend Samir’s life.

In October 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court green lighted the Trump Administration’s efforts to end TPS protections for Venezuelans. The ruling, and subsequent decisions, have led to the cancellation of TPS status for 13 countries to date, impacting some 1.3 million people across the country.

For Samir, the loss of TPS set off a chain of events that like dominoes fell one after another, taking apart the life he had painstakingly sought to build here.

“I notified all the schools and the union employer that I had lost my TPS,” recalled Samir, noting that without the legal designation he no longer had work authorization. “They all told me, ‘Please let us know how we can help you, and if anything changes, please come back… but without a work permit, we can’t keep you.’”

A ‘digital pipeline for deportations‘

Along with his employment status, Samir also lost his health insurance and, because he no longer had a valid Social Security Number, his bank shuttered his accounts. He then got a notice from the California DMV alerting him that his state issued ID was no longer valid.

“That was all I had, that was my only current, valid identification,” said Samir. “All my IDs are expired. I don’t have anything from Venezuela, I don’t have anything from Mexico, and I don’t have a passport because there is no [Venezuelan] embassy here.”

These days Samir relies on friends across the Bay Area for shelter and part-time gigs, including cataloging and archiving vinyl records for local collectors.

“If it weren’t for the help of all these people…” he pauses, catches his breath, at a loss for words, before continuing. “I have felt sort of protected, helped, loved, and accompanied.”

And while he admits he thinks of leaving, that option carries its own set of complications.

“The only way I could leave is by driving down to the border and crossing into Mexico,” said Samir, “[which] can’t issue me a passport because I’m not a citizen there, and without a passport, I can’t fly anywhere.”

‘Like Venezuela all over again’

In the meantime, Samir spends his days navigating the matrix of cameras and surveillance tools that have proliferated across San Francisco, a system he describes as a digital pipeline for deportations.

In late September, the city announced it would continue to deploy the cameras with certain limits, including who can access the data and for how long it will be stored. Reporting by 404 Media found that more than 4,000 queries carried out across ALPR networks were explicitly tagged with terms like “ICE,” “immigration,” or “ICE+ERO,” that latter referring to Enforcement and Removal Operations.

In Samir’s telling, it “feels like watching Venezuela all over again.”

He explained, “In Caracas, when state repression began, many looked the other way, thinking danger only threatened street protesters or active dissidents.”

Pointing to conditions here, he added, “Today, people say, ‘It’s just the immigrants, it’s just undocumented people.’ But that’s an illusion. When you hand the state the power to monitor, track, and categorize a group of people without limits or oversight, you hand it control over the entire society.”

Omar has long maintained that she became a US citizen at the age of 17 when her father was naturalized in 2000, but sources with direct knowledge of the federal raid on her DC bungalow said the Department of Justice is looking for evidence that claim is a lie.

Follow live updates on the federal criminal probe of lefty ‘Squad’ Rep. Ilhan Omar

If the Somali-born Omar’s citizenship was procured by the concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation — either by herself or by her father, Nur Omar Mohamed — on immigration paperwork, then the feds will seek to denaturalize and deport her, one of the sources confirmed.

The 44-year-old congresswoman was at home with her husband Tim Mynett when agents executed a search warrant and removed the items, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Criminal charges could only be brought if the alleged immigration fraud occurred within the past 10 years, while if it concerned false statements there would be a five-year statute of limitations, according to federal defense attorney Todd Spodek.

Securing a criminal conviction for “knowingly procuring naturalization unlawfully requires revocation of citizenship,” Spodek said, though a member of US Congress has never been denaturalized before.

There’s no similar statute of limitations if civil denaturalization is pursued. President Trump’s DOJ has pursued a record-breaking number of civil denaturalizations, with almost 200 cases filed since the beginning of the president’s second term in January 2025.

Of those cases, just 20 have been closed with the defendants put into deportation proceedings, according to an analysis by the left-leaning group Democracy Forward.

The Post confirmed Wednesday that prosecutors in Minnesota are leading the immigration fraud probe into the “Squad” member, while the office of DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro is pursuing an inquiry into Omar and Mynett’s finances.

Some records list Omar’s birthdate as Oct. 4, 1981, while others give the same date in 1982. If the former date is accurate, Omar would have been of legal age at the time her father received citizenship and thus would have been ineligible for the minor benefit.

The Post reported Tuesday that in the spring of 2019, following Omar’s initial election to the House of Representatives, her staff pressed the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, the Biographical Directory of the United States Congress, and Wikipedia to record her birth as happening in 1982 rather than 1981.

Months earlier, in the fall of 2018, Omar’s campaign had told the Associated Press that she didn’t have a birth certificate due to her family’s displacement by the long-running Somalia civil war.

Omar has repeatedly denied any wrondoing, with her office insisting in a statement to the Journal Wednesday: “President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this.”

The Omar family emigrated first to Kenya during Somalia’s bloody civil war in the early 1990s, eventually arriving in the US in 1995. Omar’s father died of complications from COVID-19 in 2020.

More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have also been issued to family members of the Minnesota congresswoman, including her sister, Sahra Noor.

text:
For almost two years, President Donald Trump’s Republican Party has had unified control over two of the three branches of government. That’s likely to shift in November.

Polling currently shows Democrats in a strong position to win a majority of seats in the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate, and Democrats are already planning what they’ll do if they win control of one or both chambers. The to-do list is long and ambitious: Democrats say they will end the Iran war, find ways to address affordability, restore healthcare subsidies, investigate President Trump and his family, and more.

But a majority isn’t everything. Particularly if they only win control of the House, Democrats will have a platform, but passing laws or imposing the checks they want on presidential power will be a struggle.

“The reality is, when you are the majority party in one half of one third of the national government, there’s not a whole lot you can do,” says Matt Green, a professor of politics at Catholic University.

Some of the thorniest problems Democrats want to address, like expanding health insurance coverage and making everyday life more affordable, aren’t easily solved by one party alone, analysts say. Still, Democrats will take advantage of the opportunities that a majority would provide them. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is lining up plans to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and has established working groups to address high costs of living. House Democrats slated to lead major committees are preparing to investigate various administration actions.

“We’re going to use every tool in the toolbox,” Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told CNN regarding his committee’s plans.

Prepping for investigations

If Democrats win a majority in either chamber, one of their biggest tools will be the ability to investigate the Trump administration. The majority party controls committees, giving them the power to hold hearings, issue subpoenas, and launch investigations.

Prospective committee leaders have already laid out extensive plans for using this power. Democrats on the Judiciary and Oversight committees want to examine ways Mr. Trump and his family have profited while in office, including alleged conflicts of interest regarding the family’s cryptocurrency ventures.

Leaders of these and other committees have also discussed investigations into military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean, protester killings by federal immigration enforcement agents in Minneapolis earlier this year, and the administration’s withholding or redacting of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“That’s really where you’re going to see the most action,” says Eric Schickler, co-director of the Institute of Governmental Studies at the University of California, Berkeley.

Experts expect the Trump administration will fight back. In August, the Department of Justice issued a legal opinion saying executive privilege can cover some conversations the president has with advisers outside the executive branch. That lays the groundwork for the White House to withhold information from Democrats trying to investigate it.

Ten Democrats, led by California Sen. Adam Schiff, sent an August letter asking the White House to confirm it would cooperate with “current and future congressional inquiries.” They have not received a response, per Senator Schiff’s office.

Still, Dr. Green says these investigations could be damaging to the administration.

“You can just burden the executive branch with tons of requests, and for every request they deny, you then take them to court,” he says. “This White House is not immune from public embarrassment.”

Pushing for legislative change

Leader Jeffries, who is in line to replace Mike Johnson as House Speaker if Democrats take the majority, has outlined specific priorities he says his party will tackle in a new Congress. He wants Democrats to pass laws to overturn the president’s tariffs, continue to hold votes opposing the Iran war, and reverse cuts to Medicaid that congressional Republicans passed last year. Democrats would have to overcome steep challenges to enact any of these into law, even with House and Senate majorities.

Mr. Jeffries has already established working groups to tackle what he sees as five key issues in affordability: housing, healthcare, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and caregiving. The groups will recommend actions that Democrats can take within the first 100 days of the next Congress, as well as throughout the year, Mr. Jeffries told reporters at a virtual press conference Oct. 4. Each working group is headed by one centrist and one progressive Democrat, according to reporting by The Associated Press.

Affordability is “what unites Democrats across the ideological spectrum,” said Mr. Jeffries.

Even if Democrats win both chambers, they’ll be faced with a 60-vote threshold in the Senate for most legislation. And Mr. Trump can veto laws, which would force Congress to muster a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.

Divided government “is not always a recipe for a lot of legislative productivity,” says Molly Reynolds, director of Governance Studies at the Brookings Institution and an affiliate with the Center for Effective Lawmaking.

Still, some experts say cooperation might not be impossible. Mr. Trump likes to be seen as a dealmaker, even frustrating Republicans during his first term by working with Democrats on issues like raising the debt ceiling.

Democrats may also try to attach their priorities to bills that Congress knows it has to pass. For example, when lawmakers tackle the debt limit and yearly spending bills, Democrats could try to slip in provisions that defund immigration enforcement or require the administration to spend money Congress has set aside.

Mr. Jeffries has been reluctant to say whether Democrats will impeach Mr. Trump, though he has consistently declined to rule it out. Progressive Democrats like California Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ro Khanna support pursuing impeachment, while others like former – and hopeful – Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown say it would be little more than a distraction. Experts predict the party will face serious pressure from its base to try to impeach the president a third time.

text:
SACRAMENTO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today marked his 100th lawsuit against the Trump Administration since it began on January 20, 2025, just 21 months ago. This regrettable milestone comes as the President continues to break our laws with a frequency and intensity surpassing even the lawlessness that characterized his first term in office. Within hours of being sworn into office, President Trump attempted to rewrite the Constitution by issuing an illegal executive order that sought to end the birthright citizenship promised under the Fourteenth Amendment. Attorney General Bonta filed California’s first lawsuit against the President less than 24 hours later and took this fight all the way up to the U.S. Supreme Court — and won. In the following months, Attorney General Bonta has returned to court to stop the President’s unlawful federal funding cuts for education, research, housing, healthcare, and infrastructure; get the National Guard off our streets; and defend constitutional rights like the right to vote. All of these actions clearly exceeded the President’s authority and ignored the basic constitutional framework our founders crafted with care and precision. Attorney General Bonta's 100th lawsuit, filed today, once again challenges the Trump Administration’s undermining of the rule of law and trampling over longstanding principles of justice — seeking to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) policy and practice of carrying out civil immigration enforcement in and around state courthouses.

“For the 100th time since President Trump returned to office, we’re going to court. This is a sobering milestone — and a testament to the unrelenting ferociousness with which the President is willing to steamroll over the law, our Constitution, and the fundamental values of our government,” said Attorney General Bonta. “In California, we’ve been repeated targets of this Administration. He’s gone after our funding, taken over our streets, and systematically made our communities less safe. These 100 lawsuits are a symptom, a reflection of what we’re collectively up against. The President’s epidemic of lawbreaking is the disease. No one should look at these 100 cases and think this is normal. No one should look at these 100 cases and think we want to be here today. This isn’t a fight we chose. But when the President breaks the law and goes after our state, we’ll meet him in court, each and every time."

Since January 20, 2025, President Trump and his Administration have pursued policies that have made Americans’ lives worse, not better, breaking the law 100 times in the process:

Making Your Life Unaffordable

For more than a year, President Trump has inflicted chaos on the American economy by imposing tariffs without the legal authority to do so, including through illegal attempts using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 — attempts that were struck down by multiple courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court and the Court of International Trade. A recent analysis concluded that nearly 90% of the costs of tariffs in 2025 were paid by American consumers and businesses.

At the same time, the Trump Administration attempted to starve the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of its lawful funding, threatening catastrophic harm to hardworking families and consumer financial markets nationwide. The court rejected this move after state attorneys general took it to court, ensuring it can continue its work to protect consumers from unfair, deceptive, and abusive acts by big corporations.

Undermining Civil Rights and Privacy

The Trump Administration has sought to accumulate and leverage massive troves of Americans’ personal sensitive data, attempting to illegally seize California’s voter rolls, Medicaid data, SNAP data, TANF data, and commercial drivers’ license data for purposes unrelated to their original intent like immigration enforcement and for purposes, concerningly, still unclear. California will not let programs designed to ensure children do not go hungry and to help needy families get back on their feet be exploited to fuel mass surveillance efforts.

The Trump Administration has sought to use federal funding as a bludgeon to compel states to adopt its hateful and ideological agenda — seeking to condition funding for school lunches, SNAP, and other programs that provide a critical lifeline to vulnerable communities on states’ adoption of its policy preferences around immigration, gender ideology, transgender athletes, and diversity, equity, and inclusion.

Making Our Communities Less Safe

While President Trump claimed he’d go after the worst of the worst, instead, he’s advanced policies that would have made our communities less safe, not more. Since taking office, the Trump Administration has tried to shut down a program that helps communities prepare for and mitigate the risks from disasters in advance, reallocate funding California uses to prevent and respond to acts of terrorism based on our adoption of policies the Trump Administration does not like; and impose illegal immigration enforcement conditions on emergency preparedness and crime victims grants.

Last year, Attorney General Bonta, alongside Governor Gavin Newsom, filed a lawsuit challenging the President’s unlawful deployment of California National Guard troops, securing multiple court orders blocking their federalization and deployment to Los Angeles and Portland, and finding violations of the Posse Comitatus Act. Following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in a related case, Illinois v. Trump, rejecting the Trump Administration’s nearly limitless conception of presidential authority to federalize the National Guard and the activities those troops can engage in, the Trump Administration officially withdrew the remaining troops in California and ended their deployment.

Attacking the Right to Vote

President Trump has been relentless in his attempts to restrict the right to vote, sow distrust in the integrity of our elections, and interfere with states’ constitutional authority to administer elections. Attorney General Bonta repeatedly stopped these efforts in their tracks — ensuring that November’s elections are business as usual in California.

Taking Funding Away from Our Schools and Kids

The Trump Administration has tried to stop $4.9 billion in federal education funding from flowing to California not one, not two, but three times. California has met them in court each time — ensuring the Trump Administration’s reckless actions don’t impact the educational futures of our children.

In his first month in office, President Trump also sought to pump the brakes on cutting-edge medical and public health research at universities and research institutions across the state and country — cuts that were stopped, permanently, through multistate litigation.

Rolling Back Energy and Environmental Progress

The President has spent the past 21 months writing a love letter to his fossil fuel friends — at the cost of California’s environment, public health, and clean energy future. He’s wasted taxpayer money on unnecessary and unlawful buyouts of offshore wind projects. He’s refused to implement lifesaving standards for fine particulate matter — commonly known as “soot.” And he’s tried to roll back California’s decades-old authority to set vehicle emissions standards more stringent than the federal government’s.

Ripping Away Healthcare and Social Services

As a society, we are judged by how we treat our neighbors in need. President Trump doesn’t like California’s policies — and he’s tried to punish us for them. The Trump Administration sought to freeze $5 billion in funding for childcare and family assistance programs in California, putting at risk the ability of working parents to stay in their jobs and support their families. It refused to pay out SNAP benefits last November — appealing all the way up to the Supreme Court — despite multiple courts telling the Administration it could, and in fact, should, and tried to punish states for taking steps to fund these benefits.

Targeting California’s Immigrant Communities

The President has embarked on an indiscriminate and inhuman mass detention and deportation campaign — instilling fear in California communities as ICE targets not criminals, but lawful U.S. citizens, green card holders, asylum seekers, and other hardworking contributors to our communities and economy. California has declined to use our limited resources for federal immigration enforcement, a decision that has been upheld by the Ninth Circuit. Despite this, the President has repeatedly attempted to condition transportation, crime victims, emergency services, and homeland security funding on California’s participation in immigration enforcement. These attempts have been resoundingly rejected by the courts.

…Through it All, California is Standing Strong

In just under 21 months, Attorney General Bonta has filed 100 lawsuits on behalf of California, leading or co-leading 67 of them, and separately filed more than 130 amicus briefs in support of other litigation against the Trump Administration. In this period, Attorney General Bonta has secured 57 orders granting early relief, 26 final orders, and in an additional nine cases, the Trump Administration has backed down before the case was heard on the merits. Attorney General Bonta has also celebrated major wins at the U.S. Supreme Court, protecting the right to vote and the right to birthright citizenship, defending California’s redistricting efforts, getting the National Guard off of California’s streets, and blocking the President’s illegal tariffs.

text:
The US State Department must reinstate its Diversity Immigrant Visa lottery for fiscal year 2027 by Friday, a California federal judge ruled.

The lottery must be open by Oct. 18, with registration lasting through Nov. 19, Judge Jinsook Ohta of the US District Court for the Southern District of California said Wednesday as she issued a preliminary injunction halting the green card program’s suspension.

The program offers permanent residence to up to 55,000 applicants annually from countries with historically lower levels of immigration to the US, many of them in Africa.

The Trump administration suspended the program last December, after a Portuguese national who received a visa through the program was suspected of killing four people in two separate shootings in Rhode Island and Massachusetts; the individual was subsequently found dead by suicide. In March, the administration issued a rule mandating applicants hold a passport.

California-based immigration law firm Red Eagle Law LC sued the State Department, seeking resumption of the program. Ohta had denied a temporary restraining order sought by the firm.

Last month, a Northern District of California judge found that the State Department had restarted its processing of applications for fiscal 2026 at “an unprecedented glacial pace.”

The State Department said it wouldn’t comment on pending litigation.

Red Eagle represents itself.

text:
United States immigration authorities have dramatically stepped up detentions and deportations since January 2025, when Donald Trump became president.

Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”. Officers with the Department of Homeland Security, the agency tasked with the crackdown, now make thousands of arrests a day across the country.

That includes people who are seeking asylum in the US, who are supposed to be given a chance to explain dangers they might face in their home country. And US law and international treaties, like the United Nations Convention Against Torture, prohibit authorities from deporting someone to any country in which they will be persecuted or tortured.

Many of those being detained in the US immigration crackdown say they are at risk of being hurt or killed if they return to their native countries, so the Trump administration has looked for alternative places to deport them, including places someone might have no cultural or legal ties to.

Third-country deportations, as the practice is known, have been criticised by the US as well as global rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, as well as the UN.

Critics of the practice say some of the countries taking in the deportees have a record of human rights abuses themselves, or are so dangerous that the US government tells its own citizens not to travel there. They also say there is little to ensure these third countries will give deportees a fair hearing on their cases for asylum, and in the end might send them back to their native countries to face persecution there.

Third-country deportations are not new, but rights groups say they were extremely rare before the Trump administration, and have never been used by the US at the scale they are now. Those being sent to other countries, rights groups say, would not have been deported without their consent. Some US courts have said the practice is illegal, but the US Supreme Court has allowed it to continue, including in a ruling in September.

Experts at the UN have said the practice was leading to a “cascade of human rights violations” across the globe, threatening to undo norms around how refugees and asylum seekers are treated.

A closer look at the third-country deportations

Rights groups have tried to tally forcible third-country deportations, and according to the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been subject to forcible third-country deportations so far, based on media reports and information from attorneys.

The Department of Homeland Security’s own data includes more than 16,000 cases of third-country deportations since Trump came into office in January 2025 and August 2026, the latest month for which data is available. The data, provided to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by Al Jazeera, is likely an undercount.

Deportations to these countries need the approval of authorities there, so the Trump administration has sought to make agreements, or reach informal understandings on how to send deportees to a growing list of countries.

Some countries have agreed to keep deportees in prisons, like El Salvador and Eswatini.

Others have agreed to hold deportees temporarily, with some signing Asylum Cooperative Agreements with the US, or “Safe Third Country Agreements”, which allow deportees to pursue asylum claims in a third country that has agreed to host them.

According to rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First, many of those deported have no idea where they are being sent, and end up finding themselves in countries where they do not speak the language and have little cultural understanding. Some don’t even have any documents like passports or identification cards, making it difficult to live there.

The list of countries people are being deported to has grown as the US offers financial aid, or business or visa concessions, in exchange for countries taking in third-country nationals the Trump administration wants to remove.

Liberia has agreed to take up to 1,200 deportees, for instance. The Trump administration at one point said it would extend the validity of certain visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months, and has committed $124m for the country’s health services.

In Cameroon, which agreed to take third-country nationals from the US in December 2025, the Trump administration has pledged to give $30m for the UN’s refugee work there, and $400m over the coming years for the country’s health services.

“The Trump Administration has systematically made our communities less safe with its insidious and unlawful enforcement actions in and around California courthouses,” said Attorney General Bonta.
Although ICE’s directive was vacated in late June 2026 in Pablo Sequen v. Albarran, ICE’s enforcement actions at California’s courts did not stop.
In July, after ICE’s directive was vacated, there were 28 reported incidents, resulting in 28 civil arrests.
ICE’s enforcement actions at courthouses are conducted unannounced, often by unidentified, plain-clothed officers.
text:
SACRAMENTO — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s policy and practice of carrying out civil immigration enforcement in and around state courthouses. Since the Trump Administration began authorizing and encouraging these arrests in May 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have carried out disruptive, often violent civil immigration enforcement actions at courthouses across California, without regard for the impacts on the administration of justice. Witnesses, victims, survivors of domestic violence, and others who might wish to seek redress through the state’s judicial system understandably fear that courthouses are no longer safe places to appear. ICE’s directive on courthouse enforcement and the resulting enforcement activities have had a profound chilling effect that has hindered California’s ability to enforce the law and protect public safety. In the lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, Attorney General Bonta asserts that these immigration arrests, and the directive authorizing them, are arbitrary and capricious, exceed the agency’s enforcement authority, and violate the U.S. Constitution.

“The Trump Administration has systematically made our communities less safe with its insidious and unlawful enforcement actions in and around California courthouses,” said Attorney General Bonta. “We’ve seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify. Our justice system cannot function this way. There is good reason that the common law, dating back centuries, bars civil arrests at courthouses. I’m deeply troubled that, today, we're going to court for the 100th time in less than two years to enforce the law. This is a sobering milestone. Our state’s courts should be where justice is served — not disrupted or denied.”

Since ICE changed its policy in late May 2025, immigration enforcement in and around California state courthouses has spiked. In the year that followed the policy change, the average monthly number of ICE arrests in and around California courthouses increased by more than 550% compared to prior months, with immigration enforcement actions occurring across the state, from the largest urban centers, like Los Angeles and San Diego, to rural courthouses in Shasta, Butte, and Glenn Counties. Although ICE’s directive was vacated in late June 2026 in Pablo Sequen v. Albarran, ICE’s enforcement actions at California’s courts did not stop. In June 2026, when more robust data collection began, there were 34 enforcement incidents reported at superior courts statewide, resulting in 30 civil arrests. In July, after ICE’s directive was vacated, there were 28 reported incidents, resulting in 28 civil arrests. These types of enforcement actions at California’s courts continued throughout the summer and into the fall.

ICE’s enforcement actions at courthouses are conducted unannounced, often by unidentified, plain-clothed officers. These officers have apprehended court attendees in hallways, lobbies, and parking lots of the state’s courthouses. Sometimes they follow their target from the courtroom; other times they apprehend the individual before they reach the courtroom. They have also been reported to wait in the court parking lot in certain counties for days on end, seeking to apprehend individuals who are coming to or from the courthouse. Notably, ICE’s most recent written courthouse enforcement directive does not limit who is subject to arrest — it can be anyone from a criminal defendant to a victim to individuals merely present to conduct civic business or accompany a family member. These enforcement actions have caused substantial harm, including by stymying criminal prosecutions, impeding California’s ability to provide access to justice, and disrupting court operations.

In today’s lawsuit filed against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE, Attorney General Bonta argues that ICE’s directive authorizing widespread immigration enforcement at courthouses is:

Arbitrary and Capricious in Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA): ICE failed to consider the chilling effect on access to justice and the overall functioning of state judicial systems resulting from its directive. ICE in its most recent written directive also failed to acknowledge or provide a reasoned explanation for removing an earlier restriction that barred courthouse enforcement in jurisdictions where it was prohibited.

In Excess of Statutory Authority in Violation of the APA: The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) was enacted against the backdrop of the centuries-old common law privilege that precluded civil arrests at courthouses. Congress is understood to have incorporated that privilege into the INA and thereby withheld authority for immigration officers to make civil arrests at courthouses.

Contrary to Constitutional Right, Power, Privilege, or Immunity in Violation of the APA: The states’ judicial and police powers are powers that the U.S. Constitution reserves to the states under the Tenth Amendment. ICE’s actions interfere with California’s execution of its core sovereign judicial and police functions by infringing on California’s ability to maintain and operate a judicial system, prosecute crimes, and carry out related police powers.

In Violation of the Tenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution: ICE’s directive and its courthouse enforcement infringe on California’s sovereign powers and interfere with the execution of its sovereign duties.

Attorney General Bonta is committed to holding ICE accountable and standing up for California’s immigrant communities. Earlier this year, Attorney General Bonta filed a lawsuit seeking to block the illegal development of an ICE facility in unincorporated Santa Clara County near Gilroy, California. Attorney General Bonta previously led amicus briefs in supporting Minnesota’s lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s extraordinary campaign of lawlessness during its deployment of ICE, in opposing unlawful immigration stops in the Central Valley, and to stop ICE and Customs and Border Protection from engaging in unlawful practices in Los Angeles.

text:
By Human Rights Watch

October 6, 2026

Halt Plans to Deport Thousands to Danger

(Bangkok) – Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim should press Myanmar’s junta leader, Min Aung Hlaing, to end human rights abuses during his visit to Kuala Lumpur on October 7, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today.

The Malaysian government should also halt plans to forcibly return ethnic Rohingya and other people from Myanmar, where they face persecution and other rights violations. Malaysian authorities deported about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on September 29 in coordination with junta authorities, the first batch in a series of phased returns.

“Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing to coordinate the forced return of people who fled military atrocities in Myanmar is an invitation for further abuse,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Malaysian government, which has provided protection to Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar for decades, should halt any more returns and urge the junta leader to stop the abuses that have caused millions to leave the country.”

On September 16, Prime Minister Anwar announcedthat he was inviting Min Aung Hlaing, who led the February 2021 military coup, to discuss the return of Myanmar nationals from Malaysia. This is Min Aung Hlaing’s sixth bilateral visit to an Asian country since he installed himself as president in April following sham elections and after stepping down as commander-in-chief of the Myanmar military. Min Aung Hlaing has been implicated in many abuses, and the International Criminal Court prosecutor has requested an arrest warrant for his alleged crimes against humanity.

On September 29, Malaysian authorities sent back 1,476 Myanmar nationals—1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys, and 7 girls, ages 8 to 60—accordingto Malaysia’s state news agency, Bernama, aboard two Myanmar navy ships and a hospital ship from Lumut naval base in Malaysia’s Perak state.

The deportations come amid a wave of public hostility in Malaysia toward refugees, particularly Rohingya, that government officials have fomented. The Home Ministry has describedrefugees as a financial burden, a social problem, and a security threat. Online hate speech and misinformation targeting Rohingya and migrants generally have surged this year, leading to harassment and the closure of community schools.

The transfer was the first phase of an arrangement between the Malaysian government and the Myanmar junta to return 5,000 people, initially announcedby Malaysian officials in July. Based on media reports, Malaysia’s Home Ministry said the Myanmar junta authorities had identified those slated for return. It did not disclose their ethnicity or refugee status, or say whether Rohingya were among them. The ministry was quoted as saying that further phased returns would follow once identification, documentation, and verification were complete.

Malaysian authorities have claimed the returns were strictly voluntary. But those deported were taken directly from immigration detention centers—where former detainees have reportedphysical abuse and psychological harm—raising serious concerns about whether consent was freely given.

The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) saidit had no role in the operation and was not involved in identifying those deported. Since 2019, the Malaysian government has deniedUNHCR access to immigration detention centers, preventing the agency from reviewing asylum claims or assisting detainees who are registered refugees. Consent given while in indefinite detention, without access to UNHCR or a meaningful protection assessment, cannot be truly voluntary, Human Rights Watch said.

A representative of the ethnic Chin refugee community in Malaysia told the media that community leaders knew of several asylum seekers among those deported, including one who had been recognized by UNHCR as a refugee.

There are no authoritative figures on the number of Myanmar migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers in Malaysia. More than 224,000 refugees and asylum seekers are registeredwith UNHCR in Malaysia, about 90 percent from Myanmar, the vast majority ethnic Rohingya.

Since Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, Malaysia has summarily deported thousands of asylum seekers to Myanmar without assessing their asylum claims or other protection needs, and in violation of a Malaysian courtorder. In May 2024, UNHCR issued guidancestating that people fleeing Myanmar “are likely in need of international refugee protection.”

Conditions for safe, dignified, and voluntary return to Myanmar do not currently exist, Human Rights Watch said. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity. Junta authorities have arbitrarily arrested tens of thousands of people since the coup, and thousands have experienced torture and ill-treatment or died in custody. A day before the September deportations took place, Myanmar’s military carried out an airstrike near a market in the town of Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, killing 50 people.

Rohingya face particular danger if they are forcibly returned. Myanmar authorities have long denied them citizenship and subjected them to atrocity crimes, including the ongoing crimes against humanity of apartheid, persecution, and deprivation of liberty. In Rakhine State since late 2023, Rohingya civilians have been caught in the fighting between the junta and ethnic Arakan Army forces. Both parties have carried out grave abuses, including extrajudicial killings, widespread arson, and unlawful recruitment.

Malaysian Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said on September 30 that 3,524 people had been approved for a second phase of deportation from a list Myanmar authorities submitted in a diplomatic note dated August 13. Malaysia is awaiting a date from Myanmar. About 10,400 Myanmar nationals are held in Malaysian immigration detention, according to recent reports from the Malaysian Home Affairs Ministry.

Malaysia has not ratified the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or its 1967 protocol, but it is still obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, which prohibits countries from returning anyone to a place where they would face a real risk of persecution, torture or other serious ill-treatment, a threat to life, or other comparable serious human rights violations.

The Malaysian government should immediately suspend all deportations to Myanmar, including its planned second phase, and grant UNHCR full and unimpeded access to all immigration detention centers.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) should maintain the ban on Min Aung Hlaing and other junta leaders participating in the regional bloc’s meetings. ASEAN members should refrain from organizing bilateral visits that undermine their collective ban on junta officials.

Concerned governments should press Malaysia to halt the returns, and expand resettlement places and support for countries hosting refugees from Myanmar. They should not treat returns arranged with Myanmar’s military-backed authorities as evidence that the country is safe.

“The Malaysian government should not be outsourcing the decision about who can safely return to Myanmar to the junta authorities,” Pearson said. “Prime Minister Anwar should stop the next ships before they set sail, and provide the UN refugee agency access to refugees and asylum seekers.”

text:
NEW YORK – A man who was shot by federal immigration officers in New York had his first hearing before an immigration judge Thursday, appearing remotely via video livestream from the federal jail where his lawyers say he is being held in solitary confinement.

Oscar Belgal, 28, barely spoke during the brief court session. His injury from the shooting wasn't apparent on the video feed, but his lawyers say he needs surgery to remove a bullet lodged in the back of his neck.

Belgal, a native of the Dominican Republic, tried to say something to the judge about his living conditions at the jail, but his lawyer advised him against it and cut him off.

Karene Brown, of the Legal Aid Society, said Belgal has been on 24-hour lockdown at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn with no access to a phone to speak with his family.

She told Judge Dara Reid that she has asked Immigration and Customs Enforcement to move him from solitary confinement but it has so far not honored the request. Reid said she has no say in where he’s placed within the facility — the same jail holding former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

ICE officers confronted Belgal on Oct. 8 while he was trying to find a parking spot after picking his son up from school. The boy, age 5, was in the car when an ICE officer ran up and smashed one of the car windows.

In a court filing Wednesday, Belgal's lawyers said the ICE officer then fired several shots into the vehicle as Belgal attempted to drive away. The officers never identified themselves and wore masks and civilian clothes, the lawyers said.

Department of Homeland Security officials maintain the officers believed their lives were in danger and opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.

New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively show how the shooting happened.

Belgal’s next immigration court hearing is Oct. 29. His lawyers have also filed a petition in federal court seeking his release.

description:
That doesn’t mean U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-San Antonio) has been sitting this election out.
Instead, Castro is standing outside the gates of immigration detention centers in South Texas, drawing national attention to the issue of detained children and families and criticizing the Trump administration for brutality.

text:
When redistricting took a primarily West Side district to one that encompasses nearly all of downtown San Antonio, the 20th Congressional District turned bluer than ever, effectively curbing any Republican challenger’s bid for the seat.

That doesn’t mean U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-San Antonio) has been sitting this election out.

Instead, Castro is standing outside the gates of immigration detention centers in South Texas, drawing national attention to the issue of detained children and families and criticizing the Trump administration for brutality.

He’s also working to help Democrats statewide and nationally take control of Congress during the upcoming midterm elections, he said.

Castro’s opponent on the ballot is Edgardo Báez, a U.S. Army veteran, retired medical professional and lawyer whose campaign looks to pick up the voters shifted in during redistricting.

While Castro’s office may not be up for easy grabs, it’s clear from the recent San Antonio rally in San Antonio headlined by President Donald Trump that the state of Texas is, Castro said.

“Polling has made consistently clear that our candidates for senator and governor are on the cusp of winning for the first time in a generation, and that’s because the people of Texas are fed up with this out-of-control Republican leadership in our state,” Castro said in an interview with the Report ahead of early voting, which kicks off Monday.

Texans are “fed up” with the war in Iran, tariffs and what he calls a mass deportation campaign, issues that when combined are making it hard for consumers to make ends meet and for businesses to keep their doors open, he said.

Texas is within striking distance of turning blue this cycle, Castro said — and campaigning to try to make it happen is an opportunity he can’t ignore.

Native son

Born in 1974, Castro grew up on San Antonio’s West Side and attended public schools with his identical twin brother, former three-term mayor and District 7 Councilman Julián Castro.

Their mother, Rosie Castro, is first-generation Mexican American, a longtime American civil rights activist and educator and former interim District 7 council member. Their father, Jessie Guzman, is a retired mathematics teacher in the Edgewood Independent School District.

Castro attended Stanford University in California and earned a law degree from Harvard University.

In 2002, when he was 28, Castro ran for Texas’ 125th House district seat, and in the Democratic primary, defeated incumbent Arthur Reyna. In the general election, he defeated Republic nominee Nelson Balido.

Castro is an attorney who has represented Texas’ 20th Congressional District since 2013. He serves on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

On Thursday evening, Castro is attending a District 1 town hall with Texas congressmen Rep. Diego Bernal and Sen. José Menéndez (San Antonio), and City Councilwoman Sukh Kaur.

Kaur said Castro works for all residents in the community on issues big and small, including, recently, the quiet zones in areas of the city where the railroad passes and also bringing an American family back from India after their travel was blocked.

“He’s been an amazing leader truly in the immigration conversation and ensuring that all of the residents in our community feel safe,” she said.

“I got into public service because I fundamentally believe that one of the main roles of people in government is to help create an ‘infrastructure of opportunity’ for the people they represent,” Castro said.

“In addition to the issues that we’re dealing with very intensely at any given time, I always come back to working on building that infrastructure of opportunity for folks,” he said.

Castro served as campaign chair for his brother during Julián Castro’s failed 2020 presidential bid.

In recent years, while holding down his day job in Congress, Castro has also coped with surgery and treatments following a 2022 diagnosis of neuroendocrine cancer. He said that remaining tumors in his liver have not grown, evidence that his monthly treatment at the Mays Cancer Center in San Antonio is working.

The experience has been a reminder of why he fights for universal health care, he said.

Detention centers

Since last year, Castro has made nine visits to the South Texas Family Residential Center in the town of Dilley since the Trump administration reopened the facility.

He’s been to ICE facilities in the South Texas cities of Karnes, Pearsall and Laredo multiple times, and to an Office of Refugee Resettlement camp in San Benito.

There, he’s met with detained immigrants, pointed to inhumane conditions and called for the “trailer prisons” to be shut down.

“Congressman Castro has been on the front lines of this administration’s attacks on immigrant communities and is dedicated to ensuring everyone knows what’s happening to kids in detention,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the Texas Civil Rights Project Action Fund and a supporter. “It’s an honor to stand next to him in so many of our fights for civil rights.”

Castro has worked for detainees to be released in high-profile immigration cases, like Liam Conejo Ramos, a 5-year-old Minneapolis boy detained in January while wearing a bunny hat and a Spiderman backpack, and later, teenage mariachi-performing brothers from McAllen who had once performed at the White House.

“The people of my district have asked for help,” he said. “I literally get outreach every single day on different platforms … from people asking for help because this mass deportation campaign has devastated so many families in San Antonio and South Texas, and also it’s devastated many businesses.”

When Trump announced he would headline a recent rally in San Antonio, Castro invited the president to visit Dilley “to see the lifelong lasting trauma he’s caused to these kids, to see what he’s doing in the name of Americans.”

Castro said it did not surprise him that the president did not accept.

“These decisions that have been so ugly and so cruel have been made from Washington, D.C., by many people who have never visited the border, never visited South Texas, and are completely unfamiliar with our communities,” he said.

The brothers spent their recent 52nd birthday block-walking and writing get-out-the-vote postcards with the Bexar Democrats at the St. Paul Community Center.

Castro has also been a frequent speaker on the campaign trail supporting other Democratic candidates, including lieutenant governor nominee Vikki Goodwin and gubernatorial hopeful Gina Hinojosa.

“This mass deportation campaign in Texas is as much [Gov.] Greg Abbott’s as it is Donald Trump’s,” he said during a panel at the recent Texas Tribune Festival.

‘On a new course’

If his party flips the chamber this November and takes control of the House, Castro said he wants to see a special commission investigate ICE, including deaths in custody and at the hands of agents, and to pursue legislation overhauling the agency.

For now, Castro and the Democrats are in defensive mode.

“But the longer-term goal is to get Congress to do its job of passing immigration reform,” he said, which it came close to doing in 2013. “I feel like that we could have avoided a lot of the ugliness that has come in American politics if the Congress had just passed that bill back then.”

He said he believes the election in November is going to set the nation “on a new course.”

In the meantime, Castro is working on American foreign policy and, if Democrats take control of the House, would chair the Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere in the Foreign Affairs Committee.

That subcommittee oversees U.S. relations with Venezuela, Mexico, Cuba and other countries.

“This president, more than any in generations, has focused a real spotlight on Latin America,” he said. “I disagree with many of the policies that the administration has pursued, but there’s no question that there is a renewed spotlight and interest in our relationship with Latin America.”

Castro is proud of his San Antonio roots and that he represents the city in Washington. “I think every day about how I could help make the lives of San Antonians better,” he said.

title: Chicago mother sues ICE contractor that jailed her and her baby in a hotel room
