text:
This story was published in partnership with The Intercept, a nonprofit news organization dedicated to holding the powerful accountable through fearless, adversarial journalism. Sign up for The Intercept’s newsletter.

After being detained for five days in an airport hotel, a mother filed suit against a longtime Immigration and Customs Enforcement contractor on behalf of herself and her now 23-month-old son, alleging false imprisonment among other counts.

The lawsuit was filed on September 29, more than a year after an investigation by Injustice Watch and The Intercept revealed MVM Inc. had confined Valentina Galvis, an asylum-seeker from Colombia, and her then seven-month-old infant, a U.S. citizen, in a room at the Sonesta Chicago O’Hare Airport Rosemont last summer. In that reporting, Galvis had described her captivity in stark terms, detailing how she and her son were locked in a room with no way to communicate with the outside world and no idea when, if ever, they would be set free.

Galvis is seeking monetary damages for the alleged harm and injury she and her child suffered as a result of the detention following their arrest by ICE at a Chicago immigration court in June 2025. Galvis named the Sonesta International Hotels Corporation and affiliated companies that own and operate the hotel as defendants in the complaint.

The lawsuit also named five Sonesta and two MVM executives and employees. It identifies JoAnna Granado as the MVM employee who transported Galvis and her son from the hotel to a federal office in Chicago on the day they were released, drawing on the original reporting in which Granado confirmed she was involved in the family’s detention.

Granado and other individuals named in the suit couldn’t be reached for comment. MVM didn’t respond to questions about the lawsuit. During the original investigation, Sonesta said that it “does not condone illegal behavior of any kind” at its hotels. The company declined to comment on the lawsuit.

The suit accused both the ICE contractor and the hotel of detaining Galvis and her child for profit, and alleged the companies engaged in a civil conspiracy by working together to use the hotel room as a detention cell.

“MVM, a federal contractor, physically seized, transported, and confined Ms. Galvis and her infant son,” the suit claimed. “Sonesta knowingly provided and maintained the hotel room used as a makeshift detention cell, profiting from the arrangement while a mother and her infant were locked inside.”

The suit seeks more than $50,000 in compensatory damages, plus punitive damages, and demands a jury trial.

In the complaint, Galvis alleged that her detention at MVM’s hands caused her and her baby a range of physical, emotional, and caregiving harm. Her son had just recently started transitioning to solid foods before the pair were seized by ICE; the suit alleged the infant was provided only scraps of food that were nutritionally inadequate for his age. Meanwhile, confinement-induced stress caused Galvis to decrease her breastmilk production at a time when her son needed it most.

Her baby suffered sleep disturbance and a worsening skin condition, the lawsuit claimed. While MVM had given Galvis an adequate change of clothing, the garments provided for her baby didn’t fit him. Because no laundry service was available, Galvis “washed [the infant’s] clothing in the bathroom sink multiple times,” she stated in an affidavit filed with the court, hanging “the wet clothes near the bed where the air conditioning would dry them quickly.” The infant wore only diapers while his clothes were being washed, and left the hotel on a Tuesday wearing the same outfit he’d worn since he and Galvis were detained by ICE the previous Thursday, according to the affidavit.

In court documents, Galvis alleged MVM confined her and her infant to a room near O’Hare International Airport. Galvis said she was sometimes told she would be taken to a Texas detention center and, on one occasion, that she would be deported to Colombia. She was released by MVM after a federal judge ordered that Galvis and her baby couldn’t be removed from Illinois.

The practice of using hotel rooms as makeshift detention sites has drawn little media attention; far more scrutiny has centered on conditions inside the growing network of ICE detention centers around the country. An inspector general’s report published last month found that ICE had failed to manage its detention space contracts. When asked about it at a September 30 press conference, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended facility conditions, saying detention centers meet and often exceed federal standards — and that comfort isn’t the department’s priority.

“We’re not providing Holiday Inns,” said Mullin.

While ICE agents don’t generally place people in hotels, the agency contracts with MVM to transport immigrant children and families; the contractor sometimes places them in hotel rooms across the U.S. Since fiscal year 2020, MVM has received more than $1.3 billion in ICE contracts, much of it for transporting families.

The lawsuit doesn’t name the federal government as a defendant.

William G. McLean III, who represents Galvis and her baby, underscored the companies’ role in their confinement. “The corporate defendants in this case unlawfully imprisoned and permanently traumatized my clients,” he said, “over five terrifying days after the Department of Homeland Security illegally arrested them.”

Galvis remains at risk of deportation — a final decision on her asylum claim is still pending in immigration court. She’s currently in therapy after an evaluation determined she’s experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the detention.

“I isolate myself to avoid anything that reminds me of what happened. I stay home and I do not go outside unless I really need to,” she said in an affidavit.

“Even now, when I go out, I get very nervous, and I feel terror.”

title: S.F. educators have a new role: Getting families through ICE appointments. - Mission Local
description:
For at least 50 immigrant families in San Francisco facing immigration appointments or court hearings, public-school teachers and staff have become a lifeline.
And, though volunteers across the country accompany immigrants to court and check-ins, the San Francisco program is the only known example of educators being organized and trained to attend appointments with students and students’ families.
Since January, 137 students and families in the San Francisco school system have been accompanied.
One morning, she was meant to meet two middle-school sisters at their school and take them to their immigration court hearing.
The relationships between educators and families is “building a web of community support” to counteract an immigration system that creates fear.
text:
On a recent Thursday, Carolina woke to loud, high-pitched electronic beeps from the bulky wrist monitor the federal government makes her wear.

The nerves set in. That morning, she had two immigration appointments in downtown San Francisco. The only saving grace: Ernesto Rodriguez, a social worker at her son’s elementary school in the Portola neighborhood. He was set to accompany her to the check-ins, as he has for about 10 other families from his school.

For at least 50 immigrant families in San Francisco facing immigration appointments or court hearings, public-school teachers and staff have become a lifeline.

Educators in 20 schools in the district have been trained to accompany students and families to immigration appointments as part of a collaboration between the school district, a nonprofit and the teachers’ union.

Missing a single appointment can mean a deportation order. For families too frightened to show up to a federal building alone, the presence of a familiar face can mean the difference between staying in the country and being forced out.

Still, fear kicks in. “I feel kind of strange … I feel bad, anxious, my back hurts,” Carolina, a pseudonym, told Mission Local that morning.

She decided to keep her two sons, 6 and 14, home from school while she went downtown.

Rodriguez, who had planned to pick her up at the school, quickly changed course and went to her home.

The educator-accompaniment program is a collaboration between the San Francisco Unified School District’s RiseSF office, which supports immigrant families; the nonprofit Faith in Action; and the teachers union.

If an appointment or court hearing results in an arrest, educators are trained to call the Rapid Response Hotline to find a lawyer to file a habeas petition for the immigrant’s release.

And, though volunteers across the country accompany immigrants to court and check-ins, the San Francisco program is the only known example of educators being organized and trained to attend appointments with students and students’ families. The teachers’ union covers the cost of a substitute teacher for the time away.

Since January, 137 students and families in the San Francisco school system have been accompanied. None have been arrested so far.

The morning check-in with ICE

After Carolina went downtown, she joined a line on the sidewalk outside 630 Sansome St., where dozens of immigrants waited, gripping folders with documents that could determine their future.

Carolina trembled as she neared the front of the line outside the federal building where she was scheduled to complete her first appointment of the day.

At the front, she said goodbye to Rodriguez, who would wait outside the building during her appointment, texting her sporadically to check in.

“My freedom has been stolen,” Carolina said as she stepped inside the building, where she would go through security and into her appointment alone. The woman behind her, who spoke Cantonese, cried as she, too, entered the building.

Fear of showing up

Most days, at least one immigrant walks into 630 Sansome for an appointment only to be arrested and taken through a back exit to a detention center, according to volunteers and activists who camp out during the day in front of the building.

But staying away from the building carries its own risk. One of the main ways the federal government deports people is by ordering them “removed in absentia” for missing a court hearing or appointment.

Jenny Tseng, a social worker at Aptos Middle School, saw how close a family can come to that outcome. One morning, she was meant to meet two middle-school sisters at their school and take them to their immigration court hearing. It was too dangerous for their parents to chaperone them.

Like Carolina, the family never showed up to school that morning. Tseng, two school counselors, and a volunteer went into emergency mode, called the mother, convinced her to meet them at a cafe and then took the girls to the courthouse.

In the end, the judge at San Francisco’s immigration courthouse rescheduled the case. But had they not shown up, the sisters could have been ordered removed, opening them up to arrest.

“That is how they win,” Tseng said.

Carolina’s first appointment that Thursday went smoothly.

Afterward, her 6-year-old son called to ask if she was done and would be home soon.

“I’m almost done, because now I have the check-in with the other immigration office,” she told him in Spanish.

He said he loved her.

“Yo también te amo, papi,” she said — “I love you too, sweetie.” She added, “Que Dios te proteja.” “May God protect you.”

Carolina’s second appointment

And so it’s on to the second appointment, a check-in at the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program on Tehama Street run by BI Incorporated, the private company contracted to provide ankle monitors and other surveillance gear to track immigrants.

Carolina reflected on the accompaniment program. “Thank God, along the way I found angels,” she said.

Matt Alexander, co-director of Faith in Action and a San Francisco school board member, said touchpoints between educators and immigrant families can also greatly improve how students fare at school.

When he takes children to these appointments, he said, “Their whole body is tense — they’re experiencing it as trauma. Once we leave and it’s clear nobody’s being detained or deported, and the case is moving forward, they’re relieved, they’re happy.”

A web of support

When Carolina initially had an issue with her asylum application but did not have a lawyer, Rodriguez, the social worker, pooled his money with Stefanie Eldred, another social worker at their school, to pay for a consultation.

“I’m just going to do this shit to do it,” said Rodriguez, whose mom is from Mexico. He said that in his family, supporting the community is a no-brainer. “​​It’s something you do.”

Rodriguez said he has accompanied around 10 parents of children from his school. He has also surveyed students to see who needs help connecting with immigration resources, and has found at least 30 such families at his school.

At International High School in Potrero Hill, which has a large number of immigrant students, Antoine Lagarde, a senior seminar instructor, noticed two of his students were worried and asked them what was going on.

The two students, 16 and 17, confided that their sister, a Peruvian mother of two whom they live with, was having problems with her immigration case. She was terrified she would be arrested at an upcoming court hearing and taken from the family.

Lagarde, who also volunteers with Faith in Action, invited the sister to one of the group’s meetings.

The 34-year-old mother was distraught.

“I was really worried, in a bad way. I didn’t want to eat,” she said in Spanish.

The contact with the teacher and Faith in Action meant she went to court with an entourage: Lagarde, another teacher from International High School, a SFUSD-contracted attorney who was there to observe, a Catholic priest, and Alexander. In the end, the woman’s hearing was rescheduled for next year.

“They gave me the strength to face going to court,” the woman said. The relationships between educators and families is “building a web of community support” to counteract an immigration system that creates fear.

Rodriguez, the social worker, recalled the moment when he got back to his school after a morning at an appointment with the mother of a second grader. The mother had asked him to let her daughter know all had gone well

He found the child on the playground and delivered the news.

“She got so happy, it was as if someone said, ‘It’s your birthday,’” Rodriguez said.

He watched as she ran to tell her friend the news, and then grabbed her friend’s hand to go play.

“This is the work that I love to do,” Rodriguez said.

A ride home

The day’s work with Carolina was done. As he got ready to drive her home, Rodriguez helped her log in to an SFUSD app where she could check her children’s grades and message teachers.

From the front seat of Rodriguez’s car, she used her phone to log in to the online course she is taking through City College. “She felt good. It was really sweet to see,” he said.

After dropping her off, Rodriguez felt relief. It had gone smoothly. He hopes to help more families. “I really want to get the word out so newcomer families do not feel like they’re alone,” he said. “We are not shying away from this.”

text:
US government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation".

The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.

The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.

Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved.

What is Omar being investigated for?

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband.

The Wall Street Journal reported that her cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time.

Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports.

Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.

Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.

Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship.

Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams".

US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.

How did Omar obtain her citizenship?

Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he has "no concerns" about her citizenship.

Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000.

According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18.

If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately.

Who is Omar's father?

After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker.

Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications.

According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee".

The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship.

Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991.

"[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator."

The BBC has reached out to Omar for comment.

Can Omar be deported?

The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected.

According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration.

Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is taken away. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process.

description:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday granted emergency relief for the Trump administration’s Federal Communications Commission in a dispute over political broadcast advertising rates ahead of the midterms.
A divided panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit sided with them again, accusing the FCC of “gamesmanship” ahead of the midterms.
The administration leaned on Wilkinson’s dissent when it turned back to the Supreme Court, seeking to halt the appellate order and Oct. 9 deadline.

text:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday granted emergency relief for the Trump administration’s Federal Communications Commission in a dispute over political broadcast advertising rates ahead of the midterms.

Over dissent from Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, it’s the second time in as many months that the high court has acted on the matter after backing Republicans in an earlier round as well.

At the heart of the litigation is the question of whether federal law only gives candidates themselves certain favorable rates, or whether political parties and joint fundraising committees with noncandidate members can also benefit. The FCC and GOP groups have argued for the latter interpretation, which stands to benefit them politically because Democratic candidates generally raise more money than their committees, and vice versa for Republicans.

Last month, the justices said that a federal appeals court lacked jurisdiction when it sided with four Democratic congressional candidates: Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio and former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina. Jackson dissented from that ruling.

The Democrats then brought another challenge to force the merits of the issue. A divided panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit sided with them again, accusing the FCC of “gamesmanship” ahead of the midterms.

“If allowed to continue dragging its feet, the FCC will have evaded meaningful judicial review of its newly created rule,” Judges Robert King and James Wynn wrote Oct. 7. The majority gave the FCC a 12 p.m. ET deadline on Oct. 9 to resolve the candidates’ application to review their challenge to the agency’s interpretation.

GOP-appointed Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III dissented from the Democratic-appointed majority’s order, calling it “a direct affront” to the high court’s prior ruling that favored Republicans.

The administration leaned on Wilkinson’s dissent when it turned back to the Supreme Court, seeking to halt the appellate order and Oct. 9 deadline. Chief Justice John Roberts, who fields emergency requests from the 4th Circuit, granted the agency temporary relief pending further word from the court.

More articles

In their opposition to the FCC, the Democrats said the agency was engaging in “blatant procedural trench warfare to stave off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is too late to matter.” They told the justices that they’re “up for election in just over three weeks” and are “experiencing exactly the deluge of party spending at the candidate rate that Republican Party committees promised to unleash to ‘obliterate’ them in response to the challenged agency directive.”

The national GOP senatorial and congressional committees brought a parallel Supreme Court challenge to the 4th Circuit order, which the Democrats likewise opposed.

The full Supreme Court weighed in on Wednesday, backing the administration in an unsigned opinion that said the appeals court improperly tried to force the FCC to act on that deadline.

“The Communications Act requires the Commission to act on every application it receives, but it does not obligate the Commission to act within a particular timeframe,” the court said over noted dissent from two of the court’s three Democratic-appointed justices, Sotomayor and Jackson. The pair did not explain their reasoning for dissenting.

The majority said it would be wrong to make the agency “triage its ongoing deliberation process and prepare a final order on an extremely expedited timeline.”

text:
Federal authorities investigating Minnesota U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar have seized her phone and issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to reports. The moves escalate a probe into her immigration paperwork as President Donald Trump renews attacks on her citizenship just weeks before the midterm elections.

The latest developments come two days after federal agents searched the Democrat's Washington, D.C.-area home and a day after Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro confirmed a separate investigation into the congresswoman’s financial disclosures, as Newsweek previously reported.

The Department of Justice told Newsweek that the October 12 search was part of “an ongoing federal criminal investigation” and confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in Washington.

Read More on News

Newsweek reached out to Omar’s campaign for comment via email Wednesday night.

What We Know About the Ilhan Omar Investigation

The subpoenas were issued by a grand jury gathering evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities investigate potential fraud involving Omar’s immigration paperwork, according to a person briefed on the probe who spoke to the Associated Press (AP) on condition of anonymity.

The Trump administration’s investigation into Omar is aimed at building a case to revoke her U.S. citizenship and deport her, according to a report Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal, which cited U.S. officials and others familiar with the probe. Investigators are examining how Omar obtained citizenship after arriving in the United States from Somalia, including actions taken by her late father, the outlet reported.

The investigation led federal agents to search Omar’s Washington-area residence.

The scope of the probe remains unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities are examining potential crimes related to Omar’s family immigration paperwork, according to the AP. Omar has not been publicly charged with a crime in connection with the investigation.

On Tuesday, Pirro said that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar, confirming that her office was also investigating the congresswoman’s financial disclosures.

“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said in an interview with Fox News.

Authorities have not publicly established if the financial investigation and immigration-related criminal probe are connected.

Trump Renews Attacks as Questions About Omar’s Citizenship Resurface

The investigations come amid renewed attacks from Trump, who has repeatedly questioned Omar’s background and called for scrutiny of her immigration history.

At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday, the president criticized Omar’s Somali origins and questioned her right to invoke the U.S. Constitution.

“She’s a disaster. She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said, prompting members of the crowd to chant “deport.”

On Tuesday, Trump called Omar a “terrible person” and a “terrible congresswoman.” He also declined to take a position on whether he wanted her deported.

Omar arrived in the United States as a refugee and became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000. She has represented Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District since 2019 and is seeking reelection in November.

The administration’s scrutiny of her immigration history has centered in part on a longstanding allegation that she married her brother to facilitate his entry into the United States. Omar has repeatedly denied the claim, which remains unproven.

Constitutional law professor Jonathan Turley said earlier Wednesday that Omar could face denaturalization if the government proves she provided false information that affected her eligibility for citizenship.

“The U.S. government’s position has always been that if you have information there that is untrue, where you would not have been made a citizen, then you can be denaturalized,” Turley said during a Fox News interview. He added that the standard of proof in denaturalization cases is high.

Omar Calls Search 'Political Intimidation' Ahead of Midterms

Omar condemned the search of her home, accusing the Trump administration of using federal law enforcement to target political opponents.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote on X.

“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced,” she added.

The search comes less than three weeks before the November midterm elections, drawing criticism from top Democrats, who called the raid “deeply disturbing.”

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” an October 12 joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats reads.

“Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”

title: Blue cities ask SCOTUS to rescue Biden-era immigration rule from backdoor deal
description:
At issue is a 2024 rule codifying a longstanding practice allowing immigration judges to temporarily pause removal proceedings under certain conditions.
They also request that the court prevent the Justice Department from enforcing the rule or enacting similar regulations in the future.
They said the “egregious collusion” in Texas’ case made it a compelling candidate for the court’s review.
And the Justice Department asked for a permanent injunction preventing future administrations from reinstituting the policy even though the government has previously acknowledged the harms of indefinitely binding future administrations.
The Supreme Court did not immediately respond to the cities’ application.
text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — A group of Democratic-led cities called for the Supreme Court on Thursday to disrupt a deal between Texas and the Trump administration ending a longstanding immigration practice through friendly litigation.

The cities say a Texas judge ignored their request to defend the Biden-era rule and instead rushed to approve an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice terminating the policy. They urged the Supreme Court to step in, warning against allowing the case to become an example for leveraging court rulings to achieve desired policy without the necessary review process.

“As long as this judgment serves as a viable template, this court’s holding that agencies must ‘use the same procedures when they amend or repeal a rule as they used to issue the rule in the first instance’ will be effectively a dead letter,” the cities wrote.

At issue is a 2024 rule codifying a longstanding practice allowing immigration judges to temporarily pause removal proceedings under certain conditions. The practice known as administrative closure could be used when an individual was pursuing protections through the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. And advocates say it often helped law enforcement secure cooperation from immigrant crime victims and witnesses.

Two years after the rule was adopted by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, Texas filed a lawsuit claiming the policy exceeded the agency’s authority. And the Lone Star State argued it allowed individuals without legal status to remain in the U.S. indefinitely.

Hours after the lawsuit was filed, Texas and the Department of Justice jointly asked the lower court to declare the 2024 rule unlawful and vacate it. They also request that the court prevent the Justice Department from enforcing the rule or enacting similar regulations in the future.

Later that day, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor, a George W. Bush appointee in the Northern District of Texas, agreed to eliminate the 2024 rule nationwide and permanently restricted the federal government from adopting similar protections in the future.

Legal services provider Centro Legal de la Raza moved to intervene along with the cities of Baltimore, Maryland, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut. The cities said if the judgment were to result in more deportations of noncitizens as Texas suggested, it would harm their revenue because their taxpayers would be deported.

Centro Legal de la Raza, which represents immigrants facing removal proceedings, said the judgment imposed substantial uncompensated legal work on the group.

Under what is known as rulemaking-by-collusive acquiescence, a new administration that is hostile to a regulation by its predecessor can leverage litigation brought by a friendly party to circumvent the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirements. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza said this case represents an “egregious new extension of this phenomenon.”

“The government did not merely leverage a convenient loss to undo agency action, but rather, announced in advance that it would not defend a disfavored regulation and then colluded with the challenger from the moment that suit was filed,” the cities wrote. “The result is that a significant regulation that established certain important procedures in immigration courts was erased over the course of a single day, without meaningful judicial review, public participation or adherence to the APA’s rulemaking requirements.”

In 2021, the Supreme Court attempted to answer whether interested states could intervene in similar cases where the federal government refused to defend its own rule, but the appeal was dismissed due to another change in administration.

The cities urged the justices to use their case to address these litigation tactics, noting that the practice of regulatory repeal by acquiescence has become increasingly common and effective. They said the “egregious collusion” in Texas’ case made it a compelling candidate for the court’s review.

“Texas sued more than two years after the rule was issued and only after the federal government announced that it ‘could not — and will not — defend’ the rule ‘against legal challenge,’” the cities wrote. “On the day Texas sued in the Wichita Falls Division of the Northern District of Texas, the parties jointly asked the sole district judge assigned to that division for identical relief.”

The cities also noted that the Justice Department didn’t challenge Texas’ standing even though the state’s theory of injury was similar to the arguments the Supreme Court recently rejected in a different case the federal government brought against the Lone Star State. And the Justice Department asked for a permanent injunction preventing future administrations from reinstituting the policy even though the government has previously acknowledged the harms of indefinitely binding future administrations.

“DOJ’s abandonment of the defenses it ordinarily presses confirms the absence of a genuine controversy,” the cities wrote.

The Supreme Court did not immediately respond to the cities’ application.

text:
If the rule is finalized, USCIS officers could still consider an earlier approval but would no longer begin from a position of deference to it.

On October 14, 2026, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), published a proposed rule (91 FR 65119; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529) that would remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). That regulation currently requires USCIS to defer to its prior eligibility determination when adjudicating a Form I-129 petition involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there is a material error, a material change or new material information that adversely affects eligibility. Comments are due November 13, 2026, providing a 30-day public comment period for interested parties to submit feedback on the proposed rule. Comments must reference DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529 and be submitted through regulations.gov by November 13, 2026.

Historical Background

USCIS first instructed officers to defer to prior approvals in a 2004 memorandum, citing consistency and efficiency. USCIS rescinded that guidance in 2017, reinstated it in the USCIS Policy Manual in 2021 and DHS codified it in December 2024 in the H-1B Modernization Final Rule. The current proposal would reverse that codification.

Key Change

If the rule is finalized, USCIS officers could still consider an earlier approval but would no longer begin from a position of deference to it. USCIS would also revise its current guidance requiring officers to explain, and obtain supervisory approval for, a decision not to defer. The change would impact every Form I-129 classification, including H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E and P petitions. It would most directly affect extensions with the same employer and could also affect certain amendment petitions.

The current regulation remains in effect unless and until a final rule is published and takes effect.

DHS’s Rationale

DHS argues that deference effectively shifts the burden of proof from the petitioner to the officer, discourages officers from requesting evidence and allows erroneous or fraudulent approvals to be carried forward. DHS estimates that deference applies to about 208,429 petitions a year and projects roughly 6,044 additional Requests for Evidence (RFEs) annually. DHS released the proposal the same day as a final rule confirming the end of automatic extensions for most employment authorization documents (EADs).

Impact on Employers and Foreign National Employees

If finalized, the rule is expected to have the following consequences:

Independent Review of Every Extension Petition

USCIS would make a new eligibility determination each time an extension petition is filed, without presuming that its prior approval was correct. Officers could therefore reconsider issues previously approved, including whether a position qualifies as a specialty occupation, a manager meets the L-1A requirements or a worker continues to satisfy the O-1 criteria.

More RFEs and Longer Processing

Petitions receiving an RFE took a median of 64 more days to decide, making adjudication times less predictable and workforce planning more difficult.

Work Authorization Continuity Risk

When an extension petition for the same employer is timely filed, the worker may generally continue working for up to 240 days after the authorized stay expires while the petition is pending. Longer processing times increase the likelihood that a petition filed under regular processing will remain pending beyond the 240-day period, requiring the worker to stop working until USCIS approves the petition. For families, delays are compounded by the end of automatic EAD extensions for dependents such as many H-4 spouses.

Greater Importance of Initial Filings

An initial approval would no longer serve as an anchor for later extensions. Job descriptions, wage levels, worksite information, organizational charts and qualifications presented in a new petition should be accurate and sustainable over the life of the worker's employment because inconsistencies between filings would be more likely to be questioned.

Recommended Employer Action Items

To reduce risk, employers should work with immigration counsel to:

Prepare extensions as full filings that document eligibility anew, rather than relying primarily on the prior approval notice and a short employer letter.

Identify petitions that will need extensions in the coming year and begin preparation well in advance, allowing time for a possible RFE.

Consider requesting premium processing with the extension petition or early enough to obtain a decision before the 240-day automatic extension of work authorization expires.

Compare each filing against prior petitions, Labor Condition Applications and visa applications, and address any changes in duties, worksite, compensation or corporate structure up front.

Draft initial petitions with the full life of the case in mind, and retain prior petitions, supporting evidence, RFE responses and approval notices for use in later filings.

Consider submitting a comment. Comments must reference DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529 and be submitted through regulations.gov by November 13, 2026. Comments submitted by email, mail or hand delivery will not be considered, and submitted comments, including personal information, will be made public.

Next Steps

We are closely monitoring this rulemaking. Employers should begin reviewing upcoming extensions and filing practices now and may want to consider budgeting for higher cost of extension filings, including possible RFE responses and premium processing fees.

For More Information

text:
This story was reported and produced by Injustice Watch, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago that investigates issues of equity and justice in the court system. Sign up here to get their weekly newsletter.

After being detained for five days in an airport hotel, a mother filed suit against a longtime Immigration and Customs Enforcement contractor on behalf of herself and her now 23-month-old son, alleging false imprisonment among other counts.

The lawsuit was filed on September 29, more than a year after an investigation by Injustice Watch and The Intercept revealed MVM Inc. had confined Valentina Galvis, an asylum-seeker from Colombia, and her then seven-month-old infant, a U.S. citizen, in a room at the Sonesta Chicago O’Hare Airport Rosemont last summer. In that reporting, Galvis had described her captivity in stark terms, detailing how she and her son were locked in a room with no way to communicate with the outside world and no idea when, if ever, they would be set free.

Galvis is seeking monetary damages for the alleged harm and injury she and her child suffered as a result of the detention following their arrest by ICE at a Chicago immigration court in June 2025. Galvis named the Sonesta International Hotels Corporation and affiliated companies that own and operate the hotel as defendants in the complaint.

The lawsuit also named five Sonesta and two MVM executives and employees. It identifies JoAnna Granado as the MVM employee who transported Galvis and her son from the hotel to a federal office in Chicago on the day they were released, drawing on the original reporting in which Granado confirmed she was involved in the family’s detention.

Granado and other individuals named in the suit couldn’t be reached for comment. MVM didn’t respond to questions about the lawsuit. During the original investigation, Sonesta said that it “does not condone illegal behavior of any kind” at its hotels. The company declined to comment on the lawsuit.

The suit accused both the ICE contractor and the hotel of detaining Galvis and her child for profit, and alleged the companies engaged in a civil conspiracy by working together to use the hotel room as a detention cell.

“MVM, a federal contractor, physically seized, transported, and confined Ms. Galvis and her infant son,” the suit claimed. “Sonesta knowingly provided and maintained the hotel room used as a makeshift detention cell, profiting from the arrangement while a mother and her infant were locked inside.”

The suit seeks more than $50,000 in compensatory damages, plus punitive damages, and demands a jury trial.

In the complaint, Galvis alleged that her detention at MVM’s hands caused her and her baby a range of physical, emotional, and caregiving harm. Her son had just recently started transitioning to solid foods before the pair were seized by ICE; the suit alleged the infant was provided only scraps of food that were nutritionally inadequate for his age. Meanwhile, confinement-induced stress caused Galvis to decrease her breastmilk production at a time when her son needed it most.

Her baby suffered sleep disturbance and a worsening skin condition, the lawsuit claimed. While MVM had given Galvis an adequate change of clothing, the garments provided for her baby didn’t fit him. Because no laundry service was available, Galvis “washed [the infant’s] clothing in the bathroom sink multiple times,” she stated in an affidavit filed with the court, hanging “the wet clothes near the bed where the air conditioning would dry them quickly.” The infant wore only diapers while his clothes were being washed, and left the hotel on a Tuesday wearing the same outfit he’d worn since he and Galvis were detained by ICE the previous Thursday, according to the affidavit.

In court documents, Galvis alleged MVM confined her and her infant to a room near O’Hare International Airport. Galvis said she was sometimes told she would be taken to a Texas detention center and, on one occasion, that she would be deported to Colombia. She was released by MVM after a federal judge ordered that Galvis and her baby couldn’t be removed from Illinois.

The practice of using hotel rooms as makeshift detention sites has drawn little media attention; far more scrutiny has centered on conditions inside the growing network of ICE detention centers around the country. An inspector general’s report published last month found that ICE had failed to manage its detention space contracts. When asked about it at a September 30 press conference, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended facility conditions, saying detention centers meet and often exceed federal standards — and that comfort isn’t the department’s priority.

“We’re not providing Holiday Inns,” said Mullin.

While ICE agents don’t generally place people in hotels, the agency contracts with MVM to transport immigrant children and families; the contractor sometimes places them in hotel rooms across the U.S. Since fiscal year 2020, MVM has received more than $1.3 billion in ICE contracts, much of it for transporting families.

The lawsuit doesn’t name the federal government as a defendant.

William G. McLean III, who represents Galvis and her baby, underscored the companies’ role in their confinement. “The corporate defendants in this case unlawfully imprisoned and permanently traumatized my clients,” he said, “over five terrifying days after the Department of Homeland Security illegally arrested them.”

Galvis remains at risk of deportation — a final decision on her asylum claim is still pending in immigration court. She’s currently in therapy after an evaluation determined she’s experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the detention.

“I isolate myself to avoid anything that reminds me of what happened. I stay home and I do not go outside unless I really need to,” she said in an affidavit.

“Even now, when I go out, I get very nervous, and I feel terror.”

At issue in the citizenship inquiry is whether Omar or her late father altered her age in immigration paperwork to indicate that she was 17 rather than 18 when her father applied for citizenship, the Journal reported.

According to the newspaper, investigators are examining whether that allowed her to acquire citizenship through her father rather than having to undergo a separate application process.

Omar’s father died in 2020, complicating efforts to collect evidence on whether Omar lied about her own age – which, according to a former top immigration official in the Justice Department, the Trump administration would hinge its case on – or whether her father lied on her behalf.

The Journal also reported that Homeland Security Investigations officials examined a similar allegation during the administration of former President Joe Biden but did not pursue it because they lacked evidence of fraud.

The newspaper did not report that anyone had filed a lawsuit seeking to revoke Omar’s citizenship. Such a case would require court proceedings, as the investigation itself does not revoke her citizenship or authorise her deportation.

The newspaper reported that a nonpartisan congressional watchdog had earlier cleared Omar of wrongdoing over disclosures that overstated her assets.

Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), searched Omar’s home under what the department called a “judicially authorized search warrant”.

On Monday morning, agents blocked off the street around Omar’s home and removed boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.

Omar, a prominent progressive Democrat, has faced years of attacks from Trump and his allies over her Somali background and immigration history.

Hours after the Monday raid, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.

title: Undocumented students still eligible for in-state tuition after federal court ruling
authors: Allie Pitchon, Charlottesville Tomorrow, Charlottesville Inclusive Media, Atlee Webber, Alana Bittner, Andra Landi, Jessie Higgins
description:
Undocumented students in Virginia still qualify for in-state college tuition after an Oct. 5 ruling from a federal judge, but the legal battle is likely to continue, as reported by 29 News.
For example, a first-year student eligible for in-state tuition at the University of Virginia’s college of arts and sciences would pay approximately $20,000 in tuition and fees compared to nearly $60,000 for an out-of-state student.
After Attorney General Jay Jones, a Democrat, took office in January 2026, he immediately moved to defend the Dream Act in court.
