text:
Undocumented students in Virginia still qualify for in-state college tuition after an Oct. 5 ruling from a federal judge, but the legal battle is likely to continue, as reported by 29 News.

The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Virginia in December 2025 to challenge the Dream Act, a 2020 Virginia law granting in-state college tuition and financial aid eligibility to some immigrant students. To be eligible, they must have attended Virginia high schools for at least two years and have filed (or their parents have filed) state income taxes for at least two years.

The DOJ argued that the Virginia Dream Act conflicts with the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act by granting educational benefits to undocumented students that are not available to U.S. citizens from other states. On Dec. 30, former Republican Attorney General Jason Miyares agreed to seek a court order preventing the state from enforcing the law.

The following day, the Legal Aid Justice Center and American Civil Liberties Union filed motions on behalf of Virginia’s Dream Project to intervene in the lawsuit, arguing that the Dream Act only offers a pathway to in-state tuition for those who meet specific Virginia high school and tax requirements.

Legal Defense Fund Senior Counsel Antonio Ingram agreed with the LAJC and ACLU.

“I think the logic that the DOJ is utilizing is very faulty,” Ingram told Charlottesville Tomorrow in January 2026. “They’re essentially saying undocumented students are getting benefits that citizens from other states cannot get in Virginia, but I think that’s a faulty framing, because the comparative population is fellow Virginia residents, not U.S. citizens.”

“That’s why the Dream Act in Virginia was passed,” Ingram added. “Because they grew up in these communities, they went to high school in these communities, and they have no other country to call home.”

In state-tuition is typically significantly less costly than the alternative. For example, a first-year student eligible for in-state tuition at the University of Virginia’s college of arts and sciences would pay approximately $20,000 in tuition and fees compared to nearly $60,000 for an out-of-state student.

After Attorney General Jay Jones, a Democrat, took office in January 2026, he immediately moved to defend the Dream Act in court.

However, the legal battle is likely to continue, with the federal judge’s opinion describing an appeal as a “virtual certainty,” 29 News reported. According to the outlet, Jones’ office is prepared to continue defending the law if the federal government appeals. An appeal would first go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and could ultimately reach the U.S. Supreme Court.

For now, the ruling allows eligible immigrant students to continue receiving in-state tuition.

The Virginia legal battle is part of a broader national push by the Trump administration to end in-state tuition for eligible undocumented students.

The DOJ has filed 25 lawsuits challenging such policies across the country since June 2025, as reported by Inside Higher Ed. So far, Virginia and Minnesota have upheld their policies, while in Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska, Republican attorneys general joined the federal government in seeking to end their states’ policies. A federal judge struck down Illinois’ tuition law, as reported by The Washington Post (registration or subscription required).

While we can’t cover every story that’s important to you, we do our best to be responsive to your needs. We use tips from readers to choose which stories to cover, to incorporate information into broader reports or to help us decide how to grow Charlottesville Tomorrow. Here’s where you can tell us what you think we should be covering.

name: Litigation
title: Bring Judicial Transparency Into the Internet Age | Knight First Amendment Institute
description:
The common law has long acknowledged just this, recognizing an affirmative, qualified, public right to inspect and copy judicial records.
Many courts—state and federal—have found that the First Amendment independently ensures public access to most judicial records.
Yet, many state criminal court records, tax court records, and even records of certain federal civil proceedings are not available for inspection online.
It is high time to end this impediment to meaningful judicial transparency and mandate online, electronic access to judicial records as the default rule.
Tax Court Rule 27(b) draws a strict line between party access and public access, providing public online access only to the docket and any court opinion or order.
text:
Public confidence in our justice system demands transparent proceedings and open records. Transparency in criminal prosecutions “guards against the miscarriage of justice by subjecting the police, prosecutors, and judicial processes to extensive public scrutiny and criticism,” 1. Sheppard v. Maxwell, 384 U.S. 333, 350 (1966).and transparency in civil litigation similarly empowers the press and public to check abuse and promotes “the appearance of fairness so essential to public confidence in the system.” 2. Press-Enterprise Co. v. Superior Court, 478 U.S. 1, 9 (1986) (internal marks and citation omitted).

The transparency imperative applies to the records of judicial proceedings just as fully as it does to the proceedings themselves. Access to records in criminal cases is essential because nearly all prosecutions today are resolved through plea deals, with no formal evidentiary proceedings. 3. According to the U.S. Sentencing Commission, in FY2023 more than 97% of the sentences imposed in federal court were entered on a plea of guilty to the crime charged. U.S. Sentencing Commission, 2023 Annual Report at 16, https://www.ussc.gov/about/annual-report-2023The same is true in civil litigation, where federal data shows that trials are held in less than 1 percent of civil lawsuits, with most resolved through dismissal, summary judgment, or settlement. 4. Jeffrey Smith and Grant McQueen, “Going, Going, But Not Quite Gone: Trials Continue to Decline in Federal and State Courts. Does it Matter?”, Judicature, Vol. 101, No. 4 (Winter 2017), https://judicature.duke.edu/articles/going-going-but-not-quite-gone-trials-continue-to-decline-in-federal-and-state-courts-does-it-matter/The public’s ability to follow and understand what transpires within the justice system is merely theoretical if the motion papers and other material filed with the court are not available for review. The common law has long acknowledged just this, recognizing an affirmative, qualified, public right to inspect and copy judicial records. 5. See, e.g., Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 597 (1978); United States v. Amodeo, 71 F.3d 1044, 1048 (2d Cir. 1995); In re Cont’l Ill. Sec. Litig., 732 F.2d 1302, 1308 (7th Cir. 1984). Many courts—state and federal—have found that the First Amendment independently ensures public access to most judicial records. 6. E.g., U.S. v. Ochoa-Vasquez, 428 F.3d 1015, 1030 (11th Cir. 2005); In re Search Warrant, 855 F.2d 569, 573 (8th Cir. 1988); In re NBC, Inc., 828 F.2d 340, 346-47 (6th Cir. 1987); In re N.Y. Times Co., 828 F.2d 110, 114 (2d Cir. 1987); Associated Press v. In re Washington Post Co., 807 F.2d 383, 390 (4th Cir. 1986); In re Globe Newspaper Co., 729 F.2d 47, 52 (1st Cir. 1984); Associated Press v. U.S. Dist. Ct., 705 F.2d 1143, 1145 (9th Cir. 1983); Grube v. Trader, 420 P.3d 343, 353 (Haw. 2018); Daily Press, Inc. v. Commonwealth, 739 S.E.2d 636, 640 (Va. 2013); Republican Co. v. Appeals Ct., 812 N.E.2d 887, 892 n. 8 (Mass. 2004); Skolnick v. Altheimer & Gray, 730 N.E.2d 4, 16 (Ill. 2000); Wichita Eagle Beacon Co. v. Owens, 27 P.3d 881, 883 (Kan. 2001); State v. Schaefer, 599 A.2d 337, 342 (Vt. 1991).

Yet, many state criminal court records, tax court records, and even records of certain federal civil proceedings are not available for inspection online. It is high time to end this impediment to meaningful judicial transparency and mandate online, electronic access to judicial records as the default rule. This can largely be done without new technology investments, without undermining privacy interests, and without imposing new administrative burdens on court clerks.

State Court Transparency Problems

At the dawn of the internet, when court records were filed on paper and transferred to digital form by the clerk’s office, many states adopted rules prohibiting public online access to criminal court records to protect private data and to avoid the dissemination of incorrectly transcribed information. 7. See, e.g., Electronic Access to Criminal and Family Court Records: Hearing on S. 246 Before the U.S. Judiciary Comm., 2007-2008 Leg. (Vt. Jan.11, 2008) (audio recording , pt.2, at 10:03-14:16); Electronic Access to Criminal and Family Court Records: Hearing on S. 246 Before the S. Judiciary Comm., 2007-2008 Leg. (Vt. Jan.11, 2008)(audio recording, pt.3, at 30:09-31:31) (indicating that Vermont prohibited online criminal record access out of concern that dockets placed online could contain errors generated by court clerks transcribing information from paperfiles by hand, and to protect litigants’ ostensible privacy interests).But today, lawyers are nearly universally required to file motion papers electronically and have an ethical obligation to redact certain private data from judicial records. The reasons for the initial restrictions on remote electronic access no longer apply, yet many persist. Nearly two-thirds of states still have rules limiting public online access to criminal court records to some degree even though the need for online record access applies with particular force to criminal proceedings, where the public and press’s interest in real-time oversight is at its peak, and where criminal defendants, once charged, possess significantly diminished privacy interests in the unsealed records of their cases.

The access restrictions vary from state to state. Typically, the technology is in place to allow online access to the court file in a criminal prosecution, but remote access is restricted to the parties and their attorneys. The public is denied remote access to motion papers and related filings in criminal prosecutions, so these can be viewed only at the courthouse, in person, during operating hours, where the records are accessed electronically through an online terminal, just as they could readily be accessed from home or an office. These bans on remote access make it extremely burdensome for journalists and members of the public to follow the course of a criminal prosecution and to monitor the functioning of the criminal courts. Simply learning the reasoning behind the parties’ motions or assessing the reasonableness of their positions requires a significant investment of time and effort. And to obtain a copy of a record for future reference, a reporter must generally pay the clerk to print a hard copy or take pictures of each page on the court terminal with a phone.

Federal Court Transparency Problems

The same prohibition against public online access to motions and other filings readily available to the parties exists in federal tax courts. Tax Court Rule 27(b) draws a strict line between party access and public access, providing public online access only to the docket and any court opinion or order. Full electronic access to case files is only available in person at the courthouse.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2(c) similarly prohibits online press or public access to, inter alia, any “action or proceeding relating to an order of removal, to relief from removal, or to immigration benefits or detention.” Under this rule, “[u]nless the court orders otherwise,” public online record access is restricted to the docket sheet and any court order ultimately entered; individuals must travel to the courthouse to access motion papers, supporting evidentiary submissions, and all other records through an online terminal. Because of Rule 5.2(c), more than 50,000 habeas corpus petitions filed in recent immigration cases are public only in theory. 8. Madeleine O’Neill, “The Rabbit Hole: How the search for one court record became a nationwide movement.” Court Watch (June 7, 2026), https://www.courtwatch.news/p/the-rabbit-hole-how-the-search-for-one-court-record-became-a-nationwide-movement.

Each of these state and federal rules reverses the working presumption at common law that judicial records are not hidden from public view. They deny meaningful access to records the public has a substantial interest in seeing, make it more likely that misconduct and abuse will go undetected, and reduce public confidence that justice is being done.

A Straightforward Solution

Because most courts now require parties to submit records online in digital format, and maintain those records electronically, the public right of access must be recognized as a right to access those records where they exist, online. The internet has become the “principal source[] for knowing current events,” 9. Packingham v. North Carolina, 582 U.S. 98, 107 (2017). and requiring a courthouse visit to inspect a record imposes a serious impediment to the transparency that is “pivotal to public perception of the judiciary’s legitimacy and independence.” 10. U.S. v. Aref, 533 F.3d 72, 83 (2d Cir. 2008) (internal quotations and citation omitted).

This impediment can readily be removed by amending the offending court rules or, if needed, through legislation declaring a qualified right of online public access to court records. Such a law would:

Contain legislative findings about the importance of transparency to maintain confidence in our system of justice and affirm the value of contemporaneous online public access to court records;

Define broadly the “judicial records” presumptively available for online public inspection to include everything filed with a court that is relevant to the performance of the judicial function and useful in the judicial process, regardless of whether a judge ultimately chooses to use the record in determining a litigant’s substantive legal rights; and

11. See Lugosch v. Pyramid Co. of Onondaga, 435 F.3d 110, 121-123 (2d Cir.) (explaining need for broad definition of the “judicial records” presumptively available for public inspection).

Require that such judicial records must be available to the public online, absent a judicial determination, made on a record-by-record basis, that a compelling governmental interest requires an exemption from the requirement for online access.

The law would remove any requirement for physical presence in a courthouse to examine a judicial record but would not limit a court’s ability to seal records from public view under existing standards. Privacy, safety, and other considerations currently deemed sufficient to justify sealing a record or otherwise restricting public access would not be altered, but the practice of keeping large categories of court records behind a barrier would be ended.

Acknowledgements

This comment draws on research by Yale Law students Hannah Berkman, Abi Heath, Ara Johnson, Nick Jones, Bryce Morales, Ryan Fore, and Anna Selbrede.

name: Human Rights
title: Complicity and Consequence: U.S. Alignment with El Salvador's Human Rights Violations
description:
Moreover, El Salvador’s human rights violations are a threat to the reputation and legality of the U.S. deportation system both domestically and internationally.
Years of unfettered human rights abuses reveal a systemic pattern: Human rights violations are enabled and empowered by leadership at the top and carried out across the many branches of government and security forces.
El Salvador’s gang crisis did not begin in El Salvador but in the U.S.
The State Department omitted all accusations of “significant human rights violations” from its 2024 Human Rights report.
Considering the changes in scope and omitted content in its 2024 Human Rights Report, the State Department’s 2025 Human Rights Report on El Salvador will likely downplay El Salvador’s human rights violations, if it is published at all.
text:
As the U.S. continues to deport a record number of people as part of U.S. President Donald Trump’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants, El Salvador has become a key partner in the country’s immigration enforcement apparatus. That partnership has evolved from diplomatic to transactional, as the State Department has paid El Salvador $6 million since January 2025 to detain a combination of Salvadoran deportees and third-country deportees.

The United States’ immigration enforcement apparatus already operates in breach of its international legal obligations, including the principle of nonrefoulement. Financing detention in a country whose security forces have faced sustained, well-documented allegations of torture, including in the State Department’s own reporting, compounds that exposure. It places U.S. enforcement further along a continuum of complicity in serious human rights abuses. Any such arrangement should therefore be conditioned on verifiable standards for detention conditions and treatment, so that U.S.-supported detention does not facilitate foreign torture or other abuses.

The State Department’s El Salvador 2024 Human Rights Report (HRR) omitted significant abuses, a clear break from over 20 years of consistent documentation. This marks a crucial shift in either the State Department’s monitoring or substantial reform to El Salvador’s security apparatus. In 2024, the same year the HRR covers, El Salvador’s incarceration rate climbed to the highest in the world, approximately 1,917 per 100,000 people, under a state of emergency that suspended due process and was linked to arbitrary detentions and deaths in custody. With emerging evidence on El Salvador’s current abuses, it appears that the State Department’s reporting will continue downplaying the ongoing abuse in pursuit of this administration’s immigration agenda.

To ensure the credibility and validity of its immigration/deportation apparatus, the U.S. government should distance itself from El Salvador. This complicity in El Salvador’s abuses degrades the long-standing credibility of the HRRs’ findings. Moreover, El Salvador’s human rights violations are a threat to the reputation and legality of the U.S. deportation system both domestically and internationally. Outsourcing immigration enforcement to governments with entrenched records of abuse binds U.S. policy to partners it cannot control. Each documented violation becomes a legal, diplomatic, and political liability that Washington inherits, handing adversaries a ready-made case against U.S. credibility and exposing the arrangement to litigation, congressional backlash, and collapse.

El Salvador, among other countries examined by the State Department, has perpetrated significant human rights abuses for decades. As early as 1999, the State Department noted poor prison conditions, prison abuse, arbitrary detentions, and corrupt judges. By 2001, El Salvador’s own pretrial detention data shows over half the prison population was being held before conviction, a widely recognized indicator of systemic overcrowding. This pattern of overcrowding and abuse continues for the following 22 years.

The consistency of this reporting reveals a persistent institutional failure to uphold basic human rights standards. The repetition of similar violations year after year suggests that the problem isn’t a lack of awareness, but a lack of political will to reform the security policies driving mass incarceration.

According to the 2011 report, prison conditions were “dangerously substandard.” In the 2012 report, the State Department flagged evidence of El Salvador’s government restricting freedom of speech and the press from covering the situation in the prisons. This marked a turning point. As the government silenced journalists and human rights watchdogs, accountability became increasingly difficult, and abuses of prisoners could expand unchecked. Beginning in 2012, the scale and scope of human rights abuses escalated.

In 2023, credible evidence of the military arbitrarily killing or disappearing people, serious government corruption, invasion of privacy, and intimidation/censorship/legal attacks on journalists and human rights organizations, accompanied by the aforementioned prison abuse, informed that year’s human rights report. Years of unfettered human rights abuses reveal a systemic pattern: Human rights violations are enabled and empowered by leadership at the top and carried out across the many branches of government and security forces.

Salvadoran presidents have repeatedly thrown their support behind security forces, streamlined the arrest process, and dehumanized detainees in public rhetoric, thereby creating the conditions for widespread abuse. Including the military in enforcement, the police in arrests, and the government in fast-tracked prosecution in a system of abuse is legally significant as it transforms scattered incidents of abuse into conduct attributable to the state itself.

El Salvador’s gang crisis did not begin in El Salvador but in the U.S. Both MS-13 and Barrio 18 formed in Los Angeles among Salvadoran refugees fleeing their country’s civil war. Following waves of mass deportations back to their country in the 1990s, thousands of gang-affiliated youth arrived in an El Salvador that had almost no institutional capacity to handle them. By the early 2010s, the two gangs had turned El Salvador into one of the most violent countries on earth. In 2015, the country’s murder rate was the highest in the world. President Nayib Bukele was elected in 2019 on promises of anticorruption initiatives and a stronger security apparatus to solve the gang problem. This same expansion of detention later made the country an attractive partner for Trump’s deportation policy.

Bukele promised an “iron fist” approach to crime upon taking office, shifting El Salvador’s crime-ridden trajectory substantially. In 2022, when gang violence spiked, so did Bukele’s strategy in response. In March 2022, he announced a state of emergency. With this increased authority, each increase in crime became a vehicle for amassing Bukele’s executive power. The U.S. State Department’s 2023 report suggests that prior to the state of emergency, Salvadoran prisons were already well beyond capacity. The mass arrests that followed, many without evidence, further exacerbated prison overcrowding.

The scale of these arrests is central to understanding the current crisis. By prioritizing rapid detention over evidence-based arrests, the Salvadoran government effectively traded due process for immediate security gains. While this approach yielded reductions in crime, it simultaneously overwhelmed the capacity of the prisons and eroded any remaining legal safeguards designed to prevent abuse.

Despite the opening of mega-prisons like CECOT, El Salvador’s largest Terrorism Confinement Center, Salvadoran prisons remained widely overcrowded and rife with human rights violations. According to accounts from prisoners held at CECOT, most deportees held were subject to abuse in some form. The abuses included instances of food and water deprivation, inadequate sanitation, denial of medical services, sleep deprivation, beatings, rape, and torture, documented in the State Department’s 2023 report and in another report by Human Right Watch. The U.S. role in transporting deportees into these dangerous conditions constitutes a serious breach of national, regional, and international laws.

Given the documented conditions inside Salvadoran prisons, continued U.S.-supported detention should be conditioned on independent access to detention facilities and detainees and continuous human rights monitoring. Regular monitoring would provide a mechanism to verify conditions rather than relying solely on assurances from the Salvadoran government. Such oversight need not preclude cooperation with Bukele, despite criticism of his treatment of alleged gang members, he remains widely popular among the Salvadoran population and internationally.

The Trump administration pursued mass removals as a signature priority, but doing so meant finding a partner willing to detain migrants the U.S. labeled as gang members or “terrorists“. Bukele’s El Salvador, with its state of emergency and CECOT, offered a solution.

Early in his second term, Trump moved quickly to formalize a deportation arrangement. In exchange for the confinement of approximately 300 Venezuelans and Salvadorans, Trump would send $6 million to El Salvador, with another $15 million allocated for the detention of additional deportees. Bukele could arrange the holding location for U.S. deportees, and in exchange, the U.S. could provide financing for El Salvador’s struggling economy.

Because U.S. funds directly support this detention arrangement, Washington retains leverage over the conditions under which cooperation continues. That leverage could include suspending funding or transfers when Salvadoran authorities fail to meet established human rights benchmarks such as the Nelson Mandela rules.

This continued stream of deportees worsens El Salvador’s detention crisis. Sending additional detainees into prisons already operating beyond capacity increases the risk of abuse and expands the number of people exposed to it. More importantly, transferring U.S. detainees into a detention system marked by credible reports of torture and inhumane treatment may itself violate U.S. and international legal obligations.

The International Law Commission’s draft Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts is central to understanding the implications of this arrangement. Under international law, a state may be responsible for its direct actions as well as for aiding or assisting another state in committing internationally wrongful acts. By knowingly transferring deportees into a system where cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment are well documented, and paying El Salvador for it, the United States risks being complicit in those violations.

The principle of nonrefoulement, which prohibits transferring people to a state in which they face a substantial risk of torture or inhumane treatment, further governs this arrangement. Given the State Department’s extensive documentation of abuse in Salvadoran prisons, the threshold for “knowledge” is arguably met. This evidence transforms the deportations into a legally actionable violation. At minimum, the United States must verify the legal basis and destination of each transfer before deportation occurs to avoid potential state responsibility, sanctions, or civil and criminal liability. Such verification should include an assessment of whether the receiving country presents a foreseeable risk of torture, arbitrary detention, or other prohibited treatment.

With Trump and Bukele’s arrangement, hundreds of deportees were funneled into CECOT in March and April 2025, where CECOT’s director greeted them with, “Welcome to my prison…. You are here as convicts…. The only way out of here [is] in a black bag.” This showcases exactly what they were going to be subjected to in CECOT and other detention facilities in El Salvador: no due process, no expectation of release, no appeal to law, and being held incommunicado.

Many deportees were removed without a trial in the United States, leaving their alleged violations untested in court and the legality of the deportations themselves unsettled in several Supreme Court cases. Furthermore, the limited documentation surrounding the deportations made it difficult to trace where individual deportees were sent within El Salvador, amounting to what Human Rights Watch claims to be enforced disappearances and arbitrary detention. Without adequate tracking, these individuals are at high risk of abuse. A disappearance into a massive prison system without the means of communicating outside that system means that prison casualties could go unreported.

By limiting transparency regarding who is deported, where they are sent, and under what legal authority, both governments reduce the likelihood of legal challenges and public scrutiny. This obfuscation complicates efforts by families, lawyers, and human rights organizations to track detainees or advocate on their behalf. Documentation gaps further shield officials from accountability by making it difficult to determine which agency, official, or government authorized a specific transfer, detention, or act of abuse. Closing these documentation gaps should therefore be a prerequisite for continued transfers. The United States and El Salvador should maintain accessible records identifying who is transferred, the legal authority for each transfer, and the facility in which each individual is held.

These deportees were not given due process in the United States. The Trump administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act, allowing for the deportation of immigrants without a standard trial, but due process remains a key concern for judges, politicians, and academics alike, as well as a foundational right in the U.S. Constitution. In March 2025, one of the many planes shuttling El Salvadoran and Venezuelan deportees to CECOT was blocked from taking off by a federal judge. Despite the verbal order, the plane took off anyway.

The Immigration and Nationality Act, international treaties such as the U.N. Convention Against Torture (UNCAT), and various inter-American treaties (signed and ratified by El Salvador) note that U.S. and El Salvador are in violation of treaty obligations. The American Convention on Human Rights​ and the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture​ provide legal pathways for El Salvador’s prosecution.

Despite El Salvador’s disregard for international law, the State Department’s response has been to narrow, rather than expand, its reporting of abuses. The State Department omitted all accusations of “significant human rights violations” from its 2024 Human Rights report. Released in August 2025, the report on El Salvador in 2024 omits the prison conditions that featured prominently in each of the preceding reports. The 2024 report’s omission of previously documented abuses coincides with the period in which the U.S.-El Salvador detention arrangement was being formalized, a point that warrants additional scrutiny given the absence of independent evidence that conditions improved. El Salvador’s violations in the reports notably peaked in 2022, only two years prior.

Human Rights First President and CEO Uzra Zeya has described the broader rewrite of the reports as an abandonment of values integral to U.S. national security, arguing that the administration has bent human rights policy tools toward rewarding abusive partners rather than scrutinizing them. An accompanying Human Rights First press release warns that the HRRs particularly misrepresented countries that are aligned with the Trump administration’s political interests. These discrepancies warrant an independent review of the 2024 Human Rights Report and the methodology used to assess detention conditions by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO). Restoring confidence in State Department reporting requires determining whether the omissions reflected changes in conditions or shortcomings in the reporting process.

Other warning signs suggest that El Salvador is doing its part to restrict independent reporting and civil society access. In July 2025, Cristosal, El Salvador’s leading human rights organization, fled the country after a series of government threats and arrests, including the head of Cristosal’s anti-corruption and justice program, Ruth Lopez.

The forced exit of one of El Salvador’s only human rights organizations further entrenches the lack of transparency surrounding prison conditions and detainee treatment. Without independent observers on the ground, the flow of reliable information diminishes, allowing abuses to continue with even less scrutiny. Now, more than ever, a push for transparency from both the U.S. and El Salvador is necessary to ensure accountability.

Established legal mechanisms are in place to address immigration law violations, and states retain the sovereign right to control their borders. The method of enforcement of these civil offenses is equally important. Deportation cannot become a vehicle for exposing individuals to torture, indefinite detention, or inhumane treatment. The distinction is critical: When enforcement practices drift outside legal boundaries, they do more than violate statutory and treaty obligations; they erode U.S. credibility, weaken its ability to assert moral authority abroad, and expose it to reputational and diplomatic consequences.

Key members of Trump’s Cabinet, such as Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, describe immigration as an invasion in sweeping justifications of U.S. deportations. Framing this issue as a binary choice between border security and human rights is both misleading and dangerous. Effective immigration enforcement and adherence to legal and ethical standards are not mutually exclusive; in fact, they are complementary. When enforcement mechanisms violate human rights, they undermine the legitimacy of the laws they are intended to uphold.

The U.S. decision to partner with El Salvador in this capacity reflects a broader willingness to prioritize expediency over legality and human rights, the same shift El Salvador made just a few years ago. In doing so, the United States risks the foundational values that underpin its legal and political system.

Without a change in course, the trajectory outlined above – continued transfers, documentation gaps, and divergence between State Department reporting and independent findings – carries numerous consequences. Abuses within El Salvador’s detention system will continue without the external scrutiny that accurate reporting is designed to enable. Simultaneously, continued reliance on expedited removals and wartime authorities such as the Alien Enemies Act weakens the due process protections that constrain executive power domestically. Moreover, the U.S. pattern of noncompliance with judicial orders to return wrongfully deported individuals establishes precedent for executive action operating outside judicial review, reducing the incentive for accountability.

The cumulative effect extends beyond legal exposure and diplomatic standing. It sets a precedent for treating reporting obligations, judicial oversight, and human rights commitments as optional. Addressing these risks requires three measures: conditioning U.S. cooperation on verifiable human rights standards, ensuring legal and documentary transparency in deportations, and establishing independent monitoring of detention facilities.

Considering the changes in scope and omitted content in its 2024 Human Rights Report, the State Department’s 2025 Human Rights Report on El Salvador will likely downplay El Salvador’s human rights violations, if it is published at all. This year’s HRR is months past its due date. If future reports with other relevant partners also omit or minimize the size and scope of abuse, it would reinforce a narrative of cooperative policy over legal standards. A continuation of this dynamic diminishes the credibility of the HRRs, which have historically served as some of the strongest tools to assess global human rights conditions.

Simultaneously, external pressure from human rights organizations, investigative journalists, and international bodies is likely to intensify. As more evidence emerges, or as the deportation crisis worsens, the gap between official narratives and documented reality may become increasingly difficult to sustain. Although El Salvador has tightened media restrictions, the Trump administration will struggle to do the same in the U.S.

In the immediate future, U.S complicity in these abuses will generate further stigma about U.S. immigration enforcement for the public. That reputational harm can make other countries more reluctant to cooperate with U.S. deportation efforts, further shrinking an already limited set of states willing to accept non‑nationals.

Suspend Transfers and Condition Cooperation

Congress should immediately suspend all funding and impose a moratorium on all deportation transfers to El Salvador pending a formal review of detention conditions. The U.S. should only resume cooperation if El Salvador demonstrates verifiable compliance with international human rights standards, including prohibitions on torture and other abusive methods. To prevent future cases of abuse, Congress and the U.S State Department should establish clear, enforceable benchmarks: legal access, humane conditions, and transparency, with automatic suspension mechanisms in place for non-compliance.

Ensure Legal Integrity and Transparency

The U.S. Department of Justice should verify the legal basis of all deportations to ensure compliance with due process and nonrefoulement obligations. The State Department should publicly release the terms of United States-El Salvador agreements to restore transparency and accountability. The U.S. Government Accountability Office should conduct and publish a formal review of the 2024 Human Rights Report to assess whether its omissions are consistent with available evidence and to preserve the credibility of State Department reporting.

Establish Independent Monitoring

The international community should implement independent, third-party monitoring of Salvadoran detention facilities, including regular and unannounced inspections by the U.N. Special Rapporteur on Torture and the Inter‑American Court of Human Rights. El Salvador should ensure full access to detainees, facilities, and records, including paperwork and CCTV recordings. The international community should require public reporting of findings, and the U.S. should link continued cooperation to demonstrated, sustained improvements in prison conditions.

text:
Calls to remove ICE from 250 Delaware Avenue are increasing in volume, literally.

Protesters gathered Wednesday evening outside the Statler Building, calling for Carl Montante to end the lease that allows ICE to rent the space. Montante was inducted to the Buffalo Business Hall of Fame on Wednesday at the Statler, so protesters held a simultaneous “Hall of Shame” event outside.

Several local businesses voiced support for Evict ICE. ICE’s presence impedes their ability to help customers, Good Moon Bodywork Founder Jaz Frazier said.

“ICE's ethos is the very antithesis of what Buffalo and our surrounding areas need," they said. "Good Moon welcomes immigrants and welcomes that diversity in our communities because I know that it makes all of our experiences that much richer.”

In addition to the demonstration outside, 10 members of Evict ICE entered the banquet as guests. They started criticizing Montante and were escorted out by security.

The goal is to project a collective voice and appeal to government leaders as well as business figures, said Shane Keyes a spokesperson for Evict ICE from 250 Delaware, a local advocacy group.

“While people are in there celebrating, having cocktail hour, we're out here bringing attention to the fact that in our own downtown, families are being detained, separated, and shipped to God knows where," he said. "And we don't want to stand for it."

ICE does have short-term holding rooms at its 250 Delaware offices.

Montante is executive chairman and founder of Uniland Development Company, which owns the building. The current lease ends March 31, though Uniland has not announced its future plans.

authors: Tia Maggio, Graham Cawthon, Pedro Lopez
description:

text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. —

Download the WJCL app for breaking news alerts: Apple, Google Play

A now-former Savannah police officer gave her husband, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, access to the police department’s Flock license plate reader system, which he used to conduct hundreds of searches tied to ICE investigations, according to newly obtained documents reviewed by WJCL 22 News.

The records show Amber Harpe's husband did not have his own Flock account through the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Harpe acknowledged giving him her Savannah Police Department username and password.

Her husband told investigators he used the account to locate ICE targets who had active arrest warrants. He said every search was related to his federal law enforcement work and denied using the system for personal reasons.

The Savannah Police Department fired Harpe after concluding that she knowingly gave an unauthorized person access to a sensitive police system, violated department policy and compromised safeguards designed to track who was using law enforcement data.

RELATED: Six Savannah police employees fired after alleged misuse of license plate reader system

Nearly 1,000 searches across six states

The investigation began after an internal audit flagged an unusually high volume of searches through Harpe’s account between January and July 2026.

The audit identified 983 search entries involving 97 identifiable license plates from Georgia, New Jersey, Maryland, Florida, South Carolina and North Carolina.

South Carolina plates represented most of the activity. Forty-eight South Carolina plates accounted for 788 search entries, according to the records. Department documents also noted that most registered vehicle owners identified in the audit were Hispanic.

During a July 27 administrative interview, Harpe told investigators she did not recognize the names connected to many of the searches. She said her husband performed most of them.

Harpe attributed the searches involving Maryland and South Carolina plates, along with most of those involving Georgia vehicles, to her husband.

She said she rarely used Flock herself and generally accessed it to help investigate missing-person cases involving behavioral health patients.

Harpe acknowledged that she allowed her husband to use her credentials and understood she was not permitted to share her access.

Below file video: Savannah city leaders defend Flock technology after alleged misuse by police employees

Husband said searches targeted wanted people

Harpe’s husband’s name is redacted in the documents obtained by WJCL 22 News. However, audio from interview between Savannah Police and the husband identifies him Tyler Harpe, a federal ICE agent.

During an Aug. 3 interview with Savannah police investigators, Harpe confirmed that he asked his wife for her login information because he did not have Flock access through his federal job.

He said ICE had already developed “target packages” for the people he searched and that those individuals had active arrest warrants. Flock allowed him to try to locate them while working in the field, according to the investigative report.

Tyler Harpe estimated that he used the account for about four months. He said he stopped roughly three weeks before his interview because the agency no longer conducted vehicle stops and he no longer needed the system.

Harpe gave investigators a slightly different timeline, saying her husband stopped about a week before her interview because he was concerned she could face discipline.

He denied searching for relatives, former romantic partners or anyone for personal reasons. He maintained that every person he searched was an ICE target and said the Flock information helped his agency locate wanted people with criminal histories.

He also acknowledged that using another officer’s account could violate policy.

“The investigation established that Amber Harpe provided her Flock Safety credentials to her husband,” the final report said. “Both provided consistent statements that the searches involved ICE targets and were conducted for law-enforcement purposes.”

RELATED: Former Savannah officer fights to get job back after Flock misuse firing

SPD raised concerns about immigration enforcement

In the documents, Maj. Michelle Halford wrote that SPD does not participate in federal immigration enforcement. She said the demographic pattern identified in the audit, combined with Harpe’s husband’s role as an ICE agent, raised concerns that department resources had been used without authorization to further immigration enforcement.

Harpe’s decision gave her husband the ability to search for and track people through a Savannah police system even though he did not have independent access through his federal employment, Halford wrote.

She said the arrangement exposed the Police Department to legal and reputational risks.

“Public trust is non-negotiable,” Halford wrote. “These tools exist to keep our community safe, not for personal or unauthorized use.”

The investigation did not find that Harpe violated Georgia’s law governing automated license plate readers. The disciplinary case instead centered on an SPD information-management policy prohibiting employees from allowing unauthorized people to access city or department software.

Below file video: 6 Savannah police employees fired after alleged misuse of Flock cameras

Supervisors disagreed over punishment

Department leaders agreed that Harpe violated policy, but they initially disagreed over whether she should be fired.

Interim Maj. Max Nowinsky sustained the allegation and recommended an eight-hour suspension.

Nowinsky wrote that Harpe showed poor judgment by providing direct access to her husband. However, he also emphasized that investigators found no evidence the searches were conducted for personal reasons or personal gain.

He cited Georgia law allowing law enforcement agencies, including federal agencies, to exchange captured license plate data for legitimate law enforcement purposes.

Nowinsky also considered Harpe’s work history. She joined SPD in March 2020, served in the Behavioral Health Unit and had no prior disciplinary record. Department documents described her as a well-respected employee.

Halford rejected the proposed one-day suspension and recommended termination, citing the intentional sharing of credentials, recurring unauthorized access and scale of the activity.

Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin agreed that Harpe should be fired.

Gavin acknowledged that state law permits law enforcement agencies to share license plate information for legitimate purposes. He said that authority did not allow Harpe to share her personal login information or let another person access the system under her identity.

“Credentials are assigned to one authorized user to ensure accountability, audit integrity, and system security,” Gavin wrote.

Because the searches were recorded under Harpe’s account, the system’s audit trail identified her — not her husband — as the user.

Gavin concluded that Harpe knowingly allowed her husband to bypass SPD’s security protocols and undermined the department’s ability to oversee the use of sensitive information.

RELATED: Former Savannah police employees appeal firings over alleged Flock camera misuse

Harpe said she was helping another agency

Harpe accepted responsibility for sharing her credentials but argued that firing her was excessive.

In her appeal, Harpe said her husband was a certified federal law enforcement officer and that every search was conducted for law enforcement purposes.

“The violation occurred because I gave my husband, who is a certified law enforcement officer with the Department of Homeland Security, access to my Flock account,” Harpe wrote. “Every search he conducted was for law enforcement use only and not for personal gain.”

Harpe said she was trying to assist another agency in the same way she would expect another agency to help Savannah police.

She also argued that the result would have been no different if she had personally conducted each search at her husband’s request and then provided him with the information.

“There was no malicious intent, no personal gain, and no intent to harm the Department or undermine public trust,” Harpe wrote.

She asked department leaders to consider her clean disciplinary history, years of service and the investigation’s finding that the searches were related to law enforcement work. She requested a written reprimand or, at most, the one-day suspension Nowinsky recommended.

Gavin denied her appeal Aug. 11, and the police chief’s office agreed with the termination recommendation two days later.

Below file video: GBI arrests 4 ousted Savannah Police employees

Civil Service Board appeal withdrawn

Harpe requested a hearing before Savannah’s Civil Service Board on Aug. 19. City records show her termination took effect Sept. 26.

She withdrew the appeal around Sept. 28, and her Oct. 13 Civil Service Board hearing was canceled.

The newly obtained documents do not explain why she withdrew the appeal.

Harpe’s case was part of a wider SPD investigation into alleged Flock misuse. Several other former employees were accused of searching for romantic partners, former partners or other people for personal reasons.

title: Immigration Lawyer on Trump's 'Constellation of Attacks' on Newcomer Children - The 74
description:
Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Heather Yountz, senior immigration attorney with the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute, spent 13 years shepherding children and families through immigration court.
Which Trump immigration initiatives impact kids most at this moment?
Since abused, abandoned and neglected children are considered a vulnerable population, these children have been given special protections under the TVPRA.
There were also procedural protections in immigration court.
The Trump administration has hired these ‘legal service’ groups.
text:
Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

Heather Yountz, senior immigration attorney with the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute, spent 13 years shepherding children and families through immigration court.

She was mostly successful in helping them stay in the country, she said, adding that she stopped representing individual clients in 2021.

What she’s seeing now — the targeting and deportation of the youngest immigrants and those with statuses once considered among the most protected — is unprecedented.

“Honestly, the deportation of children — particularly unaccompanied children — is a very new phenomenon,” said the lawyer, who now spends much of her time drafting legislation, lobbying for pro-immigrant policies and testifying in support of state bills.

Yountz also trains and advises state and federal legislators, as well as the offices of the Massachusetts governor and attorney general.

It’s not any one element of child immigration that is being targeted: what’s happening instead, she said, is a full-scale assault on every conceivable right.

I spoke with Yountz recently as part of my reporting on how the Trump administration’s latest enforcement wave is affecting students, families and schools. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Which Trump immigration initiatives impact kids most at this moment?

It’s really a constellation of policies attacking children right now, and it’s all part of this really well coordinated effort to strip immigrant children of their status so that they’re going to be easier to deport.

So, one of the biggest ones is the funding cut to legal service organizations. By statute, unaccompanied immigrant children who are under 18 and are in the custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement — or who were recently released from ORR custody — the Trump administration, like every presidency and executive branch, is required to provide funding for their legal representation. And they have not done so since December of 2025.

Their biggest contract was with the Acacia Center for Justice. In late 2025, the Trump administration said, ‘We will give you this funding if you provide us with certain information about the children’ — and that information was confidential and protected. It was identifying information, so of course, the attorney said, ‘No, that’s a violation of attorney-client privilege.’ And of course, there’s a huge amount of fear that the Trump administration would essentially datamine this to make determinations about who they could deport most easily.

A lawsuit was filed, and essentially it all came to a head on July 31, 2026, when the contracts were set to be renewed and the Trump administration let the contracts lapse. The result was that about $65 million was lost: More than 24,000 children lost funding for their representation.

That coincided with a number of other attacks on children.

Like what?

One of the biggest is the attack on Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) status. The Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, a federal statute, governs the treatment of Special Immigrant Juvenile status. Since abused, abandoned and neglected children are considered a vulnerable population, these children have been given special protections under the TVPRA.

Additionally, the Biden administration created Deferred Action for SIJs, a four-year protection from deportation that allowed work authorization. There were also procedural protections in immigration court. Children with SIJ status who were waiting for their green card would have their deportation case in immigration court “administratively closed” or placed on the status docket so that they would not have to keep coming into court while they waited to be eligible to apply for a green card.

Prior to 2015, obtaining a green card from an SIJ status was a relatively fast process: Children could get one shortly after their SIJ status was approved. The whole process would take about a year.

Now, it can be three to six years, and that’s because of the backlog. Essentially, each applicant for a green card has a “priority date” to adjust to green card status based on the kind of status you are eligible for and the country that you’re from. If your priority date has not come up yet, then you are waiting in a backlog.

And starting in about 2015, when there were a number of unaccompanied children who came over the border, a backlog formed. Unfortunately, Congress hasn’t created an exception for these children from the typical visa process to take them out of that backlog.

And, children used to be in ORR (Office of Refugee Resettlement) custody for around 35 days. Now it’s gone up to 200-plus days.

But aggressive enforcement isn’t the government’s only tactic in pushing kids out of the country, right?

Immigration courts are changing critical hearing dates without properly notifying people.

It’s not uncommon at all for immigrants to check their online account to find out that suddenly they have a hearing today. They may have never received notice but suddenly they have to drop everything and go to court — and if they don’t, they’re going to get an in absentia deportation order, which means they’re going to be ordered deported.

So these changes have come at a time when kids are particularly vulnerable.

That’s not a coincidence. Who’s gonna challenge this? All of the (lawyers) who just got fired, right?

How do the changes to SIJ materially impact kids?

Suddenly these children are having to go in what we call a rocket docket, which is when they go in front of a judge every three weeks in large groups of children — we call it “cattle” in courts — and it’s to create this artificial rush which results in children feeling pressured to give up their status and self-deport.

Is that the only way the government is pressuring school-aged kids to leave the country?

Similarly, in the Office of Refugee Resettlement facilities themselves, we are hearing stories of children being pressured by the staff — even offered money to leave the country.

And the paperwork for various immigration claims is extremely complex, right? Not something that can be easily done without a lawyer?

Right, and that’s another piece of the constellation of attacks. The overcomplication, the slow walking of each step of the process of guardianship — and the added costs. All of it is to make it as difficult as possible to allow any immigrant to get status in the United States. It’s part of this large deportation effort, to deport as many people as possible, and convince as many people to self-deport.

That is the absolute fingerprint of the Trump administration’s immigration policy.

Tell me more about these packed immigration hearings, the ones attorneys call “cattle.”

We are hearing heartbreaking stories about some of these hearings down in Texas that have 80 children in them, and the judge will say something like, ‘Raise your hand if you want voluntary departure.’ There’s kids on the floor with crayons. There’s a 3-year-old playing with a microphone. We just heard about a 1-year-old who was told by a judge, ‘You have three weeks to file your asylum application, or else we’re going to have to order you deported.’ That baby had no effective legal representation.

Has there been any legal group that has taken the place of those that used to represent these kids?

The Trump administration has hired these ‘legal service’ groups. They’re not advocating for the kids to stay, certainly. In one case, an attorney who had been paid to represent these children stood in the courtroom, watched the whole thing, didn’t intervene, didn’t say a word. The 1-year-old I just mentioned was told to go. It’s a kangaroo court at the highest level.

What could bring about change for these children?

The way to stop the Trump administration’s executive orders, declarations, administrative actions, is by statute. Congress has the power to override an executive order or policy memo by passing a statute.

Could Congress, right now, prevent the deportation of Haitians? Yes, they could.

They could prevent the deportation of SIJs by statute. They could make all of these children green card holders.

The problem is you need to have not just a majority in Congress in order to pass this in both the House and the Senate: Trump’s going to veto it. So, you’ve got to be able to override that veto (which requires a two-thirds majority in both houses).

If there was some check or balance that could be put into place by the House or the Senate or both, the Trump administration would not be able to steamroll immigrants in this unfettered fashion.

A lot of this work has to be done at the state and local level. States and local cities and towns have authority to protect the people living within their confines.

Here in Massachusetts, we just passed the PROTECT Act that put in place some protections for immigrants. (The legislation, according to the state’s website, “strengthens public safety by ensuring residents can access schools, child care programs, medical care, and courts without fear of immigration enforcement; reinforces constitutional protections and due process rights; and restricts state and local involvement in federal immigration enforcement.” It also provides stronger protections for parents who are detained or deported, bans new 287(g) agreements — cooperation agreements between local law enforcement and ICE — “and allows civil rights claims to be made against government officials, including ICE agents.”)

How is Trump’s current stance on these issues different than in his first term?

The Trump administration is appealing all of these challenges to the Supreme Court — and winning largely. The Supreme Court is rubber stamping his attacks and abuses on immigrants, and that’s a marked difference from Trump 1.

If he went to the Supreme Court (in the past), there was actually a weighing of the constitutionality of these aspects that took place among the justices that was not as political as it appears to be now.

And there has been a big change in terms of the immigration judges hearing these cases, right?

Immigration judges are not real judges. They are part of the administrative branch of the federal government and technically are administrative judges. They are not under the judicial branch of the federal government.

Here in Boston — but really in many parts of the country — judges with experience who have been doing this work for many years are getting fired and they’re being replaced with new judges. Sometimes they’re temporary, sometimes not. Many of them have been in the military.

Most of the immigration judges we have encountered have no or very little immigration experience. They don’t fully comprehend the law that they’re actually required to apply.

It’s complex, ever-changing, and applies from the tiniest little memo that was produced this morning all the way through state law, federal law, administrative orders, executive orders, everything — international treaties.

These new judges seem to be reading scripts from the stand, and don’t appear to be using discretion as required. Basically they’re doing what they’re told or they’ll be fired.

text:
A Mexican national who lived in the United States for nearly two decades is asking a federal judge to facilitate his return. He says that immigration authorities deported him without a valid removal order and despite his repeated refusal to leave.

Ernesto Zuniga Hilario says that Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained him in Texas in September. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) subsequently removed him to Mexico without giving him a meaningful opportunity to understand or challenge the government's legal basis for doing so. His attorneys filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.

Zuniga Hilario said he last entered the United States without inspection around 2008 and lived near Lometa, Texas, before his detention. He is married to Obdulia Cervantes Vega, whom the filing identifies as a lawful permanent resident, and has four U.S.-citizen children, according to the petition.

Read More on News

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek: "Any allegation that Ernesto Zuniga Hilario didn’t receive due process is FALSE. Zuniga Hilario signed his voluntary departure form on September 6 in blue ink. He left the United States and returned to Mexico on September 16. Breaking our country’s laws is always a bad decision."

The agency's account directly conflicts with the man's petition, which says he repeatedly declined voluntary departure because he wanted an opportunity to present his case and expected to appear before an immigration judge.

DHS said that Zuniga Hilario was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on September 6 following a traffic stop conducted by the Lampasas County Sheriff’s Office. The agency said he entered the United States illegally "at an unknown date and time by sneaking across our border on foot."

Newsweek has contacted the man's legal team for comment via email on Wednesday and is awaiting a response.

Under the Trump administration's mass deportation policy, there have been cases of wrongful deportations and removals carried out in defiance of court orders. Federal judges are squaring off and going toe to toe with the administration over wrongful removals and, in some cases, ordering DHS to facilitate the returns of individuals who were improperly deported.

The lawsuit says that immigration authorities lacked a legal basis to deport Zuniga Hilario because he was not subject to an expedited removal order or one issued by an immigration judge. Although he acknowledges previous encounters with immigration authorities, he says none resulted in a removal order.

Immigration officers apprehended Zuniga Hilario while he was traveling with his family in connection with a therapy appointment, according to court filings. He was subsequently held at the T. Don Hutto detention facility in Taylor, Texas. A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainee-locator record submitted in court filings as an exhibit also identifies the facility as his detention location.

During his detention, Zuniga Hilario alleges officers repeatedly asked whether he wanted to depart voluntarily. He declined because he wanted to present his case and expected an opportunity to appear before an immigration judge, according to the petition.

Instead, the filing alleges, authorities placed him on a bus, transported him to an airport, and flew him to Mexico City without giving him a meaningful opportunity to challenge the legal basis for his removal. Zuniga Hilario maintains that his departure was involuntary.

The lawsuit also alleges Zuniga Hilario was denied due process. His attorneys say that, if officials were reinstating an earlier removal order, they were required to notify him and give him an opportunity to contest the decision, which he alleges did not happen.

The petition acknowledges that Zuniga Hilario faces a potential jurisdictional hurdle because he had already been removed when the case was filed. His attorneys argue his case is different because they allege the government removed him without an underlying removal order and without giving him a meaningful opportunity to challenge the action.

text:
SAN DIEGO (CN) — A federal judge in San Diego ordered the U.S. Department of State on Wednesday to reopen the diversity visa lottery for 2027, also known as the Green Card Lottery.

U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta’s preliminary injunction will allow for up to 55,000 people from around the world to apply for permanent residence in the United States.

The Trump administration, which has opposed the program, did not open the program’s registration period on time for this year and subsequently argued that it was too late to do so.

Red Eagle Law, a Southern California law firm that helps immigrants apply for the program, sought a preliminary injunction that would require Secretary of State Marco Rubio to reopen the registration period for the lottery. Red Eagle Law filed a lawsuit against Rubio in August.

The government’s failure to reopen the period resulted in a de facto cancellation of the program, Red Eagle Law founder and owner Curtis Morrison argued.

“We won,” Morrison said in a social media video after the ruling was announced.

“This means that when George Herbert Walker Bush made it the law in 1990, the Trump administration can’t just ignore the laws they don’t like,” Morrison told Courthouse News in a phone interview after the ruling was announced. “We have judges here to make sure they follow the law. I think the judge did a really good job analyzing the arguments.”

Ohta ordered Rubio to publicly announce the registration period for the program no later than midnight on Oct. 15.

“The announcement shall identify the opening and closing dates of the registration period, the website through which individuals may submit electronic entries, and the requirements for participating in the program,” Ohta, a Joe Biden appointee, wrote. “Defendant shall further disseminate this information through the State Department’s other customary public notification channels, including the Federal Register.”

Additionally, the registration period must last 30 days, Ohta ruled.

Morrison said he filed a joint motion to extend that deadline to two weeks later to prevent any hiccups.

The ruling also requires the State Department to accept electronic entries submitted during the registration period, provided that applicants meet eligibility and documentation requirements.

Finally, the ruling requires the State Department to notify the individuals selected for the diversity visa lottery and process their applications under its usual procedures until all available visas have been issued or until the fiscal year ends at the end of September 2027.

In previous court hearings, Morrison argued that the State Department gaslit Red Eagle Law and potential lottery applicants by saying the Green Card Lottery was undergoing some changes and would be delayed this year. But Morrison said that this was a tactic used by Rubio and the Trump administration to delay the program until they could argue it was too late to implement it.

President Donald Trump has opposed the program going back to his first term in office. The law was established under the Immigration and Nationality Act.

The Department of Justice did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Reflections on ICE Shooting in the Bronx - Immigration Research Initiative
description:
Last week, ICE agents shot a man in the neck while attempting to arrest him in the Marble Hill section of the Bronx.
Once he was in stable condition, ICE agents completed their arrest, removed him from the hospital, and took him into custody.
This is just the latest in a growing list of ICE encounters with the public that have turned violent.
So far, there have been 30 shootings involving ICE in 2026, resulting in nine deaths and 13 injuries.
In the early part of my career, I was a crime and politics reporter in the Bronx, and Marble Hill was part of my coverage area.
text:
Last week, ICE agents shot a man in the neck while attempting to arrest him in the Marble Hill section of the Bronx. Homeland Security says they were trying to detain 28-year-old Oscar Belgal when officers fired seven rounds into his car with his 5-year-old son in the back seat. Belgal was hit in the neck and taken to the hospital. Once he was in stable condition, ICE agents completed their arrest, removed him from the hospital, and took him into custody.

This is just the latest in a growing list of ICE encounters with the public that have turned violent. So far, there have been 30 shootings involving ICE in 2026, resulting in nine deaths and 13 injuries.

But for me, this one hit close to home.

In the early part of my career, I was a crime and politics reporter in the Bronx, and Marble Hill was part of my coverage area. In fact, the corner of West 225th and Marble Hill Avenue — where Belgal was shot — is one I have walked dozens of times either reporting on a story or simply living my life.

Located just over the Broadway Bridge from the northern tip of Manhattan, Marble Hill is a residential area that has long been a working-class community of color.

When I heard about the shooting, I was in shock. There was a time in my life that I might have been the person to break the news. Or I would have been on the scene deep into the night as protesters and elected officials gathered to mourn the violence befalling their community and decry the actions of the federal agents involved.

But last Thursday I felt — as I so often do under the current administration — powerless. Someone in a community I love and care about deeply was shot. His kid was in the car. The block where it happened is full of residential buildings and at 4 in the afternoon, when the shooting occurred, who knows how many people could have been hurt.

Two weeks ago, I and the rest of the IRI team were at a conference with colleagues from around the country who were envious of how nice it must be to live in New York during this time, with a local government that cares about immigrants. And it is nice. Since Mayor Zohran Mamdani has taken office, things have felt special in New York. From rent freezes for rent-stabilized apartments, to expanded public daycare for 2-year-olds, to the Knicks winning an NBA championship, things in New York have felt different than in the rest of the country.

But Thursday’s shooting reminds us that we are not immune. Indeed, we have not been immune. There is a limit to what any city or state can do when the federal government is out of control.

According to data from DHS compiled by the Data Deportation Project, ICE arrested nearly 4,000 people in New York this summer alone and has arrested over 19,000 people since January 2025. Mostly operating below the radar of national media, ICE has abducted thousands of New Yorkers who are doing what we all do in this city: Trying to get by.

We simply must do more to protect our friends and neighbors from the horrible realities of the deportation regime.

text:
WASHINGTON – Today, Representatives April McClain Delaney, Glenn Ivey, Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Sarah Elfreth, and Johnny Olszewski and U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks (all D-Md.) released the following statement regarding last night’s ruling by a federal judge, temporarily halting the Trump Administration’s efforts to close the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center (BARC) in Beltsville, Maryland.

“As we’ve said time and again, this Administration’s attempts to shutter BARC are not only unwise – they’re illegal. BARC conducts critical research that helps farmers across our nation put food on the table for American families – including combatting serious threats to our agriculture, like cyclospora and avian flu. Last night’s ruling from a federal judge made plain: the Administration’s efforts are in clear violation of Congressional intent. We will continue fighting back against the Trump Administration’s lawless attempts to close this facility, undermining its crucial research on behalf of American farmers and families.”

title: More than 160 councillors condemn government's immigration and asylum policies
description:
Over 160 cross-party councillors have signed a joint statement expressing their solidarity with their constituents and condemning the government’s policies “targeting people who have migrated here, people seeking asylum, and people who are refugees”.
The councillors call on the government to “change course and reverse these policies and actions, which risk causing great harm and fractures in our society and communities”.
They have a message to their residents which is “we are on your side.
We will continue to build communities of safety, solidarity and hope.” This intervention comes at a time of growing local resistance and opposition to the British government’s harsh policies on immigration.
As many as eight councils around Britain have now pledged to protect their residents from Home Office immigration raids and refuse to co-operate with immigration enforcement.
text:
Over 160 cross-party councillors have signed a joint statement expressing their solidarity with their constituents and condemning the government’s policies “targeting people who have migrated here, people seeking asylum, and people who are refugees”.

The councillors, from the Greens, Labour, Lib Dems, local parties and Independents, said that they “represent wards, parishes and districts where people of all backgrounds live, work and build communities together”, and “support each other, learn from each other and celebrate each other.”

They say that as a result, they “cannot and will not be silent about policies and actions which affect the people and communities we represent and which make their lives harder in a way that benefit no-one.”

The councillors’ statement, co-ordinated by the Migrant Champions Network, comes in response to a raft of legislation and policy changes by the current government, under successive Labour Prime Ministers, that would affect their residents and constituents. This includes extending routes to settlement and making refugee status temporary, ending refugee family reunion, giving immigration officers the power to handcuff and use force against children, removing support for people seeking asylum and putting pressure on completely overstretched local authorities, bringing forward yet another Bill on immigration and asylum which would dismantle basic and fundamental human rights protections for people seeking asylum, and increasing immigration raids on people in their homes.

The councillors call on the government to “change course and reverse these policies and actions, which risk causing great harm and fractures in our society and communities”.

They have a message to their residents which is “we are on your side. You are not alone, and we will always advocate for you. We will continue to build communities of safety, solidarity and hope.”

This intervention comes at a time of growing local resistance and opposition to the British government’s harsh policies on immigration. As many as eight councils around Britain have now pledged to protect their residents from Home Office immigration raids and refuse to co-operate with immigration enforcement. Last week, Newham council joined six other London councils, and Edinburgh city council, in committing to refuse to share data with the Home Office and provide support for businesses and residents targeted by raids, alongside other measures.
