title: Restoring Congressional Power to Enable Effective U.S. Foreign Assistance - FCNL .org
description:
Congress needs to ensure future foreign aid dollars are spent responsibly and effectively.
The Power of the Purse Every year, Congress passes 12 appropriations bills that determine how much funding federal agencies receive and how they should spend it.
The executive branch is then required to spend the money as Congress intended within set timeframes.
The federal spending process broke down this year, particularly for vital foreign assistance funding.
As Congress debates the final appropriations bills for FY27, it must enact the necessary guardrails to ensure future foreign assistance funds are spent as intended and with best practices.
text:
September 30 marked the end of the fiscal year. With it came the deadline to spend billions of dollars in congressionally appropriated funding for foreign assistance programs, including global health, economic development, peacebuilding, and support for United Nations agencies. While much of these funds were spent before expiration, a last-minute flurry of spending leaves questions about where the money ended up and why spending was held off until the deadline. Congress needs to ensure future foreign aid dollars are spent responsibly and effectively.

The Power of the Purse

Every year, Congress passes 12 appropriations bills that determine how much funding federal agencies receive and how they should spend it. The executive branch is then required to spend the money as Congress intended within set timeframes. This process is rooted in Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution which states: “No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law.” However, if funds are not spent by the established deadlines, the funds expire and cannot be used as intended, and the executive branch violates the Impoundment Control Act (P.L. 93-344).

The State Department rushed to spend $4 billion in expiring aid, leaving a murky picture of where the money was spent and which entities received it.

The federal spending process broke down this year, particularly for vital foreign assistance funding. In the last week of the fiscal year, the State Department rushed to spend $4 billion in expiring aid, leaving a murky picture of where the money was spent and which entities received it. Much of the funding was distributed through extremely large grants, which thwarts efforts to localize foreign aid and empower community organizations closest to the specific challenges. Best practice calls for funding to be disbursed at regular intervals where staff can make careful decisions about how and where to spend funds rather than having to make these major decisions all at once and under pressure.

Delayed spending was not the only problem this fiscal year. According to court filings and separate letters from Senators Brian Schatz (HI) and Patty Murray (WA) and Senator Susan Collins (ME), $2.5 billion in global health and development assistance was used for administrative costs to shutter USAID instead of countering the recent Ebola outbreak, providing vaccines, and supporting maternal and child health. In addition, $725 million in emergency non-military funding for Ukraine, $3 million for possible anti-personnel landmine clearance and nearly $2 million for human rights and democracy provided by Congress was allowed to expire.

These actions by the Trump administration hurt vulnerable communities and undermine Congress’ power of the purse, shaking the very foundations of our democracy.

Pocket Rescissions

Beyond delaying and redirecting funds, the administration also cancelled millions of congressionally appropriated funds in a move known as a “pocket rescission.” Following a July 2025 rescissions package that cancelled billions in congressionally appropriated refugee and displaced-population assistance, the Trump administration once again rescinded funds for vulnerable immigrants in late September 2026. This did not give Congress ample time to review and vote on the package before the end of the fiscal year, causing the funds to expire and drawing sharp criticism from both parties.

This ignoring of congressional authority will leave refugees without aid as they rebuild their lives and subject more immigrants to family separation and prolonged detention.

The President’s pocket rescission for this past fiscal year included over $567 million from the Refugee and Entrant Assistance account, which supports recently resettled refugees, and $15 million from case management programs for asylum seekers awaiting court proceedings from safely within their communities instead of detention centers. Such sums of money are hard to conceptualize, but the harm is clear. This ignoring of congressional authority will leave refugees without aid as they rebuild their lives and subject more immigrants to family separation and prolonged detention.

A Moment for Bipartisan Leadership

Congress has an opportunity to lead so there is not a further breakdown in the federal spending process. Protecting constitutional authorities and ensuring taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly and effectively should unite leaders across parties.

Right now, the federal government is under a short-term stopgap funding agreement. As Congress debates the final appropriations bills for FY27, it must enact the necessary guardrails to ensure future foreign assistance funds are spent as intended and with best practices. This can be achieved, for example, by increasing congressional oversight and strengthening congressional notification requirements for the use of funds, requiring spending plans, mandating timely and accurate public reporting through tools such as foreignassistance.gov, and ending pocket recissions.

Congress must act to prevent harm to vulnerable communities and to protect our democracy. Through a commitment to our democracy and love for our neighbors, Congress can help achieve the world we seek.

name: Policy
title: Why Voting in the Midterms Matters for Refugees and Immigrants - HIAS
description:
But there is another issue on the ballot, whether candidates are talking about it or not: how the United States can welcome refugees and immigrants.
Congress Determines Funding for the Immigration System Congress has the power of the purse.
Congress also determines funding levels for immigration enforcement operations, the immigration courts, and efforts to reduce immigration application backlogs.
Refugee resettlement, asylum, and immigration policies do not emerge from the White House alone.
Refugees and immigrants deserve policies rooted in safety, dignity, and fairness.
text:
As Americans prepare to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, much of the public conversation is focused on the economy, health care, and national security. But there is another issue on the ballot, whether candidates are talking about it or not: how the United States can welcome refugees and immigrants.

While media coverage often focuses on the immigration policies of President Trump, it is Congress that writes the laws, controls the funding, and has oversight over refugee resettlement, asylum processes, and immigration reform.

Here are four ways Congress shapes refugee and immigration policy and why your midterms vote can impact people seeking safety in the U.S.

Congress Can Pass Legislation to Reform our Immigration System

While presidential administrations have a lot of power when it comes to policies about refugee resettlement, asylum, and immigration, it is the job of Congress to develop the laws that are the foundation of our refugee program and asylum system. We have seen groundbreaking legislation such as the Refugee Act of 1980, which created a formalized U.S. refugee resettlement program and established procedures for people to apply for asylum. More recently, we have also seen devastating congressional action, including legislation that strips refugees and asylees of essential food and medical assistance. Critically, Congress has not passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986.

Congress Determines Funding for the Immigration System

Congress has the power of the purse. It decides how federal dollars are spent, including funding for refugee resettlement, the U.S. immigration system, and humanitarian assistance for displaced people around the world. While the president submits an annual budget request, it is Congress, not the president, that sets the federal budget, determining how much funding goes to the agencies that are responsible for responding to humanitarian crises around the world, processing refugees overseas, admitting them to the United States, and helping them integrate once here. Congress also determines funding levels for immigration enforcement operations, the immigration courts, and efforts to reduce immigration application backlogs.

Congress Can Hold the Executive Branch Accountable

One of Congress’ key responsibilities is to provide oversight of the executive branch. The management of the appropriations process is a significant way that Congress can limit or expand administration programs. In addition, through a variety of mechanisms, including congressional hearings and investigations, Congress can demand information from an administration, scrutinize administration actions, and demand transparency on how it operates. When an administration makes dangerous decisions that receive little public attention—such as establishing the Office of Remigration in the State Department or removing basic due process from asylum procedures—congressional inquiries and hearings can help bring greater scrutiny and pressure to stop policies and practices that might otherwise continue largely unnoticed.

Congress Can Influence Refugee Protection Priorities

The president decides annual refugee admissions goals. However, the 1980 Refugee Act requires that before the president makes that official decision, a few steps must be taken that involve Congress. The president must submit the administration’s refugee admissions goals in a report to Congress. Then the president must send cabinet-level officials to meet with members of the House and Senate Judiciary Committees prior to the finalization of the admission plans for the upcoming fiscal year. The consultations are an important opportunity for members of Congress to ask the administration representatives tough questions about their resettlement plans, including the populations that they want to prioritize for admissions.

Refugee resettlement, asylum, and immigration policies do not emerge from the White House alone. The decisions Congress makes can affect whether families fleeing persecution find safety, whether asylum seekers receive a fair hearing, and whether humanitarian programs have the resources they need. As you prepare to vote, ask candidates where they stand on these issues and make your voice heard.

Refugees and immigrants deserve policies rooted in safety, dignity, and fairness. Learn how you can take action.

text:
In one of his first major campaign appearances since a bout with the flu forced him out of the spotlight, U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said he would not seek to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as an agency but compared their current conduct to that of a "secret police force."

Asked if he supported abolishing ICE, Talarico replied, "No, and I never have. We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that's not what we're seeing. What we've seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that's what we don't want in this country. We don't want masked men in unmarked vehicles coming through and terrorizing our communities."

Talarico, a Democratic state representative running against Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said the Biden Administration had "failed us" in securing the southern border.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Several Democrats, including ones in Texas, have called for significantly overhauling or abolishing ICE following widespread immigration raids under the Trump Administration. Former Congressman Colin Allred, who ran against Ted Cruz for Senate in 2024 and is now seeking a return to Congress, has called to abolish ICE. Congressman Christian Menefee has said ICE "needs to be torn down to the studs."

RELATED: Family of man struck by ICE vehicle and advocates dispute DHS’ story, demand appropriate medical treatment

Asked for further clarification about his vision for the role ICE should play in immigration enforcement, a spokesperson for Talarico only alluded to the candidate's remarks during the town hall appearance and his "extensive prior comments on immigration."

Previously in February, Talarico had said he wanted to "tear down this secret police force and replace it with an agency that is actually going to focus on public safety." In July, Talarico said during a campaign stop, “ICE should be cracking down on the cartels, not on our communities. ICE should be deporting gang members, not small business owners. ICE should be hunting down human traffickers, not moms and babies.”

His comments Wednesday came during an evening town hall in Fort Worth hosted by CNN and Jubilee. CNN said it had also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton. The two candidates have not debated, despite bipartisan pressure and previous pushes from each campaign.

In criticizing ICE's work under the Trump Administration, Talarico referenced the July killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who had lived in the United States without permanent legal status for decades and was shot by an ICE agent in Houston.

"Lorenzo Salgado [Araujo] was a child of God, endowed with infinite worth," Talarico said. "Lorenzo, our fellow Texan, deserves justice. And that's exactly what I'll fight for in the U.S. Senate.”

Representatives from Paxton's campaign did not immediately return a request for comment regarding Talarico's comments on ICE, nor his criticisms of Paxton as "the most corrupt politician in Texas."

In a post on social media, Paxton argued that Talarico "tried to dismantle the oil and gas industry and repeatedly tried to destroy the Texas economy." During the town hall event, Talarico said he would push for both the oil and gas industry and the renewable energy industry.

Paxton also wrote on social media that Talarico "has spent his career embracing the most radical policies imaginable and voting for every tax increase he could. His agenda would tax Texans into oblivion."

Talarico spent much of the town hall appearance positioning himself as a centrist who will work with both parties in the Senate. He also walked back some of his previous statements from his political career. When asked, for example, about a previous statement calling capitalism an "oppressive system," Talarico said he was a capitalist but that the current system of government is "crony capitalism." When asked by a voter who identified as Republican about a statement Talarico made where he called God "non-binary," Talarico said, "When I said that, I was being provocative, and I want to admit that and come clean about that, but I think what I was saying is actually not controversial theologically."

"I will always do what’s best for Texas, even if that means standing up to my own party," he said. "If the Democratic Party is going after the good-paying oil and gas jobs here in Texas, I’m going to stand up against them. I’m going to call out Democrats like Joe Biden who failed us on our southern border because we need border security here in Texas."

"I will always do what’s best for Texas, even if that means standing up to my own party," he said. "If the Democratic Party is going after the good-paying oil and gas jobs here in Texas, I’m going to stand up against them. I’m going to call out Democrats like Joe Biden who failed us on our southern border because we need border security here in Texas."

Tensions ran high at Wednesday’s Encinitas City Council meeting as residents voiced outrage over recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity in the community, demanding greater action from city leaders and saying the arrests have left neighbors fearful.

Dozens of residents filled the council chambers before and during the meeting, chanting “ICE out” and urging officials to address what they described as an increase in immigration enforcement in Encinitas.

Among those speaking out was Joshua Lazarson, who said he has lived in Encinitas for 33 years. He told ABC 10News that people in his neighborhood have been affected by recent arrests.

“They have taken people across the street from me in the apartments. They have taken a father from a school around the corner who is dropping off his child,” Lazarson said. “This is happening, if not on a daily basis, then regularly.”

Lazarson said he attended the meeting because he believes residents must support one another during difficult times.

“We need to stand up for one another when horrific things are happening. I'm here because horrific things are happening,” he said.

Other residents criticized the City Council, arguing that local leaders have not done enough to address community concerns.

Resident Jody White accused the council of failing to adequately support community members affected by the enforcement activity.

Jeremy Ross, an organizer and activist, said the issue extends beyond those directly targeted by immigration enforcement.

“We're all impacted because if one person's rights are under attack, all of our rights are under attack,” Ross said. He also accused councilmembers of making promises about local control without delivering meaningful action.

During the meeting, the city addressed two recent incidents involving immigration enforcement in Encinitas. According to comments made during the meeting, one incident involved a man arrested for an immigration violation.

Residents also raised concerns about a lack of advance notification to local authorities. During the discussion, a speaker said the San Diego County Sheriff's Department and the city had not received prior notice of an incident.

Videos submitted by residents reportedly showed encounters with ICE agents in the area earlier in the week.

ABC 10News reached out to ICE for comment late Wednesday but had not received a response at the time of reporting.

Despite the discussion at City Hall, residents said they want more concrete action from local officials to address their concerns and help restore a sense of safety in their neighborhoods.

“The people that they are taking and the people that they're putting fear into are our neighbors,” Lazarson said.

For many who attended Wednesday's meeting, the message to city leaders was clear: they want their concerns heard and their neighbors protected.

text:
Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agrees to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals, Shabana Mahmood has warned.

VIPs and officials from the east African country have already been stripped of fast-track access to UK visas after their government refused to cooperate with the return of its nationals, the home secretary said.

The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year, the Home Office said.

Refugee organisations have warned that the UK should not get drawn into rejecting applicants for asylum from Eritrea because it is a war-torn country and the UK usually accepts the vast majority of applicants, who are often escaping famine and conflict.

Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.

Mahmood said: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.

“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.

“I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”

The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.

Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.

In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.

Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.

Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.

After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.

India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.

About 84% are successful on first application and more will be successful on appeal, she said.

“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”

Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.

The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”

UN experts say that the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.

“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.

“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.

“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”

Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.

“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”

Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.

“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

text:
By Bernard Rorke

The trial of Panayote Dimitras of the Greek Helsinki Monitor, a member of the Roma Rights Network, was postponed by a Rhodes court until 6 April 2027. Panayote Dimitras and his co-accused, Tommy Olsen (director of the migrant aid NGO Aegean Boat Report), are on trial for ‘complicity in human trafficking’ and ‘criminal activities’.

This is nothing more than a show trial, a politically-motivated and arbitrary abuse of criminal law by the Greek authorities, for as Mary Lalor UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights memorably stated: “Solidarity should never be punished and compassion should never be put on trial.”

While Olsen is resident in Norway, and the Norwegian authorities have rejected the Greek application for extradition, the situation is different for Dimitras. Since 2023, the pretrial measures authorities imposed on him include a ban on leaving the country, a duty to regularly report to the police station, and a bail payment of €10,000. As Dimitras said:

“This prosecution had the sole aim to harass us and severely limit our work documenting human rights violations at Greece’s borders. It has left me stigmatized and has prevented me from travelling abroad to continue our human rights advocacy at an international level for more than three years.”

Human Rights Watch condemned the ongoing prosecution of both men as “a politically-motivated attempt to silence their efforts to expose abuses against migrants”, and called on Greek prosecutors to drop this blatant drive to intimidate Dimitras and Olsen, and criminalise their legitimate human rights work.

Amnesty International described the charges as a “gross misuse of anti-smuggling legislation”, and the action of the Greek authorities as a “new low” in their long-standing record of harassing human rights defenders: “For the first time, human rights workers are being referred to trial for helping people access asylum procedures. Construing this as ‘smuggling’ is not only a distortion of international and domestic law but a dangerous vilification of NGOs’ valuable work.”

In its statement, Amnesty asserted that there is no evidence to support the authorities’ case that Dimitras and Olsen establised and participated in a criminal organisation that jointly facilitated the unlawful entry and unlawful stay of third-country nationals in Greece; and no indication that the men’s work went “beyond the legitimate activities of assisting people in legally exercising their human rights and documenting the situation.” If convicted, they could face up to 20 years in prison.

These prosecutions are part of a wide and well-documented pattern of official harassment and intimidation targeting human rights defenders who work with migrants and asylum seekers in Greece. As stated on the news portal Kontra, even when charges are dropped, the consequences of prosecutions – which include “years of waiting, financial exhaustion, travel restrictions, public humiliation, and professional isolation” – are such that the criminal process itself is intrinsic to the repression.

In 2023, in her conclusions following a country visit to Greece, the UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders Mary Lawlor expressed her concerns at the criminalisation, smearing and intimidation of human rights defenders, “vilified as traitors, enemies of the state, Turkish agents, criminals and smugglers and traffickers”, and at the extent to which

“Human rights lawyers, humanitarian workers, volunteers and journalists [working on migration in Greece] have been subjected to smear campaigns, a changing regulatory environment, threats and attacks, and the misuse of criminal law against them, to a shocking degree.”

In a subsequent tweet on X in 2023, Lawlor made specific mention of "disturbing news" about restrictions placed on Dimitras, “including on his right to continue his legitimate human rights work. Along with Tommy Olsen, he is facing what strongly appears to be an arbitrary criminal investigation.”

Recommendations from international bodies have not only gone unheeded, but the right-wing Greek government has doubled down on its repression. As HRW reported, on 5 February 2026, the Greek Parliament passed a government-led migration law that associates humanitarian work with criminal conduct by making membership in a nongovernmental organization an aggravating factor in migration-related offenses.

According to Human Rights Watch, the law, which also grants the migration minister unchecked authority to deregister groups at his discretion and without a court ruling, is part of a surge in state-led intimidation of civil society. The group called on the European Commission to launch a formal assessment of this migration law and to ensure Athens adheres to its commitments to protects critics from legal harassment.

The ramifications of the case against Dimitras and Olsen are even more significant as EU migration policy lurches even further rightwards; at a time when the passing of EU legislation to increase deportations – described by Amnesty as “absurd, cruel and discriminatory” – was greeted by rightwing MEPs in the European Parliament chanting “send them back.”

This prosecution is just the latest chapter in the Greek state’s persistent judicial harassment against Panayote Dimitras, which has amounted to one SLAPP after another – Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation designed to exhaust and silence those who dare to dissent. Dimitras, has over the decades relentlessly defended the human rights of Roma, the LGBT+ community, migrants, asylum seekers, and any others who face discrimination, state oppression, and far-right intimidation. This is an attack on the foundations of European democracy, and by punishing solidarity and compassion, an assault on our common dignity.

text:
Note from our Editor-in-Chief:

This article is part of our series on the ‘Four Horsemen of the Trump-ocalypse.’ With several weeks left in the 2026 midterm elections, we believe this is the moment to capture the damage the Trump administration has inflicted throughout the U.S. and the world – and profile some of the people most responsible. In the days before the 2020 election, a group of Donald Trump supporters surrounded a Biden-Harris campaign bus in Texas, seemingly trying to force it off the road.

“We love what they did, but here’s the thing they don’t know,” Marco Rubio said shortly after. “We do that in Florida every day.”

It was one of several moments that revealed how the Florida senator was changing.

“That was not who I thought I knew – who I always thought was really respectful of democracy, and worked well with Democrats,” a former Rubio Senate staffer tells Zeteo. “Being flippant about some of these things that either were, or were adjacent to, political violence… this crossed the line, for me anyway.”

Others saw something else.

“That’s typical Marco Rubio, trying to get something positive out of it, because he knows deep down that was wrong,” Mike Fasano, a former Florida state legislator who served alongside Rubio, says with a chuckle. “Marco Rubio has still a great future in his political life – and I can understand why he says some of the things he says, because I’ve seen firsthand how you get elected. You have to appease the primary voter.”

One of the most successful Republicans in the modern era, Rubio has consistently meant different things to different people. He has climbed from a state legislature, to the U.S. Senate, to one of the most powerful offices in the world, leading the State Department in Trump’s second administration.

Rubio rose on the strength of his backstory, the son of Cuban exiles. He was seen as a conservative but reasonable Republican, a supporter of immigration reform, free speech, human rights, and foreign aid as soft power. That’s all changed.

It is a feature of the Trump era that most Republicans have put aside supposed morals and beliefs in order to maintain – or gain – power. Perhaps none have debased themselves as conspicuously, thoroughly, and successfully as Rubio.

text:
MDC began accepting ICE detainees on June 20, 2025, after the Department of Homeland Security signed an interagency agreement with the Bureau of Prisons to house them at the facility, making it the only long-term ICE detention center in New York City. Currently, about 200 immigrants are held at MDC, including Belgal, whose case has drawn renewed attention to conditions inside the facility.

According to a statement issued by the Legal Aid Society and Make the Road New York, Belgal has not received adequate medical care. He said the left side of his face is numb and he can barely hear out of his left ear. He also has a shoulder wound caused by shattered glass during his arrest. Belgal said he has not eaten a single meal since his arrest and has been told the only water available to him comes from a bathroom sink.

The rally preceded the MDC Brooklyn Community Support group’s weekly Tuesday vigil, which for the past year and a half has brought together local prison justice groups, immigrant rights groups, faith leaders, concerned neighbors and people currently and formerly detained at MDC to protest inhumane conditions and demand a halt to the intake of immigrants arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Holding signs reading “ICE Out of NYC” and “Free Belgal,” coalition members and local lawmakers gathered outside the prison to call for justice. During the rally, incarcerated people could be heard banging on the windows, and attendees waved back in response.

Anna Sugrue, co-founder and co-director of the Remedy Project, a youth-led prisoners’ rights advocacy group, told rally attendees that Belgal’s treatment was consistent with reports of torturous conditions at MDC shared by incarcerated people. Those reports included medical neglect, with doctors unavailable after 5 p.m. and on weekends, rotten food, staff retaliation and civil rights abuses.

“We cannot tolerate these conditions in our borough and in our city, and we cannot trust the Bureau of Prisons, the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, to maintain basic humane standards of living in this facility,” Sugrue said. “It’s up to us here to demand these humane conditions on behalf of the people behind us, and not stop until these demands are met.”

New York City Public Advocate Jumaane Williams condemned the shooting and detention of Belgal, saying nothing justified shooting someone several times in front of their child and then holding them in solitary confinement with a bullet in their neck. Williams also criticized President Donald Trump and federal officials for using faith and government power to justify violence in an effort to strip Black and Brown people of their humanity.

“You should not be in solitary confinement with a bullet in your neck after you’ve been shot with your child in the car. We should not have to say that in the United States of America in 2026. If these things were occurring in any other country, we would be sitting down, figuring out how we intervene to assist those folks. But we have liars, thieves, convicted crooks who are in charge of an agency that can be as violent as they want to be,” Williams said, vowing to stand up against the Trump administration’s cruelty and protect all immigrants.

“We’re going to stand here and fight for everyone who’s behind us, including Oscar, who is in solitary confinement with a bullet in his neck after being shot in front of his five-year-old child in a car on a busy street, at 4 p.m. picking his child up,” Williams went on. “That is an incredibly insane statement to have to say in Trump’s America. But that’s where we are, and I’m so proud to be a part of the better America.”

Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander said the danger ICE poses to children, including Belgal’s 5-year-old son, was not an isolated case. He shared that for the past couple of months, he has been attending detained juvenile dockets, where minors must appear in deportation proceedings.

Detained minors have either been separated from their parents, held despite having relatives ready to care for them, or used as bait to pressure their parents to come forward, only to end up detained or deported themselves. Although the Trump administration canceled funding for legal services intended to provide children with legal representation, minors, some of whom do not speak English, must appear before an immigration judge without a lawyer to help them navigate their cases.

“We are living with an immigration system paid for with our tax dollars, by our government, in our name, that is putting immigrant children in harm’s way every single day. And last week, it was with a hail of bullets that could have killed that kid, for, as we hear, no reason that has been presented,” Lander said. “Let’s be clear: no reason that could justify endangering the life of a child.”

City Council Member Alexa Avilés, whose district includes Sunset Park, noted that MDC has long been a site of pain for incarcerated people and their families. The facility, which currently houses high-profile inmates including former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and Luigi Mangione, has long been plagued by serious issues. In 2019, a power outage left prisoners without heat in the dead of winter, prompting national outrage. In 2024, a federal judge described conditions at the facility as “barbaric.”

“The conditions in this facility have been persistently horrific, and this needs to end. If the state cannot care for the people in its custody, it has no business holding people in its custody,” Avilés said, calling for solidarity in the fight against Trump’s inhumane deportation agenda and thanking MDC Brooklyn Community Support for its weekly vigils, which serve as a reminder not to lose faith amid cruelty.

“When this administration wants to do nothing but dehumanize and normalize cruelty, it is this community that stands here to remind us not to fall into that fray.”

After the rally, the coalition proceeded to the corner of Third Avenue and 29th Street for its weekly vigil, which featured speeches and interfaith songs. Some protesters lined up along Third Avenue holding signs, while passing drivers honked their horns in approval.

Assembly Member Marcela Mitaynes stressed the need to understand the gravity of the situation and organize the community to protect immigrant neighbors. She told Brooklyn Paper that Belgal’s inadequate medical care reflected the inhumanity of the Trump administration.

Mitaynes said she was disturbed that an ICE agent fired seven shots from a military-style rifle at a car carrying a child but was not surprised, given the aggressiveness ICE agents have displayed in other states. She also questioned why agents would approach and shoot someone who was on probation and not fleeing.

“The fact that he had any priors also does not justify the aggressiveness with which they came. We’re talking about a military-style rifle at 4o’clock in the afternoon, daylight in a residential area,” the pol said. “It’s clear that they have no training. They have no idea what they’re doing, and that makes them more dangerous. And that’s the scary part.”

Rev. Juan Carlos Ruiz, pastor of Good Shepherd Lutheran Church in Bay Ridge and one of the weekly vigil’s organizers, told Brooklyn Paper that the federal government was deliberately using the lack of medical care as a weapon to break detained immigrants’ spirits and force them to self-deport.

“Every four or five days, we have somebody in these detention centers killed. These are preventable deaths. But given the lack of medical care, the inhumane conditions that many of them are living in, that’s the result. It’s a deterrent kind of a policy. It’s cruelty,” Ruiz said, noting that ICE was escalating its presence even though New York City is a sanctuary city.

Lisa Raymond-Tolan, an organizer with Indivisible Brooklyn, encouraged New Yorkers to participate in the “No Kings; Vote Early” events on Oct. 17, including a parade and voter outreach event in Bay Ridge, New York City’s only swing district.

“This, in many ways, could be our last stand to save our democracy, and as Trump and the MAGA regime are increasing their horrific tactics in an effort to make them normal, we have to up our game as well,” Raymond-Tolan said. “The midterms are not always on everybody’s radar, and we need to educate voters that this may be your last chance to vote for democracy. We don’t know what’s going to happen during the election, after the election. So much is at stake that everybody needs to come together and get ready to confront the horrors still to come.”

The URL has been copied

A new report by the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe finds FIFA put revenue ahead of human rights at the 2026 World Cup.

The Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe have published a 50-page report, “Profit Over People: The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup”, assessing the tournament hosted across Canada, Mexico and the United States. It concludes that FIFA’s leadership did not put its own human rights commitments into practice, and that the drive for record revenue came at the expense of fairness and equality.

The 2026 edition was the first men’s World Cup held under FIFA’s 2017 Human Rights Policy, with human rights criteria built into the bidding process and a dedicated human rights framework for the 16 host cities.

What the report found

Fans priced and locked out: record ticket prices, costly visas, a lack of affordable transport between host cities and US travel restrictions on more than 39 countries excluded many supporters, particularly those on low incomes, from the Global South or with disabilities.

Immigration enforcement: citing Human Rights Watch research, the report notes more than 167,000 immigration arrests in and around 11 host cities in the run-up to the tournament, with enforcement surging during it.

Teams and officials affected: members of Iran’s squad had US visas delayed or refused, and a Somali referee with a valid visa was denied entry after an 11-hour interrogation.

Protest, press and housing: police in Mexico used tear gas on planned protests and detained two journalists, while host cities in Canada cleared unhoused residents from the streets.

Safeguarding gaps: at least eight players facing pending sexual assault cases or allegations took part, raising questions about how FIFA applied its own eligibility rules.

Limited access to remedy: FIFA’s grievance mechanism was barely publicised, so the full extent of harm remains unknown.

Andrea Florence, Executive Director of the Sport & Rights Alliance, said:

The 2026 World Cup exposed how the priorities and direction set by FIFA's leadership put profit over people.”

What the coalition is calling for

With a FIFA presidential election due in 2027, the coalition is asking FIFA and every candidate to:

make human rights requirements binding in host agreements for future men’s and women’s World Cups, with independent monitoring and consequences for breaches;

create a transparent, survivor-centred eligibility framework for athletes and officials facing serious misconduct or sexual violence allegations;

guarantee access without discrimination for fans, athletes and journalists, and protect freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and press freedom at tournaments;

ensure fair ticket access, including free companion seats for supporters with disabilities;

make grievance mechanisms visible, restore an independent Human Rights Advisory Board, reform the Ethics Committee and set up a permanent Remedy Fund.

The full report is available to download as a PDF.

Read the full announcement on the Sport & Rights Alliance website.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security finalized a rule Wednesday ending automatic work permit extensions for certain immigrants awaiting renewal approval, leaving affected workers at risk of losing their authorization to work while federal officials process their applications.

Published October 14, 2026, the final regulation permanently adopts restrictions that took effect under the Trump administration on October 30, 2025. Immigrants covered by the policy must generally receive approval from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) before their existing work permits expire, even when they submit renewal applications on time.

The restrictions replaced a protection that allowed eligible immigrants to continue working for up to 540 days while USCIS processed their renewal requests. The Biden administration had expanded that extension period to prevent employment interruptions caused by federal processing backlogs.

Affected applicants include certain asylum seekers, immigrants awaiting green card decisions, and qualifying spouses of foreign workers who depend on employment authorization documents, commonly known as EADs. Those whose permits expire before renewal approval may face interruptions in employment and income while their applications remain pending.

DHS estimates that between 20,000 and 33,000 work permits could lapse during an 18-month period beginning in May 2027, potentially affecting 1,700 to 2,800 employers. Its midpoint estimate of approximately 27,000 uses a 90-day renewal filing benchmark, assuming applicants submit requests three months before their existing permits expire. The department acknowledged that filing patterns, application volumes, and processing times could substantially change those projections.

Employers could incur approximately $312.1 million in labor turnover costs as they seek replacements for affected employees, according to the agency's economic analysis. DHS also projects $138.1 million in lost productivity for businesses unable to fill positions easily, along with a potential $14.5 million reduction in federal tax revenue over the same period.

The administration defended the restrictions as necessary to strengthen immigration screening and verify continued eligibility before granting additional work authorization. DHS argued that the previous policy allowed applicants to remain employed for months while officials conducted background checks and reviewed information that could affect their eligibility.

The department received 653 public comments on the restrictions, including submissions from immigration attorneys, legal service providers, labor unions, professional organizations and advocacy groups. Some raised concerns about staffing shortages in healthcare, education, agriculture and manufacturing as employees await renewal decisions, while others urged DHS to retain automatic extensions of 120, 180 or 240 days to reduce workplace disruptions.

Federal officials rejected those alternatives, maintaining that even shorter extensions would allow applicants to continue working before updated background checks and eligibility reviews were completed. DHS acknowledged the potential employment interruptions but concluded that its screening and security priorities justified the restrictions.

The rule also places additional importance on federal employment verification requirements. Employers must confirm that employees remain authorized to work and complete Form I-9 reverification when required. Federal law generally prohibits businesses from knowingly continuing to employ individuals who lack authorization, potentially forcing affected workers off the job while their renewal applications remain pending.

Automatic extensions granted through eligible renewal applications filed before October 30, 2025, remain valid under the previous rules. Separate protections established by federal law or Federal Register notices, including certain extensions involving Temporary Protected Status, also remain available.

text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. -- Witnesses say Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers targeted four workers who were repairing the roof at The Grand Marlin on Pensacola Beach on Tuesday following Hurricane Isaias.

Those close to the workers say they had all the right paperwork.

Witnesses say the armed agents -- wearing uniforms and identifying themselves as police -- were there for more than two hours, demanding the workers to come down. But some of the workers stayed on the roof until the officers eventually left.

"They were scared. They said they're not coming down," said Eric McKnight, a friend of the workers who witnessed the incident.

McKnight recorded part of the standoff on his cell phone.

He says the workers called him to the site to help translate, bringing them water and their documentation.

McKnight says it wasn’t until he and other bystanders mentioned the word “immigration” that got the officers to leave.

"As soon as we said that word, it's like a switch flipped. And they got in panic mode," McKnight said. "And I sent you the video. They were gone. They jumped in their cars and they were spinning tires out of there. As soon as we blew their cover. So they weren't honest with who they were."

Tuesday's encounter was just the latest ICE sighting in the area.

"That's not anything that anybody needs right now," said Grace Resendez McCaffrey, owner & editor of La Costa Latina Newspaper. "We're in disaster mode, trying to recover from a terrible catastrophe. We need everybody's help in in recovering from that."

Resendez McCaffrey is an advocate for the Spanish-speaking immigrant community.

She says she received several calls from the families of those workers who are worried that their relatives wouldn’t make it home.

"We hope that the community will step up and tell our state legislators that we don't want this type of patrolling in the area," Resendez McCaffrey said. "We don't want people being harassed from the rooftops that are just trying to help put things back together."

WEAR News asked Congressman Jimmy Patronis on Wednesday if he knew about immigration enforcement during recovery efforts.

"I have not personally seen it," he said. "I've just been focused on trying to make sure that the trains are running on time, that the power's getting turned back on."

WEAR News also reached out to The Grand Marlin, which provided this statement:

Following Hurricane Isaias, The Grand Marlin Pensacola Beach contracted a reputable local roofing business, with whom we have maintained a longstanding working relationship, to assist with repairs to our property.

We are aware of yesterday’s incident involving the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at our location. We have no further comment about the incident.

The Grand Marlin Pensacola Beach is open and operating as usual. Our focus remains on supporting our team, serving our guests, and being part of the communities we are proud to serve.

Knight says his friends plan to return to work, but likely won’t go back to The Grand Marlin.

text:
The Human Rights Center began a movement ten years ago by launching the first university-based open source investigations lab to document human rights violations and other violations of domestic and international law. The Investigations Lab has given more than 500 students from multiple disciplines tools and techniques to find, verify, and analyze publicly accessible information — social media posts, satellite imagery, digital databases and more — for lawyers, investigative reporters, human rights defenders, and researchers. The Lab has inspired more than two dozen university-based efforts of its kind worldwide and sparked the first international protocol on digital open source investigations: The Berkeley Protocol.

To mark our 10th anniversary, Alexa Koenig, Investigations Lab director, is hosting a series of conversations among Lab alumni, current students and partners in the work. Our first conversation is about investigating human rights abuses related to immigration.

The first conversation in the Lab’s 10-year anniversary series features Haley Willis, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who spent seven years with the New York Times visual investigations team before recently taking a “sustainability break”; Noah Bullock, executive director of the nonprofit Cristosol, who researches the conditions at El Salvador’s CECOT prison; and Talia Harter, a current Investigations Lab student who has led research on the experience of migrants at CECOT.

Willis, whose visual investigations at The New York York Times have spanned international and domestic human rights contexts, recounts coverage of ICE in Minneapolis. She talks about the importance of digging for information to piece together the truth and how terrifying it can be that “all the evidence can be there and nobody wants to look at it.”

Current student Harter discusses the Lab’s open source work on the removal of immigrants to third countries — often countries where they have no connection and do not speak the language — and the “architecture of cruelty” that surrounds the policy. Lab students, she says, are analyzing the agreements the US has made with countries, but also documenting the stories of immigrants shipped to those countries.

Bullock talks about Cristosol’s work in El Salvador and specifically in CECOT prison. He says one of the reasons he appreciates working with students in Berkeley’s Investigations Lab is because he began human rights work while in college.

“Great change has been possible over time because individuals in every generation have imagined something better,” Bullock said. “We all have to find a way in our own moment to contribute to pushing that legacy forward or it begins to move backwards.”

In this moving conversation, the speakers explore how to make the most impact for survivors and communities. Willis said she isn’t sure what form that will take for her in the future but that she’ll continue trying to “fulfill the conviction that the world doesn’t have to be the way that it is.”

text:
Batavia, N.Y. (WHAM) — Eduardo Machado recalled receiving an unexpected phone call from his partner Tuesday, telling him that his father, German Machado, had been detained by federal immigration agents outside his Batavia home as he prepared to leave for work.

"His car was there, unlocked, his lunch was still there, and the house just looked like he was ready to go for work," Eduardo Machado said.

BACKGROUND: SUNY Brockport employee detained by ICE outside home, union says

German Machado works in the IT department at SUNY Brockport. His family told 13WHAM they fled Venezuela in 2016 and sought asylum in the United States. Their asylum application has remained pending since then.

"We left in 2016 because my mom's a journalist and she was in danger in Venezuela with the dictatorship," Eduardo Machado said.

Eduardo said his family has work authorization and believes his father should not have been detained.

"We have legal status in the US. We have a pending political asylum. All of us have an authorized work authorization card. So we are legally working here. We're legally living here. There is no reason for my father to have been detained. He has no criminal record, a stable job, a house."

The Department of Homeland Security told 13WHAM on Wednesday that German Machado legally entered the United States in August 2016 with authorization to remain until February 2017.

The agency said Machado "overstayed his welcome by almost a decade and failed to depart."

Eduardo disputed the circumstances surrounding his father's detention, saying his family has followed the asylum application process.

"It's very worrisome," he said. "Having an ongoing, pending legal case should prevent something like this from happening. We came here and went through the right process. We are doing everything we can to abide by the law."

He said the arrest has also raised concerns about the rest of his family's safety.

"The lawyer said that if they got my father, they could come after us as well. So, we do have to remain as safe as we can."

SUNY Brockport said it "has been alerted to an off-campus federal law enforcement matter involving one of our employees and is in contact with the employee's family."

United University Professions, the union representing SUNY employees, is calling for Machado's immediate release.

"This is yet another well-loved member of our community, and there's no reason for him to be in detention," said Alissa Karl, vice president for academics with United University Professions at SUNY Brockport. "We want to make sure he has full due process, and we want him back at home where he belongs."

Eduardo said the outpouring of support reflects his father's importance to the university and the community.

"We're trying to do everything we can through the legal process to get him back," he said. "And I'm sure we will."

A DHS spokesperson said work authorization or a pending immigration application does not, by itself, confer lawful immigration status in the United States. The agency said Machado will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

Union members plan to rally in support of Machado on Thursday from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the SUNY Brockport student union.

Machado's other son, Samuel Machado, also released a statement to 13WHAM Wednesday, providing additional details about the family's immigration history.

My father, German Machado, is currently being held in immigration custody at the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia, New York.

Due to political persecution and the deteriorating conditions in Venezuela, my family sought refuge in the United States through lawful means. On August 30, 2016, we entered the United States through John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), where we were lawfully inspected and admitted pursuant to valid B-2 nonimmigrant visas. As reflected in our respective Forms I-94, our authorized period of admission extended through February 27, 2017.

On September 16, 2016, well within our authorized period of admission, my family timely filed an Application for Asylum and for Withholding of Removal (Form I-589) with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). My mother, Maria Velazquez de Machado, was designated as the principal asylum applicant, with my father, German Machado, included as her derivative spouse. My brother, Eduardo Machado, and I, Samuel Machado, were also included as derivative applicants, as we were both unmarried children under the age of 21 at the time of filing.

Since submitting our asylum application, our family has remained in the United States while awaiting adjudication of the pending application. In connection with these proceedings, we have been issued Employment Authorization Documents (Form I-766) and Social Security numbers, enabling us to obtain lawful employment in the United States.

Our asylum application has remained pending before USCIS for approximately ten years, and we have yet to be scheduled for an asylum interview. According to the information currently reflected in our USCIS case records, the application remains pending adjudication. To our knowledge, no removal proceedings have been initiated against any member of our family, nor has any final order of removal been issued. We have continued to maintain employment authorization pursuant to the applicable immigration regulations.

Notwithstanding these circumstances, my father was apprehended by officers of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at our family residence while preparing to leave for work (SUNY Brockport). He was subsequently transferred to the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia, New York, where he remains detained.

Our family has had virtually no communication with him since his apprehension. Our last contact occurred on August 13, at approximately 9:12 a.m., when he was permitted to make a telephone call lasting approximately one minute. During that brief conversation, he informed us that he had been taken into ICE custody. Since that time, we have been unable to speak with him or obtain meaningful information concerning the legal basis for his continued detention, his current circumstances, or any anticipated proceedings.

We are deeply concerned by his detention, particularly given the longstanding pendency of our family's asylum application, our documented lawful admission into the United States, and the absence of any known removal order. We are very grateful to the US for the opportunity to apply for asylum,

In light of these circumstances, we respectfully request assistance in obtaining clarification regarding the legal grounds for my father's apprehension and continued detention, confirmation of his current immigration status and any pending proceedings, and information concerning the steps necessary to seek his release while our family's asylum application remains pending.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection need to improve oversight and guidance for federal immigration officers' use of body-worn cameras, according to a Wednesday report from independent federal investigators.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security, however, resisted a recommendation in the report from the Government Accountability Office that ICE change its current policy, in which agents choose when to manually turn on body cameras, as opposed to automatic activation.

In a response to GAO, the department — which oversees both agencies — argued that automatic activation on a body camera presents a risk to ongoing operations, such as recording sensitive interactions with informants or victims or inadvertently filming bystanders.

GAO said that statement was insufficient. “However, DHS’s response did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective, or other controls that could help ensure compliance with activating cameras when required by policy,” according to GAO.

Multiple shootings

The report came after multiple high-profile cases of federal immigration officers shooting and killing people during interactions and enforcement actions, prompting calls for wider body camera use.

GAO made seven recommendations to the Department of Homeland Security to update its guidance for body cameras.

The department agreed with six, but disagreed with implementing automated camera activation controls, arguing that ICE’s current policy is sufficient. CBP does have automatic camera activation, which means the body camera turns on and starts recording when a weapon is drawn or emergency lights are turned on.

“Without reliable control activities, ICE risks gaps in documentation and video evidence that can make reviews of incidents more challenging,” according to GAO.

After federal immigration officers killed two U.S. citizens in January during an aggressive deportation drive in Minneapolis, the Trump administration directed body cameras to immigration agents.

In June, there were two back-to-back killings of immigrants in Texas and Maine that prompted border czar Tom Homan to announce that during traffic stops at least one ICE officer will wear a body camera.

Democrats have also pushed for all federal immigration officers to wear body cameras in the wake of the killings and violent interactions from agents that were recorded by bystanders.

Thousands of body cameras distributed

GAO investigators found that as of April, ICE issued 4,800 body cameras, splitting them evenly between its deportation wing of Enforcement and Removal Operations and the investigative law enforcement arm of ICE, Homeland Security Investigations.

And in June, CBP issued approximately 11,500 cameras, mostly to Border Patrol.

But GAO found problems in the cameras’ deployment.

“Most CBP and ICE offices have not developed specific operational guidance that explains how personnel should use, or not use, cameras under their unique operational circumstances,” according to the report. “The lack of guidance at this operational level increases the risk that CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy.”

DHS agreed to the recommendations from GAO that the leaders of ICE and CBP should update their body camera program to include changes in requirements and costs and plan for any contingencies based on current risk.

The department also agreed that CBP and ICE should implement goals to ensure effectiveness for the body-worn camera program and that both agencies should ensure their sub-agencies are also given proper guidance on the expectations and appropriate uses of the body cameras.

text:
Scientists fear losing control. Government leaders in the United States and abroad are debating how to keep increasingly capable models from causing harm.

These concerns must be taken seriously. But as a physician, I worry that fear of AI will cause our nation to overlook an extraordinary opportunity: harnessing narrower applications to improve patient care and save lives.

Consider a question I often pose to medical professionals. If you had time to check on patients every day, could you detect complications earlier and improve outcomes?

Almost always, the answer is yes.

For postoperative patients, that could mean identifying a surgical wound infection early enough to begin antibiotics without delay. For patients with chronic heart failure, it could mean treating at the earliest signs of acute decompensation. And for people with diabetes or hypertension, it could mean monitoring closely enough to maintain effective blood glucose and blood pressure control.

I saw the value of more frequent outreach and evaluation as CEO of The Permanente Medical Group. From 2000 to 2015, heart-disease and stroke mortality among Kaiser Permanente members declined roughly twice as fast as it did nationally. TPMG also controlled hypertension in 85% of patients, compared with 54% nationally.

However, that kind of care requires substantial clinician time and organizational resources. Most medical groups cannot afford to provide that level of attention consistently. There are not enough doctors, hours or dollars to do so nationwide.

Generative AI agents could change that calculus. These are software tools designed for specific tasks. They could monitor data, respond to health changes, and take predefined steps without direct clinician oversight.

Consider, for example, how AI might help one of the 6.7 million Americans living with chronic heart failure. A cardiologist monitoring a patient at home would look for increases in weight, ankle swelling, and fluid in the lungs. Combining those signs with reduced endurance and difficulty lying flat comfortably would indicate worsening heart failure.

These assessments are neither especially complex nor beyond what AI could do today. Bluetooth can connect agents to electronic scales and stethoscopes. Video monitoring would allow other agents to evaluate ankle swelling, measure stair-climbing ability, and assess whether the patient can lie flat comfortably.

In each case, these agents would augment what the doctor already does, not replace it. The potential benefit is significant. Across dozens of randomized trials, remote monitoring of patients with heart failure has reduced hospitalizations by roughly 20%. AI agents could make that kind of continuous monitoring easier and more affordable nationwide.

The same logic applies to chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes. Nearly 120 million American adults have high blood pressure, and 38 million live with diabetes. Both illnesses can damage the heart, kidneys, and blood vessels when poorly controlled.

Yet treatment still depends primarily on information collected during office visits, several months apart. Millions of patients already own home blood pressure cuffs or glucose monitors, but doctors rarely have the time to evaluate those readings. AI agents could track them, recognize when control is failing and notify physicians based on the same clinical parameters they would use if they could review the information frequently.

Consider the upside for patients with hypertension. The CDC estimates that better “team-based control” of high blood pressure could prevent roughly 92,000 heart attacks, 139,000 strokes and 115,000 cardiovascular deaths over five years. AI agents could support that care by making monitoring and evaluation easier.

A third opportunity comes after surgery. Once home, patients are instructed to watch for signs of infection at the incision site: redness, drainage, and pain. But because some of those changes are normal after surgery, patients may struggle to recognize when they signal a complication.

If surgeons could see patients daily, they would compare the wound’s appearance with how it looked the day before. AI agents could do the same by collecting photos or video from the patient’s phone, analyzing progression for signs of improvement or deterioration, and asking about pain or drainage.

If the application identified a likely problem, it could send the images and findings to a clinician, who could quickly determine whether the patient needed to be seen. Patients with concerns could still contact the surgeon directly.

Surgical-site infections add about $3.3 billion to U.S. health care costs each year. Earlier recognition would bring patients to medical attention sooner, when treatment — including antibiotics — would be more effective.

These opportunities to improve quality and save lives raise an important question. If Bluetooth, video, and conversational AI already exist, why haven’t they been assembled into tools that augment what physicians do today?

The biggest barrier is the complexity and expense of obtaining regulatory approval for medical tools used by patients. But Medicare offers a starting point. Its new ACCESS model supports technology-enabled chronic care and rewards providers for improving outcomes rather than simply delivering more services. Working with the FDA and NIH, ACCESS could provide a structured setting to test these agents, determine whether they improve medical outcomes, and create a path toward approval.

A second barrier is collaboration. Safely developing these agents for patient use at minimal cost will require clinicians, medical societies, and health systems to work with AI companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. In parallel, independent researchers will need to test reliability and ensure that false alarms do not overwhelm clinicians.

The existential risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems demand serious safeguards. But our nation should not treat every use of AI as equally dangerous. Yes, the risk of moving too fast is real. So is the danger of standing still.

Robert Pearl, the author of “ChatGPT, MD,” teaches at both the Stanford University School of Medicine and the Stanford Graduate School of Business. He is a former CEO of The Permanente Medical Group.

Self-governance is more than voting. It is informed judgment, civic participation, accountability, and constitutional responsibility. It means knowing our history, understanding our rights, questioning power, evaluating information, speaking when something is wrong, and participating rather than surrendering our voice. That power is difficult for a president to take because it begins with the citizen.

Self-governance is not only political — it is internal. It means governing one’s thoughts, emotions, and actions with discipline, awareness, and integrity. People who self-govern are composed, ethical, accountable, and purpose-driven. They recognize manipulation, resist pressure, and refuse to surrender independent judgment. A president can attempt to control institutions, pressure agencies, attack the press, manipulate information, and test constitutional boundaries. But a president cannot control a citizen who governs themselves. That is the power of self-governance.

The framers understood the danger of concentrated power. They created separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism, elections, and a free press because government was never supposed to depend on one person’s restraint. Constitutional government depends on citizens who recognize when these protections are being weakened — and are willing to act.

When executive power expands beyond constitutional limits, citizens must understand what is happening and what they can do. Executive overreach is not only a political problem; it is a constitutional warning signal. When Congress refuses to investigate, legislate, oversee, or use its constitutional powers, citizens cannot conclude that nothing can be done. When independent journalism is attacked, citizens must defend the information needed to make informed decisions. When elections are questioned or threatened, citizens must understand that elections belong to the people, not to any president or political party. Self-governance is how citizens respond.

Consider what happens when information becomes contested. A president who attacks reporters, restricts access, retaliates against dissent, or tries to replace independent reporting with a preferred narrative is not merely fighting with the press. He is affecting the information citizens need to govern themselves. Without reliable information, self-governance becomes harder. Propaganda is not just an attack on truth — it is an attack on the citizen’s ability to govern.

Citizens who know their rights and understand the constitutional system can distinguish fact from fiction. They can question claims, verify information, read beyond headlines, recognize manipulation, and reject conspiracies designed to make them distrust every institution. They can ask what was promised, what was done, who benefited, who was harmed, and what constitutional authority was used.

Self-governance is remembering. A nation that forgets becomes vulnerable to having its history rewritten. National memory belongs to the people. When history is altered to flatter power, citizens lose knowledge they need to recognize manipulation. Self-governance requires Americans to remember what leaders did, what institutions allowed, what rights were challenged, and what consequences followed. That memory shapes how citizens understand the present.

Reports indicate that Trump’s approval rating has reached historical lows, even as he urges voters to support candidates “as if his name were on the ballot.” After the administration revoked press passes for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, a federal judge ordered their access restored, according to court filings. Continued restrictions on entry to certain events, however, have raised further concerns about the independent reporting citizens rely on. Additional reporting has also raised concerns about possible federal interference in elections, including ballot seizures, and altered election rules. These developments and warnings raise constitutional questions citizens must understand rather than dismiss or accept without scrutiny.

Elections are not personal loyalty tests. The press is not an enemy of the government. Constitutional rights do not belong to presidents. Public institutions do not belong to officeholders. They belong to the people.

Congress also matters because citizens cannot exercise self-governance fully if they do not hold their representatives accountable. Congress has constitutional powers designed to restrain executive overreach. When it fails to use them, accountability does not end — it shifts to the people. Citizens cannot perform Congress’s constitutional duties, but they can demand that their representatives fulfill them. That means more than complaining. It means contacting representatives, writing letters, making calls, attending town halls, supporting independent journalism, asking for roll-call votes, and remembering how elected officials responded when constitutional limits were tested. It means voting — not waiting for Election Day. Self-governance happens between elections.

And it happens close to home. City councils, school boards, county commissions, and other local bodies make decisions affecting education, safety, zoning, budgets, public resources, and community life. Citizens who attend meetings, speak at meetings, question officials, examine budgets, and serve on boards are not merely participating in government. They are governing.

Self-governance is not simply having a government that represents you. It is accepting responsibility for decisions that shape your community and country. This responsibility belongs to everyone — conservatives, moderates, independents, and progressives. It does not require agreement on every political issue. It requires agreement on something fundamental: government must remain accountable to the people, and constitutional limits must apply to those who hold power.

The people cannot protect what they do not understand. But civic understanding is not reserved for experts or elected officials; it can be learned, strengthened, and shared. Americans need to know what the Constitution protects, what each branch of government is empowered to do, where those powers end, and what citizens can do when leaders cross those boundaries. The Constitution is not simply a document government officials swear to uphold. It is also a framework that gives citizens authority to hold those officials accountable.

Self-governance is both a right and a responsibility. It means refusing to surrender judgment because politics is exhausting, refusing to accept propaganda because truth is inconvenient, and refusing to remain silent because speaking up feels powerless. It means remembering that government derives its legitimacy from the people and that elected officials serve the public — not the other way around.

The Republic drifts when citizens disengage and recovers when they use self-governance deliberately. Institutions can fail, and executive power can go unchecked, but neither makes the people powerless. Americans must use the power they possess: informed judgment, voting, civic participation, public pressure, independent journalism, constitutional knowledge, and accountability. They must question power rather than fear it, defend truth rather than surrender to narrative, and demand that Congress use its constitutional authority with courage and persistence. They must participate where government is closest to them — in their communities, schools, councils, commissions, and elections.

The people are not powerless. They are the sovereign. Self-governance is how they exercise that power. It is how they defend their rights when institutions fail, protect truth when history is manipulated, and demand accountability when leaders abuse authority. It is how the Republic survives, how the nation remains accountable to its people, and how Americans remain free.

Self-governance is America’s last defense against executive overreach — and the one defense no president can ever take unless the people surrender it.

Carolyn Goode is a retired school principal and an adjunct university instructor who writes about civic literacy, constitutional accountability, and the responsibilities citizens share in sustaining democratic governance.
