text:
Lawyers for Oscar Belgal, the undocumented Dominican immigrant shot by ICE agents in New York City last week, are asking for his immediate release, claiming that agents never identified themselves before the shooting and, six days later, their client still hasn’t been allowed to undergo surgery despite having a bullet lodged in his neck.

The Legal Aid Society, which now represents the 28-year-old father, filed a habeas corpus petition in Brooklyn Federal Court Wednesday, calling Belgal’s arrest illegal and demanding his “immediate release on reasonable conditions.”

“Anything less fails to adequately address Oscar’s imminent risk of complete and irreversible harm,” reads the motion, filed by Legal Aid immigration lawyer Perry McAninch, noting, “He has experienced a loss of sensation in half of his face, as well as hearing loss in his left ear.”

Belgal’s lawyers said he had picked his boy up from school and taken him to McDonald’s before ICE agents swarmed his car.

“After ICE shot him, Oscar exited his vehicle and pleaded for medical assistance, fearing that he was dying,” the Legal Aid motion reads. “And believing the same, his son began yelling that the masked individuals had killed his dad.”

Belgal claims in court papers that ICE agents never identified themselves as they approached the car with guns drawn.

“It wasn’t until later, when Oscar woke up in the hospital with one of their bullets lodged in his neck, that the individuals would declare themselves as ICE officers,” his attorneys said in the court filing.

Belgal, who was initially detained in New Jersey after his shooting, was moved to the notorious MDC Brooklyn federal jail on Friday.

“Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five-year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” McAninch and fellow Legal Aid attorney Elyssa Williams said in a joint statement Wednesday. “With a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk. The Court must intervene and order his immediate release.”

The Daily News has covered several instances of medical mistreatment at the jail, including two cases where staff botched inmates’ cancer treatment. In one case, court documents detail how jail staff ignored an inmate’s CT scan result for months, allowing a tumor in his lung to triple in size. He died last November.

Belgal’s case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Hector Gonzalez, a Biden appointee who has ruled against ICE in the past.

Judge Gonzalez gave the Department of Homeland Security until Monday at 10 a.m. to file paperwork explaining why Belgal shouldn’t be released. He also ordered that Belgal remain in New York until DHS files its paperwork.

An earlier habeas corpus petition brought by Belgal’s attorneys in Manhattan Federal Court following the shooting is expected to be dismissed after his then lawyers acknowledged Tuesday that he wasn’t in the Southern District of New York when they filed it.

An ICE agent fired seven bullets into a silver Honda Civic driven by Belgal on Marble Hill Ave. near W. 225th St. Thursday afternoon, hitting him in the neck. His 5-year-old son was in the back seat.

While video of the actual shooting has not been released, agents were in plainclothes, some disguised as construction workers, when they ran up to Belgal’s car, their weapons raised toward him.

Belgal’s attorneys say ICE didn’t have a warrant for their client’s arrest.

“Respondents have failed to meet the most elemental requirements for their arrest and detention authority, not even having charged Oscar as a removable immigrant before arresting him,” McAninch wrote.

After shooting him, ICE agents stood by doing nothing as he bled on the ground, attorneys claim. Responding NYPD officers took him to New York-Presbyterian Allen Hospital.

The court filing doesn’t identify who shot Belgal, though it names Supervising Deportation Officer Brenden Cuni as one of the agents present. He’s not believed to be the shooter.

Cuni has been named in several cases alleging violence against immigrants during arrests, and he’s been called to task by name by at least two Brooklyn Federal Court judges in cases where agents made arrests before writing up arrest warrants.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin has repeatedly defended the agents, painting Belgal as a “dangerous” criminal with ties to the Trinitarios — though the government hasn’t described what those ties might be — and saying that he “weaponized his vehicle” and accelerated at ICE officers as he tried to escape.

Belgal may have direct or indirect knowledge of a shooting of a Customs and Border Protection officer in Manhattan last year, Mullin said.

When asked to comment on Legal Aid’s petition to have Belgal released, DHS only sent quotes that Mullin said Friday, calling the detainee one of the “worst of the worst.” The federal Bureau of Prisons said they “do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or medical status.”

On May 22, Judge Gonzalez ruled against ICE in the case of Ecuadorian immigrant Oscar Alexander Curimilma Quille, who was surrounded and arrested without a warrant during a vehicle stop outside his Patchogue home on April 30. The agents were targeting another person when they surveilled the vehicle.

In that case, ICE agents failed to include accurate information in those initial documents to show that Quille had the opportunity to explain he wasn’t dangerous or a flight risk, and gave “inconsistent” evidence about whether he tried to run from them.

“If the government did not accurately record the truth, Petitioner’s detention was a foregone conclusion. If the government did not even consider the truth and instead recorded what it thought would justify detention, that is far worse. Under either scenario, Petitioner was not afforded due process,” the judge wrote at the time.

text:
This week’s pick of news and commentary about solitary confinement:

A man who was shot by ICE in New York City last week still has a bullet lodged in his neck, according to his attorneys. The man, Oscar Belgal, is a 28-year-old immigrant from the Dominican Republic who was shot in his car by ICE while driving with his five-year-old son. Since the shooting, Belga has been held in solitary confinement at the federal Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn after a short stint at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital. According to his legal team, Belgal has been denied proper food, been forced to drink water from the bathroom sink, and has lost feeling in the left side of his face. Harold Solis, an attorney with Make the Road New York, said, “It’s not clear to us why a person with a bullet in their body is in solitary confinement and hasn’t been seen by medical specialists that apparently even the hospital told him he needs.” A statement by Belgal’s legal team said the “deliberate indifference” from ICE agents and Belgal’s mistreatment at the jail represent “further examples of the cruelty and disregard for basic human dignity that have long defined this agency.” Gothamist

A 29-year-old man, Emil Encarnacion, died last week in an apparent suicide in the “behavioral assessment unit” (BAU) at MCI-Norfolk, a medium security prison in Massachussetts. The Massachusetts Department of Corrections claims that the BAUs are an alternative to solitary confinement. However, individuals in the BAU are held in their cells alone for up to 21 hours a day, which is only one hour less than the 22 hours of in-cell time in the solitary confinement “restrictive housing” unit. Prisoners often refer to BAUs as “the hole” and say the promised access to services like recreation, phone calls, and case management are not available as advertised. If officially ruled a suicide, Encarnacion’s death would be the fourth suicide in a Massachusetts BAU since April 2025. MassLive

A U.S. Air Force Major who called for President Donald Trump’s impeachment has been imprisoned in solitary confinement since August, according to his attorney. Major Jason Watson was originally arrested on July 1 for standing on the steps of the U.S. Capitol holding a sign that read “Impeach. Convict. Remove.” on the grounds that his action violated the “rarely used” Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which prohibits military personnel from using “contemptuous words” against the president. After criticizing Trump in an interview with CNN on August 18, Watson was placed into military pretrial detention, where his lawyer says he has been held in solitary confinement for 24 hours a day. Watson’s lawyer says the U.S. government is preparing to try him in a general court martial, the military’s most serious form of trial. Military.com

Idris Makhmudov, a lead organizer of a hunger strike with over 500 participants at an immigration detention center in Georgia, was placed in solitary confinement this week. Makhmudov and dozens of participants began their strike October 6 after spending an average of 20 months at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE Processing Center, the nation’s largest immigration detention complex. Detained immigrants, the majority of whom are confined for merely seeking asylum, have written a report of conditions inside the facility, including gravely inadequate medical and dental care; moldy, spoiled food; undrinkable water that causes rashes; cramped sleeping areas; and “xenophobic treatment” from staff. Advocates say Makhmudov’s move to solitary confinement is an act of retaliation for his role organizing the hunger strike. Another man, Andrei Gerdiukov, was also placed in solitary for participating in the strike, according to his wife. The detained immigrants’ report also alleged that detention center staff “frequently threaten detained immigrants with solitary confinement.” Latin Times | The Guardian | The Current

The trial for a class-action lawsuit alleging abuse in solitary confinement at Virginia’s supermaximum Red Onion State Prison was canceled this week, after both sides reached a proposed settlement. The suit was filed by the ACLU on behalf of over a hundred incarcerated plaintiffs held in solitary confinement for as long as 24 years, alleging plaintiffs were subjected to physical abuse, racist harassment, recreation in feces-covered cages, and extended stays in solitary confinement through a program allegedly meant to “transition” them out of solitary. WJLA

A mother in Alabama, Tanisha Thomas, is suing the state Department of Corrections after her son died in August 2026 from complications resulting from a suicide attempt in solitary confinement three years earlier. Thomas says she was only notified that her son William Andrell Thomas was found hanging in his cell from another incarcerated man, not from prison officials at St. Clair Correctional Facility. While William survived the hanging attempt, he sustained severe brain injuries that took away his ability to speak and walk. He was moved from the hospital back to prison seven months after regaining consciousness, while still in critical condition. After finally returning home on a medical furlough, William passed away from his injuries in August. WHNT

Martin Soto has been released from Delaney Hall immigration detention center in New Jersey after four months in solitary confinement. A judge ordered his immediate release after Soto’s attorney argued that holding Soto in solitary—and the ensuing severe psychological damage, including suicidal thoughts—constituted unconstitutional conditions, especially considering his deportation was not “reasonably foreseeable,” or imminent. Soto’s petition for release also alleged the unconstitutionality of involuntary servitude at the detention center, where detained immigrants are forced to work 12 hours a day for $1—or less, if they do not reach the 12-hour mark. Soto was placed in solitary as retaliation for organizing a hunger strike at Delaney Hall against the unsanitary conditions, according to his lawyer. Soto, originally from Peru, was detained while picking up diapers for his two children. NJ.com

Three transgender women allege mistreatment—including physical abuse from staff, verbal harassment from both staff and other detained people, medical neglect, isolation, and invasive strip searches—at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena, Louisiana. New Orleans-based attorney Mich González said, “There is nothing in the system that is built to recognize their full humanity as trans people, and now there’s no mechanisms in place to protect them from transphobic violence, from abuse of solitary confinement,” referring to the Trump administration’s 2025 executive order blocking protections and care for trans people in prisons and detention centers. Though ICE claims their placement in solitary is for their own protection, Sofia, one of the detained trans women, said, “[Solitary] isn’t protection, it’s torture.” The three women were seeking asylum in the United States and have no active criminal charges. Verite News New Orleans

Children in Connecticut can be kept in rooms for “ED [Emergency Department] boarding” in a practice that is “more than simply dehumanizing; the experience is tantamount to solitary confinement,” writes child advocate Larissa Pitts in an opinion piece. Pitts describes visiting one of her 16-year-old clients in a room with no windows and limited human connection, where she was held for three days awaiting foster care placement. Faced with the trauma of returning to ED boarding, the child chose to stay at the first foster care placement offered to her, despite the family’s teenage son sexually harassing her in her room at night. The practice of isolation is often used on children in the state’s foster care system, like Pitts’ client. Connecticut Mirror

text:
Fresno, Calif. (KRGV) — The Fresno County District Attorney’s Office charged a 32-year-old ICE agent from McAllen with the assault on a 72-year-old Fresno homeowner and the homeowner’s daughter.

David Gonzalez III pleaded not guilty Wednesday to charges of assault, elder abuse, vandalism, and battery in connection with the incident, Central California ABC affiliate ABC 30 Action News said, adding that investigators said Gonzalez appeared drunk during the incident.

Gonzalez appeared in court in a wheelchair, the ABC 30 Action News said.

READ MORE: ICE agent accused of assault in Fresno held position less than a year

According to a release from the district attorney’s office, Gonzalez was found sleeping on the front lawn of a Fresno home during the early morning hours Oct. 9, 2026, when the homeowner asked him to leave.

“Gonzalez assaulted him, causing him to fall to the ground and sustain visible injuries. During the incident, Gonzalez also threw the victim into a neighbor’s parked vehicle, causing significant damage to the side of the car,” the news release said. “When the homeowner’s daughter intervened to help her father, Gonzalez assaulted her as well, causing her to fall to the ground.”

Fearing for his safety and his daughter’s safety, the unidentified homeowner shot Gonzalez. He was later hospitalized.

The DA’s office says Gonzalez faces a maximum sentence of nearly five years if convicted on all charges.

Fresno County jail records show Gonzalez was released on bond Wednesday. ABC 30 Action News said the bond for Gonzalez was set at $37,000, and he’s required to remain in California after posting bond.

The Hidalgo County Sheriff’s Office confirmed to Channel 5 News that Gonzalez worked as a sheriff’s deputy before becoming an ICE agent in December 2025.

Channel 5 News reached out to an ICE spokesperson on Wednesday night regarding Gonzalez's arrest and employment status. Updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

text:
Nearly a week after he was shot during an encounter with Immigration Customs and Enforcement officers in Manhattan, the man remains held at a detention center with the bullet still inside him, his attorneys alleged in a court filing Wednesday.

Oscar Belgal was shot Thursday in his car while his 5-year-old son was in the back seat, authorities said. Attorneys with the Legal Aid Society said in a habeas petition that the bullet is still "lodged in his neck" and he is only being given ibuprofen for the pain.

"With the bullet still lodged in his neck, the entire left side of Oscar's face remains numb. He struggles to hear anything out of his left ear, describing what he does hear as sounding as if it were far off in the distance," the petition said.

The 28-year-old Dominican national is allegedly being held in a segregated unit at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, as federal prosecutors seek to remove him from the country, according to the petition.

A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily barred the Trump administration from deporting Belgal or transferring him outside of the Southern District of New York, the Eastern District of New York or the District of New Jersey. A different judge ordered a similar block on Belgal's deportation last week.

In his order Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Hector Gonzalez is also asking the government to explain why it believes Belgal warrants mandatory detention despite recent rulings, including one by the same judge, that limits the government’s ability to detain someone without bond or consideration of their individual circumstances.

Belgal's attorneys contended ICE agents arrested Belgal without a warrant.

ICE did not immediately comment on the latest court filing from Belgal's attorneys.

Last week, the Department of Homeland Security alleged that Belgal, who they claim has "associations" with a gang and a criminal record, "weaponized his vehicle," when ICE agents tried to box him in with their vehicles during the arrest. Belgal denies having involvement with the gang and his attorneys say ICE has not provided any evidence?

Surveillance footage shows Belgal parked in his SUV when two officers in plainclothes approach him with guns drawn.

It is not immediately clear what the two armed men were saying to Belgal.

Belgal is seen reversing and then driving out of the parking spot as one of the armed men punches the driver's side window and breaks the glass. He is seen driving off.

Nidia Delfín, Delfín’s sister, said her brother was handcuffed in the backseat of the ICE vehicle when it hit Parra, adding that he was on his way to breakfast with employees when he was apprehended by ICE. She said that Delfín is not a criminal, that he has no arrest warrants and that he was in the process of getting his green card, which means he was on the path to being a legal permanent resident.

“He owns his own small company. He hires people from the community. He is a good man,” she said, adding that he witnessed “this horrific incident.”

She said that she, her parents and her brother are afraid but that they are speaking up so Parra “can get justice.” She pleaded with others in the community who witnessed the incident — she said she has seen videos on social media — to do the same and share the information they have.

“What was done to him is not OK,” she said, referring to Parra. “It’s not how we’re supposed to treat other human beings.”

Cesar Espinosa of FIEL Houston, an immigrant civil rights organization who is representing Parra’s family, said the men held in the ICE vehicle “witnessed everything that happened,” including “the moment when Mr. Miguel [Parra] was run over.”

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News on Tuesday that videos gathered by his office suggest that Parra was struck intentionally. Teare said his office is seeking to interview the witnesses as it investigates the case.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

A senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News on Tuesday that ICE officers on the scene were wearing body cameras and that the agency is reviewing video for an internal investigation.

ICE has said allegations that the agency intentionally struck Parra are “RECKLESS and FALSE.”

Espinosa said that if there is video from body cameras, it should be turned over to the district attorney’s office immediately.

A government watchdog report released Wednesday found that Customs and Border Protection and ICE have not developed specific operational guidance to explain how their personnel should use body cameras.

Without that guidance, “CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy,” the Government Accountability Office said in its report.

The Trump administration issued guidance two weeks ago that dictated that officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

DHS and ICE did not immediately respond to questions about the release of the bodycam video, whether they planned to deport witnesses to the incident and the status of the ICE officer who drove the vehicle that hit Parra.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.

At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction.

The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

Teare, a Democrat, told NBC News the investigation could lead to charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Espinosa said at the news conference that Parra does not feel safe at the hospital. The ICE officers who were there when he was struck “are the same crew that are watching him 24/7” at the hospital, Espinosa said. He did not know whether the driver of the vehicle was among those guarding Parra.

ICE did not immediately confirm whether the ICE officers involved in Saturday’s incident are with Parra at the hospital.

Espinosa, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno and Parra’s family demanded at the news conference that ICE keep Parra at the hospital where he is being treated for his multiple injuries.

Without the proper medical care, he could end up with infections and other problems that could be life-threatening, “so we need him to get the best medical care possible,” Espinosa said.

Espinosa and Bruno said Parra still has not been processed by ICE, which has said that he is in the country illegally. Bruno and Espinosa confirmed that Parra was undocumented and said they could not provide further information about whether he was seeking other status.

Parra, who works applying stucco, has been in the country 34 years, having arrived at age 14, Espinosa and Bruno said.

The man who was driving the truck with Parra and also ran away was identified at the news conference as “Omar.” He does not have a criminal record or any open immigration warrants, Espinosa said.

At the news conference, advocates criticized ICE for pursuing Parra with the immigrants handcuffed in their car, endangering everyone, according to Espinosa.

Teare, who served several years as the chief of the district attorney’s vehicular crimes division, also criticized ICE’s tactics.

“The behavior of this agency and these agents on our streets is so dangerous to everyone that lives in these communities,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

ICE did not immediately respond to allegations that it was conducting an immigration stop while it was transporting immigrants it had previously apprehended.

ICE has said in statements that it was pursuing a man it identified as Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. It has said Parra was not its target.

Espinosa repeatedly held up a photo of Mendoza at the news conference and said no one, including Parra, recognized him or knew who he was. He also showed a photo of Omar, the man who was with Parra in the car before they fled, to show it was not Mendoza.

“If he [Mendoza] does exist, he must be taken into custody, and a proper thorough investigation must be done so that he may be looked at,” Espinosa said.

text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer appeared to intentionally drive a vehicle into a Mexican construction worker in Houston, then fled the scene, a prosecutor said Wednesday, rejecting the agency’s claim the man stepped in front of the vehicle while running from authorities.

A family member of Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, also disputed the identity of a man who ICE says was with him and had been the target of Saturday’s operation, saying they had never seen or heard of that person before.

Both called into question the details provided by ICE surrounding the encounter that has added fuel to fiery criticism of immigration enforcement operations in Houston, where local prosecutors are already investigating a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.

Surveillance footage shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, told The Associated Press the video clearly shows Mr. Parra running away from the unmarked vehicle driven by an ICE officer. The agency has claimed Parra Hernandez ran in front of it.

“That vehicle jumped a median, drove into a parking lot and drove directly at and then over Mr. Parra,” Teare said.

Parra Hernandez underwent surgery for a broken leg later Saturday and also needs surgery on his ankle, his lawyer, Kim Bruno, said during a news conference Wednesday. He remains in ICE custody in the hospital, she said.

Harris County DA is looking at criminal charges

Teare said ICE already had two detainees in the SUV — a Jeep Cherokee — when it ran over Parra Hernandez, and his office will get statements from both of them before making a charging decision, likely next week.

His office spoke with Parra Hernandez on Tuesday in the hospital.

“What I’ve seen so far indicates to me that this agent intentionally struck this person and ran him over,” Teare said.

After Parra Hernandez was hit, the Harris County Sheriff's office and the Harris County District Attorney's Office went to the scene with a tow truck to impound the ICE vehicle and download crash data, Teare said.

But the same ICE officer who drove the vehicle into Parra Hernandez had fled the scene in the SUV, thus keeping the vehicle in ICE's possession, Teare said. Driving a vehicle that has been involved in a collision writes over or erases the data recorded by the vehicle, he said.

“Any law enforcement officer knows those facts. ICE, either intentionally or through gross negligence, destroyed potential evidence in this case,” Teare said.

Teare said his office is evaluating several possible charges to bring against the ICE officer, including assault with a deadly weapon.

ICE denies intentionally striking Parra Hernandez

Allegations that officers intentionally struck Parra Hernandez are “reckless” and “false,” ICE said in a statement. Parra Hernandez had been in a vehicle with the target of an enforcement operation, and when officers tried to stop the car, the two men fled on foot, the agency said.

He “ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” ICE said.

Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization, flatly denied this claim during a news conference Wednesday, citing the surveillance video.

Attorneys and relatives of others who were arrested by ICE during the operation Saturday denied during the news conference that the man ICE named as the target of its operation — Jose Mendoza-Cervantes — was even in the white van, saying they didn’t know anyone of that name.

Espinosa said Parra Hernandez is from Mexico and has been in the U.S. for 34 years. He declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status, but said he is living in the U.S. without authorization.

He said two ICE officers were in the room when he visited Parra Hernandez at the hospital.

Prosecutors are still investigating a fatal ICE shooting in July

Teare said ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.

text:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday seemed likely to let a lawsuit brought by a Tennessee man alleging that a website owned by entertainment giant Paramount Global violated a 1988 video privacy law when it shared information with Facebook go forward, at least for now. After nearly 90 minutes of oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, the justices appeared poised to agree with Michael Salazar that the law, the Video Privacy Protection Act, applies to any consumer of the products sold by a company that provides videos. Although some members of the court expressed concerns about the possibility that allowing Salazar’s suit to proceed could open the door to lawsuits against a broad swath of U.S. companies, those concerns appeared to be assuaged in part by the prospect that other provisions of the law could serve as a check on such suits. Moreover, some justices suggested that companies could easily avoid suits in the future by obtaining their customers’ consent to share their personal information.

The law before the court on Wednesday has its origins in the 1987 battle over the nomination of Judge Robert Bork to fill the vacancy left by the retirement of Justice Lewis Powell from the Supreme Court. A Washington journalist, Michael Dolan, obtained and published a list of the videos that Bork had rented from his local video store.

Bork’s nomination failed, with 58 senators voting against him and only 42 for him. That likely had little to do with his taste in movies, which included (as Dolan later recounted) “whodunits and Brit films, costume drama and otherwise.” But Dolan’s article spurred Congress to enact the Video Privacy Protection Act, which bars a “video tape service provider” from “knowingly disclos[ing], to any person, personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider.”

In 2022, Salazar subscribed to an email newsletter distributed by 247Sports.com, a Paramount-owned website that covers college sports recruiting. Salazar says that he watched videos on the 247Sports.com site while he was logged into his Facebook account. Paramount, he says, then used a code known as a Pixel that it had installed – without Salazar’s consent – on 247Sports.com to provide Facebook with information about the videos that Salazar had watched on the site.

Salazar filed a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Nashville, Tennessee, alleging that Paramount’s disclosure of his video-viewing history without his consent violated the VPPA. He asked the court to award $2,500 in damages (the maximum available under the law) for the alleged violation of the VPPA to him and the other members of the class, as well as (among other things) punitive damages and attorney’s fees.

U.S. District Judge Eli Richardson dismissed Salazar’s case. He ruled that, for purposes of the VPPA, Salazar was not a “consumer,” because a “consumer” must be “‘a subscriber of goods and services in the nature of audio-visual content.’” Salazar could not be a “subscriber,” he wrote, because the 247Sports.com newsletter was not “audio-visual content.”

A divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit upheld that ruling. Writing for the majority, Judge John Nalbandian wrote that although, standing alone, “the expression ‘goods or services’ is not limited, its association with surrounding words cabins its meaning. The full definition of ‘consumer’ in the statute does not encompass consumers of all ‘goods or services’ imaginable, but only those ‘from a video tape service provider.’”

Salazar came to the Supreme Court last fall, asking the justices to weigh in, which they agreed in late January to do.

On the one hand, although the question was not actually before them, some justices were skeptical that Paramount Global fell within the definition of “video tape service provider” at all. Justice Clarence Thomas was the first to make this point. He told Joshua Hammack, who represents Salazar, that the statute only applies to an entity that rents, sells, or delivers “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.” How, Thomas asked, would that extend to videos streamed over the internet?

When Hammack countered that the law does not require a tangible object, but instead also covers videos that someone plays on their phone or at their house, Thomas suggested that streaming a movie on TV might be closer to traditional television (which is not covered by the VPPA) than picking a video up from a movie rental store.

Thomas made the same point with Paul Clement, who represents Paramount Global, asking how 247Sports.com qualifies as a video tape service provider. It does not naturally seem, Thomas said, to be in the business of providing videos.

But Clement also indicated that the definition of “video tape service provider” sweeps more broadly than companies whose sole business is selling or renting video tapes. When Congress enacted the VPPA, he noted, it “did make it pretty clear” that a department store that sold videos would be considered a video tape service provider.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett echoed Thomas’ question, asking Hammack why the videos that 247Sports.com played on its site made it analogous to a 1980s-era movie-rental store and therefore a “video tape service provider.” She appeared unpersuaded by Hammack’s contention that when 247Sports.com plays videos on its site, it has a “profit motive,” telling him that “basically every other business” with a website has a profit motive. “[I]f I’m on Nordstrom’s website,” she said, “and I click to … see the model show me what the shoes are going to look like … that’s a profit motive.”

Justice Samuel Alito also appeared doubtful at times that Paramount Global was a “video tape service provider,” telling Hammack that the VPPA was a “law that is based on the technology of the 1980s.” He questioned whether Paramount was selling or renting videotapes, and what it meant for a product to be “similar” to videotapes. “[I]t is not similar,” he noted, “in the sense that you go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, who was relatively quiet during Wednesday’s argument, suggested that Salazar’s interpretation of the VPPA was inconsistent with Congress’ goal of protecting a consumer’s video-viewing history. He harkened back to what he described as a favorite hypothetical of retired Justice Stephen Breyer, involving a sign that proclaims “no pets in a park.” Does that mean, Roberts queried, that someone who has a pet snail in his pocket can be prosecuted, or does it mean that we should look at the purpose of the rule?

Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed both lawyers on a key argument made by Paramount Global: whether allowing Salazar’s lawsuit to move forward would open the floodgates to lawsuits against all kinds of businesses that stream videos on their websites.

Hammack stressed that federal trial courts have ruled that businesses such as, say, Chick-fil-A are not “video tape service providers” and therefore not subject to suit under the VPPA.

That response prompted Kavanaugh to ask Clement how the court should think about what Kavanaugh characterized as the “sky-is-falling concern” when Paramount Global could still prevail on two separate questions that are not actually before the court – what constitutes a “video tape service provider” and whether the kind of information that Paramount disclosed to Facebook qualifies as “personal identifiable information.”

Kavanaugh then suggested that a “very easy solution” to the problem facing Paramount Global and other similarly situated companies would simply be to obtain their customers’ consent before disclosing any information obtained from them.

Justice Elena Kagan made the same point, telling Clement that a company could avoid liability under the VPPA in two ways: first, by getting consent; and, second, by ceasing the practice of selling people’s personal information.

Kagan also indicated that, in her view, this case was precisely the kind of case that Congress intended to cover in the VPPA. She described a scenario in which a judge watched many videos of women wrestling on a sports website like 247Sports.com, with the potential for embarrassment if that video-viewing history were disclosed. “[C]ouldn’t this case kind of be the paradigmatic” example, she asked, of a case to which the VPPA would apply?

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared sympathetic to Salazar’s position. She told Clement that he had “a line-drawing problem.” The point of the VPPA, she said, “was the unlawful disclosure without consent of personally identifying information.” But under Paramount Global’s interpretation, she continued, the application of the statute would hinge on “what particular item the consumer purchased” from the video tape service provider. “And I don’t understand why that should be the dividing line or why that makes any sense in this concept.”

Barrett also questioned whether Salazar has a legal right to sue, known as standing. She emphasized that Salazar’s information had not actually been disclosed to a person, no matter “what this Pixel thing is.”

Hammack pushed back, responding that Salazar’s video-viewing history had gone to Facebook, the world’s largest social-media company.

Barrett raised the question again with Clement, asking whether Paramount Global conceded that Salazar has a right to sue.

Characterizing the information that had been disclosed to Facebook as “gobbledegook,” Clement offered to provide additional briefing on the question of whether Salazar could bring his lawsuit at all.

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Two people were allegedly in the back seat of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle when an agent struck a man during a pursuit in Texas on Saturday and are now sought for questioning by local investigators, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said.

DA Sean Teare told ABC News Wednesday that his office identified the two ICE detainees who were in the vehicle when the unidentified agent struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez at a strip mall outside Houston.

"We were not able to interview them at the scene," Teare told ABC News, adding that federal agents had already moved the two persons away to a detention facility.

The DA said his office alleged that ICE had picked up the two people before the incident with Parra-Hernandez earlier in the day.

Teare said he reached out to the federal government to let them know the two men, who are still in a detention center, are material witnesses in their investigation into the incident.

ICE said in a statement that an agent was pursuing Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national who they allege had a criminal record and a final order of removal by a judge, and observed him get in a vehicle with Parra Saturday morning.

The ICE agent attempted a car stop, and Mendoza-Cervantes and Parra-Hernandez, who the agency alleged is also undocumented, fled their vehicle on foot, according to ICE and the Harris County Sheriff's Office.

Surveillance video of the incident reviewed by ABC News appears to show the ICE vehicle moving in the direction of the man running and striking him.

An ICE spokesperson alleged in a statement that Parra "ran in front of an ICE vehicle" when he was hit.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct," the spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.

ICE did not comment on Teare's claims that there were two men in the back seat of the vehicle during the incident. Mendoza-Cervantes remains at large as of Wednesday afternoon, according to ICE.

The DA said his office interviewed Parra on Tuesday in the hospital, where he is in stable condition. The DA said he has not been charged with a crime.

The DA said he is also collecting more evidence from the incident and could possibly issue charges against the ICE agent for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Teare said his office will attempt to interview the ICE agent.

"Context is important. We want to see what led up to the confrontation," the DA said.

“Stopping the DMV-to-DHS Data Pipeline” examines four ongoing pathways through which driver and vehicle data held by state Department of Motor Vehicles (DMVs) is accessed by federal immigration enforcement agencies, via a “DMV-to-DHS pipeline.” These pathways include: 1) directly through database access; 2) through the interstate querying system known as Nlets; 3) through sale to data brokers, who may in turn sell it to ICE/CBP; and 4) through local law enforcement who pass data to ICE/CBP.
Researchers examine the experiences of four states—Maryland, Minnesota, New York, and Washington—all of whom have passed state laws to curtail the DMV-to-DHS pipeline, and yet, all of whom, to different extents, continue to experience vehicular immigration arrests.

The Trump administration scored a victory at a liberal-leaning appeals court Wednesday, which temporarily blocked a section of a California law requiring plainclothes federal law enforcement agents to show their badges and identification when carrying out operations.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- The ICE agent accused of drunkenly attacking a 72-year-old Fresno man and his daughter made his first court appearance Wednesday, pleading not guilty to all charges.

The defendant, David Gonzalez, is charged with three felony counts, including assault likely to produce great bodily injury, elder abuse and vandalism, along with a misdemeanor battery charge.

The 32-year-old appeared in court bound to a wheelchair as he formally entered his plea.

Action News legal analyst Tony Capozzi said the case appears to be shaping up as a self-defense claim by the victims.

"I think the DA and the police look at this as a self-defense case in trying to protect themselves. So the question now is: Will the federal government do something to try to protect this agent?" Capozzi said.

Capozzi noted that because Gonzalez is charged with violations of California law, federal authorities cannot simply dismiss the case or issue a federal pardon.

The legal analyst also pointed to Gonzalez's choice of representation. Rather than being represented by a federal prosecutor or Department of Justice attorney, Gonzalez is being defended by local attorney Brian Andritch.

"If they did, it gives the impression that he was working within the scope of his employment," Capozzi said. "He makes that allegation, then the victims in this case have a great lawsuit to sue not only the agent but the federal government."

According to Fresno police, Gonzalez was discovered sleeping in the front yard of a central Fresno home. Investigators allege that when the homeowner confronted him, Gonzalez appeared intoxicated and became violent, assaulting the 72-year-old man and allegedly slamming him into a neighbor's parked vehicle.

"We weren't sure what it was in the morning, but from what it looked like to us the altercation extended out to our car," neighbor Frederick Lisitsa said.

Police say Gonzalez then allegedly attacked the victim's daughter when she attempted to intervene.

Investigators say the elderly victim, fearing for his life, armed himself and shot Gonzalez during the confrontation.

Gonzalez has worked as an ICE agent for less than a year. Prior to joining the federal agency in December, he worked as a deputy with the Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office in Texas.

He joined the department as a detention officer in 2017 before becoming a deputy in 2022.

Gonzalez left the department for his federal immigration position in December of 2025.

In court Wednesday, attorney Brian Andritch indicated Gonzalez is expected to post bond, which has been set at $37,000. If released, he will be required to remain in California while the case proceeds.

Action News reached out to ICE regarding Gonzalez's employment status and was referred to the Department of Homeland Security. A response had not been received as of Wednesday evening.

Gonzalez is scheduled to return to court next week.

title: Immigration – Habeas corpus - Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly
description:
Where habeas corpus relief has been requested by a petitioner arguing that his continued detention by immigration authorities violates his due process rights, the petition should be denied because the petitioner has received all the process to which he is entitled.
Accordingly, the Court lacks jurisdiction over the petition to the extent it seeks release based on the vacatur of Petitioner’s convictions.
… “On the merits, however, the Court finds that Petitioner is not entitled to relief.
As other courts have observed, the government may generally continue its detention of noncitizens denied bond while it appeals adverse immigration rulings to the BIA.
Accordingly, he is not entitled to further relief.” Vieira Da Costa v. Moniz, et al.
text:
Where habeas corpus relief has been requested by a petitioner arguing that his continued detention by immigration authorities violates his due process rights, the petition should be denied because the petitioner has received all the process to which he is entitled.

“Petitioner contends that his ongoing detention violates his due process rights because (1) the conviction that formed the basis for his removal proceedings has now been vacated, and (2) an immigration judge has already granted him discretionary relief from removal. …

“Petitioner first contends that his detention cannot lawfully continue because the aggravated felony conviction upon which the government bases his removal proceedings no longer exists. … In essence, his argument is that the Due Process Clause forbids the government from detaining individuals pending an administrative decision on their removability if it lacks a basis for their removal. In response, Respondents argue that this Court lacks jurisdiction to provide Petitioner’s requested relief because adjudicating his claim would require the Court to opine on Petitioner’s removability in violation of 8 U.S.C. §1252(b)(9). … Respondents are correct. …

“Federal law provides a discrete pathway for noncitizens to obtain judicial review of issues concerning their removability: by appealing a final order of removal to the relevant United States Court of Appeals. … Section 1252(b)(9) ‘strips federal courts of jurisdiction to decide legal and factual questions arising from an alien’s removal in any other context, including on a petition for a writ of habeas corpus.’ Gicharu v. Carr, 983 F.3d 13, 16 (1st Cir. 2020). …

“… Petitioner contends that due process requires his release because, after the vacatur, he is now ‘neither removable nor subject to mandatory detention under 8 U.S.C. §1226(c).’ … As in Flores-Powell [v. Chadbourne, 677 F. Supp. 2d 455 (D. Mass. 2010)], Zaoui [v. Horgan, No. 13-cv-11254, 2013 WL 5615913, at *1 (D. Mass. Aug. 23, 2013)], and Alphonse [v. Moniz, No. 21-cv-11844, 2022 WL 279638, at *4–5 (D. Mass. Jan. 31, 2022)], adjudicating this claim would require the Court to inquire into whether Petitioner is properly removable under 8 U.S.C. §1227(a)(2)(A)(iii), and therefore require the Court to review ‘questions of law and fact … arising from any action taken or proceeding brought to remove an alien from the United States.’ 8 U.S.C. §1252(b)(9). This, the Court cannot do. Accordingly, the Court lacks jurisdiction over the petition to the extent it seeks release based on the vacatur of Petitioner’s convictions. …

“Petitioner further argues that his continued detention is unlawful because an immigration judge has already granted Petitioner a discretionary waiver of removal under INA section 212(c), so there is no longer a lawful basis to detain him pending a decision on his removability. …

“On the merits, however, the Court finds that Petitioner is not entitled to relief. As other courts have observed, the government may generally continue its detention of noncitizens denied bond while it appeals adverse immigration rulings to the BIA. … While this practice strikes the Court as potentially unjust given the often-protracted nature of BIA appeals, and particularly so when the government lacks a strong basis to appeal, the Court cannot conclude that it is categorically beyond the government’s power, at least where a petitioner has received an appropriate individualized bond hearing. …

“Here, Petitioner has had three bond hearings, the latter two of which followed, and were expressly premised on, the changed circumstances presented by Petitioner’s receipt of section 212(c) relief. … Another session of this Court has already found that the second of Petitioner’s two post-relief bond hearings satisfied the requirements of due process. … At this point, Petitioner has received all the process to which he is entitled, and which this Court has the power to grant, with respect to his detention during the pendency of his immigration proceedings. Accordingly, he is not entitled to further relief.”

Vieira Da Costa v. Moniz, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-523-26) (9 pages) (Burroughs, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-cv-13620-ADB) (Sept. 30, 2026).

text:
Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the officer who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.

The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.”

The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal's release, said he had picked up his son from school on Oct. 8 and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.

“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way," Belgal's lawyers wrote. "Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”

New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn't conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.

The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.

A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.

Whatever happened next didn't appear on the NYPD's security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal's damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.

Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.

DHS didn't comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal's lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.

Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and is suffering from impaired hearing.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

“Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, the lawyers representing Belgal.

At a news conference last week, Marcos Charles, the head of ICE's enforcement and removal operations, said Belgal refused orders to exit his vehicle and then accelerated and smashed into two government vehicles as ICE officers tried to block him from driving away.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has maintained officers didn’t know a child was in the car and blamed Belgal for putting his son's life in danger.

description:
Where a petitioner has moved for an order reinstating his deferred action status and returning his work authorization, the petitioner’s motion should be allowed because the revocation of his deferred action status violated his procedural due process rights and was arbitrary and capricious.
… Respondents’ revocation of Petitioner’s deferred action status was therefore in violation of his due process rights.
… “Petitioner further contends that the revocation of his deferred action status was arbitrary and capricious in violation of the APA.
… Petitioner responds that Respondents’ argument misrepresents existing USCIS policy, which states that existing SIJS deferred action recipients will ‘generally retain this deferred action.’ … “Petitioner is again correct.
… “Viewing the record holistically, the Court finds that the revocation of Petitioner’s deferred action status was plainly arbitrary and capricious.
text:
Where a petitioner has moved for an order reinstating his deferred action status and returning his work authorization, the petitioner’s motion should be allowed because the revocation of his deferred action status violated his procedural due process rights and was arbitrary and capricious.

“Respondents argue first that Petitioner is seeking relief unavailable in a habeas action, as the remedy he requests goes beyond release from confinement. … Petitioner responds that the further relief he requests is appropriate because it seeks to abate a ‘collateral consequence’ of the unlawful action upon which his detention was based. … The Court agrees with Petitioner. …

“Respondents also contend that this Court is precluded under the Immigration and Nationality Act (‘INA’), 8 U.S.C. §1252(g), from reviewing the decision to terminate Petitioner’s deferred action. … Petitioner argues that Section 1252(g)’s jurisdictional bar on claims challenging removal proceedings or orders is inapposite to claims challenging the termination of deferred action. … The Court again agrees with Petitioner. …

“Respondents next argue that the Court cannot review Petitioner’s challenge to the revocation of his deferred action status under the Administrative Procedure Act (‘APA’) because deferred action is simply a nonenforcement decision, and such decisions are ‘committed to agency discretion by law.’ … Petitioner responds that the regulatory process for granting deferred action to recipients of [Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS)] like Petitioner ‘involves clear standards against which to assess the agency’s discretion’ because it involves mandatory criteria and clear-cut forms of relief. … Once again, Petitioner has the better argument. …

“Having concluded that Petitioner’s challenge to the revocation of his deferred action status is within the Court’s jurisdiction, reviewable under the APA, and a proper subject of habeas relief, the Court turns now to the merits of Petitioner’s claims. …

“Petitioner contends that he had a protectable property interest in his deferred action status, and that Respondents’ decision to revoke that status without any sort of pre-deprivation process violated his due process rights. … Respondents argue that Petitioner has no due process rights related to his deferred action status because it is a discretionary form of relief that does not create a constitutionally protected liberty or property interest. …

“Contrary to Respondents’ position, SIJS deferred action status is not so discretionary that it is exempt from the protections of the Due Process Clause. …

“Accordingly, courts have repeatedly found that continuation of deferred action status is both a property interest and a liberty interest protectable under the Due Process Clause. … Petitioner is therefore entitled to due process with respect to the revocation of his deferred action status.

“The question becomes, then, whether Petitioner received such process. The Court finds that he did not. Respondents summarily revoked Petitioner’s SIJS deferred action status with no pre-deprivation notice, no explained rationale, no pre-deprivation opportunity to be heard, and no opportunity to contest or appeal the revocation. … Respondents do not even argue that the process Petitioner received was adequate in the event the Due Process Clause applies. … Whatever level of process is due in these circumstances, it exceeded what Petitioner received.

“Courts have repeatedly found that such arbitrary and unexplained revocations of deferred action status — particularly those which, like Petitioner’s, appear designed to serve as post-hoc justifications for detention — violate due process. … Respondents’ revocation of Petitioner’s deferred action status was therefore in violation of his due process rights. …

“Petitioner further contends that the revocation of his deferred action status was arbitrary and capricious in violation of the APA. … Respondents argue that their revocation was justified because the government had withdrawn the policies under which Petitioner was granted deferred action. … Petitioner responds that Respondents’ argument misrepresents existing USCIS policy, which states that existing SIJS deferred action recipients will ‘generally retain this deferred action.’ …

“Petitioner is again correct. …

“Viewing the record holistically, the Court finds that the revocation of Petitioner’s deferred action status was plainly arbitrary and capricious. Although the Court’s review under this standard is deferential, the government may not simply revoke a benefit Petitioner had relied upon for years with no explanation, no process, and no apparent consideration of reliance interests, based on circumstances that have not changed in any articulated way. … That is particularly true where, as here, the agency’s conduct appears contrary to its own existing policies. … Accordingly, the revocation of Petitioner’s deferred actions status was unlawful under the APA.”

Padilla Posadas v. Hyde, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-513-26) (12 pages) (Burroughs, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-cv-10276-ADB) (Sept. 30, 2026).

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a United States agency that has taken a central role in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, has rejected a government report calling for its agents to wear body cameras that automatically activate.

On Wednesday, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan agency that provides research to Congress, released a report recommending an update to ICE guidelines for camera usage.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests

list 2 of 3DHS defends ICE shooting in NYC, says officers believed they were in danger

list 3 of 3Ilhan Omar says she ‘will not be silenced’ after US agents raid her home

end of list

It suggested that “automated camera activation” would be helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel”.

“Given the important role of body-worn cameras in law enforcement activities, we maintain that additional controls are needed to help ensure that ICE personnel capture footage in accordance with policy,” the report said.

Automatic activation, it added, would address difficulties ICE agents face in manually turning on their cameras during enforcement operations.

But ICE has rejected the recommendation for automatic activation, which could be triggered by an agent pulling a gun or turning on a car siren. The agency cited privacy concerns.

But the Trump administration faces public pressure to improve transparency during its immigration raids.

Agents from ICE and other agencies such as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have faced accusations of excessive force and civil liberties violations.

In January, two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were shot to death in separate shootings in Minneapolis, Minnesota, during immigration operations.

The New York Times estimated in July that immigration agents had opened fire on at least 25 people since the start of Trump’s second term. A CBS News review updated this week counts at least 30 shootings, with nine people killed and 13 others wounded.

ICE has often blamed such incidents on aggression against its agents, and it has argued that its officers have opened fire to defend themselves from danger.

But in several cases, that rationale has come under scrutiny.

Critics argued that video footage in Good’s fatal shooting disproved government statements alleging that she had weaponised her vehicle against agents. Her car, according to observers, appeared to be turning away from agents, not towards them.

In another case, ICE agent Christian Castro was accused of making false statements about a shooting that resulted in injury to Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man living in Minneapolis.

Castro faces federal charges for allegedly lying about being attacked with a snow shovel and broom before the shooting, after video footage contradicted his account. Castro pleaded not guilty last month.

More recently, on October 8, immigration agents shot a man named Oscar Belgal in New York City while his five-year-old son was in the backseat of his car. ICE stated that Belgal appeared to be “going towards officers” in his car when they opened fire.

On Tuesday, a judge rejected the government’s effort to have Belgal deported.

Activists say better recording procedures for body camera footage could help clarify what happened in such incidents.

But the Trump administration has largely refused to implement reforms to ICE protocol.

Earlier this year, Democrats in Congress delayed funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, on the basis that significant changes needed to be made to reduce incidents of excessive force.

The department said on Wednesday that automatically recording cameras could result in “the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”.

The agency added that all ICE offices had received body cameras as of August 5, but that training in their use was still ongoing and would be finished “soon”.

text:
HOUSTON -- A Texas prosecutor says a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent appeared to use a vehicle to intentionally strike a man who took off running in Houston and that an investigation opened by his office could result in criminal charges.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, needed surgery for a broken leg after being hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man's family.

The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors have also investigated a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.

RELATED: ICE agent strikes man with car during pursuit in Texas, authorities say: VIDEO

“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”

Tim Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston, said in a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday that “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Spokespersons for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday.

Parra Hernandez has been in the U.S. for 34 years and was on his way to work when the encounter began, according to Espinosa. Espinosa declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status.

He said he saw two ICE agents in Parra Hernandez's room while visiting him at the hospital.

“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.

Teare said ICE and DHS have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

text:
After a federal immigration agent struck a man with his vehicle on Saturday, immigrant rights advocates and family members are demanding witnesses be protected from deportation — and disputing the official account of the event.

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) claimed Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an agent's vehicle while they were trying to arrest a different man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes. The ICE spokesperson asserted the two men were in the same car, and Parra-Hernandez was fleeing the scene after an attempted traffic stop.

However, FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez did not know the man ICE was trying to arrest, and he said they weren't in the same car. A different man, who was not the target of the ICE investigation, was in the car with Parra-Hernandez, Espinosa said.

"They have to stop pulling people over just because they fit a description. Just because they might seem like the person. Just because they're driving a white truck on their way to work," Espinosa said during a Wednesday press conference. "When I grew up, that was called racial profiling, and that is what's happening today."

ICE said they were seeking to detain Mendoza-Cervantes because he had a criminal record and a final order of removal. Houston Public Media was unable to find any criminal cases involving Mendoza-Cervantes in a search of local Dallas County and Harris County court records.

In a statement to Houston Public Media, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) re-iterated ICE's account of the incident Saturday.

"During surveillance, ICE observed their target and Miguel Parra-Hernandez, another illegal alien from Mexico, enter the vehicle," a DHS spokesperson said. "ICE then attempted a vehicle stop. The illegal aliens then pulled over and fled on foot. As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck."

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office may pursue felony assault charges against the ICE agent who struck Parra-Hernandez with a vehicle. At the press conference on Wednesday, Espinoza said the witnesses should be protected from deportation so they can assist with the investigation.

DHS did not respond specifically to a request for comment about the possible criminal charges, but denied that an ICE agent intentionally ran over Parra-Hernandez.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," a DHS spokesperson said in its statement. "The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct."

According to FIEL, Hernandez sustained three fractures to his right leg as well as injuries to his left and is still in custody while receiving treatment. Parra-Hernandez's brother, Rodolfo Parra, said the family hopes ICE will allow him to receive appropriate medical treatment.

“We’re asking all people in any level of power to please request that they do not move my brother because he is in a delicate state of health, and that we’re still continuing to fight for justice," Parra said.

title: How ICE Puts the NYPD in an Impossible Position - Vital City
description:
ICE agents attempted to arrest Oscar Belgal, who was in his car with his 5-year-old son.
Nor can NYPD officers obstruct federal agents because their activities are unpopular or distasteful.
This misunderstanding is but one example of the no-win position federal immigration enforcement has put the NYPD in.
Responding to violence is not the same as providing security for an ICE enforcement and removal operation.
Nor is intervening to prevent a confrontation from escalating into further violence the same as assisting ICE with immigration enforcement.
text:
Those pointing fingers at the police department in the wake of the Marble Hill shooting fail to understand its legal constraints and responsibilities.

Last November, protesters gathered outside a parking garage near Canal Street to prevent federal immigration agents from leaving to conduct a raid on the nearby illegal street vendors of counterfeit goods in Chinatown. They blocked the exit with garbage and their own bodies. The NYPD responded to the gathering, ordered the protesters to move and ultimately cleared a path that allowed ICE vehicles to exit. NYPD officers also arrested more than a dozen protesters for disorderly conduct.

The NYPD said it hadn’t coordinated with ICE and that officers were responding to complaints about a disorderly crowd blocking the street. This wasn’t particularly persuasive to the protesters who saw officers as clearing a way for federal immigration agents.

This month, tensions have understandably run even higher after an ICE agent shot a man in Marble Hill. Par for the course in this political climate, many elected officials have been blaming the NYPD for supposedly picking sides, as though it made a conscious decision to facilitate ICE actions. The belief that the PD was complicit in President Donald Trump’s deportation machinery has led to calls for Jessica Tisch to be removed as commissioner.

In fact, the NYPD has very little choice when it comes to responding to a federal law enforcement agency, even a hyperactive and undisciplined agency like ICE. City law prohibits the NYPD from using its personnel and resources to assist civil immigration enforcement, except in a narrow set of circumstances. But it still has a responsibility to keep the peace and prevent escalation, regardless of whether ICE is involved, and under well-established law police cannot interfere with the lawful execution of federal duties, however repugnant, distasteful or seemingly contrary to New York City values they may be.

For example, when local officers engage with crowds or guard protest zones — both important functions we should expect of our police — they risk being seen as ICE collaborators. When they refrain, they face accusations of neglecting to protect New Yorkers.

The NYPD has to respond to violence, protect demonstrators and bystanders, and intervene when crowds or federal agents create a danger to the public or each other. These are basic responsibilities of local policing, not discretionary favors to ICE, and the department cannot abandon them to avoid the appearance of cooperation or appease popular sentiment.

We can look across the river to Newark to see what happens when local police leave ICE to manage these confrontations. In May, federal agents clashed repeatedly with protesters outside of the Delaney Hall detention center, using pepper spray and batons. These escalations — and the relative absence of local cops to help manage the situation — compelled Gov. Mikie Sherrill to send state police to take over crowd management and establish protest zones. Even Newark Mayor Ras Baraka, who had himself been arrested by ICE, then defended local police involvement and subsequently put city officers in greater control of the area.

The Newark pattern is playing out in New York: The feds cause a mess, and local police take much of the blame.

The “targeted operation” on Oct. 8 in Marble Hill is a classic example of the problem. ICE agents attempted to arrest Oscar Belgal, who was in his car with his 5-year-old son. The video shows ICE rushing the car, guns out, in plain clothes. An ICE agent fired seven rounds, wounding the driver as he appeared to pull out of his parking space. We still don’t know exactly what happened or whether the shooting was justified, but ICE claims that he “weaponized” the vehicle. (Further investigation may clarify what happened, but that agency has made similar claims in the past. It hasn’t exactly earned the benefit of the doubt.)

Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark has opened an investigation, as have federal authorities. Whether those investigations produce a full public accounting of what happened, and any accountability for anyone involved, remains to be seen. Department of Homeland Security policy prohibits firing at the driver of a moving vehicle unless deadly force is justified. But even without deciding what threat the driver posed, rushing at and firing into a moving car were at a minimum bad tactics — especially for an apprehension that was presumably “targeted” and intentional.

The NYPD is taking its share of blame, but the question is why. It didn’t participate in this operation. Its officers arrived afterward, as they do whenever they get reports of gunshots. They rendered aid and transported Belgal to the hospital in the back of their car. They set up a crime scene so that the shooting could be investigated. All of that is proper procedure.

Those taking the NYPD to task for supposedly enabling ICE fail to understand that the NYPD operates under a substantially different set of laws and responsibilities than the feds — indeed, a different set of laws and responsibilities than many other police departments.

New York City’s sanctuary laws prohibit most forms of cooperation with civil immigration enforcement. Officers are not permitted to detain someone because federal authorities want to deport them. This has a public safety purpose: Immigrants must be able to report crimes, seek assistance and cooperate with investigations without fearing that these interactions will get them deported.

Under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, however, New York City cannot prohibit ICE from exercising its lawful federal authority. Nor can NYPD officers obstruct federal agents because their activities are unpopular or distasteful. And for those who might say “but ICE is not exercising lawful authority; it’s running amok,” it’s essentially impossible for a local police department to make that determination in real time. Besides, the NYPD must still respond when called, protect people — including federal law enforcement — from violence, and maintain public safety.

Some of the criticisms have been especially ignorant. There’s a viral video being circulated on social media that purportedly shows NYPD officers being instructed to turn off their body cameras at a protest. The accusation is that Tisch ordered this action so that officers could conceal their conduct, a bullet point in the arguments of those calling for her dismissal.

Those objecting, however, appear to be unfamiliar with the 50-year-long policy conversation that the city has had around protests and surveillance. The NYPD’s Patrol Guide, its policy manual, says officers should not activate body cameras merely because they are present at a demonstration. That rule stems from the Handschu litigation, which began in 1971 when activists sued the NYPD for spying on them, infiltrating their groups and gathering intelligence on political organizations. The resulting agreement placed substantial restrictions on police investigations involving political activity. While its protections have changed over the decades, the underlying principles are the same: People shouldn’t become subjects of police intelligence gathering for merely exercising their First Amendment rights.

Body cameras create a difficult problem. They’re valuable tools for documenting police conduct, but they also record people standing in front of officers. With hundreds of officers attending demonstrations, the department could collect an enormous archive of people involved in political activity — including people’s faces, conversations and associations. Is that really what the critics want?

This misunderstanding is but one example of the no-win position federal immigration enforcement has put the NYPD in. Local police are told not to help ICE, not to stand by while ICE abuses people and not to allow dangerous confrontations to develop on our city streets. In some situations, officers cannot do all three.

Clearing a street to prevent injury and mayhem isn’t the same as clearing it so ICE can move in to make an arrest. Responding to violence is not the same as providing security for an ICE enforcement and removal operation. Nor is intervening to prevent a confrontation from escalating into further violence the same as assisting ICE with immigration enforcement. Federal officers aren’t immune from investigation if they engage in potentially criminal conduct. However, those lines aren’t always clear, and federal agents enjoy some legal protection against state and local interference when performing their lawful duties.
