text:
Washington state officials have made it harder for immigration agents to access driving records during deportation raids, but keep getting played by Trump’s deportation goons.

That’s according to a new report from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights (UWCHR). The report released Tuesday claims that current Department of Licensing practices still likely violate state laws protecting Washington state drivers from the disclosure of names, addresses, and license plate information for civil immigration enforcement.

Cruising around neighborhoods, malls, and other public spaces in Washington, ICE is able to look up driver information from state databases, despite laws prohibiting them from doing so.

“Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles,” said Guillermo Rivera, with Eastside For All, at a presentation of the report in a corner of a UW library. “We need accountability, and we need leadership now, not months from now.”

Titled “Stopping the DMV-to-DHS Data Pipeline,” the report compares vehicle and driver data sharing between state and federal immigration across Washington, Maryland, Minnesota, and New York. The report identifies four pathways which driver data reaches immigration agents: directly through state databases, an interstate messaging system called Nlets, local law enforcement, and private data brokers.

The report looked at states with so-called “sanctuary” laws that profess to protect drivers’ privacy from federal immigration agents. (California, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Virginia, and Oregon didn’t share their data.)

Despite significant actions inconveniencing ICE, Washington still lets Customs and Border Protection (Border Patrol agents and Customs officers) access to car owner names and addresses through the interstate messaging system called Nlets.

In one example cited by the report, the interstate messaging platform Nlets was accessed by CBP to lead to an ICE arrest with no CBP agents present, suggesting ICE logged in with a CBP username, or asked for a lookup.

Immigration agencies blocked by Washington are logging in “just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy.

The news comes amid conflicting reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Washington state, but a clear uptick in ICE enforcement nationwide ahead of the midterm elections. ICEwatch tracker IceOut.org published evidence Monday based on local arrest reports that some of the ICE enforcement in Washington has been shifted to California.

Gov. Bob Ferguson has attempted to disrupt the DOL to DHS data pipeline, according to the report. To understand what he’s been up to, here’s a refresher on immigration agency jargon:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) goes after immigrants internally using Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) agents to arrest. Those agents used to operate separately from ICE’s detective wing, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Those real cops used to focus squarely on human trafficking and other transnational crime. Customs and Border Protection, which is supposed to guard the border, has also been reassigned under Trump, sending agents to back up ERO.

Here’s what Ferguson has done:

Terminated direct access to the state’s Driver and Plate Search for two ICE subagencies (ERO and HSI), and suspended CBP’s account, but it could regain access.

Blocked Nlets, the more basic interstate driver lookup tool, to queries from ICE-linked usernames, first to ERO last November, and then to HSI, finally, in January of this year.

Blocked some individual CBP-linked usernames for the Nlets interstate database. The report says this began in April 2026 and that five CBP usernames were blocked as of September 18, 2026.

Sound complicated? Well, if the state simply required a warrant from immigration agencies to use its data, it wouldn’t be. According to the report, that’s what New York State did, and it’s closed a lot of loopholes.

Washington’s approach is piecemeal. Under Ferguson, the state is trying to balance the role of federal agencies going after criminals and the White House hijacking criminal investigators to carry out mass deportations. It’s a game of whack-a-mole that Washington has accepted for the remainder of Trump’s term.

For example, according to Ferguson, CBP still needs access to Nlets to combat human trafficking and firearm access.

“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” Ferguson’s statement read. “Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data.”

Ferguson’s office told The Stranger how many queries it has blocked from immigration agents (174,349 from November 2025 to October 2026), but not how many were granted. The report says 3,696,147 data searches for driver and vehicle information have happened—though the numbers are not completely comparable because they are over a broader time frame (January 2025 to May 2026).

The UW report questions why that game should be played. It points out that victims of various immigration authority data theft have apparently never been notified of their data being given away illegally. A spokesperson for the governor declined to name an example of a notification, and did not contract the report’s finding.

The deportation machine, long focused on targeting immigrants who posed safety threats, is ramping up to unprecedented levels of not just xenophobia but illegality. Racial profiling, rubber stamped by the Supreme Court, is now the norm. Apprehending legal immigrants, and lying to courts to cover up illegal arrests, are shockingly common. And HSI, which used to quietly work with local police to solve international crimes, has been demoted from detective to beat cop.

Responses to these problems have been stronger in other states. Not only is New York state demanding warrants, it’s also historically funded immigrant legal defense at higher levels.

Many immigrants across Washington were already afraid to get in their cars, take their kids to the park, or even go grocery shopping in this so-called sanctuary state. As I’ve reported before, even immigrants who have beaten ICE in court travel nervously, packing an absurd number of documents with them as a kind of safety blanket against anticipated arrests and harassment.

Immigrants in Washington state keep getting arrested, with the assistance of data produced by their own tax dollars, in a regressive tax state where they contribute disproportionately to their income. Their data is casually released by politicians who are supposed to represent their interests (yes, non-voters are constituents), and answer to the family members and neighbors who voted them in. The report is a reminder that the laws voters supported to protect immigrants’ civil rights aren’t fully being enforced.

text:
Immigration, inflation, health care, AI, data centers, and flock cameras were topics of discussion Wednesday (Oct. 14) during the debate between Arkansas’ Third Congressional District candidates. The debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election was hosted by Arkansas TV.

Democrat Robb Ryerse, Libertarian Bobby Wilson, and U.S. Rep. Steve Womack, R-Rogers, participated in the almost hour-long debate.

Ryerse, in response to the first question about immigration and border security, said if elected he would work to make sure “ICE isn’t knocking at your door, ripping your family apart.” Ryerse said the federal government should spend less money on detention centers and more on “infrastructure that makes immigration easier.”

Wilson said voters have been clear that they want less immigration, but the Trump Administration has been “very brutal” and needs to find less harsh ways to deal with immigrants. He also said Democrats and Republicans have both failed to develop an immigration policy that best fits with American values.

Womack gave the Trump Administration “very high marks” on how they’ve handled immigration issues.

“Under the Biden Administration millions of people were just literally walking across the border and coming into our country, and then disappearing into the shadows,” Womack said. “It’s quite the contrast now. The Trump Administration and Homeland Security have shut down that border.”

INFLATION

The rate of inflation, especially with food and energy, has been an issue nationwide for many federal and state races. On Wednesday, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that prices for all items rose 3.7% in September compared with September 2025. The index for energy was up 20.4% in September compared with September 2025, and the year-over-year index for food was up 2.5%. Shelter prices are up 3.2% year over year, according to the BLS report.

Wilson, the Libertarian, again blamed both parties, saying their policies that result in deficit spending are “like groundhog day again” and have a major role to play in inflation. He also said the U.S. attack on Iran has resulted in recent inflation.

Womack said his support of the One Big Beautiful Bill, a major federal reconciliation bill pushed by President Donald Trump, prevented a “massive tax hike” on Americans and included provisions to address inflation. He also said to lower long-term energy prices the country needs to “unleash the potential” of the energy industry.

Ryerse cited three reasons for a majority of inflationary pressures.

“There are three specific reasons things why everything costs too much,” Ryerse said. “Number one, there is the war in Iran. The war in Iran has caused the price of gasoline and diesel to skyrocket which has driven up the price of everything. Number two is Donald Trump’s chaotic tariff war. … And number three, major corporations throughout this country have been posting record profits and I wonder if they’ve been doing that by gouging American families.”

AI, DATA CENTERS, FLOCK CAMERAS

Wilson said AI development and its growing use in the economy is “the most important thing going on right now,” but Congressional oversight could stifle development. However, he said there should be “standardization” to protect communities from data center developments, and Congress has a role in addressing privacy concerns.

Womack said AI “is here to stay” but it can’t operate unfettered. He also said if regulations shut down data centers or make them difficult to build and operate, resource will go to countries that may not be friendly with the U.S. He said Congress has a regulatory role, but going too far could result in a weaker national defense, and stifling AI could result in unintended consequences, like slowing innovation in medical research.

“We need to have some guardrails,” Womack said. “I think Congress has a role in that. But I think that we’ve got to be careful that we don’t go too far to where we cede a lot of that technology to adversaries that have nefarious intentions for our country.”

Ryerse said he is pro technology, “but technology can get out of control in a hurry.” He said there have been many periods in history where technology moves faster than societal rules and bad things happen to the environment and humans. He said Congress should do more and the country “must pump the brakes on AI and data centers.”

As to the growing concern with Flock and other automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras, Womack said “Flock cameras are a tool, and like any tool, they can be misapplied.” He said there are privacy concerns, but Flock has helped solve many crimes and has a public safety purpose. He said Congress should not have a “blanket approach” with such cameras, and should instead let communities decide how they are used.

Ryerse said local governments do have control, but Flock and some law enforcement agencies continue to allow privacy violations. He said Congress needs to enact privacy protection rules, and “rein in the use” of such cameras. He said no one should be comfortable living in a society with unregulated AI and ALPR cameras.

Wilson said the “horse has left the barn” in terms of cameras being everywhere, including the cameras on cellphones. He said Congress should make sure law enforcement agencies receive warrants to get info instead of relying on ubiquitous and unregulated surveillance systems.

HEALTH CARE COSTS, RURAL ACCESS

All three candidates agreed that costs are too high and access is becoming a problem. Wednesday’s BLS report on inflation also noted that costs for medical care services are up 2.5% between September and September 2025.

Womack again pointed to the federal One Big Beautiful Bill, saying it provides billions of dollars to expand rural care and addresses costs. He also said he has sponsored legislation that allows veterans to have more access to telehealth services. He also touted his support of a community program that placed the first MRI in a Mercy system facility in Carroll County.

Ryerse said health care should be a human right, and should be accessible to all people no matter where they live. He also said healthcare for all places medical decisions with the patient and doctor, instead of having insurance companies involved. He said “healthcare crisis stories” are one of the top things he hears on the campaign trail.

Wilson again said sending Democrats and Republicans to Congress will not fix the country’s healthcare system. He said it’s just “a yo-yo back and forth” with the two parties.

title: DOMINICAN REPUBLIC: 'We are part of this country and we have the right to nationality'
description:
The Constitutional Court ruled that people born in the Dominican Republic to migrant parents in an irregular situation were the children of foreigners ‘in transit’ and therefore not entitled to Dominican nationality.
Law 169-14 established a naturalisation pathway for this group, providing for access to Dominican nationality after two years.
We are Dominican citizens born in the Dominican Republic.
Because of their physical features, many young people are mistaken for undocumented Haitians, regardless of where they were born or their right to Dominican nationality.
We Dominicans of Haitian descent are part of this country and have the right to have our nationality recognised.
text:
The Constitutional Court ruled that people born in the Dominican Republic to migrant parents in an irregular situation were the children of foreigners ‘in transit’ and therefore not entitled to Dominican nationality. On this basis, it denied nationality to over 200,000 people of Haitian descent. Many already held documents, were studying or working and had spent their entire lives in the country. Their parents had come from Haiti to work in the sugar industry, in many cases under agreements between the two countries.

Until 2010, being born on Dominican territory conferred the right to nationality. The only exceptions were the children of diplomats and of foreigners ‘in transit’, meaning those passing through. Amendments to the Constitution in 2010 extended the exceptions to include the children of undocumented foreigners, but only those born from that point onwards. The ruling extended this exclusion retroactively. It interpreted the former exception for people ‘in transit’ as including undocumented migrants.

The ruling also ordered the Central Electoral Board, the body in charge of the Civil Registry, to review birth records and transfer these people to the foreign nationals’ register. Consequently, those born before 2010 lost a nationality the Constitution had recognised as theirs at birth. Even before the ruling, the Central Electoral Board had been administratively denying them nationality and refusing to issue them birth certificates.

Law 169-14 was passed in 2014 to reverse the effects of the ruling, but its scope has been limited. It divided those affected into two groups. Group A comprised those who were already registered with the Civil Registry and were due to have their nationality recognised once again. Group B comprised people born in the Dominican Republic who had never been registered with the Civil Registry and who, due to barriers to obtaining recognition of their nationality, had remained stateless. Law 169-14 established a naturalisation pathway for this group, providing for access to Dominican nationality after two years.

Problems persist in both groups. Some people in Group A were transferred to a civil registry other than the standard one and continue to face difficulties with their papers. In Group B, only a very small proportion have managed to obtain Dominican nationality, while many people remain stateless and without a definitive solution, even though the law set a deadline for completing the process. Also, the state closed offices that served Dominicans of Haitian descent, leaving them without an effective means of resolving their situation.

Thirteen years after the ruling, its effects are still being felt. Young Dominicans of Haitian descent still face obstacles to accessing services, studying, travelling and working.

It affects us directly, even though we are not migrants. We are Dominican citizens born in the Dominican Republic.

Those most at risk are those who are still unable to prove their nationality, because without papers, the risk of detention is greater. Our young people are detained in their communities, in their homes and even when they go to hospital. They may be transferred to immigration processing centres pending deportation, and some have been deported to Haiti before we could intervene to prove that they are Dominican.

Behind these detentions lie racial profiling and structural racism. Because of their physical features, many young people are mistaken for undocumented Haitians, regardless of where they were born or their right to Dominican nationality.

The government’s measures against Haitian migrants also affect us in another way, as many of those migrants are our parents, grandparents, aunts and uncles.

We organise and train young people in human rights, and we carry out advocacy work, make public complaints and hold protests. We run awareness-raising campaigns in the media and participate in decision-making forums to draw the authorities’ attention to these issues.

This year, on the 13th anniversary of the ruling, we mobilised to denounce the obstacles that persist and demand effective measures from the state. We have also launched a social media campaign calling for full recognition of nationality and an end to statelessness.

This work involves risks. Those of us who speak out against discrimination and racism receive death threats and are subjected to stigmatisation and smear campaigns on social media. There have also been attempts to disrupt our activities and physically attack us.

We demand that it comply with the Constitution and Law 169-14, guarantee full recognition of our nationality and put an end to statelessness. The 2010 constitutional amendment must no longer be used to deny the rights of those of us who were born before then and were already entitled to nationality. We need an effective solution that protects our rights and redresses the historical harm caused to our community.

The government has a duty to protect the rights of all people, not just one part of society. We Dominicans of Haitian descent are part of this country and have the right to have our nationality recognised.

text:
Los Angeles, Calif. (Oct. 14, 2026) — The California Immigrant Policy Center (CIPC) today condemned a wave of indiscriminate immigration arrests that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has reportedly launched across California without public announcement. According to news reports, the operation, which ICE has reportedly named “Operation Safe California,” began in the San Diego area earlier this month, will last at least 45 days, and directs federal agents to arrest anyone they believe lacks immigration status.

CIPC has heard from partners in the Central Valley, the Central Coast, and San Diego about increased arrests. In Fresno and Madera counties, dozens of people have been arrested since early October, most of them at traffic stops, according to the Fresno Bee and local rapid response groups. One of the people arrested was Luis Arreguin, a father who has lived in Fresno since age 5. He was pulled over on his way to work on Oct. 1 and taken into ICE custody.

In Santa Maria, Allan Hancock College officials confirmed that federal immigration officers detained a student’s father in a campus parking lot on Oct. 5 as he dropped his daughter off at school.

Communities are answering with collective action. In Fresno, more than 350 people packed a community meeting on Oct. 11 to organize rapid response, know-your-rights education, voter protection, and emergency support for families whose loved ones have been separated and detained by ICE.

“Every family in California should be able to drop their kids at school, show up for work, and go to their place of worship without fear of being racially profiled and taken by federal agents from the people they love,” said Sukaina Hussain, Deputy Executive Director of the California Immigrant Policy Center. “What our partners are describing is not public safety. It is fear by quota.”

“The mass immigration raids are coming just weeks before a highly contested election. When parents are being detained on their way to work and while dropping their kids off at school weeks before Election Day, that is not a coincidence. Our communities will not be intimidated,” Hussain said. “California has made a choice: our state and local resources go to keeping all of us safe, not to tearing families apart. We call on state and local leaders, from Sacramento to Fresno City Hall, to hold that line and stand with the communities being targeted right now.”

authors: Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press, Anna Wilder, Report For America

text:
The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors are also investigating a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern Tuesday over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.

READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows

"The most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon," Teare told FOX 26 Houston. "Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened, based on the surveillance footage."

ICE denies intentionally striking Parra Hernandez

Allegations that officers intentionally struck Parra Hernandez are "reckless" and "false," ICE said in a statement. Parra Hernandez had been in a vehicle with the target of an enforcement operation, and when officers tried to stop the car, the two men fled on foot, the agency said.

He "ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck," ICE said.

Espinosa flatly denied this claim during the news conference Wednesday, citing surveillance video.

The footage shows a man running from the white truck as a black SUV approaches him from behind. The video does not show the car hitting the man — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches from the man before stopping. After, the man is on the ground behind the car.

Attorneys and relatives of others who were arrested by ICE during the operation Saturday denied during the news conference that the man ICE named as the target of its operation — Jose Mendoza-Cervantes — was even in the white van, saying they didn't know anyone of that name.

Espinosa said Parra Hernandez comes from Mexico and has been in the U.S. for 34 years. He declined to share Parra Hernandez's status, but said he is living in the U.S. without authorization.

He said two ICE officers were in the room when he visited Parra Hernandez at the hospital.

"He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we're waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle," Espinosa said.

He remained in ICE custody Wednesday, Espinosa said.

Prosecutors are still investigating a fatal ICE shooting in July

Teare said ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

Wilder reported from Austin, Texas.

text:
ORLANDO, Fla., October 9, 2026 — Colombo & Hurd, PL announced that Patrick J. Glen has joined the firm as Counsel in its Federal Immigration Litigation Practice. Glen comes to the firm after nearly two decades at the U.S. Department of Justice, most recently as Senior Litigation Counsel in the Office of Immigration Litigation, where he briefed seven merits cases before the U.S. Supreme Court.

He joins a practice led by Sarah Wilson, a former senior DOJ official, that has spent the past year in federal court challenging some of the most consequential immigration policies of this administration.

Nearly two decades inside the government’s immigration litigation shop

As Senior Litigation Counsel in DOJ’s Office of Immigration Litigation, Glen wrote the government’s Supreme Court merits briefs with the Office of the Solicitor General, prepared the arguing attorney, and sat at counsel’s table before the Court. He also handled numerous petition-stage filings, including petitions for certiorari and briefs in opposition, and developed office-wide guidance on significant litigation issues.

Earlier, as a Trial Attorney, he briefed cases in every geographic federal court of appeals and argued in the Second, Third, Sixth, Ninth, and Eleventh Circuits.

While detailed to the Office of Management and Budget, Glen reviewed proposed and final regulations for statutory authority and legal sufficiency. Those are the same questions at the heart of the Administrative Procedure Act challenges the firm brings today.

He has taught immigration law and appellate practice at Georgetown University Law Center and Penn State Dickinson Law. He holds an LL.M. from Georgetown, a J.D. from Ohio Northern University, and a B.A. from Dickinson College, and is admitted before the U.S. Supreme Court.

“Patrick spent his career writing the government’s side of these cases, all the way to the Supreme Court,” said Sarah Wilson, Partner and leader of Colombo & Hurd’s Federal Immigration Litigation Practice. “He knows how agencies defend their decisions and where those arguments break down. That makes us stronger for every client we represent.”

A litigation team built from DOJ’s own ranks

Glen joins two other DOJ veterans in Colombo & Hurd’s Federal Immigration Litigation Practice:

Sarah Wilson, Partner and Practice Leader, is a former Assistant Director in DOJ’s Office of Immigration Litigation and served in 2025 as Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General in the Civil Division.

David Kim, Senior Litigation Counsel, is a former Acting Assistant Director in DOJ’s Civil Division, where he led class actions and APA challenges to federal immigration policy.

The team spent years defending the government’s immigration decisions. Now it holds the government to the law.

Impact litigation with national reach

The practice has been at the center of two of the year’s most significant immigration cases.

Striking down the 75-country immigrant visa ban. On August 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York vacated a State Department policy that suspended immigrant visas for nationals of 75 countries, nearly 40% of the world’s nations. In Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC) v. Rubio, Judge Jeannette A. Vargas found the policy “patently unlawful,” vacated it nationwide, and set aside every visa refusal based solely on it. Colombo & Hurd litigated the case with coalition co-counsel on behalf of families and workers whose lives had been put on hold.

Challenging new green card restrictions. On October 5, 2026, the firm joined Democracy Forward, the American Immigration Council, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association in filing American Association of University Professors et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al. in Boston. The suit challenges two 2026 USCIS policies that penalize applying for a green card from inside the U.S. and allow denials without a chance to submit more evidence.

The practice also brings APA challenges to unlawful rules, sues over improper denials in high-skilled categories like EB-1A and EB-2 NIW, and files mandamus actions to force decisions on delayed cases.

text:
BROCKPORT, N.Y. — Students at SUNY Brockport said they were shocked and wanted answers after an employee was detained by ICE at his home in Batavia.

RELATED: Union leader speaks in support of SUNY Brockport employee detained by ICE

Students on campus said they felt confused and hurt by the situation, especially since Brockport has about 150 international students.

“When things like this happen close by, it’s so different than seeing it online. And when you actually go and see it here. It makes you realize these issues aren’t just present out there – they are happening in my smaller community,” said Brockport student Liam Eveleigh.

Machado came to the U.S. in August 2016, and the Department of Homeland Security said he had until February 2017 to stay legally.

The United University Professions union told News10NBC on Tuesday that Machado had authorization to work until 2029. DHS told News10NBC, “work authorization or a pending application does not mean legal status in the U.S.”

“German was here on a work visa that was set to expire three years in the future. So why was he suddenly detained? The lack of transparency that really actually bothers me,” said Brockport student Samuel Robinson.

Members of student club Turning Point USA said they did not have enough details on what happened but said they do support ICE.

Robinson does have a message during this time of unease.

“Try to stick with your friends as much as you can. Don’t be afraid. A democracy only functions when you can engage in an open dialogue. Try to keep an open mind. But stick to your guns. Don’t be passive. Just keep love in your hearts,” Robinson said.

There is a planned “Visibility Event” at the college Thursday to support Machado at the student union. It’s from 11 a.m.-1 p.m.

Statement from the Department of Homeland Security

“On October 13, 2026, ICE arrested German Machado Guillen, an illegal alien from Venezuela, during a targeted enforcement operation in Batavia, New York. Machado Guillen lawfully entered the United States on August 30, 2016, with permission to stay until February 27, 2017. In violation of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome by almost a decade and failed to depart. He will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

To be clear: work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status in the U.S.

Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Statement from United University Professions union

“United University Professions, the nation’s largest higher education union, today called for the immediate release of one of our members, a SUNY Brockport employee who was taken into custody by ICE agents this morning in front of his Batavia home. German Machado, a SUNY Brockport IT technician, was picked up by ICE agents as he was preparing to leave for work, according to his wife, Maria Velázquez. A journalist, Velázquez said the couple fled the Maduro regime in Venezuela in 2016 and sought asylum in America.

She said that Machado has a valid Employment Authorization Document to work at SUNY Brockport; the EAD expires in 2029. Issued by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an EAD proves that a noncitizen is legally authorized to work in the U.S. for a specific period of time. Machado is being held in the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia.

‘German Machado is a good man and a hard worker who is in this country legally and who is legally authorized to work in this country,’ said UUP President Fred Kowal. ‘As a union, we will do all that we can to push for German’s release, including ensuring that his federal rights are not violated in any way by the Trump administration.‘

‘We are not criminals, we are good citizens trying to live a life in peace. We just want to live in safety,’ said Velázquez. ‘We own a home here. We are all professionals with university degrees. We work here and we pay taxes. (ICE) had no reason to do this to (Machado).‘

Velázquez said she believes that ICE agents were waiting for her husband to leave their house this morning to apprehend him. His car is still in the garage but his wallet and keys are gone.

She said the couple came to the U.S. because the Maduro regime threatened and harassed Velázquez for being a journalist. They applied for asylum in 2016 and they’ve been waiting for the case to be adjudicated since then.

‘We have complied with the laws, we’ve been doing everything we can,’ said Velázquez.”

We have been trying to get in contact with Machado’s wife, with no luck. The student journalism program at Brockport told us she’s trying to stay out of the public eye right now.

text:
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) is currently reviewing a proposed regulation that, if finalized, would amend the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) premium processing timeframes. Currently, premium processing timeframes are 15, 30, or 45 business days, depending on the immigration benefit being requested.

Once the proposal clears OMB review, it will be published in the Federal Register for comments from the public, generally for a period of 30 to 60 days.

Though details of the proposal will not be known with specificity until publication, it is possible that USCIS could seek to lengthen existing premium processing timeframes.

USCIS offers expedited adjudication – called premium processing – of certain immigration benefits for an additional fee that ranges from $1,780 to $2,965 depending on the case type. The fees and premium processing timeframes differ based on the immigration benefit sought. Expedited adjudication can mean the receipt of a decision on the case, or the receipt of a request for evidence (RFE) or notice of intent to deny (NOID) within the designated premium processing timeframe. In recent months, USCIS has more frequently exceeded premium processing timeframes even where the additional fee has been collected.

Premium processing is currently available for Form I-140, most Form I-129 filings, and certain Forms I-765 and I-539 with the following corresponding timeframes:

Form I-140 for EB-1C multinational manager/executive or EB-2 national interest waiver: 45 business days

Form I-765 employment authorization applications for F-1s seeking optional practical training: 30 business days

Form I-539 change of status to F, M, or J: 30 business days

Other Form I-140 and any eligible Form I-129: 15 business days

USCIS last increased premium processing fees in March 2026, using an inflationary adjustment process that occurs every two years.

When the proposed rule clears federal review, it will be published for a public comment period of 30 to 60 days. The regulation would not take effect until the rule is finalized, which can take several months.

Once the proposal is published, feedback from employers will be important to inform the government of the impact of the proposal on the business community. If your organization wishes to comment, Fragomen’s Government Strategies and Compliance Group can assist.

Federal immigration authorities are continuing to use Washington driver data to track down and arrest immigrants despite state sanctuary laws designed to prevent data sharing.

Loophole allows ICE data access in WA

What we know:

According to a new study from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights, ICE agents are exploiting loopholes to access driver information from the Department of Licensing database. The report identifies four main pathways used by agents, with a non-profit firm called "Nlets" cited more than 100 times. State troopers and other law enforcement agencies use Nlets to share driver data across state lines during traffic stops.

Researchers found that previous efforts by Washington state to restrict or eliminate access to DMV records have proven ineffective.

DOL data access linked to 356 ICE arrests in WA

"They apparently decided that requiring ICE and the Border Patrol to sign statements promising not to use it for civil immigration enforcement was enough," said UW Center for Human Rights director Angelina Godoy. "Well, it's not enough. As of today, the UW Center for Human Rights has documented 356 incidents of arrests carried out on our streets and highways following federal agents querying the DOL for our data."

Researchers expect federal queries to increase for the foreseeable future as federal authorities say they will continue to "flood the zone" in sanctuary cities like Seattle.

What we don't know:

It remains unclear whether plain-clothes federal agents who recently arrested two men on I-5 South near the 85th Street exit in Seattle used Department of Licensing data to track them down.

Recent immigration enforcement operations in WA

Washington state passed sanctuary laws forbidding state agencies from sharing driver data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for civil immigration enforcement. description:

CBP does have automatic camera activation, which means the body camera turns on and starts recording when a weapon is drawn or emergency lights are turned on.
After federal immigration officers killed two U.S. citizens in January during an aggressive deportation drive in Minneapolis, the Trump administration directed body cameras to immigration agents.
Democrats have also pushed for all federal immigration officers to wear body cameras in the wake of the killings and violent interactions from agents that were recorded by bystanders.
Thousands of body cameras distributed GAO investigators found that as of April, ICE issued 4,800 body cameras, splitting them evenly between its deportation wing of Enforcement and Removal Operations and the investigative law enforcement arm of ICE, Homeland Security Investigations.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection need to improve oversight and guidance for federal immigration officers' use of body-worn cameras, according to a Wednesday report from independent federal investigators.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security, however, resisted a recommendation in the report from the Government Accountability Office that ICE change its current policy, in which agents choose when to manually turn on body cameras, as opposed to automatic activation.

In a response to GAO, the department — which oversees both agencies — argued that automatic activation on a body camera presents a risk to ongoing operations, such as recording sensitive interactions with informants or victims or inadvertently filming bystanders.

GAO said that statement was insufficient. “However, DHS’s response did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective, or other controls that could help ensure compliance with activating cameras when required by policy,” according to GAO.

Multiple shootings

The report came after multiple high-profile cases of federal immigration officers shooting and killing people during interactions and enforcement actions, prompting calls for wider body camera use.

GAO made seven recommendations to the Department of Homeland Security to update its guidance for body cameras.

The department agreed with six, but disagreed with implementing automated camera activation controls, arguing that ICE’s current policy is sufficient. CBP does have automatic camera activation, which means the body camera turns on and starts recording when a weapon is drawn or emergency lights are turned on.

“Without reliable control activities, ICE risks gaps in documentation and video evidence that can make reviews of incidents more challenging,” according to GAO.

After federal immigration officers killed two U.S. citizens in January during an aggressive deportation drive in Minneapolis, the Trump administration directed body cameras to immigration agents.

In June, there were two back-to-back killings of immigrants in Texas and Maine that prompted border czar Tom Homan to announce that during traffic stops at least one ICE officer will wear a body camera.

Democrats have also pushed for all federal immigration officers to wear body cameras in the wake of the killings and violent interactions from agents that were recorded by bystanders.

Thousands of body cameras distributed

GAO investigators found that as of April, ICE issued 4,800 body cameras, splitting them evenly between its deportation wing of Enforcement and Removal Operations and the investigative law enforcement arm of ICE, Homeland Security Investigations.

And in June, CBP issued approximately 11,500 cameras, mostly to Border Patrol.

But GAO found problems in the cameras’ deployment.

“Most CBP and ICE offices have not developed specific operational guidance that explains how personnel should use, or not use, cameras under their unique operational circumstances,” according to the report. “The lack of guidance at this operational level increases the risk that CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy.”

DHS agreed to the recommendations from GAO that the leaders of ICE and CBP should update their body camera program to include changes in requirements and costs and plan for any contingencies based on current risk.

The department also agreed that CBP and ICE should implement goals to ensure effectiveness for the body-worn camera program and that both agencies should ensure their sub-agencies are also given proper guidance on the expectations and appropriate uses of the body cameras.

title: Approximately 500 participate in hunger strike at Folkston immigration detention center
authors: Jabari Gibbs, The Current GA, Jabari Gibbs, The Current GA, Atlanta Community Press Collective, Matt Scott, Alessandro Marazzi Sassoon, The Columbus Times
description:

2026 5:32 p.m. A previous version of this story said that Sam Hamilton represented clients who are participating in the strike.
text:
Approximately 500 people in a Coastal Georgia immigration detention center are on a hunger strike, protesting conditions at the facility as well as what they say are violations of asylum protocols by U.S. authorities, according to family members and legal representatives.

Samantha Hamilton, senior litigation staff attorney at Asian Americans Advancing Justice Atlanta (AAAJ), said most of the people participating in the civil disobedience came to the United States seeking asylum from authoritarian and repressive national governments. The hunger strikers say they were following the legal process for their immigration claims, yet have been at the privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Folkston for months or years awaiting judicial hearings.

The hunger strike is the latest controversy at the Charlton County facility, which is run by The GEO Group and, despite numerous complaints about unsafe conditions, is expanding to become the largest ICE detention center in the nation.

“There’s nothing illegal about seeking asylum. There’s nothing illegal about seeking sanctuary,” said Hamilton. “So this is just the natural next step in a long-time struggle of people being detained at this facility.”

Hamilton said that as of Oct. 8, around 372 men confined to Folkston’s F building and K5 pod are participating in the hunger strike, along with an estimated 150 more detainees in other buildings.

The numbers come from numerous sources associated with the Campaign to Shut Down Folkston ICE Processing Center (FIPC), activists who have different lines of communication with detainees there, as well as family members of detainees, according to Hamilton.

The new civil protest among detainees is part of a monthslong struggle for redress, Hamilton said. For months, detainees have been seeking redress from the courts, with an increase in petitions filed in U.S. Federal Court in Waycross asking the U.S. government to show cause for their detention.

In September, 14 Russian-speaking detainees published a letter in which they complained about inadequate conditions at Folkston.

A larger group agreed to join a hunger strike ahead of a planned Oct. 6 inspection of the facility, according to a letter signed by 45 of the protesters and a video explaining the rationale for the mass protest.

“Some of us have been detained for months. Some people have been here for years. We are not serving criminal sentences. We are asking the United States for protection,” one of the detainees said in an audio recording obtained by The Current GA. “We are afraid that what inspectors see will not show how we normally live. We have serious concerns about the food, sleep conditions, medical care, and the length of our detention.”

Polina Chertushkina, the 26-year-old wife of a Russian national who signed the September letter, said her husband deserved a day in court because he never broke the law.

She and her husband Andrei Gerdiukov sought asylum in America after entering the U.S. at the Texas border in February 2024. Immediately afterward, they were allowed to live peacefully as the government processed their file, she said. The couple settled in New York and purchased an apartment and a car. But they were detained in Miami by U.S. border officials. Officials transferred her husband to the D. Ray James facility in Georgia. She was released under an alternate program which requires electronic monitoring, Chertushkina said.

“We didn’t do anything. We didn’t commit any crimes, and we didn’t break any law. We followed all the requirements and all things that the government told us to do,” she said.

Folkston has been the focus of criticism for years by the Department of Homeland Security’s own auditors. The Current GA has previously reported on the 2024 death of 57-year-old Jaspal Singh. That story found that an ICE report said the facility’s medical care “deviated beyond safe limits and directly contributed to his death.”

Despite a checkered track record, the government awarded The GEO Group a new $47 million contract to expand the number of beds to 3,000, a size that would make the center the largest permanent ICE facility in the United States.

In the last two years, conditions have deteriorated, according to Hamilton, who has visited Folkston multiple times. The water is undrinkable, forcing detainees to join the voluntary work program that pays $1 a day so they can afford the water bottles sold at commissary, she said.

“People have reported seeing bugs in the water. People have reported getting rashes, presumably from the water that they never had. Skin rashes that they’ve never had before,” she said ”People have reported their hair falling out as a result of taking showers from the water, and because the water is so disgusting, people really try to avoid it at all costs.”

The GEO Group declined to comment, instead directing The Current to direct questions to ICE. ICE did not respond to requests for comment.

Congressman Earl “Buddy” Carter did not respond to requests for comment. Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock also did not respond to requests for comment.

Chertushkina said that her husband, Andrei Gerdiukov, was placed in solitary confinement for participating in the strike and engaging in a group demonstration.

She hopes that Gerdiukov can be released soon, as she relies on him to support her through her medical issues.

“We came here because America was so welcoming, and we didn’t expect it because nobody informed us that we could go through all these hard things here. I think if we had known about it, maybe we wouldn’t have come,” said Gerdiukov.

Correction: Oct. 12. 2026 5:32 p.m. A previous version of this story said that Sam Hamilton represented clients who are participating in the strike.

Editor’s note: In addition to her role as an immigration attorney, Samantha Hamilton also serves as Atlanta Community Press Collective’s attorney and has represented the outlet in previous litigation. Hamilton was not involved in ACPC’s decision to publish this story.

title: More Trump propaganda videos posted to YouTube despite court order - Democracy Docket
description:
The Trump administration posted more political ads on the official White House YouTube Monday, appearing to defy a court order that blocked the ads from being aired, pro-democracy groups told a federal court.
Despite a New York judge granting Common Cause and a coalition of other pro-democracy groups’ motion Sunday for a temporary restraining order blocking the political ads, the Trump administration posted four new political ads on YouTube the next day.

text:
The Trump administration posted more political ads on the official White House YouTube Monday, appearing to defy a court order that blocked the ads from being aired, pro-democracy groups told a federal court.

Despite a New York judge granting Common Cause and a coalition of other pro-democracy groups’ motion Sunday for a temporary restraining order blocking the political ads, the Trump administration posted four new political ads on YouTube the next day. These ads, though not aired on television, have garnered a cumulative 189,000 views in the two days they have been live.

In a notice filed Tuesday, Common Cause raised concerns about these new ads and asked the Trump administration if they were developed, created or published using the $20 million that the administration diverted from immigration enforcement without congressional approval.

Common Cause also wrote that two of the ads challenged in their lawsuit, titled “America Will Never Be a Socialist/Communist Country” and “Mount Rushmore,” are still up on the White House YouTube channel. These two ads have a total of 70,000 views.

The Trump administration continued to air some of its ads despite the court order, blaming internal email delays over the weekend for the initial failure to comply.

Common Cause originally filed its lawsuit against the Trump administration on Oct. 7 for using taxpayer dollars to produce and distribute political ads “glorifying” President Donald Trump in an effort to support Republican candidates as midterm voting begins.

The pro-democracy groups alleged Trump told Office of Management and Budget director Russel Vought to find government funds for these ads despite prohibitions on using public funds for political advertising. Common Cause argued these ads violated the Administrative Procedure Act and the U.S. Constitution and asked the Court to block the Trump administration from producing and airing them.

District Court Judge Jennifer Rochon granted the temporary restraining order on Oct. 11, writing that Common Cause provided a “strong showing” and it was likely to win its lawsuit.

The court will hold a hearing Wednesday to determine whether the Trump administration violated the restraining order when it ran ads after the order was issued.

text:
U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the Democratic incumbent, and her Republican challenger, state Sen. John Braun, debated issues of affordability, housing, data centers, immigration, social issues and other big topics in the KATU studios on Tuesday night in closely watched race that may help determine which political party controls Congress.

The seat that the two are fighting over is the 3rd Congressional District in southwest Washington.

Braun, the minority leader in the Washington state Senate and a former U.S. Navy captain, is looking to flip the seat to red by defeating Gluesenkamp Perez, who is serving her second term in Congress.

Watch the full debate below:

During the debate, Gluesenkamp Perez blamed President Donald Trump’s war in Iran for the cause of the spiking cost of everyday items like groceries and gasoline.

“The war in Iran has been a disaster,” she said. “The administration has failed to articulate a clear goal or strategy to achieve it, and I voted against it six times.”

Gluesenkamp Perez said the cost of housing was a major problem for people in southwest Washington and said she helped pass the Build Now Act to get more houses built.

Braun did not mention the war in Iran in his response to a question about what the federal government could do to lower prices, but he blamed many of the problems of affordability on local and state policies.

“There are only a few things that you can do at the national level,” he said. “Taxes. And we’ve made some progress in the last year and a half to get taxes lower, competitive, stable -- we have more work to do.”

Debate over Data Centers

The issue of data centers has snuck into campaigns across the country this election cycle, and it was a topic of discussion in Tuesday’s debate between Braun and Gluesenkamp Perez.

Braun said every data center project needs to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, but the discussion needs to start in the community where the project is proposed.

“With the folks who want to put in the data center -- interfacing with local citizens, understanding their concerns, addressing their concerns,” as well as following all the federal, state, and local permitting rules, he said, adding that the citizens need to support the project.

On balance, he said, data centers could be beneficial to communities.

“In southwest Washington we have a generational legacy of making sure that public assets benefit the public, not a select group of insider, you know, titans of tech,” Gluesenkamp Perez said in her response to data centers.

She said citizens need to know that Congress has their backs and will protect them from things like noise pollution, the cost of energy, or impacts to their water supply to ensure that “local communities are held harmless.”

Trump’s Tariffs

The two also debated Trump’s tariffs. The president argues that his tariffs will increase manufacturing jobs in the United States.

Gluesenkamp Perez accused the Trump administration of being reckless with its use of tariffs.

“I think it is vitally important to our national strength that we reshore manufacturing, that we have a real respect, but the way that he is exercising tariff authority I think has been a disaster. I think it has just been so chaotic, and it has not led to a stronger, more prosperous or more respect for the trades,” she said.

Braun appeared to agree. He said the issue of tariffs was one place where he did not agree with the president.

“I work in manufacturing, I know quite a bit about manufacturing,” he said. “I will tell you that tariffs are not the way to do that. Perhaps in certain situations, say with China or perhaps with Russia, tariffs are appropriate, but with our allies indiscriminate use of tariffs is not helpful and ultimately lead to an increase in prices for manufacturers and consumers.”

The New Gluesenkamp Perez Ad

While the candidates sparred over the big issues of the day, which also included social issues like transgender rights and abortion during the hour-long debate, perhaps the tensest and most emotionally charged moment came near the end, when the two candidates were discussing the chemical tank implosion at the Nippon Dynawave plant in Longview in May that killed 11 people.

As that discussion was ending, Gluesenkamp Perez brought up a family she said was harmed by Braun’s company, Braun Northwest.

Earlier in the day, the two candidates released dueling news releases over a new TV ad released by the Gluesenkamp Perez campaign that was about that family.

That ad featured Colten Keller, who used to work at Braun Northwest. His father died in an accident while working for the company.

“I think everything that you need to know about how Sen. Braun will respond, how he’ll write rules, how he’ll listen to people who have actually been in accidents, you can see how he treated the family of a man who was killed in an accident at his own company,” Gluesenkamp Perez said during the debate.

In the news release and in the ad, which her campaign bought time air time right before the KATU debate to run it, the campaign accused Braun’s company of not offering the family support after the accident.

“The only response weeks later was asking when Colten would be back on the clock,” the Gluesenkamp Perez news release stated.

In responding to her new ad and her remarks during the KATU debate, Braun called it “a new low” for Gluesenkamp Perez.

“It’s an attack ad on me for not placing a phone call to the son of a man who was killed in a workplace accident at our plant two years ago,” Braun said. “Here’s the reality, I talked to the son twice that day. I didn’t call him, I talked to him in person because he also worked for us at the time, so this is just an example of what Marie, a D.C. politician, will do to keep her seat in Washington, D.C.”

“You owe that family an apology,” Gluesenkamp Perez immediately snapped back.

During the debate the two also discussed the roles for Congress in authorizing military action, immigration policy, border security, as well as what it needs to do to ensure Western states can deal with devastating wildfires.

The full debate can be watched above.

text:
A Texas prosecutor has launched a criminal investigation into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who allegedly used an SUV to deliberately run over a fleeing man in Houston, leaving him with a broken leg that required surgery.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said surveillance footage of Saturday's incident appeared to show the federal agent intentionally striking 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez, raising the possibility of aggravated assault charges.

“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”

The footage shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running away as a dark SUV pursues them. The vehicle then strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen lying on the ground moments later.

ICE has disputed the suggestion that the collision was intentional, saying Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle as officers attempted to detain him.

“As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” Tim Oberle, an ICE spokesperson in Houston, said in a statement provided to The Texas Tribune.

Victim faces further surgery

Parra Hernandez, who has lived in the United States for 34 years, was on his way to work when the encounter unfolded, according to Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant rights organization FIEL Houston.

Espinosa said Parra Hernandez suffered a broken leg and underwent surgery following the collision. He is expected to require another operation to reconstruct his injured ankle.

“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.

Espinosa, whose organization is assisting the family, declined to disclose Parra Hernandez's immigration status.

He also said he encountered two ICE agents inside Parra Hernandez's hospital room while visiting the injured man.

Prosecutor accuses ICE of refusing to cooperate

Teare, a Democrat, said ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the agency, have not cooperated with his office's investigation.

DHS officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

The investigation comes amid heightened scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement operations in Houston and elsewhere under President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

Teare's office previously investigated the fatal shooting of 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by an ICE officer in July.

The district attorney said DHS also failed to respond to his requests for information about that incident.

Salgado Araujo's death was among at least 10 fatalities involving encounters with immigration officers since the beginning of Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The latest incident has intensified criticism of federal immigration tactics, with local prosecutors now examining whether an ICE agent's actions in Houston crossed the line into criminal conduct.

No criminal charges have been announced in connection with Saturday's collision.

text:
The city of San Antonio has sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to block a proposed immigration detention facility, arguing the federal agency failed to review the plan’s environmental impact.

DHS paid $66.1 million for a 640,000-square-foot commercial warehouse in San Antonio earlier this year. In August, the agency awarded a $17.3 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services to convert the building into a detention facility that could hold 1,500 immigrants a day.

In a Tuesday federal petition, city officials said the federal agency disregarded requirements to thoroughly consider the plan’s environmental consequences and consider reasonable alternatives in violation of the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. Other communities have used the same strategy to fight ICE.

San Antonio’s filing said DHS and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials failed to upgrade the facility’s sewer and water system to ensure its operation would not discharge harmful contaminants into surface waters. It also pointed to longstanding concerns regarding health and safety conditions within ICE detention centers, such as disease outbreaks reported in Texas facilities earlier this year. In addition, the city alleged that it has received “little-to-no information” from federal officials about their plans for the warehouse.

“The Detention Conversion Project threatens the environmental, economic, public health, and safety interests of the City of San Antonio and its people,” the petition said. “These alarming conditions could endanger public health and require a response by City health officials.”

DHS said the city was more interested in thwarting President Donald Trump’s immigration policy than caring about the environment. An unnamed spokesperson also said the agency is moving swiftly with state and county partners to use existing detention space.

“From day one, DHS has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so,” the unnamed spokesperson told The Texas Tribune. “These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer’s expense.”

As of Aug. 6, just over 30% of the people arrested by ICE across the country had a prior conviction, according to federal data. In Texas, two-thirds of people arrested by ICE had no criminal convictions.

This is not the only warehouse that DHS has had eyes on in Texas.

In February, a company said it would not sell or lease a 1 million-square-foot facility in Hutchins to ICE, blocking a plan to convert it into a detention facility near Dallas that could hold 9,500 people. Meanwhile, Democratic U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar told the Tribune in August that DHS was planning to sell the three warehouses it had bought in El Paso County, which have capacity for more than 8,000 people.

The federal agency has also offloaded several other warehouses around the country that were initially bought to boost the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.

text: 🚨 Landmark decision: Children must never be detained for reasons related to their or their parents’ migration status The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child has reaffirmed this fundamental principle in Jas.K.B. and Others v. the Czech Republic (Communication No. 193/2022), finding violations of the rights of two sisters under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The case concerned two Afghan sisters detained with their parents for 34 days in a closed immigration detention centre in the Czech Republic, pending transfer to Austria under the Dublin III Regulation. The younger child was just 11 years old. The Committee made clear that: 🔹 Immigration detention of children is arbitrary: the possibility of detention as a measure of last resort does not apply in the context of migration control. 🔹 Family unity cannot justify detention: where keeping the family together is in the child’s best interests, States must pursue non-custodial alternatives for the whole family. 🔹 The best interests of the child must be meaningfully assessed, including the harm inherent in detention and the availability of alternatives. This decision is an important reaffirmation of international human rights standards and a clear reminder that describing a detention facility as suitable for families does not make child immigration detention compatible with children’s rights. The International Commission of Jurists, together with The AIRE Centre, Dutch Council for Refugees | International Strategic Litigation, and European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE) had intervened in the case by filing a legal brief with the Committee. 🔗 For more details: https://lnkd.in/ecpvpCQt #ChildrensRights #Migration #HumanRights #ImmigrationDetention #UNCRC #RuleOfLaw
