text:
Women’s Mass Incarceration:

The Whole Pie 2026 Tweet this

By Wendy Sawyer and Brian Nam-Sonenstein

October 14, 2026

Press release

With growing public attention to the problem of mass incarceration, people want to know about women’s experiences with incarceration. How many women are held in prisons, jails, and other correctional facilities in the United States? Why are they there? How are their experiences different from men’s? These are important questions, but finding the answers requires not only disentangling the country’s decentralized and overlapping criminal legal systems, but also unearthing the frustratingly limited data that’s broken down by gender.

This report provides a detailed view of the 198,800 women and girls incarcerated in the United States and how they fit into the even broader picture of correctional control. We pull together data from a number of government agencies and break down the number of women and girls held by each correctional system, by specific offense, in 446 state prisons, 27 federal prisons, 2,765 local jails, 1,277 juvenile correctional facilities, 65 Indian country jails, and 148 immigration detention facilities, as well as in military prisons, civil commitment centers, state psychiatric hospitals, and prisons in the U.S. territories. We also go beyond the numbers, including rare self-reported data from a national survey of people in prison to offer new insights about incarcerated women’s backgrounds, families, health, and experiences in prison. This report answers the questions of why and where women are locked up — and much more:

Women’s incarceration has risen by almost 60% globally since 2000. For several decades in the U.S., it grew at twice the pace of men’s incarceration, yet it still receives relatively little attention, obscured by the much larger scale of men’s incarceration. Making up just 1 in 10 people behind bars, women continue to experience confinement in systems designed for men — that is, systems that ignore important gender differences, even in the data they collect and report. Frustratingly, even as this report is updated using many of the same data sources from year to year, it is not a direct tool for tracking changes in women’s incarceration over time; we are forced to rely on the limited sources available, which are neither updated regularly nor always compatible across years. Still, particularly in light of the scarcity of gender-specific data, the disaggregated numbers presented here are an important step to ensuring that women are not left behind in the effort to end mass incarceration.

The policing and incarceration of so many women is at least partially explained by the United States’ bipartisan commitment to so-called “tough on crime” policies. Rather than cracking down on the “worst of the worst” as politicians often promise, this approach has instead made local, state, and federal governments reliant on the criminal legal system as the primary (if not only) tool for addressing a wide array of societal issues like drug use, poverty, and homelessness. As a result, governments have ensnared hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people — including nearly 200,000 women and girls — in a system that fails to resolve those issues but nonetheless returns people behind bars over and over again, destroying their lives, families, and communities in the process. The rapid expansion of a surveillant, punishing system of community supervision; the aggressive policing of “quality of life” issues stemming from disinvestment in healthcare and housing; and the commitment to long mandatory sentences under the war on drugs are just some examples of policy choices that have forced so many women behind bars.

It’s particularly notable that — in stark contrast to the total incarcerated population, where state and federal prison systems hold twice as many people as jails — more incarcerated women are held in jails than in prisons. As we explain, the outsized role of jails has serious consequences for incarcerated women and their families.

Jails loom large in women’s incarceration

Women make up about 25% of all individuals booked into jail each year. Compared to men or the total jail population, a greater share of women in jails are serving sentences, but even so, most women being held for local authorities (61%) have not been convicted of a crime and are trapped there awaiting trial.

Aside from women under local authority (or jurisdiction), state and federal agencies also pay local jails to house nearly 7,600 additional women. For example, ICE and the U.S. Marshals Service, which have fewer dedicated facilities for the people they detain, contract with local jails to hold roughly 2,900 women on a typical day. That means the number of women physically held in jails is even higher:

Women disproportionately stuck in jails: Causes and effects

Avoiding pretrial detention is particularly challenging for women. The number of unconvicted women stuck in jail is surely not because courts are considering women to be a flight risk, particularly when they are generally the primary caregivers of children. The far more likely answer is that incarcerated women, who have lower incomes than incarcerated men, have an even harder time affording money bail. When the typical bail amounts to a full year’s income for women, it’s no wonder that women are stuck in jail awaiting trial.

After conviction, the system continues to funnel women into local jails: About one-quarter (26%) of convicted incarcerated women are held in jails, compared to about 8% of all people incarcerated with a conviction. This reflects the different distribution of offense types and criminal histories between convicted men and women. Women are proportionally more likely to be serving a sentence of incarceration for a property or drug offense and less likely to be incarcerated for a violent offense as compared to men. These differences mean that women are more likely to be sentenced to a term in jail, where people typically serve shorter sentences of up to one year.

So, what does it mean that large numbers of women are held in jail — for them, and for their families? First, while stays in jail are generally shorter than stays in prison, jails can be especially deadly for women. Women have a higher mortality rate than men in jails, dying of drug and alcohol intoxication at twice the rate of men. And the number of deaths by suicide among women in jails increased by almost 65% between the periods of 2000-2004 and 2015-2019. Women are more likely than men to enter jail with a medical problem or a serious mental illness, and while incarcerated, they are more likely to suffer from mental health problems and experience serious psychological distress. Being locked up doesn’t help: research shows that incarceration can cause lasting damage to mental health.

Compounding the problem is the fact that jails are particularly poorly positioned to provide proper health care. In fact, local jails tend to offer fewer services and programs overall than prisons do, and because most programs are designed for the larger male population, women may not even have access to programming that’s available to men in the same jail. (However, this is certainly not to say that prisons are always better at meeting women’s needs, as we will discuss further.)

Jails also make it even harder to stay in touch with family than prisons do. Jail phone calls are often at least three times as expensive as calls from prison, and other forms of communication are more restricted — some jails don’t even allow real letters, limiting mail to postcards. Increasingly, both prisons and jails are doing away with real mail altogether and contracting with private companies that scan and then destroy postal mail, delivering shoddy scanned copies to the recipients. These barriers to authentic communication are especially troubling given that 80% of women in jails are mothers, and most of them are primary caretakers of their children. Children are therefore particularly susceptible to the domino effect of burdens placed on incarcerated women.

Ending mass incarceration requires looking at all offenses — and all women

Too often, the conversation about criminal legal reform begins and ends with the question of “non-violent” drug and property offenses. While drug and property offenses make up more than half of the offenses for which women are incarcerated, the pie chart reveals that all offenses — including the violent offenses that account for nearly one-third of all incarcerated women — must be considered in the effort to reduce the number of incarcerated women in this country. This fact underscores the need for policy discussions to focus not just on the easier choices but on the changes that will have the most impact. Particularly in light of the fact that many survivors of domestic and sexual abuse have been incarcerated for violent crimes that occurred in response to gendered violence and abuse, excluding entire offense categories from consideration for reform makes even less sense.

Furthermore, even among women, incarceration is not indiscriminate and reforms should address the disparities related to gender identity, sexual orientation, race, and ethnicity as well. A 2017 study revealed that one-third of incarcerated women identify as lesbian or bisexual, compared to less than 10% of men who identify as gay or bisexual. The same study found that lesbian and bisexual women are likely to receive longer sentences than their heterosexual peers, and more likely to be put into solitary confinement.

And although the data do not exist to break down the “whole pie” by race or ethnicity, we know that Black and American Indian or Alaska Native women are consistently overrepresented in state and federal prisons: Women in prison are 47% white, 18% Black, 19% Hispanic, 3% American Indian or Alaska Native, 0.7% Asian, and 13% “other.” While we are a long way from having data on the intersectional impacts of sexuality and race or ethnicity on women’s likelihood of incarceration, it is clear that Black and lesbian or bisexual women and girls are disproportionately subject to incarceration.

Prison is no answer for marginalized, traumatized women

About half of confined women and girls are held in state and federal prisons. In general, women in prison are serving longer sentences than those in jails, and they are often located far from their families and friends. In many geographically large states there is just one facility for women, making visits difficult for children and other loved ones located hundreds of miles away. To make matters worse, a lot of facilities that hold women are overcrowded, which can lead to heightened levels of violence, worse health outcomes, and longer terms of incarceration. In Wisconsin, for example, women’s prisons are 78% over capacity, compared to 30% over capacity for men’s facilities. But these are just a few of the many challenges facing women in prison, as we found in our 2022 analysis of a rich dataset published by the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the 2016 Survey of Prison Inmates.

The data from the survey offer a rare in-depth look at the backgrounds and experiences of people in prison, relying on responses from incarcerated people themselves, rather than the administrative data that’s easier to collect from prison systems. In our analysis, we focused on people held in state prisons, who make up a much larger piece of the “whole pie” than those in federal prisons. Among our findings and those of the Bureau of Justice Statistics, we see that in state prisons nationwide:

Women report childhood disadvantages at alarming rates: 12% report homelessness before they turned 18, 19% were in foster care at some point, and 43% came from families that received welfare or other public assistance. Almost half (45%) had been arrested by age 18.

Women are more likely than men to enter prison having already received a high school diploma or equivalent credential, but still over half (53%) did not finish high school.

More than 1 in 6 women (16%) experienced homelessness in the year before the arrest that led to their incarceration — a higher rate than among men (10%).

Women are more likely to be jobless (53%) than to be employed in the month before their arrest.

Women are more likely to be written up for a prison rule violation in the past year (58%), particularly for “minor” rule violations (70%).

Women report disabilities (50%) and physical and mental health problems at higher rates than men. Over half (58%) of women met the criteria for a substance use disorder the year before they went to prison, and over three-quarters (76%) had some indication of a past or current mental health problem — both significantly higher rates than among men. Yet just 47% had received treatment for a substance use disorder and just 43% had received professional mental health care since they went to prison.

Women are more likely to be parents of minor children (58%), more likely to be single parents, and more likely to have been living with their children prior to their imprisonment — making it more likely that incarceration would uproot their children and lead to termination of parental rights, permanently breaking up their families.

About 4% of women (over 3,000) were pregnant when they went to prison, and more than two-thirds (68%) of these women had no health insurance at the time. Yet only half had received any kind of prenatal care in prison apart from an obstetric exam. Only 10 states and the federal government run prison nursery programs, which are residential programs where people can live with their newborns.

These statistics confirm much of what we know about incarcerated women from previous research: By almost any measure, women in prison are worse off than men, both leading up to and during their incarceration. Furthermore, the underlying causes of women’s criminal behavior are distinct from men’s and show that they would be better served in treatment programs in their communities than by criminal legal system punishments far from home.

Mass incarceration targets girls, too

Over 5,000 young women and girls are caught up in various systems of confinement, very often for minor and even non-criminal offenses. Most (85%) are held by the juvenile justice system, but about 600 are unaccompanied migrant children held in facilities operated by the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR). While children held by ORR are not held for any criminal or delinquent offense, most are held in shelters or even juvenile placement facilities under detention-like conditions. And a not-insignificant number of confined girls are actually held in adult prisons and jails. Like their adult counterparts, confined girls often report identities that are marginalized in the U.S. along lines of race, gender, and sexual orientation.

Many girls are locked up for reasons that have nothing to do with public safety. For nearly 1 in 4 girls (24%) confined by the juvenile justice system, the most serious charge levelled against them is a non-criminal “technical” violation of probation (17%) or a status offense (7%), such as “running away, truancy, and incorrigibility.” These are behaviors that would not warrant confinement except for these girls’ status as probationers or as minors. By comparison, boys are held for these technical violations and status offenses at half the rate of girls. The use of confinement in response to status offenses is particularly troubling because those behaviors tend to be simply responses to abuse.

Girls of color and those who identify as LBTQ+ are disproportionately confined by the juvenile justice system. Black girls account for 37% of all girls in juvenile facilities, despite making up just 16% of girls under 18 nationwide; similarly, 3% of girls in juvenile facilities are American Indian or Alaska Natives, compared to less than 2% of girls nationwide. And while LBTQ+ women are overrepresented in the adult correctional systems, a staggering 40% of girls in the juvenile justice system are lesbian, bisexual, or questioning and gender non-conforming. The comparable statistic for boys is just under 14%.

While society and the criminal legal systems subject all girls to stricter codes of conduct than is expected of their male peers, Black girls in particular shoulder an added burden of adultification — being perceived as older, more culpable, and more responsible than their peers — which leads to greater contact with and harsher consequences within the juvenile justice system. In fact, about 220 girls aged 17 or younger are locked up in adult prisons and jails, the result of laws that allow the transfer of youth from juvenile to adult criminal courts. In 2023, 292 girls were “waived” to criminal courts from the juvenile system — nearly 8% of all cases “waived.” More than one-third (37%) of those girls were Black.

A look at some of the smaller “slices”: immigration and involuntary commitment

Turning to those who are locked up criminally and civilly for immigration-related reasons, we find that over 1,200 women are held for criminal charges or convictions of immigration offenses by the federal Bureau of Prisons and U.S. Marshals Service. The vast majority of people incarcerated for criminal immigration offenses are accused of illegal entry or illegal reentry — in other words, for no more serious offense than crossing the border without permission.

Under the current Trump administration's mass deportation regime, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) now civilly detains about 7,700 women and girls, not for any crime, but simply because they are facing deportation. People detained by ICE are physically confined in federally-, privately-, or state-run immigration detention facilities, andin local jails under contract with ICE or the U.S. Marshals. Many of the federally-run facilities in particular have long track records of abusive treatment and inhumane conditions. The roughly 600 unaccompanied migrant girls held in the custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) are awaiting placement with parents, family members, or friends, rather than deportation, but we include them in our count because, again, most are held in detention-like conditions.

Adding to the universe of people who are confined because of criminal legal system involvement, we estimate that about 2,900 women are involuntarily committed ina growing number ofstate psychiatric hospitals and civil commitment centers for underlying criminal charges. Many of these people are not even convicted, and some are held indefinitely. So-called “forensic patients” include people being evaluated or treated for incompetency to stand trial, as well as those found not guilty by reason of insanity or guilty but mentally ill, who may remain forcibly hospitalized for decades or for life. A small number of women convicted of sex-related crimes are involuntarily committed or detained after their prison sentences are complete. Meanwhile, at least 38 states allow involuntary commitment for substance use disorder treatment, and in many cases, people are sent to actual prisons and jails, which are inappropriate places for treatment.

The tentacles of mass incarceration have a long reach

Even the “whole pie” of incarceration in the chart above represents just one small portion (18%) of the women under any form of correctional control, which includes 819,400 women on probation or parole. Again, this is in stark contrast to the total correctional population (mostly men), where one-third (35%) are in prisons and jails.

Nearly three-quarters of women (74%) under the control of any U.S. correctional system are on probation. Probation is often billed as an alternative to incarceration, but instead it is frequently set with unrealistic conditions that undermine its goal of keeping people from being locked up. For example, probation often comes with steep fees which, like bail, women are in the worst position to afford. Failing to pay these probation fees is often a non-criminal “technical” violation of probation. Childcare duties further complicate the common probation requirement to meet regularly with probation officers, especially for women with no extra money to spend on childcare or reliable transportation across town. And probation violations — even for these innocuous and understandable reasons — can land women in jail or prison who were never sentenced to incarceration in the first place. In fact, our analysis of the 2016 Survey of Prison Inmates found that one-third (33%) of women in state prisons were on probation at the time of their arrest, which underscores how this “alternative to incarceration” often simply delays incarceration.

In the wake of the 2022 Supreme Court decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, restrictive pretrial, probation, and parole conditions can also create barriers to accessing reproductive health care. Restrictions on travel are “standard conditions” of supervision in many places, requiring approval from a probation or parole officer to make specific trips. With many states now restricting access to and criminalizing abortion, seeking an abortion or other reproductive care may be difficult or impossible for many of the hundreds of thousands of women on probation or parole in those states. We estimate that 4 out of 5 women (82%) on probation or parole nationwide are impacted by state abortion restrictions. More specifically, (excluding federal probation and post-release supervision) 82% of women on probation and 85% of women on parole live in states that (1) either completely ban abortion or restrict it based on gestational age and (2) list travel restrictions as a standard condition of supervision.

Reentry is another critical point at which women are too often left behind. Almost 2.5 million women and girls are released from prisons and jails every year, but fewer post-release programs are available to them — partly because so many women are confined to jails, which are not meant to be used for long-term incarceration. Additionally, many women with criminal records face barriers to employment in female-dominated occupations, such as nursing and elder care. It is little surprise, therefore, that formerly incarcerated women — especially women of color — are also more likely to be unemployed and/or homeless than formerly incarcerated men, making reentry and compliance with probation or parole even more difficult. All of these issues make women particularly vulnerable to being incarcerated not because they commit crimes, but because they run afoul of one of the burdensome obligations of their community supervision.

Like probation before it, electronic monitoring is touted as an “alternative” to incarceration, but it is being used to expand the scope of correctional control rather than reduce the number of people behind bars. The rapid expansion of electronic monitoring in the pretrial context has created “an entirely new path to incarceration via ‘technical violations.’” And ICE’s “Alternatives to Detention” and “Intensive Supervision Appearance Program,” which both rely almost entirely on electronic monitoring, now subject hundreds of thousands more people to constant surveillance and the threat of detention or deportation than just a few years ago. Unlike probation, electronic monitoring is so constrictive that it amounts to a form of “e-carceration.” Unfortunately, the available data are not broken down by sex or gender identity, but with nearly half a million people on electronic monitoring across the criminal legal and immigration systems in 2022, it’s safe to assume that many, many women are confined by this form of mass incarceration as well.

The need for more data

The picture of women’s incarceration is far from complete, and many questions remain about mass incarceration’s unique impact on women. This report offers the critical estimate that a quarter of all incarcerated women are unconvicted. But since the federal government hasn’t collected the key underlying data in 20 years, is that number growing? And how do the harms of that unnecessary incarceration intersect with women’s disproportionate caregiving to impact families? Beyond these big picture questions, there are a plethora of detailed data points that are not reported for women by any government agencies. In addition to the many data gaps and limitations mentioned throughout this report, we’re missing other basic data, such as the simple number of women incarcerated in U.S. territories or who are being held in federal pretrial detention by the U.S. Marshals.

As public awareness has grown about the differences between gender identity and sex assigned at birth, there has been a growing interest in the question of how transgender and nonbinary individuals experience incarceration. Unfortunately, government surveys that break down data between “male” and “female” categories often include trans men among “females” and trans women among “males,” relying on housing assignments as a proxy for gender. In recent years, the Bureau of Justice Statistics had begun collecting data on transgender and nonbinary individuals — for example, it reported data on a small sample of transgender individuals in state prisons in its 2016 Survey of Prison Inmates, which we analyzed — but removed questions about gender identity from its surveys in early 2025 when Trump took office. This further muddies the picture of women’s incarceration.

While more data are needed, the data in this report lend focus and perspective to the policy reforms needed to end mass incarceration without leaving women behind.

About the data

This briefing uses the most recent data available on the number of people in various types of facilities and the most significant charge or conviction. Because not all types of data are collected each year, we sometimes had to combine differing data sets; for example, we applied the percentage distribution of offense types from the previous year to the current year’s total count data, since prison offense data lags by one year. To smooth out these differing levels of vintage and precision among the sources, we choose to round all figures in the graphic. This process may, however, result in various parts not adding up precisely to the total.

See all the footnotes

Acknowledgements

All Prison Policy Initiative reports are collaborative endeavors, but this report builds on the successful collaborations of the many versions of this report we have produced since 2017. For this year’s report, the authors would like to thank Aleks Kajstura for her foundational work on previous iterations of this report.

Finally, we’d like to thank each of our individual donors — your commitment to ending mass incarceration makes our work possible.

About the authors

Wendy Sawyer is the Research Director at the Prison Policy Initiative. Along with directing the organization’s research priorities, Wendy is the author (or co-author) of several major reports, including Mass Incarceration: The Whole Pie, Youth Confinement: The Whole Pie, Beyond the Count: A deep dive into state prison populations, All Profit, No Risk: How the bail industry exploits the justice system and Arrest, Release, Repeat: How police and jails are misused to respond to social problems. Wendy also publishes briefings on recent data releases, academic research, women’s incarceration, pretrial detention, probation, and more.

Brian Nam-Sonenstein is a Senior Editor and Researcher at the Prison Policy Initiative. He is the author of several major reports, including Mass Incarceration: The Whole Pie 2026, Youth Confinement: The Whole Pie 2025, Cut-rate care: The systemic problems shaping ‘healthcare’ behind bars, and Bad Behavior: How prison disciplinary policies manufacture misconduct. Brian also published briefings explaining why ending mass incarceration is an economic justice issue and how providing housing can help interrupt a major pathway to prison created by the criminalization of homelessness. In addition to his work as a researcher, Brian plays a pivotal role in supporting other members of the Research Department in shaping the framing and messaging of their publications in a way that maximizes their impact and reach.

About the Prison Policy Initiative

The non-profit, non-partisan Prison Policy Initiative was founded in 2001 to expose the broader harms of mass criminalization and spark advocacy campaigns to create a more just society. Through big-picture reports like Mass Incarceration: The Whole Pie, as well as in-depth reports on issues such as probation and parole, the organization shapes the public conversation on mass incarceration and helps the public more fully engage in criminal legal system reform.

title: Caminando Fronteras takes part in CGPJ continuing training for judges on migration
description:
We brought into the room what the Pact leaves out: the rights of border victims and of the families searching for them.
The sessions examined how the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum will be implemented in Spain and what its consequences will be.
Using concrete examples, we showed how these rights are systematically violated: Families are denied access to effective judicial protection.
We explained how families organise and, from the cases we are litigating, we shared recommendations to the judges to make access to justice and rights possible.
They also show the role the judiciary can play in ensuring that the families of border victims finally have access to justice.
text:
From 9 to 11 September, in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, we took part in the continuing training sessions of Spain’s General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ), “Immigration: The European Union Pact on Migration and Asylum and its impact on national legislation”. We brought into the room what the Pact leaves out: the rights of border victims and of the families searching for them.

The sessions examined how the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum will be implemented in Spain and what its consequences will be. Our contribution was part of the round table “Guaranteeing the protection of human rights at the border”, with the presentation “The rights of victims in migration contexts: families as rights holders and agents of change”.

The Pact does not recognise victims or their rights. That is why we chose to focus on the people it never mentions: those who have died or disappeared on migration routes, and their families. Today these families are the ones driving change at the borders. They are organising, demanding that their loved ones be recognised, and claiming the rights they are entitled to.

We began with what happened in Ceuta at the end of July, when the protocol for incidents with multiple victims was applied for the first time. We looked at how applying this protocol affected coordination among everyone involved in identifying the victims, from the judicial authorities to the State security forces.

We also spoke about the dehumanisation caused by denying their rights to people who have died or disappeared and to their families. When families cannot access truth, justice and reparation, they suffer macro-victimisation: on top of the harm of their loss comes the harm done by the system itself. This discussion also opened the door to exploring restorative justice processes.

The Pact may not include them, but international human rights law does protect victims and their families. We based our presentation on the General Comment of the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances on enforced disappearances in the context of migration. Using concrete examples, we showed how these rights are systematically violated:

Families are denied access to effective judicial protection.

Investigations are neither thorough nor effective.

The authorities do not open investigations on their own initiative, so the entire burden of the search falls on the families.

Filing a complaint and providing DNA samples remain very difficult.

We explained how families organise and, from the cases we are litigating, we shared recommendations to the judges to make access to justice and rights possible.

It is essential that judges listen to civil society organisations. These encounters allow us to share knowledge and convey the daily reality of migrants and their families. They also show the role the judiciary can play in ensuring that the families of border victims finally have access to justice.

title: New economic report underscores stakes for Sonoma County in Trump's immigration crackdown
description:
Ethan Brown, executive director of the Sonoma County Economic Development Collaborative, said the economic contribution of undocumented workers is “striking” in scale.
Brown said the report’s findings are particularly important as Sonoma County faces an aging workforce, high housing costs and a contracting wine industry.
Amid that campaign, the economic council found the legal resources available to local undocumented immigrants are declining.
Bernice Espinoza, removal defense attorney with Sonoma Immigrant Services, said access to sufficient legal representation affects people’s workforce participation and economic stability.
He recently moved to Sonoma County after 10 years in the Central Valley, the nation’s most productive agricultural region.
text:
Against the backdrop of President Trump’s historic immigration enforcement and deportation campaign, a new report by a Bay Area thinktank lays bare the economic and humanitarian stakes for Sonoma County and its undocumented residents.

The report, by the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, found the more than 21,000 undocumented immigrants in Sonoma County generate an estimated $2.3 billion in economic activity, pay nearly $1 billion in state and federal taxes and comprise nearly 30% of agricultural jobs, 19% of administrative jobs and 13% of service jobs.

Concentrated deportation and detention efforts like those which have taken place elsewhere in the nation would destabilize the local economy and tear at the fabric of the local immigrant community, which is deeply integrated in Sonoma County, said Abby Raisz, vice president of research for the non-partisan institute. News and social media posts about such federal operations in other parts of the state and country have had wider ripple effects, making immigrants fearful of going to work, taking children to school and in some cases pushing them leave the country.

“The big overarching takeaway is that it does not take a deportation alone to disrupt the economy — fear alone can do so much damage,” Raisz said.

The study was conducted following the escalation of federal enforcement operations in 2025, and its findings come as operations appear to be ramping up across California, where Immigration and Customs Enforcement has reportedly launched a weeks-long surge campaign.

The Press Democrat over the past week spoke to people who described personal and economic fears over what such an enforcement operation could mean for their lives and the wider community.

Over the weekend, some joined with local immigrant rights groups in a three-day march from Petaluma to Cloverdale to call attention to what they describe as an environment of terror and fear in the immigrant community.

Rene Saucedo, an organizer with the Sonoma County Sanctuary Coalition, said the scores of those who joined was still down from the expected crowd because of the fear that ICE agents might target the procession.

“There exists very much a general fear, and I would call it terror, in the immigrant community that we were going to see massive arrests and the use of violence in our community,” Saucedo said.

North Bay Organizing Project hotline coordinator Luis Zaragoza said the group has been tracking verified reports of the surge in ICE arrests, including in the San Joaquin Valley and on the Central Coast.

“We haven’t seen increased activity in our area yet,” Zaragoza said. “But we are keeping in close communication with other rapid response networks.”

The Sonoma County snapshot from the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, released last month, follows on March report that pegged the wider potential economic cost to the nine-county Bay Area of mass deportations at $67 billion in regional GDP and $8.4 billion in annual tax revenue.

“This past week has been a stark reminder that when federal agents run rampant in our communities,” said Alex Mensing, communications director at California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice, a Bay Area nonprofit legal services group. “It’s bad for everyone.”

The data in the new report, he added, “reflects the fact that immigrant rights and worker rights are interconnected, and respect for both is crucial to our region’s wellbeing.”

Spotlight on Sonoma County

The new report found there are about 79,000 immigrants living in Sonoma County, about 17% of the population. Around one in four are undocumented, and nearly three quarters have lived in the United States for more than a decade. More than 10,000 have lived in the county for more than 20 years. Nearly 85% of those from Mexico and 89% of undocumented residents from Central America have lived in the United States for more than a decade, compared with just 17% being from Asian countries.

Ethan Brown, executive director of the Sonoma County Economic Development Collaborative, said the economic contribution of undocumented workers is “striking” in scale. Significant disruptions to this workforce would ripple throughout the local economy, “affecting businesses, household spending, tax revenues and the delivery of goods and services that residents rely on.”

“The report underscores what many of us have known or suspected as we’ve witnessed the impact of mass immigration enforcement in other locales — that these working families are our neighbors and coworkers, contributing significantly to our economy and the tax base that fuels important public services at the local, state, and federal levels,” he said in an email.

Though undocumented residents represent 26% of Sonoma County’s immigrants, according to the council report, they generate 36% of the $6.4 billion economic output from immigrant workers.

In many cases, undocumented residents live alongside “legal residents” in “mixed status” households, the authors noted. When a primary wage earner is removed from a mixed-status household through detention or deportation, that household may see its median income fall by roughly 73%, from $96,000 to $26,300, the report found. Stakeholders described children and teenagers taking on rent and household responsibilities when adults lose work.

Undocumented residents also represent 78.5% of the county’s immigrant maids and housekeepers and 44.5% of construction laborers — with many positions involving long hours of physically demanding work which are not easily replaced. The report cited the example of a local grower “who lost a long-tenured tractor driver to enforcement fear — and needed two people to replace the departed worker’s combined skills.”

In a similar statewide study conducted last year, the Bay Area Council Economic Institute found 27% of California residents are immigrants, with an estimated 2.3 million undocumented residents making up approximately 8% of the state’s workforce. The latter pay more than $23 billion a year in taxes.

Brown said the report’s findings are particularly important as Sonoma County faces an aging workforce, high housing costs and a contracting wine industry.

“Maintaining a strong and resilient economy requires recognizing the essential role immigrant workers and business owners play in our community and ensuring that Sonoma County remains a place where businesses can find the workforce they need to succeed,” Brown said.

Specter of mass deportations

Mass deportations and aggressive immigration policies have been hallmarks of Trump’s second term. In July 2025, Congress approved more than $170 billion in border enforcement funding through Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, H.R. 1, including major new resources for ICE, border protection, detention infrastructure, border facilities, technology and personnel. The federal administration has set a target of roughly one million deportations per year, a pace that would require thousands of arrests and removals each day.

By the end of 2025, the Trump Administration said its efforts had led to the deportation of 605,000 people. Another 1.9 million undocumented immigrants “voluntarily self-deported,” the administration said.

Amid that campaign, the economic council found the legal resources available to local undocumented immigrants are declining. Only 46% of the more than 5,000 pending immigration cases filed against local undocumented immigrants have legal representation — the lowest representation rate in the Bay Area, according to the report.

In addition, according to the North Bay Organizing Project, a progressive nonprofit, many people may choose to self-deport, or are kept in detention centers despite signing voluntary removal agreements.

Bernice Espinoza, removal defense attorney with Sonoma Immigrant Services, said access to sufficient legal representation affects people’s workforce participation and economic stability. Without it, “many people remain in limbo, unable to secure lawful employment or maintain stability for themselves and their families.”

“We continue to see significant policy changes affecting immigrants’ ability to work legally, including changes to work permit-validity periods and increasing filing fees”, she said. “These changes create additional financial and administrative burdens for individuals already struggling to navigate a complex system.”

Sonoma Immigrant Services has limited resources available to address the current need, Espinoza added, with one removal defense attorney. Santa Rosa-based Vital Immigrant Defense Advocacy and Services (VIDAS) has four such attorneys and International Institute of the Bay Area and University of San Francisco’s School of Law Immigration and Deportation Defense Clinic each have one. “This shortage directly impacts immigrant workers, families, and employers who rely on a stable workforce,” Espinoza said.

Sonoma County has invested in education, preparedness, and legal consultations for immigrants, but many local legal providers cannot take on new cases at low or no cost, Espinoza added. More investment in legal representation is needed, she said. “While investments in employer outreach, healthcare partnerships, and community education are important, these efforts cannot substitute for direct legal representation,” she said.

Local impetus for report

Oscar Chavez, president and CEO of the Sonoma Community Foundation, which commissioned the new study, said it reflects the economic blow more aggressive ICE operations could inflict in the area. Many employers are terrified of losing many workers, he said.

“Enforcement stops being something that happens to somebody else, and it becomes a workforce issue.”

Chavez said at the end of 2024, with Trump poised to return to the White House, many of the foundation’s nonprofit partners started calling with concerns about the threat of mass immigration enforcement and the growing fear and anxiety among their clients. In response, the foundation directed $80,000 to commission the study and meet with stakeholders to examine how federal immigration policies were impacting the local immigrant community and what could be done to help.

The foundation then created a fund for organizations providing resources for immigrants, named Fund for Belonging, which seeks to support groups that provide resources to immigrants impacted by “volatile political environments, public health crises and climate-driven disasters,” according to the foundation’s website.

Chavez said such funding infrastructure will be key to address the economic fallout that is likely when community members are threatened by expanded enforcement actions in their backyards. In 2025, the Fund for Belonging raised $1.3 million and distributed about $700,000 to organizations providing immigrant services, including mental health, legal and job training assistance.

“There is a risk we will see an increase in enforcement, and we now know ICE has the resources to ramp up,” he said. “It’s really a matter of when our community will be impacted.”

Rabbi Shalom Bochner of B’nai Israel Center for Jewish Life in Petaluma was among those who marched Monday in the immigrant-rights procession. He recently moved to Sonoma County after 10 years in the Central Valley, the nation’s most productive agricultural region. The federal government’s recent surge in ICE operations there threaten a workforce and place that “feeds our country and our world.”

“That has always been the strength of our country — it has been until recently the way the world saw us,” he said. “It pains me, no it sickens me, to see the way our democracy’s sense of justice has been twisted to persecute people that are trying to be here legally and in a law abiding way.”

Staff Writer Martin Espinoza can be reached at martin.espinoza@pressdemocrat.com. Staff Writer Natalie Hanson can be reached at natalie.hanson@pressdemocrat.com.

text:
The Justice Department on Friday issued about a dozen subpoenas as part of an investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, including to members of her family, a person familiar with the investigation said.

The congresswoman herself was not subpoenaed, the source said, adding that the orders seeking information are tied to a federal grand jury in Minnesota, Omar’s home state.

The investigation is examining matters surrounding Omar’s immigration status, and that includes, but is not limited to, her birthdate, the source said. Omar, who was born in Somalia and moved to the United States with her family in the 1990s, was naturalized when she was 17 years old, meaning she was a juvenile and able be conferred citizenship through a parent.

Investigators are attempting to speak with Omar’s sister but have not issued her subpoena yet, the source said.

The investigation is seeking information to see where it leads, the source said. For example, if records, representations related to age and immigration status contain false information, that would provide material for investigators to scrutinize further. They could also examine communications related to such matters.

The Justice Department declined to comment to NBC News, and a spokesperson for Omar didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the subpoenas.

The subpoenas came just days before federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, D.C., home as part of a yearslong criminal investigation that is partly looking into immigration fraud, a person familiar with the matter said. The investigation, which is being conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Justice Department, has involved whistleblowers, documents and witness testimony, the source added.

After the search of her house Monday, Omar said in a statement on X, “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Asked Monday if he had been aware of the search in advance, President Donald Trump said the federal government was looking at Omar “very carefully.” He also repeated is frequent attacks on her and Somalia more broadly, calling her a “terrible person” who came from a nation that’s a “non-country.”

“Then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution,” Trump said. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ.”

That evening, Trump also attacked Omar in remarks at a rally he held for Republicans in Ohio.

“I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’”

Omar, who is part of a group of progressive women in Congress known as the “squad,” has been a frequent target of Trump’s rhetoric against her and other members’ liberal positions, as well as Somalian immigrants broadly.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to tease federal action against Omar last month when he said “something’s going to happen” with her, but they were still investigating.

“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case,” Mullin said. “It’s an actual case because they did things wrong. If you decided to break the law or lie [about] the information you gave the United States to be able to come into the United States through either asylum or because you were just wanting to seek a better life, but you didn’t tell us who you actually were, you lied about certain things about your application — those things, there’s no expiration to that.”

title: Five Immigration Developments That Will Define Employer Compliance in 2026
authors: Melissa Allchin, Matthew Gorman, Betsy Morgan
description:
The State Department’s Fraud Unit has also greatly expanded investigations of U.S. employers involving visa fraud at U.S. consulates.
In October 2026, DHS also proposed a regulation that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B (and other) workers whose employment is terminated.
Key matters to monitor: $100,000 H-1B Fee: A Massachusetts federal court vacated the fee on June 8, 2026.
The outcome of this litigation is likely to affect the separate $103,265 fee proposed by DHS.
Proposed $103,265 and $70,000 Fees: If finalized, both fees are expected to face legal challenges.
text:
The immigration landscape for U.S. employers has shifted dramatically. The past six months alone have produced escalating enforcement activity, sweeping proposed changes to temporary visa categories, and reshaped adjudication standards — all while active litigation continues to alter the legal picture in real time. Below are five critical developments and recommended action items for each.

1. SURGE IN GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATIONS

Employer-facing immigration enforcement has reached levels not seen in recent memory. ICE’s rate of Notices of Inspection (NOIs) for I-9 audits has increased significantly, and DHS has broadly expanded the types of I-9 violations that can result in immediate fines.

The Department of Labor has suspended PERM labor certification processing for several major employers while also launching “Project Firewall,” which gives the Secretary of Labor broad discretion to target employers for H-1B compliance investigations.

The State Department’s Fraud Unit has also greatly expanded investigations of U.S. employers involving visa fraud at U.S. consulates.

What Employers Should Do:

Conduct audits of I-9s (including a review of audit-trail sufficiency for electronic platforms), PERM audit files, and H-1B public access files.

Review PERM recruitment methodology and strategy to ensure compliance with current enforcement trends.

Establish a protocol for responding to government site visits or subpoenas.

2. PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE H-1B PROGRAM

The H-1B program faces its most significant restructuring in decades. On August 25, 2026, DHS proposed an additional $103,265 fee for cap-subject H-1B petitions — on top of the existing $100,000 Presidential Proclamation fee (currently subject to litigation; see Section 5 below).

In October 2026, DHS also proposed a regulation that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B (and other) workers whose employment is terminated. If finalized, the rule would effectively require departure from the country immediately upon termination, without an opportunity to seek new employment or change immigration status.

What Employers Should Do:

Begin assembling your H-1B cap list earlier than usual (i.e., now) and assess wage-level classifications in light of the weighted lottery.

Model the financial impact of potential cumulative fees on your H-1B budget and determine company policy should the fees take effect this cap season despite potential litigation.

3. PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE STUDENT VISA/OPT PROGRAM

On October 7, 2026, DHS proposed a regulation that would require universities to pay $70,000 the first time an F-1 student is recommended for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT recommendation — with costs potentially passed through to students or employers. A student who uses pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, and a STEM OPT extension could generate $130,000 in total fees. DHS characterized the proposal as an anti-fraud measure, but litigation is widely anticipated. Courts have already held that DHS cannot impose fees functioning as taxes without congressional authorization — the same theory used to invalidate the $100,000 H-1B fee. The comment period closes on December 7, 2026, and publication of the final rule is expected to follow in subsequent months.

What Employers Should Do:

Review your student-visa population to better understand your risk profile should the fees become final.

4. HEIGHTENED USCIS SCRUTINY

The adjudicatory environment at USCIS has become significantly more challenging over the past fiscal year, with denial rates increasing across the board. Effective August 5, 2026, USCIS authorized adjudicators to deny petitions without issuing a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) if initial evidence is deemed insufficient — a meaningful departure from prior practice. Adjudicators may also now set response deadlines as short as 30 days for certain filing types, replacing the prior standard of up to 12 weeks.

A May 2026 policy memo further recharacterized adjustment of status as an “extraordinary form of relief,” signaling a more restrictive discretionary approach across the board.

What Employers Should Do:

Prepare visa extension and permanent residence filings as early as possible to allow time to respond to requests for evidence or overcome denials.

Build internal workflows capable of responding to RFEs within 30 days.

Factor longer processing timelines and higher denial rates into all workforce planning.

Review adjustment-of-status strategies with particular attention to filings for temporary-intent visa holders.

5. THE LITIGATION LANDSCAPE

The volume and pace of immigration litigation is itself a compliance challenge. Key matters to monitor:

$100,000 H-1B Fee: A Massachusetts federal court vacated the fee on June 8, 2026. The First Circuit denied the government’s motion for a stay on July 24, 2026, and the fee therefore remains unenforceable pending appeal. The outcome of this litigation is likely to affect the separate $103,265 fee proposed by DHS.

Adjustment of Status Memo: Legal challenges have been filed against PM-602-0199, arguing the policy guidance constitutes a substantive rule change requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA.

Student Visa Regulation: Currently blocked by a September 2026 district court decision granting nationwide preliminary relief. DHS has appealed to the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

Proposed $103,265 and $70,000 Fees: If finalized, both fees are expected to face legal challenges.

What Employers Should Do:

Develop a communication strategy for high-stakes immigration updates (e.g., town halls, targeted email communications) to reduce employee anxiety, reaffirm the company’s awareness and strategic approach, and emphasize that most changes are not yet final and remain subject to litigation.

description:

Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12, drawing condemnation from civil rights advocates, labor leaders, and progressive organizations that accuse the Trump administration of using federal law enforcement to intimidate a political opponent just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12, drawing condemnation from civil rights advocates, labor leaders, and progressive organizations that accuse the Trump administration of using federal law enforcement to intimidate a political opponent just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

The involvement of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a Department of Homeland (DHS) Security agency, has drawn scrutiny amid renewed concerns about President Donald Trump’s long-standing attacks on the Minnesota Democrat, who is up for reelection, and the state’s Somali American community. In response to a request for comment, DHS redirected Prism to the Department of Justice, which did not respond.

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement to NBC 6 that HSI “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” as “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

Omar wrote in an Oct. 12 X post that she was “ok” after the search.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and its Minnesota chapter condemned the raid in a statement, calling it an “obvious act of political persecution” against a Black, Muslim, and immigrant congresswoman who has frequently criticized Trump’s policies.

Robert Sichta, an immigration attorney with CAIR, called the raid an act of political theater and argued that its timing, shortly before the November midterm elections, raises serious questions about the government’s motives.

“What stands out is just the audacity, the abject cruelty,” Sichta said in an interview. He also predicted that the controversy could strengthen Omar politically, arguing that her constituents know her record despite the repeated attacks she has faced from Trump.

Trump has insulted Omar over social media as well as at rallies, saying she should be “sent back to Somalia” and “should be in jail.” He has also made racist comments about Somali immigrants. Minnesota is home to one of the largest Somali populations in the U.S.

Indivisible, a progressive grassroots organization against authoritarianism, joined the criticism against the raid on Omar’s house. Leah Greenberg, the group’s co-founder and co-executive director, described the raid as a dangerous escalation in the administration’s treatment of Omar.

“For a decade, Trump has targeted Rep. Ilhan Omar with grotesque, racist rhetoric that has fueled threats against her,” Greenberg said.

She said that deploying federal law enforcement against a sitting member of Congress so close to an election risked undermining democratic principles and intimidating elected officials who oppose the president.

Greenberg also connected the search to Trump’s recent rhetoric about Somali Americans and Minnesota, warning that the administration’s actions could deepen racial divisions.

“No president should be able to abuse their power to intimidate elected officials or silence dissent,” she said.

The Minnesota AFL-CIO also condemned the operation. Bernie Burnham, president of the state labor federation, said Minnesota’s labor movement stood with Omar and criticized what he viewed as the use of government resources against a political opponent.

“If Donald Trump can do this to her, he can do it to any other American citizen,” Burnham said.

He added that political disagreements should remain part of a healthy democracy, and not become grounds for the government to target its critics.

Omar represents Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District and has emerged as one of Trump’s most outspoken critics in Congress. She made history in 2018 alongside Michigan Democrat Rashida Tlaib as the first Muslim women elected to Congress. A Somali-born refugee, Omar has become a prominent voice on immigration enforcement and Islamophobia. She has called for replacing the current immigration enforcement system with one that protects immigrants’ rights.

Sichta urged people to understand their rights if federal agents arrive at their homes. He said residents should request to see a warrant, verify the agents’ identities, and seek legal advice rather than attempting to handle a potentially complicated encounter alone.

“You want your lawyer to talk to them,” he said, cautioning people against making statements without understanding the legal consequences.

Sichta said that the government must ultimately answer for its actions, even when legal challenges take time to resolve.

“Everybody obeys the law in their job. Nobody breaks the law, and nobody is unaccountable under our law,” he said.

title: Open Rights Group raises concerns over Home Office AI asylum tools and calls for their suspension
description:
The Open Rights Group examined two AI tools used by the Home Office: the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS), tool which summarises asylum interview transcripts, and the Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, which helps caseworkers search country policy information.
As the report highlights, both AI tools generate their own new text rather than merely retrieving existing text and they can filter or omit facts relevant to a decision.
The Home Office is also not planning an independent audit of its AI tools and is not listing them on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Hub.
Responses to parliamentary questions and freedom of information (FOI) requests contained contradictory accounts of staff training and testing of the AI tools, the Open Rights Group said.
In addition, the Open Rights Group questioned whether the tools had delivered the efficiency improvements claimed by ministers.
text:
A new report by the Open Rights Group (ORG) has raised concerns about the Home Office's use of artificial intelligence (AI) in asylum decisions, with a six-month investigation highlighting significant error in content generated by AI tools and a lack of transparency and independent oversight.

The 20-page report can be downloaded here.

The Open Rights Group examined two AI tools used by the Home Office: the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS), tool which summarises asylum interview transcripts, and the Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, which helps caseworkers search country policy information. Both use OpenAI's GPT-4o model through Microsoft's Azure AI Foundry.

As the report highlights, both AI tools generate their own new text rather than merely retrieving existing text and they can filter or omit facts relevant to a decision.

A 2025 Home Office pilot evaluation found that 9% of ACS summaries were inaccurate or omitted information and had to be removed from the trial. However, subsequent sampling by Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) of 203 summaries after the tool's wider rollout found that 22% failed an initial assessment and 30 of 56 summaries examined at a second stage also failed.

Whilst noting that the exact SME procedures to test for a 'fail' were unclear, the Open Rights Group noted: "Therefore, across both stage reviews 22% and 15% of sampled summaries were assessed as not fit for use – significantly higher than the 9% figure in the Home Office's published pilot evaluation."

The Open Rights Group further notes that only 203 summaries were checked by Home Office SMEs between April and July 2026, representing only approximately 0.3% of the estimated 70,000 cases processed during that period.

According to the report, the situation for the APS tool is worse and there is no equivalent ongoing quality-control process. Anna Turley, the Minister of State for Border Security and Asylum, confirmed in August that the testing of the APS tool had now ceased.

The report further criticised the Home Office for not applying the UK Government's AI Playbook to the tools, which offers guidance on using AI safely, effectively and securely. The Home Office is also not planning an independent audit of its AI tools and is not listing them on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Hub.

Responses to parliamentary questions and freedom of information (FOI) requests contained contradictory accounts of staff training and testing of the AI tools, the Open Rights Group said. Some FOI requests were refused.

The report states: "The Home Office has refused to provide key information including about staff training, the prompts being used, and how the tools are being tested for quality assurance. Their replies have been at times self-contradictory. Our findings suggest that these tools have been rolled out without proper testing, quality assurance and training. This careless approach could have catastrophic consequences for those people whose future is in the hands of Home Office decision-making."

In addition, the Open Rights Group questioned whether the tools had delivered the efficiency improvements claimed by ministers. Its analysis of Home Office data found that the average monthly number of initial substantive asylum decisions since April 2026 had fallen by about 42% compared with the same period in 2025, while the mean time between substantive interview and decision had increased by 29%.

The report calls on the Home Office to suspend both tools, commission an independent evaluation and audit, and ask the Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration to investigate their use.

It says there should be no use of AI in the asylum decision-making process without proper consultation, adherence to domestic regulations and international obligations, and full alignment with human rights principles
